p: [א] רֵאשִׁית כְּנִיסַת הָאָדָם לַעֲבוֹדַת הַשֵּׁם צָרִיךְ לִהְיוֹת בְּחִפָּזוֹן,
The initial entry of a person into the service of God must be done in haste,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁמָּצִינוּ בְּפֶסַח מִצְרַיִם שֶׁהָיָה נֶאֱכָל בְּחִפָּזוֹן, וְלֹא פֶּסַח דּוֹרוֹת.
just as we find regarding the Passover of Egypt, which was eaten in haste, whereas the Passover of subsequent generations was not.
מִפְּנֵי שֶׁהַהַתְחָלָה לְנַתֵּק עַצְמוֹ מִכָּל תַּאֲווֹת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה שֶׁהוּא מְקֻשָּׁר בָּהֶם,
Because at the start of tearing oneself away from all the physical desires of this world to which one is bound,
צָרִיךְ לִשְׁמֹר הָרֶגַע שֶׁמִּתְעוֹרֵר בּוֹ רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם,
one must seize the precise moment in which an awakening to the will of God occurs,
וְלַחְפּוֹז עַל אוֹתוֹ רֶגַע לְמַהֵר לָצֵאת מֵהֶם, אוּלַי יוּכַל.
and rush upon that very moment to hasten an escape from them, so that perhaps one may succeed.
וְאַחַר כָּךְ שׁוּב יֵלֵךְ בִּמְתִינוּת וּלְאַט, כְּדִין פֶּסַח דּוֹרוֹת.
And afterward he should go on slowly and deliberately, like the law governing the Passover of later generations.

paragraphs.text: Haste at the beginning and deliberation afterward

rich.text: Haste at the beginning and deliberation afterward

paragraphs.text: The initial awakening must be seized before the desires that bind a person overwhelm it. After that first departure, service proceeds with a slower, deliberate pace.

rich.text: The initial awakening must be seized before the desires that bind a person overwhelm it. After that first departure, service proceeds with a slower, deliberate pace.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Rav Tzadok · Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Berakhot 2:3: “Afterward, “to learn and to teach”: first one receives from his teachers, then still more from his colleagues, as is taught in Ta’anit 7a—this is “to learn”; and from his students more than from them all—this is “to teach.” These correspond to the passages “You shall love” and “And it shall be, if you listen,” as is taught in Berakhot 14b. Afterward, “to guard”: this is the reflection before an action comes into practice, from the expression “His father kept [the matter],” which signifies waiting. As is written in Asarah Ma’amarot, a mitzvah requires watchfulness and waiting so that one can prepare oneself, while the zealous act early lest death overtake them. This corresponds to “So that your days may be many.” After one has passed through all these levels, he should then be deliberate, for he is assured of “so that they may be many”: life will increase, and his desire will not cease after a time. At the beginning it is different. When a desire reaches him, he must act upon it promptly, lest the desire cease in the meantime. As we have written elsewhere concerning the Passover offering in Egypt, it is eaten in haste while one has not yet passed through the preceding levels.”

This gives a fuller account of the deliberation with which Tzidkat HaTzadik concludes.

paragraphs.text: The opening of Tzidkat HaTzadik distinguishes the urgency needed to leave an old attachment from the measured work that follows. The first moment must become a willingness to follow God, while later growth has its own pace.

rich.text: The opening of Tzidkat HaTzadik distinguishes the urgency needed to leave an old attachment from the measured work that follows. The first moment must become a willingness to follow God, while later growth has its own pace.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Rav Tzadok · Peri Tzadik, Rosh Chodesh Nisan 2:1: “The first commandment was the eating of the paschal offerings: to eat sacred meat, so that holiness would enter every Israelite through it. The commandment given concerning it was: “This is how you shall eat it—your sandals on your feet and your staff in your hand.” Why did they need this, when the eating took place at night and the departure from Egypt by day? Rather, this was the preparation of being ready to follow the LORD: “your following Me into the wilderness.” This is the meaning of “the right foot”: the work of this month is to be ready to follow the LORD, “to walk in His ways.” This is accepting the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven, represented by the final letter heh, kingship.”

rich.text: : “The first commandment was the eating of the paschal offerings: to eat sacred meat, so that holiness would enter every Israelite through it. The commandment given concerning it was: “This is how you shall eat it—your sandals on your feet and your staff in your hand.” Why did they need this, when the eating took place at night and the departure from Egypt by day? Rather, this was the preparation of being ready to follow the LORD: “your following Me into the wilderness.” This is the meaning of “the right foot”: the work of this month is to be ready to follow the LORD, “to walk in His ways.” This is accepting the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven, represented by the final letter heh, kingship.”

paragraphs.text: Explanation: Peri Tzadik asks why the Israelites ate ready for travel although their departure would occur only later. Readiness itself was their first acceptance of Heaven’s rule. This gives substance to Tzidkat HaTzadik’s initial haste: the decisive moment is used to orient oneself toward following God, before the journey has been completed. It also helps explain why the urgency of the beginning need not dictate the pace of everything that follows.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Ishbitz–Radzin · Sod Yesharim, The First Night of Pesach 25:1: “All this indicates that, in a situation where Israel clearly recognizes His blessed will, they no longer attend to any established order, but have the capacity to leap without proceeding through gradual stages, acting with great alacrity to do His blessed will. This is the meaning of: “The Passover offering that our ancestors would eat—for what reason? Because the Holy One, blessed be He, passed over.” That is, why were they commanded to undertake such intense service? “Because the Holy One, blessed be He, passed over the houses of our ancestors in Egypt”: because the Holy One, blessed be He, also leapt over, and shone salvation upon us by a leap, in haste, before the appointed time. Therefore we too were commanded, and it was fixed in our hearts, to perform such service in a short time and with great alacrity.”

paragraphs.text: Explanation: Sod Yesharim explains why Pesach can require a leap past ordinary stages: clearly recognized Divine will calls forth swift service, answering the salvation that arrived by a leap. This illuminates why Rav Tzadok treats the awakening as an opportunity that can be lost through delay. Tzidkat HaTzadik supplies the further distinction in this pair: after the initial departure, service proceeds slowly and deliberately. The comparison does not turn every impulse into authorization to skip stages.

paragraphs.text: Tanya, Part I; Likkutei Amarim 31:14-16: “This condition is the condition of the Exodus from Egypt, of which it is said, ‘For the people fled.’ At first sight this is puzzling: why was it so? Had they told Pharaoh to release them forever, would he not have been compelled to release them? Rather, the evil in the souls of Israel was still at full strength in the left chamber, for their impurity did not cease until the giving of the Torah. Their aim and desire were only that their divine soul should leave the exile of the other side, which is the impurity of Egypt, and cleave to Him, blessed be He. As it is written, ‘Hashem, my strength, my stronghold, and my refuge in a day of distress,’ and so forth; ‘my stronghold and my refuge,’ and so forth; ‘He is a refuge for me,’ and so forth. Therefore, in the future, when Hashem removes the spirit of impurity from the earth, it is written, ‘You shall not go in flight, for Hashem goes before you,’ and so forth.”

sections.en: Blessings and Awareness of the Divine

p: [ב] בְּרָכוֹת לְרֹאשׁ צַדִּיק.
"Blessings are upon the head of the righteous" (Proverbs 10:6).
לְכָךְ מַסֶּכֶת בְּרָכוֹת הַהַתְחָלָה מִשִּׁשָּׁה סְדָרִים,
For this reason, Tractate Berakhot [Blessings] is the opening treatise of the entire Talmud (the Six Orders),
שֶׁעִקַּר הַכֹּל: "דַּע אֶת אֱלֹהֵי אָבִיךָ" – וְאַחַר כָּךְ "וְעָבְדֵהוּ",
because the foundation of everything is: "Know the God of your father" (I Chronicles 28:9) — and only afterward, "and serve Him",
שֶׁצָּרִיךְ לֵידַע לְמִי עוֹבֵד.
for one must first know Whom one is serving.
וְזֶהוּ הַבְּרָכָה לִפְנֵי כָּל מַעֲשֶׂה, לְיַחֵד כָּל מַעֲשָׂיו לַהַשֵּׁם,
And this is the purpose of reciting a blessing before every action: to dedicate all of one's deeds to God,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "בְּכָל דְּרָכֶיךָ דָעֵהוּ", כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב הָרַמְבַּ"ם [רַבֵּנוּ מֹשֶׁה בֶּן מַיְמוֹן].
as it is written: "In all your ways acknowledge Him" (Proverbs 3:6), as Maimonides explained.
וְזֶהוּ עַל יְדֵי הַבְּרָכָה, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ: הַשִּׁעוּר בָּהּ קָטָן שֶׁיּוֹדֵעַ לְמִי מְבָרְכִין.
And this consciousness is achieved through the blessing; as the Sages stated regarding the qualifying age for a minor: a child who knows to Whom we recite blessings (Berakhot 48a).
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן בִּשְׁאָר מִצְוֹת, אֵין הַשִּׁעוּר שֶׁיֵּדַע לְמִי מַנִּיחִין תְּפִלִּין וְכַיּוֹצֵא.
This is unlike other commandments, where the age definition is not framed around whether he knows to Whom one dons phylacteries (tefillin) or the like.
מְבֹאָר שֶׁהַבְּרָכָה עִקָּרָהּ הַיְּדִיעָה לְמִי מְבָרְכִין, שֶׁעַל כָּךְ נוֹסְדָה.
Thus it is evident that the core essence of a blessing is the awareness of Whom one addresses, for that was its foundational purpose.
וְזֶהוּ הַתְחָלַת הַכְּנִיסָה לַתּוֹרָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "רֵאשִׁית חָכְמָה יִרְאַת הַשֵּׁם".
And this constitutes the primary gateway into the Torah, as it is written: "The beginning of wisdom is the fear of God" (Psalms 111:10).
וְיִרְאַת שָׁמַיִם הוּא עַל יְדֵי "שִׁוִּיתִי הַשֵּׁם לְנֶגְדִּי תָמִיד", כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב בַּהַגָּהָה דְּרֵישׁ אֹרַח חַיִּים.
And the fear of Heaven is attained through "I have set the Lord before me always" (Psalms 16:8), as written in the gloss of the Rema at the beginning of Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim.
וְהַיְנוּ בְּרָכוֹת שֶׁכֻּלָּן מַתְחִילִין בִּלְשׁוֹן נוֹכֵחַ,
This also explains why all liturgical blessings open in the second-person direct address "Blessed are You...":
שֶׁמִּיָּד בְּהַתְחָלַת הַבְּרָכָה צָרִיךְ לִהְיוֹת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ נוֹכַח עֵינָיו כְּאִלּוּ עוֹמֵד עָלָיו וּמְצַוֵּהוּ.
for at the very start of the blessing, the Blessed Name must be directly present before one's eyes, as though He is standing over him and issuing the command.
וְהַסִּיּוּם לְשׁוֹן נִסְתָּר, דְּמִיָּד נֶעְלָם,
Yet the conclusion transitions into the third person "...Who has sanctified us", because He immediately recedes into transcendence,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "עַל גּוֹזָלָיו יְרַחֵף" – נוֹגֵעַ וְאֵינוֹ נוֹגֵעַ, כַּיָּדוּעַ.
as it is written: "Over its fledglings He hovers" (Deuteronomy 32:11) — touching yet not touching, as is well known [Rashi on Deuteronomy 32:11].

paragraphs.text: Sod Yesharim follows the blessing through eating to the use of the strength that the food supplies.

rich.text: Sod Yesharim follows the blessing through eating to the use of the strength that the food supplies.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Ishbitz–Radzin · Sod Yesharim, Simchat Torah 1:2: “At the beginning we bless, “Who brings bread forth from the earth,” as the Sages said in Berakhot: “Ha-motzi means ‘who brought forth.’” Blessing is also an expression of drawing forth: one draws to oneself the utterance of God’s mouth clothed within the food. As it is written, “For a person does not live by bread alone, but by everything that proceeds from God’s mouth.” The blessed will that, from the creation of the world, brings into being and gives life to everything in the world is clothed within the bread and gives life to the person. Through the blessing, the person breaks through the garments and finds and draws forth to himself the blessed will that gives him life. Before eating, at the time of the blessing, the person gives to the food, for through the blessing the food is raised. But at the time of eating, the food is called the giver, because the person is nourished by it. After eating, the person prevails over the food, because the choice is then in his hands: according to the way he serves God with the strength of that eating, so will be the ascent of that food.”

paragraphs.text: Explanation: Sod Yesharim develops the present siman’s instruction to dedicate one’s deeds to Hashem through the blessing. Recognition before eating uncovers the divine will within the food, but the account continues afterward: the person chooses how to serve Hashem with the received strength. Knowing before Whom one blesses thus begins a relationship that governs the ensuing action; it is more than an acknowledgment that ends when the words of the blessing end.

paragraphs.text: Mishneh Torah, Human Dispositions 3:3: “Someone who conducts himself according to medicine, but intends only that his body and limbs should be sound and that he should have children to perform his work and labor for his needs, is not following a good path. Rather, he should intend that his body be sound and strong so that his soul may be upright in knowing Hashem, for one cannot understand and contemplate wisdom while hungry or ill, or while one of his limbs is in pain. He should intend to have a son who may become wise and great in Israel. Thus, one who follows this path throughout his life serves Hashem continually, even while doing business and even during marital relations, because his intention in everything is to obtain what he needs so that his body will be sound for serving Hashem. Even while sleeping, if he sleeps deliberately so that his mind and body may rest, lest he become ill and be unable to serve Hashem because of his illness, his sleep is service of the Omnipresent, blessed be He. Concerning this, the Sages commanded, ‘Let all your deeds be for the sake of Heaven.’ This is what Solomon said in his wisdom: ‘Know Him in all your ways, and He will make your paths straight.’”

paragraphs.text: Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 1:1: ““I have set Hashem before me always” is a great principle of the Torah and of the virtues of the righteous who walk before God. A person’s sitting, movements, and affairs when alone at home are unlike his sitting, movements, and affairs before a great king. His speech and free expression as he wishes among his household and relatives are unlike his speech in the king’s presence. All the more so, when a person takes to heart that the great King, the Holy One, blessed be He, whose glory fills all the earth, stands over him and sees his deeds—as it is said, “Can a person hide in secret places and I not see him? declares Hashem”—fear and submission in awe of Hashem, and shame before Him, will immediately come upon him continually.”

sections.en: The Yoke of Heaven by Day and Night

p: [ג] עִקַּר הַקְּרִיאַת שְׁמַע: קַבָּלַת עוֹל מַלְכוּת שָׁמַיִם וְעוֹל תּוֹרָה וּמִצְוֹת, כִּדְאִיתָא (בְּרָכוֹת יג.),
The core purpose of the recitation of Shema is the acceptance of the yoke of the Kingdom of Heaven and the yoke of Torah and commandments, as taught in the Talmud (Berakhot 13a),
וְצָרִיךְ בַּיּוֹם וָלַיְלָה.
and this obligation applies both by day and by night.
וְלֹא בְּבֹקֶר וָעֶרֶב, אֶלָּא "בְּשָׁכְבְּךָ וּבְקוּמֶךָ", עַיֵּן שָׁם י"א עַמּוּד א'.
Notice that the Torah did not formulate the obligation as "in the morning and evening," but rather "when you lie down and when you rise up" (cf. Berakhot 11a).
דְּיָהֵיב הַזְּמַן בָּזֶה מִשּׁוּם דְּהַבֹּקֶר וָעֶרֶב הֵם שִׁנּוּיִים בָּעוֹלָם וְלֹא בָּאָדָם,
The Torah framed the requirement in terms of human posture because morning and evening represent astronomical changes in the cosmos, not internal shifts within man;
וְהָיָה דַּי בְּקַבָּלָה אַחַת לִשְׁנֵיהֶם.
and were that the sole factor, a single daily acceptance of the yoke would have sufficed for both periods.
רַק מִפְּנֵי הַשִּׁנּוּיִים שֶׁבָּאָדָם,
Rather, it is instituted because of the practical changes taking place within the human being:
שֶׁבַּיּוֹם קָם וְעוֹסֵק בִּמְלַאכְתּוֹ, וְצָרִיךְ קַבָּלַת עוֹל מַלְכוּת שָׁמַיִם שֶׁכָּל מַעֲשָׂיו יִהְיוּ לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם,
for during the daytime a person rises and engages in worldly work, needing the acceptance of Heaven's yoke so that all worldly labors are directed toward the service of Heaven,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (עֵירוּבִין סה.): "אֲנַן פּוֹעֲלֵי דִּימָמָא", כְּפוֹעֲלִים הָעוֹשִׂים מְלָאכָה שֶׁכָּל מַעֲשֵׂיהֶם לָאָדוֹן,
as the Sages remarked (Eruvin 65a): "We are day-laborers," comparable to hired workers whose every effort belongs exclusively to their master,
וַאֲפִלּוּ בְּבִרְכַּת הַמָּזוֹן מְקַצֵּר בִּשְׁבִיל עֲבוֹדָתוֹ (בְּרָכוֹת טז.).
such that a laborer even curtails the wording of Grace After Meals to return promptly to his employer's task (Berakhot 16a).
וּבַלַּיְלָה, עֵת שְׁכִיבָה וּמְנוּחָה, צָרִיךְ גַּם כֵּן קַבָּלַת עוֹל מַלְכוּת שָׁמַיִם,
At night, however, which is an interval of reclining and passivity, there is likewise a need to accept the yoke of the Kingdom of Heaven:
שֶׁגַּם בְּשָׁכְבוֹ עַל מִטָּתוֹ יֵדַע לִפְנֵי מִי הוּא שׁוֹכֵב, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב בַּהַגָּהָה דְּרֵישׁ אֹרַח חַיִּים.
so that even resting upon his bed, he remains cognizant of before Whom he is lying down, as noted in the gloss at the beginning of Orach Chayim.
וְזֶה מְלָאכָה יוֹתֵר גְּדוֹלָה.
And this internal discipline during inactivity is an even greater spiritual labor.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי בָּזֶה עַל פָּסוּק "וַיַּחֲלֹם יַעֲקֹב", שֶׁמֵּהַחֲלוֹמוֹת נִכָּר מַעֲלַת הָאָדָם,
This aligns with what I heard expounded on the verse "And Jacob dreamed" (Genesis 28:12): that a person's true stature is revealed through dreams,
אִם גַּם כְּשֶׁאֵינוֹ עוֹשֶׂה כְּלוּם, רַעְיוֹנָיו רַק "וְהִנֵּה הַשֵּׁם נִצָּב עָלָיו".
demonstrating whether even when inactive and unconscious, his thoughts remain fixated on "and behold, the Lord stood above him" (Genesis 28:13).

paragraphs.text: Sod Yesharim distinguishes the morning’s manifest recognition from the faith that sustains a person through apparent separation.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Ishbitz–Radzin · Sod Yesharim, Shabbat Chol HaMoed Sukkot 11:2: ““To declare Your kindness in the morning.” When Abraham’s morning shines before a person—as in “one called to another,” translated “they receive from one another”—one explicitly recognizes “the kindness of God all day.” “Your faithfulness in the nights” means that when Abraham’s morning is concealed, a person does not recognize the connection. This concealment is called night: “One did not approach the other all night.” As the Midrash explains, when people become separated from one another it is called night, appearing as separation and interruption. Then the person’s only counsel is to hold to greater faith. This is “Your faithfulness in the nights.” Through faith, the whole of a person’s existence can be strengthened. In truth, a person’s essential existence corresponds to the faith established in his heart. As the Zohar says, “‘Her husband is known in the gates’—this is the Holy One, blessed be He, who becomes known according to what each measures within his heart, as much as each can cleave ….” According to the faith that each establishes in his heart, God dwells within him and gives him existence and endurance.”

paragraphs.text: Explanation: The Radziner passage explains the inward meaning of night: the connection is not apparent, so faith must carry the person’s existence and endurance. This clarifies why the present siman requires a separate acceptance for lying down and calls that inactive service a greater labor. The night’s avodah is not simply a second performance of the daytime task. It carries allegiance to Hashem into a condition in which ordinary conscious activity and visible reassurance have receded.

p: [ד] מִצְוָה רִאשׁוֹנָה שֶׁנִּתְחַיֵּב הָאָדָם כְּשֶׁנַּעֲשָׂה הָאָדָם בֶּן שְׁלֹשׁ עֶשְׂרֵה שָׁנָה הוּא קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע שֶׁל עַרְבִית, שֶׁהוּא הָרֵאשִׁית כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל,

The very first commandment a young man becomes obligated in upon reaching thirteen years of age [the threshold of Bar Mitzvah, at nightfall] is the recitation of the evening Shema, which serves as the foundational beginning, as mentioned above.
כִּי הוּא וּבִרְכוֹת אֶחָד,
For it [Shema] and blessings are one and the same,
רַק שֶׁהַבְּרָכוֹת בִּפְרָט הַמַּעֲשִׂים, וְזוֹ בִּכְלָל עַל כָּל מַעֲשֵׂה הַקִּימָה וְעַל כָּל מַעֲשֵׂה הַשְּׁכִיבָה.
except that blessings pertain to specific, individualized actions, whereas Shema is a comprehensive acceptance governing the entire act of rising and the entire act of lying down.
וְשֶׁל עַרְבִית קוֹדֵם, כִּדְפָתַח בֵּיהּ תַּנָּא: "דִּקְרָא קָאֵי",
And the evening Shema comes first chronologically, as the Mishna opens with the evening time: "The Tanna relies on the Scriptural verse,"
וְיָלֵיף מִבְּרִיָּתוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם לְעִנְיַן קַבָּלַת עוֹל מַלְכוּת שָׁמַיִם:
deriving the principle from the cosmic order of Creation regarding the acceptance of the yoke of Heaven:
דִּבְרֵישָׁא חֲשׁוֹכָא,
namely, that darkness precedes light ("first there was darkness, and then there was light").
צָרִיךְ קַבָּלַת עוֹל מַלְכוּת שָׁמַיִם אַף מִתּוֹךְ הַחֹשֶׁךְ וְהַסִּכְלוּת וְהֶעְדֵּר הַמַּעֲשִׂים,
A person must accept the yoke of Heaven's sovereignty even from within obscurity, ignorance, and the absence of spiritual deeds;
וְאָז סוֹפוֹ לְקַיְּמָהּ בְּעֹשֶׁר וּנְהוֹרָא דִּימָמָא,
and subsequently, one will merit to fulfill it amid spiritual abundance and daytime illumination—
הַשָּׂגָה הַבְּרוּרָה שֶׁעַל יְדֵי זֶה נִמְשָׁךְ הַמַּעֲשֶׂה.
achieving that clear, luminous perception of the Divine through which active, tangible deeds are drawn forth into reality.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Ishbitz–Radzin · Sod Yesharim, The First Day of Pesach 15:2: “Israel had to clarify the difference so that it could be seen explicitly: between Israel’s flock, a flock for a commandment, and Egypt’s flock, a flock of idolatry. A flock hints at the evening before the morning, as the Gemara asks: “Why do goats walk first and then sheep? Like the world’s creation: first darkness and then light, as it says, ‘There was evening and there was morning.’” My holy father explained that this is what the Sages meant in saying that Egypt’s idolatry was the flock. All their service was directed to the darkness preceding the light; they made that primordial darkness their object of fear, so that all their deeds would remain in darkness and they could receive every flow of good without any service, above their understanding. This is called darkness: proceeding without knowledge. Light is when a person proceeds with knowledge and reckoning. The Zohar says concerning this, “Flock was bound to flock”: outwardly, Israel too follow without knowledge or calculation, above their apprehension. They were even called “a hasty people, who put your mouth before your ears,” not calculating whether they would have the strength to bear it. Of this it says that Israel were bound in this for four hundred years, until the distinction would be explicitly clarified and separated from its knot. It would become apparent that Israel’s entire purpose in following beyond their apprehension was to reach the source at the root of His will, which is a light far higher than the light called light from the human side. Such following without knowledge and reckoning is called a flock of a commandment. Egypt’s flock, by contrast, is called idolatry: they do not wish to look at the light. They say that His will intentionally emanated evening before morning in order to conceal the light from human eyes, so that a person would always walk in darkness and not in light, with deeds in darkness. The Zohar speaks of the clarification’s not being easily untied because this is truly a very fine distinction; it is not easy to show the difference between flock and flock explicitly to human eyes.”

rich.text: Sod Yesharim, The First Day of Pesach 15:2

: “Israel had to clarify the difference so that it could be seen explicitly: between Israel’s flock, a flock for a commandment, and Egypt’s flock, a flock of idolatry. A flock hints at the evening before the morning, as the Gemara asks: “Why do goats walk first and then sheep? Like the world’s creation: first darkness and then light, as it says, ‘There was evening and there was morning.’” My holy father explained that this is what the Sages meant in saying that Egypt’s idolatry was the flock. All their service was directed to the darkness preceding the light; they made that primordial darkness their object of fear, so that all their deeds would remain in darkness and they could receive every flow of good without any service, above their understanding. This is called darkness: proceeding without knowledge. Light is when a person proceeds with knowledge and reckoning. The Zohar says concerning this, “Flock was bound to flock”: outwardly, Israel too follow without knowledge or calculation, above their apprehension. They were even called “a hasty people, who put your mouth before your ears,” not calculating whether they would have the strength to bear it. Of this it says that Israel were bound in this for four hundred years, until the distinction would be explicitly clarified and separated from its knot. It would become apparent that Israel’s entire purpose in following beyond their apprehension was to reach the source at the root of His will, which is a light far higher than the light called light from the human side. Such following without knowledge and reckoning is called a flock of a commandment. Egypt’s flock, by contrast, is called idolatry: they do not wish to look at the light. They say that His will intentionally emanated evening before morning in order to conceal the light from human eyes, so that a person would always walk in darkness and not in light, with deeds in darkness. The Zohar speaks of the clarification’s not being easily untied because this is truly a very fine distinction; it is not easy to show the difference between flock and flock explicitly to human eyes.”

paragraphs.text: Explanation: Both passages invoke darkness preceding light, but Sod Yesharim explains why the direction of the response matters. Israel follows beyond present comprehension in order to reach the source of Hashem’s will; Egypt treats the preceding darkness as a place in which to avoid accountable service. This sharpens the present siman’s first acceptance of Heaven’s yoke: one begins faithfully without clarity so that clearer understanding and deed can follow, rather than making lack of understanding an end in itself.

p: [ה] וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁעִקַּר חִיּוּב קַבָּלַת עוֹל מַלְכוּת שָׁמַיִם בִּקְרִיאַת שְׁמַע,
Although the primary obligation to accept the yoke of the Kingdom of Heaven occurs during the recitation of Shema,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם חִיּוּבָהּ נִמְשָׁךְ לְעוֹלָם,
nevertheless, its obligation continues at all times,
שֶׁאֲפִלּוּ רֶגַע אֶחָד לֹא יָזוּז מִמֶּנּוּ הָעוֹל.
such that not even for a single moment should this yoke depart from him.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאוֹמְרִים: "עַל חֵטְא שֶׁחָטָאנוּ לְפָנֶיךָ בִּפְרִיקַת עוֹל",
And this is like what we say in the confessional prayer: "For the sin we committed before You by casting off the yoke,"
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב הַבַּעַל שֵׁם טוֹב עַל פָּסוּק: "אַשְׁרֵי אָדָם לֹא יַחְשֹׁב הַשֵּׁם לוֹ עָוֹן".
and as the Baal Shem Tov explained on the verse: "Praiseworthy is the person to whom the Lord imputes no iniquity" (Psalms 32:2).
וְקַבָּלַת עוֹל מַלְכוּת שָׁמַיִם שֶׁל עַרְבִית זְמַנָּהּ כָּל זְמַן הַשְּׁכִיבָה,
Now, the acceptance of the yoke of Heaven in the evening applies to the entire duration of lying down,
שֶׁכָּל הַלַּיְלָה צָרִיךְ לִהְיוֹת נוֹשֵׂא בְּעוֹל.
meaning that throughout the entire night one must carry this yoke.
אֲבָל שֶׁל שַׁחֲרִית רַק בִּתְחִלַּת הַקִּימָה,
In the morning, however, the direct obligation applies only at the initial moment of rising,
וּכְמוֹ הַבְּרָכָה בִּתְחִלַּת הַמִּצְוָה סַגִּי עַל כָּל הַמִּצְוָה, אַף שֶׁנִּמְשֶׁכֶת זְמַן מַה.
just as the blessing recited at the start of a commandment suffices for the entire duration of the mitzvah, even if it continues for a while.
לְפִי שֶׁקַּבָּלַת הָעוֹל דַּי בִּתְחִלַּת הַמַּעֲשֶׂה, וְאַחַר כָּךְ קְדֻשַּׁת הַמַּעֲשֶׂה מַמְשֶׁכֶת.
For accepting the yoke at the very beginning of the deed is sufficient, and thereafter the sanctity of the act carries itself forward.
וּכְמוֹ "בִּלְשְׁמָהּ" גַּבֵּי גֵּט, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב בְּתַנְיָא פֶּרֶק מ"א,
This parallels the requirement of intent "for her sake" in writing a bill of divorce, as explained in Tanya, Chapter 41;
הָכָא נַמֵּי בַּיּוֹם, שֶׁהוּא עֵת הַמַּעֲשֶׂה, הוּא רַק בִּתְחִלַּת הַמַּעֲשֶׂה.
so too regarding the day, which is the time of active deed, the explicit acceptance is needed only at the inception of action.
וּכִדְדָיֵיק קְרָא "בְּשָׁכְבְּךָ" – הַיְנוּ כָּל הַלַּיְלָה דְּשׁוֹכְבִין.
And this is precise in the wording of the verse: "when you lie down" (b'shokhbekha) denotes the entire night during which one remains lying.
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן "וּבְקוּמֶךָ" הוּא רַק בִּתְחִלַּת יוֹם, דְּאָז קָמִין וְעוֹמְדִין,
In contrast, "when you rise" (u'vekumekha) refers only to the start of the day, when people arise and stand up,
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן כָּל הַיּוֹם הוֹלֵךְ וְיוֹשֵׁב, וְלֹא שַׁיָּךְ "בְּקוּמֶךָ".
whereas for the rest of the day one walks and sits, so the term "when you rise" would no longer apply.
וְהַיְנוּ דְּעַל יוֹם מַעֲשֶׂה, כְּלָלוּת הַקַּבָּלַת עוֹל מַלְכוּת שָׁמַיִם בִּתְחִלַּת הַיּוֹם דַּי.
This demonstrates that for an active workday, the general acceptance of the yoke of Heaven made at the outset of the day is entirely sufficient.

paragraphs.text:
Sefer HaZikhronot 1:27–29: “I found in Pesikta Zutarta, Parashat Ekev, concerning “Beware lest you forget”: this is one who casts off the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven, eating without prayer and without a blessing. It appears that forgetting is interpreted as casting off the yoke. Although blessings over enjoyment and the prohibition against eating before prayer are only rabbinic prohibitions, since Israel have already become accustomed to them, one who violates them does so through casting off the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven. Casting off the yoke is the subject of the warning against forgetting. Accordingly, this is a continual warning that there should be no moment in which he casts off the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven. This requires great mindfulness, so that the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven remains continually upon his heart, in addition to accepting the yoke in Shema morning and evening.

Sefer Yereim, section 11, explains this warning as requiring a person not to forget to accept the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven and recite Shema each day. According to the view that Shema is rabbinic, he explains that a person should continually remember his Creator and His commandments. His position is that accepting the yoke morning and evening suffices. Presumably the concluding word “continually” has the same meaning: he should remember this matter every day in the morning and evening, or at another time during the day and night. Someone who recites Shema and prays without any attention, because his heart is directed elsewhere, and who throughout the entire day never brings the remembrance of Hashem to his heart, has violated this warning according to his words.

Rabbeinu Yonah writes in Sha’arei Teshuvah, gate 3, section 27, that this is a warning to remember Hashem at all times, and the apparent meaning of his words is literally at every moment. Yet it seems that this interpretation would not be pleasing to the Master: one who forgot for a single moment would transgress a prohibition, and a person would thereby transgress countless prohibitions every day. As explained, not every person merits remaining constantly attached to Hashem, never departing entirely from remembrance of Him even while occupied with worldly affairs and the like.”

p: [ו] קַבָּלַת עוֹל מַלְכוּת שָׁמַיִם שְׁלֵמָה אָמְרוּ (בְּרָכוֹת טו.):
Regarding the complete acceptance of the yoke of the Kingdom of Heaven, the Sages stated (Berakhot 15a):
"נִפְנָה" – פֵּרוּשׁ: מִכָּל גִּלּוּלֵי תַּאֲווֹת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה הַמֻּתָּרוֹת אֲשֶׁר לֹא לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם.
"He relieves himself" — meaning an inward cleansing from all the base, worldly desires, even permissible ones, that are not pursued for the sake of Heaven.
"וְנוֹטֵל יָדָיו" – שָׁמַעְתִּי שֶׁזֶּה רְמִיזַת רְחִיצַת יָדַיִם עַל סִלּוּק נְגִיעוֹת.
"And washes his hands" — I have heard [from the Izbitzer Rebbe] that this washing of hands is an allusion to divesting oneself of personal biases and selfish motives.
וְיֵשׁ לוֹמַר עוֹד: רוֹמֵז עַל הָרְחִיצָה מִמַּה שֶּׁכְּבָר נִתְלַכְלְכוּ כְּלֵי הַמַּעֲשֶׂה מֵאוֹתָם הַטִּנּוּפוֹת, יִרְחָצֵם בְּמֵי הַדַּעַת וְטָהֵר.

And one could further suggest: it hints at washing clean the instruments of action that were soiled by those base contaminations, cleansing them in the purifying waters of divine understanding so that one becomes pure.
"וּמַנִּיחַ תְּפִלִּין" – כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב בְּיַעֲרוֹת דְּבַשׁ, שֶׁהוּא חוֹתַם שֵׁם שָׁמַיִם שֶׁנּוֹשֵׂא עָלָיו,
"And dons phylacteries" — as written in Ya'arot Devash, this is the seal of Heaven's Name that one bears upon oneself,
כְּמוֹ עֶבֶד שֶׁנּוֹשֵׂא הַנִּשְׁקָא מֵאֲדוֹנוֹ לְאוֹת שֶׁהוּא אֲדוֹנוֹ.
like a servant who wears the badge or insignia of his master to signify who his master is:
וְעַל יָדוֹ לְאוֹת לְעַצְמוֹ, וְעַל הָרֹאשׁ לְאוֹת לְכָל עַמֵּי הָאָרֶץ כִּי שְׁמָא דְּמָרֵיהּ עֲלֵיהּ.
upon his arm as an internal sign to himself, and upon the head as a visible sign to all peoples of the earth that the Name of the Master is upon him.
"וְקוֹרֵא קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע" – קַבָּלַת עוֹל מַלְכוּת שָׁמַיִם וְעוֹל תּוֹרָה וּמִצְוֹת.
"And recites Shema" — which is the explicit acceptance of the yoke of Heaven and the yoke of Torah and commandments.
"וּמִתְפַּלֵּל" – [גַּם זֶה (הַתְּפִלָּה) מִכְּלַל מַלְכוּת שָׁמַיִם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתְבוּ הַתּוֹסָפוֹת (בְּרָכוֹת יד:)].
"And prays" — [this too (prayer) falls under the category of the Kingdom of Heaven, as Tosafot wrote (Berakhot 14b)].
כִּי קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע אֵינוֹ לְנֹכַח הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן תְּפִלָּה, כִּדְפֵירֵשׁ רַשִׁ"י (בְּרָכוֹת כה רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א),
For Shema is not recited in direct personal encounter facing the Blessed Name, whereas the Amidah prayer is, as Rashi explains (Berakhot 25a);
וּשְׁלֵמוּת הַמַּלְכוּת שָׁמַיִם שֶׁיִּהְיֶה לְנֹכַח הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
and the full perfection of accepting Heaven's kingdom is achieved when standing face-to-face before the Blessed Name.
וְאַחַר כָּל הַהֲכָנוֹת אֵלּוּ, אָז מִתְפַּלֵּל.
And only following all of these sequential preparations does one then engage in prayer.

footnotes.enAnchorPrefix: Regarding the complete acceptance of the yoke of the Kingdom of Heaven, the Sages stated (Berakhot 15a):

paragraphs.text: Berakhot 15a: ‘Rabbi Yochanan also said: Someone who wishes to accept upon himself the complete yoke of Heaven’s kingship should relieve himself, wash his hands, put on tefillin, recite the Shema, and pray. This is the complete acceptance of Heaven’s kingship. Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: Anyone who relieves himself, washes his hands, puts on tefillin, recites the Shema, and prays is regarded by Scripture as though he built an altar and offered a sacrifice upon it, as it is written: ‘I wash my hands in purity and circle Your altar, Hashem.’ Rava said to him: Does the Master not hold that it is as though he immersed? For it says erchatz, ‘I will bathe [in purity],’ and does not say architz, ‘I will wash [my hands].’’

footnotes.enAnchorPrefix: "He relieves himself" — meaning an inward cleansing from all the base, worldly desires, even permissible ones, that are not pursued for the sake of Heaven.

paragraphs.text: Tzidkat HaTzadik 220:1: “This is the meaning of “tefillin require a clean body”: one should be completely clean of every desire for the affairs of this world. Bodily cleanliness in its plain sense also removes distracting thoughts. As the Jerusalem Talmud, Berakhot, chapter 3, halakhah 5, says, one keeps a distance from a child’s excrement because his thoughts are bad. The essential reason that removing excrement is called “your camp shall be holy” is the distracting and evil thoughts arising from it, for holiness is their opposite. Therefore the Sages said, “He should relieve himself and wash his hands,” and so forth: this is the complete acceptance of the yoke of Heaven. Even “he should relieve himself” is included in accepting that yoke. This is why the practice has become weak in our hands: it is difficult to attain this level, and none arose like Moses. At least during prayer a person should strive to attain it—to cleave entirely to Hashem with all his heart, soul, and resources. It is sufficient to wear tefillin then; throughout the rest of the day he should be satisfied with wrapping himself in tzitzit, so that he will at least remember to repel every distracting thought that confronts him.”

footnotes.enAnchorPrefix: "And washes his hands" — I have heard [from the Izbitzer Rebbe] that this washing of hands is an allusion to divesting oneself of personal biases and selfish motives.

paragraphs.text: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Exodus, Ki Tisa 1: “‘They shall wash their hands and feet.’ The priests’ washing from the laver signifies the removal and elimination of personal bias. Washing indicates this, as it is written concerning the heifer whose neck is broken: ‘The elders shall wash,’ and so forth, ‘and say: Our hands did not shed,’ and so forth. They declare that they have no personal involvement or share in this deed. The priest who serves also needs washing: he must remove his personal bias and nullify his judgment and will before the will of the blessed Hashem, serving only in the way that Hashem desires. So too, our command to wash our hands in the morning and before a meal means that before beginning to attend to bodily needs, a person needs to pray to Hashem. If something of this world comes to him that is, Heaven forbid, contrary to Hashem’s will, he asks Hashem to take away and remove his desire for it. Even a permitted thing contains good and its opposite. If a person eats something permitted and afterward uses that strength to commit a transgression, it becomes apparent that he did not receive the good power contained in that thing. This is the purpose of washing: a prayer to Hashem that, in everything, he receive only the good power it contains. For a person may stipulate concerning an inheritance coming to him from elsewhere that he will not inherit it. For this reason, they established the recitation of the passage of the laver before prayer and before the passages of the offerings: that we should pray only for what Hashem desires.”

paragraphs.text: Mishneh Torah, Immersion Pools 11:12: “It is clear and evident that the laws of impurity and purity are decrees of Scripture. They are not matters decided by human reason; they belong among the statutes. Immersion from impurity likewise belongs among the statutes, for impurity is not mud or filth that water can remove. It is a decree of Scripture, and the matter depends on the heart’s intention. Therefore the Sages said: if one immersed without establishing the intended degree of purification, it is as though he had not immersed. Nevertheless, there is an allusion in this matter. Just as one who intends in his heart to purify himself becomes pure upon immersion, although nothing has changed in his body, so one who intends to purify his soul from the impurities of the soul—wicked thoughts and evil opinions—becomes pure once he resolves in his heart to separate from those counsels and brings his soul into the waters of knowledge. Scripture says: ‘I shall sprinkle pure water upon you, and you shall become pure; from all your impurities and all your idols I shall purify you.’ May Hashem, in His abundant mercy, purify us from every sin, iniquity, and guilt. Amen.”

paragraphs.text: The preparations for prayer form a vessel for what Hashem bestows

rich.text: The preparations for prayer form a vessel for what Hashem bestows

paragraphs.text: Tiferet Yosef identifies the human task as humility and fear of Heaven that make room for divine Torah.

rich.text: Tiferet Yosef identifies the human task as humility and fear of Heaven that make room for divine Torah.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Ishbitz–Radzin · Tiferet Yosef, Nitzavim 10: ““For this commandment that I command you today ... is not in Heaven ... nor beyond the sea ... for the matter is very close to you, in your mouth and in your heart, to do it.” My grandfather of blessed memory asked: the Zohar repeatedly says how exalted and precious the words of Torah are; this appears to place them in Heaven and beyond the sea! The explanation follows “Everything is in the hands of Heaven except fear of Heaven.” How can one say “except,” when everything is in God’s hands? God established in this world that the vessel belongs to the person, and this is called fear of Heaven. What is the person’s vessel? Principally, that he lowers himself so that God’s majesty may rest upon him. Thus “The human being became a living soul” is translated “a speaking spirit.” The Zohar says that this spirit rises and speaks before the holy King, enters every gate, and none restrains it; therefore it is called a speaking spirit. When a person stands in prayer before God, God bestows words of Torah upon him. The words He bestows are indeed exalted and precious. The vessel the person establishes, however, is in the person’s hands. This is “The matter is very close to you, in your mouth and in your heart, to do it”: when a person lowers himself for God’s majesty to rest upon him, forming his vessel, God bestows upon him the exalted words of Torah.”

paragraphs.text: Explanation: Tiferet Yosef describes the person standing in prayer as a vessel made through lowering oneself before Hashem. This develops the progression here from removing personal bias and bearing the Master’s sign to direct encounter in prayer. The preparations do not manufacture the light by independent human power. They make the person receptive, so that accepting Heaven’s kingship is expressed not only in a declaration but in how he stands before its Source.

sections.en: The Spiritual Significance of Meal Times and Shema

p: [ז] זְמַן קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע תָּלֵי בִּזְמַן אֲכִילָה בַּמִּשְׁנָה דְּרֵישׁ בְּרָכוֹת, וְשָׁם בַּבָּרַיְתָא עַמּוּד ב'.
The time established for reciting Shema is tethered to meal times in the opening Mishna of Berakhot, and in the Baraita on 2b.
כִּי אֲכִילָה הוּא קִיּוּם הַחַיִּים, וְכָךְ קַבָּלַת עוֹל מַלְכוּת שָׁמַיִם.
For eating sustains physical life, and similarly, the acceptance of the yoke of Heaven sustains spiritual life.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאֲכִילַת הָאָדָם בַּבֹּקֶר וּבָעֶרֶב, כָּךְ קַבָּלַת עוֹל מַלְכוּת שָׁמַיִם.
And just as a person eats in the morning and in the evening, so too must one accept the yoke of Heaven morning and evening.
וּמַאן דְּאָמַר: מֵעָנִי – בְּדַעַת, שֶׁאֵין לוֹ נֵר לְהָאִיר עֵינֵי שִׂכְלוֹ וּמְמַהֵר בַּאֲכִילָה פְּשׁוּטָה,

The authority who measures this time by "when a poor man eats" refers allegorically to one poor in spiritual knowledge, who lacks a candle to illuminate his intellectual vision and quickly partakes of simple fare;
כָּךְ קַבָּלַת עוֹל מַלְכוּת שָׁמַיִם בִּפְשִׁיטוּת כְּעָנִי זֶה שֶׁאוֹכֵל רַק פַּת בְּמֶלַח.
so too his acceptance of Heaven's yoke is simple and plain, like this poor man who eats merely bread with salt.
וְחַד מַאן דְּאָמַר: דְּבָתַר רוֹב בְּנֵי אָדָם, דְּגַם כֵּן אֵין צָרִיךְ טָהֳרָה,
Another authority holds that the time follows the majority of people, who likewise require no ritual purity,
רַק מְתִינוּת קְצָת עַד שֶׁיִּהְיֶה "נֵר הַשֵּׁם נִשְׁמַת אָדָם" מֵאִיר עֵינֵי שִׂכְלָם.
requiring merely a bit of composure until "the lamp of the Lord, which is the soul of man" illuminates the eyes of their mind.
וּלְחַד מַאן דְּאָמַר: כִּבְלֵילֵי שַׁבָּת, שֶׁהַכֹּל מוּכָן מִבְּעוֹד יוֹם,
And according to the opinion comparing it to Friday evening, when everything has been prepared before nightfall:
וְדַי לִקְרִיאַת שְׁמַע שֶׁל עַרְבִית הַהַכָנָה שֶׁמִּבְּעוֹד יוֹם עַל יְדֵי מַעֲשֵׂה הַיּוֹם, וְאֵין צָרִיךְ הַכָנָה אַחֶרֶת.
the preparation made before sunset through the day's active deeds is sufficient for the evening Shema, with no further preparation needed.
וְהַהֲלָכָה כַּכֹּהֲנִים, שֶׁהֵם הַבַּטְלָנִים מִכָּל עִנְיְנֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה, שֶׁאֵין לָהֶם אֶלָּא עֵסֶק הַתּוֹרָה,
Yet the halakhic ruling follows the priests (Kohanim), who are detached from all mundane matters of this world, engaged solely in Torah,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב הָרַמְבַּ"ם [רַבֵּנוּ מֹשֶׁה בֶּן מַיְמוֹן] סוֹף הִלְכוֹת שְׁמִטָּה וְיוֹבֵל, וְכֵן שָׁמַעְתִּי בָּזֶה,
as Maimonides wrote at the end of the Laws of Shemittah and Yovel, and as I have likewise heard on this subject.
וַאֲכִילָתָם קֹדֶשׁ לַהַשֵּׁם וּצְרִיכִים טָהֳרָה,
Their eating is holy unto God and requires ritual purification;

paragraphs.text: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Talmud, Berakhot 2b:1: “The master said: ‘From the time the priests enter,’ and so forth. They raised a contradiction: ‘From the time the poor person,’ and so forth; ‘from the time the day becomes sanctified,’ and so forth; ‘from the time people enter to recline at a meal.’ This tanna refers to Scripture, explaining ‘when you lie down and when you rise,’ and asks: From when do we recite the Shema in the evening? Reciting the Shema means recognizing the light of Hashem’s abundant love. Thus, ‘From when do we recite the Shema in the evening?’ asks how a revelation of His light is found in the evening. He explains that we find the priests awaiting this time and attaining at that hour more than they attained in the sunlight. Necessarily, then, this hour contains a revelation of the light of abundant love for every soul of Israel, and reciting the Shema belongs to this time. The Gemara shows how each sage found a further sanctity at this hour. ‘The time people enter to recline’ means that on Passover there is additional sanctity at that hour; on Friday evenings, there is the sanctification of the day.”

paragraphs.text: Machshavot Charutz 9:5: “The windpipe and the food pipe are next to one another: one brings out speech and voice, and the other brings in food. They are called “signs,” because the sign of life is in them. Through the windpipe a person draws life in his breath, without which he has no life; in the human being this also gives the power of speech, making him a speaking spirit. Eating through the food pipe sustains life. The root of an Israelite’s life depends solely upon recognizing his Master and that Hashem dwells within him: “You give life to them all.” The life he receives from eating likewise comes only from Hashem’s will that he eat and receive life from it. Thus it is written, “A person does not live by bread alone, but by everything that issues from Hashem’s mouth.” This means that bread alone, separated from Hashem, does not give life; the word of Hashem together with the bread is what gives life. Without this recognition it is not called life at all for an Israelite. Through this, eating is considered like an offering, and even more precious. As the Sages explain the verse “For Hashem your God arranged it before me”: if He arranged it for your offering, all the more so for your food. The table is like an altar, and one who fills the throats of Torah scholars with wine is like one offering libations, because they are Hashem’s sanctuary and altar, and are superior to a physical altar of stones. This, however, requires complete intention for the sake of Heaven: one must not eat to satisfy his desire, but because Hashem established within creation that food sustains life, and this is therefore His will.”

sections.en: Preparation, Prayer Windows, and the Obscurity of Night

p: [ח] וּזְמַן הַהַכָנָה הַזּוֹ הַכֹּל לְפִי מַה שֶּׁהוּא אָדָם,
The duration required for this preparation depends entirely on the spiritual standing of each individual person,
וַחֲסִידִים הָיוּ שׁוֹהִים רַק שָׁעָה אַחַת לִתְפִלָּה, כִּדְאִיתָא (בְּרָכוֹת ל:).
and the pious would wait only one hour before prayer, as taught in the Talmud (Berakhot 30b).
וְזֶה טַעַם גַּם כֵּן שֶׁהִרְחִיבוּ בִּזְמַן שֶׁל עַרְבִית עַד עַמּוּד הַשַּׁחַר,
This also explains why the Rabbis extended the permissible timeframe for the evening prayer until the break of dawn:
כִּי בְּחֶשְׁכַת לַיִל קָשֶׁה לִמְצֹא בְּהִירוּת מַלְכוּת שָׁמַיִם, פְּעָמִים עַד עַמּוּד הַשַּׁחַר כּוּלֵּי הַאי וְאוּלַי.
because in the deep obscurity of night it is hard to attain the luminous clarity of Heaven's kingdom, and at times even taking until dawn is scarcely enough.
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן בַּיּוֹם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "לְהַגִּיד בַּבֹּקֶר חַסְדֶּךָ" – אָז אֶפְשָׁר לְהַגִּיד מִיָּד בַּבֹּקֶר מִתּוֹךְ אוֹר הַנִּכָּר.
By day, however, as it is written: "To recount Your lovingkindness in the morning" (Psalms 92:3), one can readily proclaim it right away in the morning amidst visible light.
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן בַּלֵּילוֹת, רַק הָאֱמוּנָה בַּלֵּב וְלֹא הַהַגָּדָה, שֶׁהוּא הַהוֹצָאָה מִכֹּחַ אֶל הַפּוֹעַל עַל הֶעָבָר,
In the night, by contrast, there is only inner faith in the heart without vocal recounting—for recounting brings past reality into dynamic actuality—
אֶלָּא הַקִּוּוּי עַל הֶעָתִיד כַּאֲשֶׁר "אָתָא בֹקֶר", גַּם בְּכָל הַלַּיְלָה כֻּלָּהּ.
and instead one can only express yearning for the future, for when "morning comes," persisting through the entire night.
וּלְכָךְ תְּפִלַּת עַרְבִית רְשׁוּת,
For this reason, the evening prayer was originally categorized as optional (reshut),
כִּי תְּפִלָּה הוּא הַכָּרַת הַנֹּכַח יוֹתֵר מִקְּרִיאַת שְׁמַע, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל אוֹת ו',
because prayer requires facing God directly even more than Shema does (as I wrote above in Section 6),
וְאִי אֶפְשָׁר לְחַיֵּב בַּלַּיְלָה, דְּ"זֶה שְּׁמִי לְעֹלָם" כְּתִיב, בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה שֶׁדּוֹמֶה לְלַיְלָה.
and one cannot impose such direct obligation at night, for it is written: "This is My Name to be concealed" (le'alem) in this world, which resembles night.
רַק רְשׁוּת לְמִי שֶׁחֲנָנוֹ הַשֵּׁם לִהְיוֹת "לַיְלָה כַּיּוֹם יָאִיר" לוֹ.
It remained optional for someone whom God granted the favor that "night shines for him like the day" (Psalms 139:12).
רַק הָאִידְּנָא, בְּעִקְּבוֹת דִּמְשִׁיחָא, קָרוֹב לְאוֹר הַיּוֹם, קִבְּלִינְהוּ לְחוֹבָה.
Only in our later era, amidst the footsteps of the Messiah when the light of day draws near, did Jewish communities accept it as an absolute obligation.
וּתְפִלַּת הַשַּׁחַר גַּם כֵּן זְמַנָּהּ עַד חֲצוֹת, יוֹתֵר מִזְּמַן קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע,
Similarly, the morning prayer may be recited until midday—extending beyond the timeframe for the morning Shema—
כִּי לְקַבָּלַת הַנֹּכַח מִמַּלְכוּת שָׁמַיִם צָרִיךְ הַכָנָה יוֹתֵר.
because achieving the face-to-face consciousness of Heaven's kingdom demands greater preparation.
וּלְכָךְ יֵשׁ תַּשְׁלוּמִין לִתְפִלָּה אֵצֶל תְּפִלָּה הַסְּמוּכָה אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁעָבַר הַזְּמַן.
And for this reason, missed prayers can be made up during the immediately following prayer even though the original time has passed;
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן בַּתְּפִלָּה הַשְּׁלִישִׁית הָוֵי "מְעֻוָּת [לֹא יוּכַל לִתְקֹן]" (בְּרָכוֹת כו.),
whereas skipping two prayers makes it "a crooked thing [that cannot be made straight]" (Ecclesiastes 1:15; Berakhot 26a),
דִּבְתְרֵי זִמְנֵי הָוֵי חֲזָקָה לְגַבֵּי אוֹתָהּ דְּלָא מָצֵי מְכַוֵּין לָהּ.
for missing twice creates a presumption of spiritual incapacity regarding concentrating properly on that missing prayer.

paragraphs.text:
Mesillat Yesharim 17:6-8: “Among the practices that guide a person toward attaining this trait is preparation for divine service and the commandments. That is, one should not begin performing a commandment suddenly, before the mind is settled and able to reflect on what one is doing. Rather, one should prepare for it and ready the heart calmly until one enters into reflection.

Then one should consider what one is about to do and before Whom one is about to do it. For once one enters into this reflection, it is easy to cast off ulterior motives and establish in the heart the true and desired intention.

You see that the early pious ones would wait an hour before their prayer and then pray, so that they might direct their hearts toward the Omnipresent. Certainly they did not spend an hour idly. Rather, they directed and prepared their hearts for the prayer they were to offer, casting away foreign thoughts and filling themselves with the requisite awe and love. Scripture says: ‘If you prepare your heart and spread your hands toward Him’ (Job 11:13).”

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Ishbitz–Radzin · Beit Yaakov on Torah, Chayei Sara 3:1: ““A time of finding” points to an ultimate purpose: the purpose of all the affairs of this world, a world of uncertainty full of concealment, is that a person refine himself as far as his strength permits. After all this, he will need prayer, praying to Hashem, blessed be He, to bring matters to a good conclusion for him. For all the refinements a person achieves according to his strength and intellectual grasp count as nothing, since creation itself was originally brought into being from nothing. He therefore needs to pray to Hashem after all his refinements, surrendering his soul and all his resources to Him and recognizing that Hashem gives him the strength to accomplish—even in his service of Hashem and his own refinements.”

paragraphs.text: Explanation: Beit Yaakov explains why prayer is still needed after a person has refined himself to the extent of his ability. This clarifies the present siman’s account of preparation differing with the person and being difficult in concealment. Preparation is a real obligation of the person’s side, yet direct encounter is also a gift for which he prays. Its success cannot be measured only by the time or effort already invested.

sections.en: The Gravity of Passive Omission

p: [ט] יָשַׁב אָדָם וְלֹא עָשָׂה מִצְוָה שֶׁחוֹבָה עָלָיו לַעֲשׂוֹתָהּ – כְּאִלּוּ עָשָׂה עֲבֵרָה.
If a person sits idly and fails to perform a commandment he is obligated to do, it is considered as though he committed an active transgression.
כָּךְ שָׁמַעְתִּי מִדִּיּוּק לְשׁוֹן הַמִּשְׁנָה דְּרֵישׁ בְּרָכוֹת: "לְהַרְחִיק מִן הָעֲבֵרָה".
Thus I heard derived from the precise wording of the opening Mishna of Berakhot: "in order to distance man from transgression."
וּפָשׁוּט הוּא, שֶׁכֵּן מָצִינוּ (רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה יז.):
And this concept is straightforward, for we find similarly (Rosh Hashanah 17a):
"פּוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּגוּפָן – קַרְקַפְתָּא דְּלָא מַנַּח תְּפִלִּין",
"The transgressors of Israel with their bodies are defined as a skull that does not put on tefillin,"
אַף עַל גַּב דְּאֵינוֹ אֶלָּא בְּ"שֵׁב וְאַל תַּעֲשֶׂה".
even though this omission is merely passive inaction ("sit and do nothing").

footnotes.enAnchorPrefix: "The transgressors of Israel with their bodies are defined as a skull that does not put on tefillin,"

paragraphs.text: Poked Akarim 4:12: “Thus it is not possible to speak of bodily transgressors of Israel who have no remedy: repentance remains possible. Even the transgressors of Israel are full of regret. Even if a person has not repented completely, one who sins only because of desire cannot fail to feel regret in his heart after the desire and appetite have passed. Although this is not complete repentance that reaches the place where penitents stand, he has nevertheless already left the category of bodily transgressors of Israel. Therefore this category is found only in “a head that does not put on tefillin,” because that is not driven by desire. The Sages also said “a head that does not,” rather than “someone who does not put them on”: a thought of regret may still pass through a person’s heart sometime in his life, for Hashem is the heart of Israel, and even Israel’s transgressors have attachment and desire for Hashem in the concealed depths of their hearts. “A head that does not,” however, means that the head itself has no connection to the holiness of tefillin: it has passed through all ten levels of evil up to the root and crown of impurity, until the mind within the head is wholly immersed in evil, without any good thought at all. Even so, the name Israel still remains upon him, for he is called one of the transgressors of Israel.”

The omission matters because tefillin embody the mind’s bond with Hashem; Rav Tzadok also preserves the significance of regret and the continuing possibility of repentance. It should not be read as classifying every isolated missed act as the extreme spiritual condition described here.

p: [י] כָּל בִּנְיַן לִמּוּדוֹ יִהְיֶה עַל הַמִּקְרָא שֶׁצִּוָּה הַשֵּׁם,
The entire edifice of a person's Torah study must be anchored upon the Scripture that God commanded,
וְזֶה יִהְיֶה נֹכַח עֵינָיו, כִּי עַל זֶה הוּא דָּן: עַל מַה שֶּׁצִּוָּה הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּתוֹרָתוֹ.
and this must remain constantly before his eyes, for this is what he is analyzing: that which the Blessed Name commanded in His Torah.
וְעַל זֶה רָמַז בְּרֹאשׁ הַמִּשְׁנָיוֹת, דְּפָתַח: "מֵאֵימָתַי", וְתַנָּא אַקְּרָא קָאֵי, כִּדִמְפָרֵשׁ בַּגְּמָרָא.
And the Sages hinted at this at the very beginning of the Mishnayot, opening with "From when...", where the Talmud clarifies that the Tanna stands anchored upon Scripture.
לְאוֹרוֹיֵי דְּכָל מִשְׁנָתוֹ רַק אַקְּרָא קָאֵי,
This teaches that his entire teaching is founded strictly on the Biblical text,
וְלֹא כְּלִמּוּד חָכְמָה מֵחָכְמוֹת.
and not like the study of standard secular disciplines and philosophies.
וְכִמְדֻמֶּה שֶׁכָּךְ שָׁמַעְתִּי גַּם כֵּן.
And I believe I heard this precise concept taught as well.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Ishbitz–Radzin · Sod Yesharim, Shemini Atzeret 17:2: “Since the light hidden and concealed within the performed mitzvah is not visible to human eyes, the act alone is insufficient: one must also learn the Torah of every mitzvah, so as to recognize its inward depth, the essential light hidden within the garment of the action. Therefore Torah study is itself one of the 613 mitzvot. The sages instituted blessings before and after Torah, for their purpose is to establish this light firmly in the heart. They likewise instituted saying before the Torah reading, “You were shown to know that the Lord is God,” indicating that this very Torah is the light hidden deep within the garments of the mitzvot. For this purpose Ezra also instituted that Israel should not pass three days without Torah. In Babylonia, Written Torah began to enter the clothing of Oral Torah. Therefore one must continually awaken, each time anew, the light hidden within this clothing, so as to recognize the light of Written Torah through all the garments.”

paragraphs.text: Explanation: The Radziner passage gives inward content to the present siman’s insistence that the Mishnah stands upon Scripture. Learning the details is a continual recovery of the divine light present in Written Torah and the mitzvah, rather than a detached exercise in ideas. Its account of Ezra’s institution explains why this recognition must be renewed: the light remains present through the garments, but the learner must keep uncovering and establishing it in the heart.

Just as the tannaim and amoraim of the Gemara studied the Mishnah, sought to understand its meaning, and explained it, so the compilation of the Mishnah was based on the Written Torah. When he studied the verse ‘when you lie down and when you rise,’ he immediately explained the time for reciting the Shema. In this way he arranged the entire Mishnah.”

p: [יא] יָלְפִינַן מִבְּרִיָּתוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם דִּבְכָל דָּבָר הַלַּיְלָה קוֹדֵם לַיּוֹם כִּדְאִיתָא רֵישׁ בְּרָכוֹת.
We learn from the creation of the world that in all matters the night precedes the day, as taught at the beginning of Berakhot (2a).
כִּי בְכָל דָּבָר הַהֶעְדֵּר קוֹדֵם לַהֲוָיָה,
For in everything, absence precedes existence;
וְ"כִי אֵשֵׁב בַּחֹשֶׁךְ" אֵדַע כִּי אַחַר כָּךְ "ה' אוֹר לִי".
and "when I sit in darkness," I know that afterward "Hashem will be a light unto me" (Micah 7:8).
כִּי כָל חַיֵּי הָאָדָם כָּךְ מוּרְכָּבִים מֵהַזְּמַן: חֹשֶׁךְ וְאוֹר, יוֹם וָלַיְלָה, כָּךְ חוֹזֵר חָלִילָה,
For a person's entire life is thus compounded of time: darkness and light, day and night, cycling repeatedly;
רַק שֶׁהַחֹשֶׁךְ קוֹדֵם, דִּקְלִיפָּה קוֹדֶמֶת לַפְּרִי.
only that darkness comes first, just as the peel precedes the fruit.
חוּץ בְּקָדָשִׁים קַיְימָא לַן: הַלַּיְלָה אַחַר הַיּוֹם,
This applies universally except regarding sacrificial holy offerings (kodashim), where we maintain that night follows day;
כִּי מִי שֶׁכְּבָר בָּא אֶל הַקֹּדֶשׁ הַיּוֹם קוֹדֵם, כְּמוֹ מִי שֶׁעוֹמֵד תּוֹךְ הַפְּרִי אֶצְלוֹ הַפְּרִי קוֹדֵם לַקְּלִיפָּה
for one who has already entered the realm of holiness has day first, like one standing inside the fruit for whom the fruit precedes the peel
וּלְכָךְ סָלְקָא דַעְתָּךְ גַּם לִקְרִיאַת שְׁמַע [וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר].
and therefore one might initially have thought this should apply to the recitation of Shema as well [as I wrote elsewhere].
וְעַיֵּין בְּתַלְמִידֵי רַבֵּנוּ יוֹנָה בְּרָכוֹת ח' עַמּוּד א' דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל "וְאוֹמֵר", דְּגַם בַּתּוֹרָה כֵּן.
And see Talmidei Rabbeinu Yonah, Berakhot 8a in the older pagination [6a of the Rif in the Vilna edition], s.v. ve-amar, showing that in Torah study it is likewise so.

paragraphs.text:
Sha'arei Teshuvah 2:5: “One who trusts in Hashem must hope amid the gloom of distress, for the darkness will become the cause of light. As it is written: ‘Do not rejoice over me, my enemy; though I have fallen, I have risen; though I sit in darkness, Hashem is a light for me’ (Micah 7:8). Our Sages, of blessed memory, said: ‘Had I not fallen, I would not have risen; had I not sat in darkness, there would have been no light for me.’

Every person, on a day of distress, should set the heart to understanding and to fasting, together with repentance and prayer, just as the community is obligated to fast and afflict itself in a time of distress, as our Sages instituted. This is a chosen fast and a day of favor. When Hashem’s chastisement comes upon a person who is pure and upright, it is a trial and serves to increase that person’s reward in the World to Come, as it is said: ‘To afflict you and to test you, to do you good in your latter end’ (Deuteronomy 8:16). Our Sages, of blessed memory, said: If a person scrutinized his deeds in a time of distress, searched and investigated, and found no sin in his hands, these are afflictions of love.”

paragraphs.text: Resisei Layla 17:1: “This is the meaning of the creation of the world: first darkness, and afterward light. The world was created in this way so that one could attain delight; that is possible only through darkness coming first. Thus it says, “When I sit in darkness”—precisely then—“Hashem is a light for me.” It also says, “He made darkness His hiding place”: the Holy One, blessed be He, conceals Himself within the darkness. The greater the darkness and concealment, the greater the light hidden within it, which one can attain through that darkness. Thus it says, “You shall seek Hashem from there”—precisely from there—and, “It is a time of distress … and from it he will be saved.” Scripture does not call bodily trouble alone “distress,” but that which truly constricts the soul as well. From that very place comes the soul’s deliverance.”

paragraphs.text: Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Berakhot 3:1: “Berakhot 2a derives the order from the creation of the world. In sacred offerings, the night follows the day, just as the blessing mentions “forming light” before “creating darkness.” Although in the creation of the world darkness came first and then light, from Hashem’s perspective creation precedes formation. Creation is darkness to us, as the Zohar explains that light can be so great that it is dark to weak eyes; therefore “creates” is said of darkness. From our perspective, ascending from below to above, formation precedes creation. Thus with offerings, which bring atonement to one who has sinned and is deficient, day comes first. In Hashem’s governance of the whole creation, however, night comes first. One might have thought that our acceptance of the yoke of Heaven depends on us, and that day therefore comes first. The Gemara teaches that it is derived from creation: as soon as one accepts the yoke of Heaven and recognizes that Hashem is one, everything returns to its source. The end is rooted in the beginning, and the lower returns to become the upper, like the flash of lightning, as I have explained elsewhere.”

sections.en: Regarding Repentance, There Are Two Facets

p: [יב] בִּתְשׁוּבָה יֵשׁ שְׁנֵי עִנְיָנִים: לְהַבָּא וְתִיקּוּן הֶעָבָר,
Regarding repentance, there are two facets: orientation for the future, and rectification of the past;
וְזֶהוּ טַעֲמָא שֶׁצָּרִיךְ שְׁנֵי דְבָרִים: טָהֳרָה עַל לְהַבָּא
and this is the reason why two elements are required: purification for the future

[בְּמֵי הַדַּעַת הוּא תּוֹרָה תַּבְלִין וּמַצְלֵי מֵעֲבֵירוֹת לְהַבָּא שֶׁהַמָּאוֹר מַחֲזִיר לְמוּטָב כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּמִּדְרָשׁ רֵישׁ אֵיכָה, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּתַנָּא דְבֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ וּבַמִּדְרָשׁ (וַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה כה) שֶׁהַתְּשׁוּבָה: לָמַד דַּף אֶחָד יִלְמוֹד שְׁנֵי דַפִּים]

[through the waters of divine understanding, which is Torah serving as the antidote saving from future sin, since its inner illumination restores one to good, as stated in the Midrash at the beginning of Eichah, and as taught in Tanna DeBei Eliyahu and Vayikra Rabbah 25:1, that repentance requires: 'if he was accustomed to study one page, let him now study two pages'],
וְכַפָּרָה הוּא לְתַקֵּן הֶעָבָר וּלְכַפֵּר הַחֵטְא,
and atonement (kapparah) to repair the past and atone for sin,
וְהוּא עַל יְדֵי קָרְבָּן וְדוּגְמָתוֹ תְּפִלָּה אוֹ תַּעֲנִית וּצְדָקָה.
which is accomplished through sacrifice, and in its absence through prayer, fasting, and charity.
וְקַיְימָא לַן כַּפָּרָה לֹא מְעַכֶּבֶת, דִּתְשׁוּבָה אֲפִילּוּ הִרְהֵר בְּלִבּוֹ הֲרֵי זֶה צַדִּיק גָּמוּר,

And we establish the halakhic rule that the lack of final atonement does not impede spiritual status, for regarding repentance, even if one merely resolved so in his heart, he is immediately deemed completely righteous;
וְזֶהוּ רַק לִתְרוּמָה הַמּוּרָם מִן הַחוֹל הַגָּמוּר לִהְיוֹת עַל כָּל פָּנִים בְּגֶדֶר צַדִּיק.
yet this level of partial purification suffices only for terumah (the priestly tithe), being elevated from pure mundane commonality so as to enter at least the category of righteous.
אֲבָל לְקָדָשִׁים הָרוֹצֶה לְהִתְקַדֵּשׁ וְלִהְיוֹת קָדוֹשׁ צָרִיךְ גַּם כֵּן לְרַפֵּא אֶת הַקּוֹדֵם.
But for sacred offerings (kodashim), one who desires to become sanctified and holy must also thoroughly heal all that preceded.
וְתָלֵי זְמַן קַבָּלַת עוֹל מַלְכוּת שָׁמַיִם בִּתְרוּמָה, דְּכַפָּרָה לֹא מְעַכֵּב לְקַבָּלַת עוֹל מַלְכוּת שָׁמַיִם וּקְרִיאַת שְׁמַע דְּהַיְינוּ תּוֹרָה,

And the timeframe for accepting the yoke of Heaven is linked specifically to terumah, because the lack of past atonement does not bar the acceptance of the yoke of Heaven and the recitation of Shema, which is Torah study;
כָּךְ פֵּירֵשׁ רַשִּׁ"י שָׁם רֵישׁ בְּרָכוֹת בְּשֵׁם הַיְרוּשַׁלְמִי וּבִמְנָחוֹת צ"ט עַמּוּד ב' עַיֵּין שָׁם.
thus Rashi explains at the beginning of Berakhot citing the Yerushalmi, and in Menachot 99b, see there.
"וְלָרָשָׁע אָמַר אֱלֹהִים מַה לְּךָ לְסַפֵּר חֻקָּי",
Scripturally, "unto the wicked God said: What right have you to recount My statutes?" (Psalms 50:16);
אֲבָל מִיָּד שֶׁנִּטְהַר עַל לְהַבָּא הֲרֵי זֶה צַדִּיק גָּמוּר וְיָכוֹל לְקַבֵּל עוֹל מַלְכוּת שָׁמַיִם.
but the moment a person resolves upon purity for the future, he is instantly fully righteous and qualified to accept the yoke of Heaven.
רַק הַעֲרֵב שֶׁמֶשׁ צָרִיךְ, דְּהַיְינוּ שֶׁעָבַר יוֹמוֹ שֶׁהָיָה טָמֵא וְהֶעֱרִיב עָלָיו הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ בְּטָהֳרָה,
He requires only the setting of the sun (ha'arev shemesh), meaning that the day in which he was defiled must pass and the sun must set upon him in a state of purity;
וְזֶהוּ שִׁינּוּי זְמַן עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁכָּתַב הָרַמְבַּ"ם (פֶּרֶק ב מֵהִלְכוֹת תְּשׁוּבָה) בְּשִׁינּוּי הַשֵּׁם, כִּלְשׁוֹנוֹ: אֵינִי עוֹמֵד עַכְשָׁו בְּאוֹתוֹ זְמַן וּגְבוּל כָּעֵת שֶׁנִּטְמֵאתִי,

and this temporal shift operates like the principle explained by Maimonides (Hilkhot Teshuvah 2:4) regarding changing one's name, as if to say: "I no longer stand within the same time and boundary as when I became defiled,"
כִּי הַהוּא יוֹמָא דְּקָא גָּרִים, שֶׁבְּכָל יוֹם הָאָדָם עוֹמֵד בְּעִנְיָן אַחֵר.
for that elapsed day caused the transition, since with each new day a person stands in an entirely refreshed state.

paragraphs.text: Vayikra Rabbah 25:1: “Rav Huna said: If a person stumbled in a transgression and became liable to death at Heaven’s hand, what should he do and live? If he was accustomed to reading one page, let him read two pages; if he was accustomed to studying one chapter, let him study two. If he was not accustomed to reading or studying, what should he do and live? Let him become a communal administrator or a collector of charity, and he will live.”

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Ishbitz–Radzin · Tiferet Yosef, Talmud Anthology, Taanit 10: “God is without limit or end, whereas the human being is limited. When a person sins, he damages a relation to One without limit or end; how, then, can repentance coming from a limited person help? But God abounds in kindness. Therefore, when a person accepts upon himself to return in repentance, God raises his perception and shows him that he has a connection with God’s light. Repentance thereby becomes unlimited, while the sin lies only within his limited perception. Of this it says, “He remembered that they are flesh,” as explained elsewhere. This is the Talmud’s statement that Rabbi Zeira said, “Let us accept it upon ourselves, and afterward observe it,” and the verse, “He said to me: Do not fear, Daniel, for from the first day that you set your heart to understand and to afflict yourself before your God, your words were heard.” If we accept the fast upon ourselves, our words will immediately be heard. This is what the sages say here: one who fasts for part of a day recites the fast-day prayer. When he accepts repentance upon himself, even though he is limited, he prays Aneinu: God shows him that he has a connection with His light, so that repentance too becomes unlimited.”

paragraphs.text: Explanation: Tiferet Yosef reads Daniel’s prayer as heard from the first day he set his heart to return. Divine kindness connects the limited person’s beginning to a light beyond his measure. This illuminates the present siman’s distinction between present purification and atonement for the past. A genuine resolve can already establish the standing needed to accept Heaven’s yoke, while the deeper healing of what preceded remains a further task.

paragraphs.text: Tanya, Part III; Iggeret HaTeshuvah 2:1-3: “All this concerns atonement and forgiveness of the sin: when a person repents completely, his past violation of the King’s command is wholly forgiven. Not a thing or half a thing is mentioned against him on the day of judgment to punish him for it, Heaven forbid, in the World to Come, and he is entirely released from judgment in the World to Come. However, to be acceptable before Hashem, pleasing and beloved before Him as before the sin, so that his service brings satisfaction to his Maker, he needed to bring a burnt offering even for a minor positive commandment involving neither excision nor execution by the court. So our Sages expounded in the Sifra on the verse ‘It shall be accepted for him’; and so it is stated in the first chapter of Zevachim: a burnt offering atones for a positive commandment and is a gift after a person has repented and his punishment has been forgiven. It is like someone who offended a king, appeased him through advocates, and was pardoned: nevertheless, he sends a gift and tribute so that the king will consent to receive him. The expression ‘atones,’ and Scripture’s words ‘It shall be accepted for him, to atone for him,’ do not mean atonement for his soul, but atonement before Hashem, bringing satisfaction to his Maker, as stated there in the Gemara and as it is written, ‘It shall be unblemished to be accepted.’”

sections.en: Time Is Composed of Day and Night

p: [יג] הַזְּמַן מוּרְכָּב מִיּוֹם וָלַיְלָה וְכֵן חַיֵּי הָאָדָם אוֹר וְחֹשֶׁךְ עוֹלֶה וְיוֹרֵד,
Time is composed of day and night, and so too is human life: light and darkness, ascending and descending,
כִּידוּעַ מַאֲמַר הַבַּעַל שֵׁם טוֹב עַל פָּסוּק "שֶׁבַע יִפּוֹל צַדִּיק וָקָם".
as is known from the Baal Shem Tov's teaching on the verse: "Seven times does the righteous fall and rise up" (Proverbs 24:16).
כִּי שִׁבְעָה יָמִים הוּא שָׁבוּעַ אֶחָד וְאַחַר כָּךְ חוֹזְרִים אוֹתָן שִׁבְעָה יָמִים חָלִילָה.
For seven days constitute one week, and thereafter those same seven days recur in cycle.
וְאָמְנָם גַּם בְּעֵת הַחֹשֶׁךְ צָרִיךְ אוֹר הַלְּבָנָה אוֹ אוֹר כּוֹכָבִים דְּנַמֵּי אוֹר הוּא כִּדְאִיתָא רֵישׁ פְּסָחִים, וְלֹא שֶׁיְּהֵא חָשׁוּךְ לְגַמְרֵי.
Indeed, even during the period of darkness one needs the light of the moon or the stars, which is also recognized as light (Pesachim 2a), so that it not be total obscurity.
וּבְבֵיתוֹ צָרִיךְ אוֹר הַנֵּר
And inside one's house, one requires the light of a candle

[מִצְוָה, וְאוֹר תּוֹרָה "שֶׁמֶשׁ וּמָגֵן ה'", זֶהוּ תּוֹרָה לִשְׁמָהּ בִּבְהִירוּת הַכָּרַת שֵׁם שָׁמַיִם, וְזֶהוּ "וְאֹהֲבָיו כְּצֵאת הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ", וּ"מַצְדִּיקֵי הָרַבִּים כַּכּוֹכָבִים" שֶׁלּוֹמְדִים תּוֹרָה נִגְלֶה לָרַבִּים].

[a mitzvah; and the light of Torah is as 'the sun and shield of Hashem' (Psalms 84:12), namely Torah studied for its own sake in radiant awareness of Heaven; and this is 'those who love Him are like the sun rising in its strength' (Judges 5:31), while 'those who turn many to righteousness are like the stars' (Daniel 12:3), teaching manifest Torah publicly].
וּפֵירוּשׁ "בְּבֵיתוֹ" – בְּחַדְרֵי לְבָבוֹ, אוֹר הַנֵּר יָפֶה לִבְדִיקָה,
And 'inside his house' means within the inner chambers of his heart, where candlelight is ideal for inspection:
שְׁאוֹר שֶׁבָּעִיסָה הַטָּמוּן בְּחוֹרִין וּבִסְדָקִין זֶה טוֹב יוֹתֵר בַּלַּיְלָה בְּעֵת הַחֹשֶׁךְ שֶׁאָז אוֹר הַנֵּר מֵאִיר
searching out the leaven in the dough hidden within holes and cracks is accomplished far better at night during darkness, when candlelight shines brightly

[מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן בַּיּוֹם אֵין מֵאִיר דִּשְׁרָגָא בְּטִיהֲרָא, וְעַיֵּין בַּיְרוּשַׁלְמִי רֵישׁ פְּסָחִים דִּבְיוֹם אַף בְּמָקוֹם חָשׁוּךְ אֵין מֵאִיר כָּל כָּךְ, בִּזְמַן שֶׁשֵּׁם שָׁמַיִם נִגְלֶה עַל כָּל פְּנֵי הָעוֹלָם קָטָן אֵין נֵר מִצְוָה חָשׁוּב לִכְלוּם],

[unlike daytime when a lamp in broad daylight yields no benefit (Chullin 60b), and see Yerushalmi Pesachim 1:1 that by day even in a dark chamber a candle does not illuminate well; for when the Divine Name is fully manifest over the micro-cosmos, the candle of an isolated mitzvah is eclipsed],
וְעַל יָדוֹ יָכוֹל לִבְדּוֹק כָּל הַמִּינֵי חִימּוּץ מִסִּדְקֵי לְבָבוֹ עַד מָקוֹם שֶׁיָּדוֹ מַגַּעַת, וְהַשְּׁאָר מְבַטְּלוֹ בְּלִבּוֹ.
and through this inspection one can purge all subtle souring impurities from the crevices of the heart as far as human reach extends, nullifying whatever remains in his heart.
וְהִנֵּה אוֹר הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ מְטַהֵר זְמַן הַיּוֹם, וְהַשְׁלָמַת הַטָּהֳרָה כַּאֲשֶׁר אִיעֲרַב שִׁמְשָׁא כִּדְאִיתָא בְּרָכוֹת ב',
And behold, sunlight purifies the hours of the day, with complete purity finalized once the sun sets (Berakhot 2b);
דְּלוּלֵי נִטְהַר לֹא אִיעֲרַב עֲדַיִן, וְכָל כַּמָּה דְּלָא אִיעֲרַב עֲדַיִן צָרִיךְ אוֹתוֹ זְמַן טָהֳרָה עַל יְדֵי אוֹר הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ שֶׁהוּא מִשְׁתַּדֵּל בְּטָהֳרָתוֹ:

for had he not immersed for purity the sun would not set effectively upon him, and so long as it has not set he still requires that interval of purification under sunlight while exerting himself toward total purity.

paragraphs.text: Sefer HaYashar 6:43: “Having explained the matter of love and aversion, we say that one who serves Hashem must recognize at the beginning of his service that love and aversion struggle with each other: sometimes one prevails, and sometimes the other. Therefore, at the beginning of his service he need not be alarmed if he grows weary of it. Such is the way of love at its beginning: it reaches a certain limit and stops, and afterward returns, gains strength, and renews itself like an eagle. If love weakens and aversion grows strong, he must not despair of the service, but know that after some days this will pass. If, however, he lacks understanding and does not recognize the delights in serving the Creator, the days of aversion will lengthen and the days of love diminish, and aversion will continue to grow. A thoughtful person must therefore accustom himself gradually at the beginning of his service, so that he does not become weary of it. When love enters his heart to perform a mitzvah, he should hasten to perform it. When he sees love diminishing and aversion beginning, some wisehearted people press themselves and do not permit themselves to cast off the task until the aversion passes. Foolish people cannot overcome their aversion: they grow weary of that practice and abandon it until it is lost to them. If they held on to part of it and did not abandon everything, it would not be lost. Therefore, when a thoughtful person sees aversion entering his heart and grows weary of the service, he should not abandon the whole practice or say, “I shall leave it all now and return to it afterward.” If he leaves it all, it will be lost to him; if he holds on to part of it, it will not be lost.”

paragraphs.text: Why the smaller light serves the search

rich.text: Why the smaller light serves the search

paragraphs.text: Concealment leaves room for the person's own work of bringing light into particular hidden places.

rich.text: Concealment leaves room for the person's own work of bringing light into particular hidden places.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Ishbitz–Radzin · Tiferet Yosef, Talmud Anthology, Pesachim 2: “This is their meaning: one does not search by the light of a torch, but by a candle, which is suited to searching. Hashem concealed His light so that there are places in this world where His light is not recognizable; these are called ‘holes and cracks.’ Through his labor and service, called a candle, a person brings the honor of Heaven even there, as it is written, ‘The soul of a person is Hashem's candle’ (Proverbs 20:27). The righteous stand before the Shechinah like a candle before a torch. This is Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's reasoning: the candle can be brought into holes and cracks. Hashem established His will that there should, as it were, be holes and cracks in this world: to human eyes, light and goodness seem absent there and the honor of Heaven seems deficient. This leaves a place for human labor, through which a person, serving Hashem with his own effort, illuminates those holes and cracks, fills them with the shining of his candle, and completes the work so that no breach remains and His honor is whole, without deficiency. This is the candle suited to searching. From the standpoint of the torch, however, there is no place for human service.”

paragraphs.text: Explanation: Tiferet Yosef explains why the candle, rather than the larger torch, suits the search of the heart. A place where the light is already seen as complete leaves no apparent deficiency for human work to address. The candle represents the person's deliberate effort to recognize and reveal holiness within the concealed particulars. This clarifies why the siman values a mitzvah's limited light precisely during darkness, while still requiring a search as far as one's ability reaches.
