paragraphs.text: Kometz HaMinchah 2:68:1: “The Sages also said that the wicked are under the control of their hearts, while the righteous are otherwise. “They” signifies the complete human form, which bestows influence, while the heart receives it. As explained elsewhere, it is compared to a woman, as in “Every wisehearted woman.” The Sages also interpreted “He built” as referring to the additional understanding given to woman, and understanding is in the heart, as stated at the beginning of Tikkunei Zohar. It also says, “A woman who fears Hashem,” and, “Fear of Hashem is His treasury”; the Sages compare a woman to a treasury. Awe is in the heart, as stated in Yoma, and the woman represents yearning and desire, as in “Your desire shall be for your husband”; this too is in the heart, as in “His heart’s desire.” This is not the place to expand further. This is the meaning of “they are under the control of their hearts”: the earthly recipient is primary, and they follow it rather than the Giver. The righteous, however, do not follow matter but form. “You shall remember that He is the One who gives you strength”: in all the good things of this world, their primary concern is knowing the Giver, so that through them He grants them awareness of His divinity, as explained above.”

paragraphs.text: Zohar, Chayei Sara 27:270: “So in the days to come, when the Holy One, blessed be He, will remember His people, the community of Israel, the Shekinah will return from exile first and proceed to her House, as the holy Temple will be built first. The Holy One, blessed be He, will then say to the Community of Israel: “Shake thyself from the dust, arise and sit down, O Jerusalem” (Is. 52, 2). She will enquire, “Whereto shall I go, since my House is destroyed, my Temple is burnt with fire?” The Holy One, blessed be He, will then rebuild the Temple first, restore the Holy of Holies, build the city of Jerusalem and then raise her from the dust. So Scripture says: “The Lord doth build up Jerusalem” first, and then, “He gathereth together the dispersed of Israel”, and afterwards, "Who healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds" (Ps. 147, 2, 3)-this being an allusion to the resurrection of the dead. Then will be fulfilled that which is written, "And I will put my spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, etc." (Ezek. 36, 27). 'Blessed be the Lord for evermore!'”

paragraphs.text: Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah 2:2: “What is the way to love and fear Him? When a person contemplates His wondrous and great works and creations, and perceives from them His wisdom, which has no measure or limit, he immediately loves, praises, and glorifies Him, and longs intensely to know the great Name. As David said, “My soul thirsts for God, for the living God.” When he reflects on these same matters, he immediately draws back in awe and knows that he is a small, lowly, obscure creature, standing with slight and limited understanding before the One whose knowledge is perfect. As David said, “When I see Your heavens, the work of Your fingers … what is man that You remember him?” In accordance with these matters, I explain broad principles concerning the works of the Master of all worlds, so that they may provide an opening for one who understands to love Hashem. As the Sages said concerning love: through this you come to recognize the One who spoke and the world came into being.”

sections.en: Even an Action That Is Not Inherently Proper

p: [ל] אַף מַעֲשֶׂה שֶׁאֵינָהּ הֲגוּנָה בְּעֶצֶם, כָּל שֶׁהִיא הֲגוּנָה כְּפִי מַחֲשַׁבַּת הָאָדָם וְהִיא מַעֲשֵׂה מִצְוָה,
Even an action that is not inherently proper, so long as it is proper according to the person's subjective intention and constitutes a performance of a mitzvah,
רַק שֶׁהָיָה לוֹ לַעֲשׂוֹתָהּ עֵצָה הַיּוֹתֵר טוֹבָה, אֵין לָנוּ לִמְנוֹעַ מִמֶּנּוּ עֲשִׂיָּתָהּ
except that he should rather have performed it in a better, more advisable way, we are not to prevent him from doing it
כִּדְמַשְׁמָע מֵאֵלִיָּהוּ שֶׁהִמְתִּין עַד שֶׁסִּיֵּים תְּפִלָּתוֹ וְלֹא מְנָעוֹ תֵּיכֶף.
as implied by Elijah, who waited until [Rabbi Yosei] finished his prayer and did not interrupt him immediately.
וְאוּלַי יֵשׁ לוֹמַר דְּלֹא הָיָה שָׁם מָקוֹם פָּנוּי לְהִתְפַּלֵּל עוֹד,
And perhaps one could suggest that there was no other cleared spot to pray there,
וְהָיָה לוֹ לְהִתְפַּלֵּל בַּדֶּרֶךְ, רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר קוֹדֶם שֶׁנִּכְנַס לַחָרְבָּה,
and he should have prayed on the road—meaning before entering the ruin;
וְאֵינוֹ בַּמַּשְׁמָע, אֶלָּא גַּם שֶׁהָיָה יָכוֹל לָצֵאת לְהִתְפַּלֵּל לֹא מְנָעוֹ מֵהִתְפַּלֵּל בַּחָרְבָּה.
yet that is not the implication of the text, but rather even though he could have stepped outside to pray, Elijah did not stop him from praying inside the ruin.
וְאוּלַי לְבַל יִתְבַּלְבֵּל בִּתְפִלָּתוֹ עַל יְדֵי זֶה, כֵּיוָן שֶׁכְּבָר הָיָה מוּכָן לְהִתְפַּלֵּל לֹא רָצָה לְמוֹנְעוֹ,
And perhaps lest he become distracted and confused in his prayer through an interruption, since he was already poised in prayer, Elijah chose not to stop him,
אַף שֶׁאֵינוֹ רָאוּי עַל פִּי דִּין לַעֲשׂוֹת כֵּן לְכַתְּחִלָּה:
even though it is halakhically improper to act in such a manner ab initio.

paragraphs.text: Berakhot 3a:12: “It was taught: Rabbi Yosei said: Once I was walking along the road, and I entered one of Jerusalem’s ruins to pray. Elijah, remembered for good, came and kept watch for me at the entrance (and waited for me) until I finished my prayer. After I finished my prayer, he said to me: ‘Peace to you, Rabbi.’ I said to him: ‘Peace to you, my rabbi and teacher.’ He said to me: ‘My son, why did you enter this ruin?’ I answered him: ‘To pray.’ He said to me: ‘You should have prayed on the road.’ I said to him: ‘I was afraid that travelers might interrupt me.’ He said to me: ‘You should have recited a short prayer.’”

paragraphs.text: Ben Yehoyada on Berakhot 3a:4: “There is, however, a difficulty: why repeat “he kept watch for me” and “he waited for me,” when shamar means waiting? It appears to me that if Rabbi Yosei had said only “he waited for me,” I would have thought that Eliyahu arrived after Rabbi Yosei was already standing in prayer, and therefore did not interrupt him but waited until he finished. Had he arrived before the prayer began, he would not have permitted him to pray there and would have brought him out at once. The repeated wording therefore teaches that Eliyahu came before he began to pray, yet did not stop him and allowed him to pray there. Why did Eliyahu not require him to recite the shortened prayer, instead of waiting while he prayed at his usual length? It appears that Eliyahu wanted Rabbi Yosei to remain there so that he would hear the heavenly voice and know how greatly the Holy One, blessed be He, grieves over Israel’s suffering. Eliyahu knew through holy inspiration the moment when the heavenly voice sounded each day, and allowed him to prolong his prayer until that time arrived and he would hear it.”

paragraphs.text: Context: Ben Yehoyada also reads the repeated wording as showing that Eliyahu arrived before the prayer. He then offers a particular explanation for the delay: enabling Rabbi Yosei to hear the heavenly voice. That explanation is retained alongside Rav Tzadok’s own tentative explanations, rather than being turned into an unrestricted rule.

sections.en: One Should Not Pray in a Place Where One Might Become Confused or Interrupted…

p: [לא] אֵין לְהִתְפַּלֵּל בְּמָקוֹם שֶׁאֶפְשָׁר לְהִתְבַּלְבֵּל בָּאֶמְצַע, אֶלָּא תְּפִלָּה קְצָרָה שֶׁלֹּא יִתְבַּלְבֵּל בָּהּ.
One should not pray in a place where one might become confused or interrupted in the middle, except by offering a shortened prayer in which one will not be distracted.
כִּי טוֹב מְעַט בְּכַוָּנָה מֵהַרְבּוֹת בְּלֹא כַוָּנָה.
For better is a little with heartfelt concentration than much without concentration.
וְכֵן בְּכָל עִנְיָן וּזְמַן, כְּשֶׁאֵין יָכוֹל לְכַוֵּין כָּל הַתְּפִלָּה,
And likewise in every circumstance and time, when a person is unable to concentrate through the entire prayer,
וְעוֹבְרֵי דְּרָכִים – דֶּרֶךְ הַמֶּלֶךְ שֶׁל עוֹלָם, חָלָל שְׂמָאלִי שֶׁבַּלֵּב – יַפְסִיקוּהוּ מֵעֲבוֹדָתוֹ,
and wayfarers—representing the highway of the mundane world, the left cavity of the heart—would interrupt him from his divine service,
יִתְפַּלֵּל תְּפִלָּה קְצָרָה עַל כָּל פָּנִים בְּכַוָּנָה:
let him at least pray a shortened prayer with true focused intention.

paragraphs.text: The short prayer can ask for wider understanding when one cannot fully clarify a particular request.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Ishbitz–Radzin · Tiferet Yosef, Talmud Anthology, Berakhot 4: “He said to him, ‘You should have prayed a short prayer.’ For when goodness proceeds directly from Hashem, there is no suffering in that goodness, as it is written, ‘Evil does not dwell with You’ (Psalms 5:5), expounded in the Midrash (Tanchuma, Tazria): evil does not descend from Heaven. Only when goodness descends clothed in the garments of this world can it appear to a person that he suffers from that goodness. A person must therefore see that no one suffers because of his good fortune. When he is distracted and cannot clarify himself in this way, the counsel is to pray a short prayer. Concerning the short prayer, the Gemara later states (Berakhot 29b): ‘Others say: The needs of Your people are many, and their understanding is limited.’ The entire prayer concerns their limited understanding: they pray to Hashem to raise their perception. They will then receive the goodness from its source and have no suffering. When a person sees that he receives goodness from its source, he has no suffering. This is the counsel when a person is distracted: to pray that Hashem raise his perception to the source, so that he will have no suffering.”

paragraphs.text: Explanation: Tiferet Yosef reads the same exchange with Eliyahu as a difficulty in clarifying one's request: under distraction, a person cannot adequately examine whether the desired benefit could burden someone else. The short prayer asks Hashem to raise the petitioner's understanding toward the source of the good. This gives positive content to the siman's preference for a short prayer that can be said with attention.

paragraphs.text: Yosher Divrei Emet, First Kuntres 19:1: “That is, those called “sons,” who possess a level of neshamah in addition to their nefesh and ruach, are bound in their thought to the blessed Creator. They may therefore go out even into the marketplace at times when they need to: because they are deeply bound to the blessed Creator, passersby will not interrupt their attachment. This is “sons go out with knots”—with attachment to the Creator in their thought. “Sons of kings” means those who have only nefesh and ruach, who are called sons of kings from the side of the kingdom of Heaven. They go out “with bells”: one must not go out idle, but, like a bell that rings and makes a sound, should continually sound forth words of Torah, prayer, and fear of the blessed God. One must not rely on attachment in thought, for passersby will interrupt it, Heaven forbid, since that attachment is weak. “And every person” means that all people are alike in this respect; scarcely anyone is to be found at the level of the “sons who go out with knots.” Rather, when the Sages spoke of “sons who go out with knots,” they spoke of what was usual—that is, of their own condition. They were speaking about themselves, not others. These are the master’s words.”

sections.en: "One Does Not Enter a Ruin" (Berakhot 3a)—meaning a Place Devoid of the Dwelling…

p: [לב] "אֵין נִכְנָסִים לַחָרְבָּה" – פֵּירוּשׁ: מָקוֹם פָּנוּי מִמּוֹשַׁב בְּנֵי אָדָם הָאֲמִתִּיִּים וּמְקוֹם מִצְוָה, רַק כָּל מַחֲשֶׁבֶת הָרְשׁוּת.

"One does not enter a ruin" (Berakhot 3a)—meaning a place devoid of the dwelling of authentic, spiritual human beings and a place of mitzvot, occupied solely by thoughts of optional, mundane pursuits.
מִפְּנֵי הַחֲשָׁד – שֶׁיַּחְשׁוֹד לְעַצְמוֹ שֶׁמָּא יֵשׁ אֵיזֶה תַּאֲוָה בַּדָּבָר.
"On account of suspicion"—meaning that a person should suspect within himself lest there be some subtle base desire motivating the matter.
וּמִפְּנֵי הַמַּזִּיקִין – דְּכָל מָקוֹם הַפָּנוּי מִקְּדוּשָׁה יֵשׁ מָקוֹם לַמַּזִּיקִין וְכֹחַ הַיֵּצֶר לְהִתְגַּבֵּר.
"And on account of harmful spirits (mazikin)"—for every place vacant of holiness leaves room for damaging spiritual forces and the power of the evil inclination to prevail.
וּמִפְּנֵי הַמַּפּוֹלֶת – דִּסְתָם חָרְבָּה רְעוּעָה שֶׁאֵין לָהּ קִיּוּם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ: "שֶׁקֶר אֵין לוֹ רַגְלַיִם".
"And on account of collapse"—for an ordinary ruin is precarious and lacks enduring stability, as stated: "falsehood has no legs to stand on."
וַאֲפִילּוּ לְצוֹרֶךְ עֲבוֹדָה [לְהִתְפַּלֵּל] אֵין לִיכָּנֵס,
And even for the sake of divine service [to pray], one should not enter,
אִם יָכוֹל [לְהִתְפַּלֵּל] בַּדֶּרֶךְ, הוּא דֶּרֶךְ הַמֶּלֶךְ, פִּילוֹן מְפוּלָּשׁ לַעֲבוֹדַת ה',
if one is able [to pray] on the road, which represents the King's highway, an open avenue for the service of Hashem;
וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁדֶּרֶךְ הַמֶּלֶךְ הוּא מָלֵא מֵעוֹבְרֵי דְּרָכִים, וְהֵם הַמַּפְסִיקִין לַהוֹלֵךְ בְּדֶרֶךְ ה',
and even though the King's highway is full of transient passersby who disturb one walking in the path of Hashem,
מוּטָב לַעֲבוֹד שָׁם עֲבוֹדָה קְצָרָה כְּפִי הַיְּכוֹלֶת מִלִּיכָּנֵס לַחָרְבָּה וּמַחֲשֶׁבֶת חוּץ לְצוֹרֶךְ עֲבוֹדָה.
it is better to perform a brief service there according to one's ability than to enter a ruin and entertain external, peripheral thoughts for the sake of divine worship.
אִם לֹא בְּחָרְבָּא חֲדַתָּא, מְחוּדֶּשֶׁת מֵאִתּוֹ,
This applies unless it is a newly made ruin (charba chadta), freshly originated by him,
וּבִתְרֵי, שֶׁאֵינוֹ יְחִידִי בַּעֲבוֹדָתוֹ עַל דֶּרֶךְ הַזֶּה,
and in the presence of two people, such that he is not isolated in his divine service along this path,
וּכְשֵׁרֵי, שֶׁכָּל כַּוָּנָתָם לַעֲבוֹדַת ה',
and they are worthy individuals whose whole intention is directed toward the service of Hashem,
וּדְלָא קָאֵי בִּדְבָרָא, שֶׁהוּא מְקוֹמָן שֶׁל כֹּחַ הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע:
and it is not situated out in an open field, which is the natural domain of the power of the evil inclination.

paragraphs.text: Yisrael Kedoshim 5:1: “The essence of complete holiness is reaching this great level: to be able to make holy use of all one’s enjoyments, without intending one’s own benefit or bodily pleasure. Rabbenu HaKadosh said of himself, in Ketubot 104a, that he had not enjoyed [this world] even with his little finger. See Tosafot there: “Delicacies did not enter his body.” Yet Avodah Zarah 11a says that neither radish nor lettuce, and so forth, ever ceased from his table. See Tosafot, beginning “shelo”: these expand the intestines to accommodate many delicacies. In the comment beginning “tznon,” Tosafot raises the difficulty from Ketubot and gives a strained answer, for the expression “their table” implies that he too ate in this manner. Moreover, why would he provide so many delicacies for his household if he did not desire them and considered them inappropriate? And the passage compares him with Antoninus. Rather, the truth is as I received it, and later saw in a certain book: the statement is to be understood literally. Although his table was full of every worldly delicacy, he nevertheless derived no enjoyment from it at all. All his eating was in exceptional holiness, in accordance with his quality of being called “holy.” This is complete holiness: for all one’s actions and enjoyments to be for the sake of Heaven, without feeling any personal enjoyment at all.”

When there are two people. If there are two, there is no suspicion either! When the two are dissolute. “Because of collapse”: But should it not be prohibited because of suspicion and harmful forces? When there are two upright people. “Because of harmful forces”: But should it not be prohibited because of suspicion and collapse? In a new ruin, with two upright people. sections.en: Although Zealous Individuals Do Not Anticipate a Mitzvah Earlier Than the Morning

p: [לג] אַף עַל גַּב דִּזְרִיזִים אֵין מַקְדִּימִין טְפֵי מִצַּפְרָא, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ פֶּרֶק קַמָּא דִּפְסָחִים (ד.),
Although zealous individuals do not anticipate a mitzvah earlier than the morning, as taught in the first chapter of Pesachim (4a),
זֶהוּ מִצַּד הַזְּרִיזוּת לַמִּצְוָה לְבַד;
that rule applies solely from the general standpoint of alacrity toward a mitzvah;
אֲבָל בִּדְבַר מִצְוָה הַנְּחוּצָה לִשְׁעָתָהּ, צֵא וּלְמַד מִפּוֹעֵל בְּעִסְקֵי הָעוֹלָם בְּדָבָר הַנָּחוּץ.
but regarding an urgent mitzvah that is pressing for that specific hour, go forth and learn from a hired laborer engaged in urgent worldly affairs.
וּלְכָךְ סָלְקָא דַעְתָּךְ בִּבְרָכוֹת [ב:] דִּלִמְלֶאכֶת בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ הָווּ מַחְשְׁכֵי וּמַקְדְּמֵי גַּם בַּלַּיְלָה, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
And for this reason, the Gemara in Berakhot (2b) initially entertained that for the construction of the Temple, workers would stay late into the night and arise early before dawn, see there.
וְיֵשׁ לוֹמַר גַּם לְמַאי דְּדָיֵיק מִקְּרָאֵי דְּלָא חָשְׁכֵי וְקָדְמֵי, הַיְינוּ מִפְּנֵי שֶׁהָיָה לָהֶם הַלַּיְלָה לְמִשְׁמָר וְגַם כֵּן לֹא הָיוּ פְּנוּיִים לְכָךְ,

And one may say that even according to the conclusion derived from verses that they did not work into the night or before dawn, it was because the night was required for guard duty and they were not available for physical building;
אִי אִיכָּא לְמֵימַר מַחְשְׁכֵי וּמַקְדְּמֵי, אֲבָל בְּלָאו הָכִי וַדַּאי לְמִצְוָה נְחוּצָה דְּעָבְדִינַן כֵּן כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל:
but otherwise, it is certainly established that for an urgent mitzvah one acts with such nocturnal exertion, as mentioned above.

sections.en: The Entire Night Was Created for Sleep

p: [לד] "כָּל הַלַּיְלָה אִיבְרִי לְשֵׁינְתָא" לְחַד מַאן דְּאָמַר בְּעֵירוּבִין ס"ה עַמּוּד א',
"The entire night was created for sleep," according to one opinion in Eruvin (65a);
וְעַיֵּין שָׁם בְּתוֹסָפוֹת דְּהַיְינוּ לֵילֵי תְּקוּפַת תַּמּוּז.
and see there in Tosafot that this denotes the short nights of the Tammuz solstice.
וְעַיֵּין תַּעֲנִית ל"א עַמּוּד א' דְּמִטַּ"וּ בְּאָב צָרִיךְ לְהוֹסִיף, וְהַיְינוּ מֵחֲצִי תְּקוּפַת תַּמּוּז,
And see Ta'anit (31a) that from the fifteenth of Av one must add time to Torah study, which corresponds to the midpoint of the Tammuz solstice;
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר דִּלְעוֹלָם הַהַתְחָלָה נִמְשָׁךְ עַד הַחֲצִי, דְּאַחַר כָּךְ רוּבּוֹ כְּכֻלּוֹ וּכְאִלּוּ כֻּלּוֹ עָבַר, וְהַלֵּילוֹת מַתְחִילִין לְהִתְגַּדֵּל.

and as I wrote elsewhere, the beginning of a period extends until its midpoint, for afterward the rule that 'the majority is like the whole' applies as if the period has entirely passed, and the nights begin to lengthen.
וְעַיֵּין בַּמִּשְׁנָה רֵישׁ בְּרָכוֹת דִּזְמַן הַהַתְחָלָה לִישַׁן עַד סוֹף הָאַשְׁמוּרָה הָרִאשׁוֹנָה,
And see the Mishna at the beginning of Berakhot, that the window for beginning to sleep extends until the end of the first watch;
וְאַף רַבָּן גַּמְלִיאֵל וַחֲכָמִים מוֹדִים לָזֶה כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּתַלְמִידֵי רַבֵּנוּ יוֹנָה
and even Rabban Gamliel and the Sages concede to this, as written in Talmidei Rabbeinu Yonah
[וְצָרִיךְ עִיּוּן אַמַּאי לֹא פֵּירְשׁוּ דִּפְלִיגֵי אַף אַזְמַן הַתְחָלַת שְׁכִיבָה, דְּאִיכָּא אֱינָשֵׁי שֶׁהוֹלְכִים לִשְׁכַּב בְּהַאי שַׁעְתָּא,
[and it requires further reflection why they did not explain that they argue regarding the start of retiring to bed as well, since there are people who go to sleep at that later hour;

footnotes.enAnchorPrefix: and even Rabban Gamliel and the Sages concede to this, as written in Talmidei Rabbeinu Yonah

paragraphs.text: Rabbeinu Yonah on Berakhot 1a:2-3: ““Until the end of the first watch”—that is, one third of the night. There are three watches in the night, as it is written, “at the middle watch”: calling it the middle implies that there is one before it and one after it. Rabbi Eliezer holds that “when you lie down” does not mean all the time people are lying in their beds, but all the time during which they go to lie down. Until a third of the night, some people delay going to bed, and it is still called the time of lying down. “The Sages say,” and so forth: The Sages and Rabban Gamliel disagree with Rabbi Eliezer about the end of the time. They interpret “when you lie down” as all the time people are lying in their beds. Even the Sages, who say “until midnight,” do not disagree with Rabban Gamliel about the interpretation of “when you lie down”: they agree that by Torah law its time extends throughout the night. Their disagreement concerns a safeguard. The Sages made a safeguard to distance a person from transgression; Rabban Gamliel did not require that safeguard. Nevertheless, both the Sages and Rabban Gamliel agree that, from the outset, one should recite it immediately at the appearance of the stars. This is evident from the passage below: “So that a person should not come from the field in the evening,” and so forth. Even when he comes from the field before its time, he should not say: Since the time for the Shema has not yet arrived, I will first eat and drink. Instead, he should read Scripture or study until the stars appear, then recite the Shema and pray, and afterward eat. Since we see that even when he arrives before its time they were concerned that he might become negligent, and required him to read or study so that he would pray immediately, we learn that everyone agrees that one should initially recite it as soon as the stars appear. They disagree only after the fact: the Sages hold that, even after the fact, he fulfills his obligation only until midnight, because of the safeguard; Rabban Gamliel holds that, after the fact, he fulfills it throughout the night.”

sections.en: One Should Not Enter a Ruin Because Harmful Spirits (mazikin) Are Commonly Found There

p: [לה] לֹא יִכָּנֵס לְחָרְבָּה דִּשְׁכִיחִים מַזִּיקִין
One should not enter a ruin because harmful spirits (mazikin) are commonly found there
[וְעַיֵּין שָׁם בַּגְּמָרָא עוֹד שְׁנֵי טְעָמִים, עַיֵּין שָׁם הַנָּפְקָא מִינַּהּ בָּהֶם].
[and see there in the Gemara two additional reasons, and examine the practical halakhic differences between them].
וְעַיֵּין בָּבָא קַמָּא כ"א עַמּוּד א' וּבְרַשִּׁ"י עַיֵּין שָׁם.
And see Bava Kamma 21a and Rashi there.
כִּי בַּיִת הוּא מָקוֹם שֶׁמַּחֲזִיק בּוֹ אֵיזֶה דָּבָר,
For a house is a structure designated to contain something,
וְכַאֲשֶׁר חָרַב מֵאֵין יוֹשֵׁב מִבְּנֵי אָדָם וְלֹא מֵחֲפָצָיו
and when it lies in ruins without human inhabitant and devoid of personal property
[וְכִדְאִיתָא בְּבָבָא קַמָּא שָׁם דְּגַם בְּמַחֲזִיק בּוֹ תִּבְנָא וְצִיבֵי סַגִּי],
[and as stated in Bava Kamma there, that even if it merely stores straw and wood it is sufficient],
אִם כֵּן הוּא מָקוֹם הָפְכִּי וּמַזִּיק לְיִשּׁוּב בְּנֵי אָדָם,
then it becomes an inverted, detrimental place that opposes human settlement;
וּלְפִיכָךְ אָמְרוּ שָׁם בְּבָבָא קַמָּא דִּמְקַלְקֵל גַּם כֵּן הַבִּנְיָן,
and therefore they stated there in Bava Kamma that an empty ruin ruins the building itself as well,
שֶׁהַבִּנְיָן מִצָּרְכֵי בְּנֵי אָדָם,
because a building exists for human needs,
וּמֵאַחַר שֶׁזֶּה הִיפּוּךְ הַיִּשּׁוּב, הוּא גַּם כֵּן הָפְכִּי וּמַזִּיק לַבִּנְיָן שֶׁהוּא מִכְּלַל הַיִּשּׁוּב:
and since the vacancy is the negation of civilized habitation, it is likewise contrary and destructive to the structure itself, which belongs to the realm of human civilization.

But the consideration that “a house that is inhabited remains settled” still applies: storage is not habitation, and the person who lived there did well and benefited the owner.”

paragraphs.text: Context: Rashi distinguishes storage, which prevents the destructive force associated with abandonment, from habitation, which also brings care for the building. Rav Tzadok’s statement that wood and straw suffice concerns the first of these benefits.

paragraphs.text: Rashi on Bava Kamma 21a:7:1-2: ““As it is said, ‘Desolation strikes the gate’”—a harmful spirit named Shaia batters the gate of a house in which no people live; therefore the person who stayed in it benefited its owner. Another explanation: A house that is desolate and alone, without people, has its gate battered: harmful forces batter it. “A house that is inhabited remains settled”—a house occupied by people retains its settled condition, because those living inside see what it needs and repair it.”

paragraphs.text: Netivot Olam, Netiv Hatorah 1:7: “This means that roads are presumed dangerous, as explained in the commentary on the chapters of Avot. The reason roads are presumed dangerous is that there is no human settlement there. Such a place is removed from the essential world, for the essential world is the settled world, and this lies outside settlement. Therefore destructive forces, which oppose the world, hold sway there, and there is reason to fear that forces outside the order of the world will prevail over a person. Thus the statement says: “One who walks on the road and has no escort.” Certainly, when he has an escort, other people accompany him; because a person is with him, it is considered as though he were within the settled world, and he is not called one who has separated from settlement. But someone without an escort and a connection to settlement—what should he do to gain that connection? He should engage in Torah, for Torah is the order that preserves the world, as explained. When he attaches himself to Torah, he has an escort and a connection to the order of the world. Preserving that order saves him from destructive forces, so that they do not prevail; such forces prevail only when a person separates from the world, as we have said. That is why all roads are presumed dangerous. But when he attaches himself to Torah, he has an escort into the world’s order, and therefore does not leave the settled world. This is a complete escort for a person. If connection to other people is considered an escort—because he is then not regarded as being alone, but connected to the creatures that make up the world—then all the more so when he attaches himself to Torah, which is the order of the whole world and in which everything is found. He has a complete escort, connects himself to the world, and is not separated from it so that destructive forces would prevail over him. This is clear.”

sections.en: A Person Should Not Enter a Synagogue Alone—this Referred to Their Ancient Synagogues Which…

p: [לו] לֹא יִכָּנֵס בְּבֵית הַכְּנֶסֶת יְחִידִי – בְּבָתֵּי כְּנֵסִיּוֹת שֶׁלָּהֶם שֶׁהָיוּ עוֹמְדִים בַּשָּׂדֶה וּמְסוּכָּנִים מִמַּזִּיקִים,
A person should not enter a synagogue alone—this referred to their ancient synagogues which stood out in the fields and were perilous on account of harmful spirits,
וּלְפִיכָךְ צְרִיכִים לְהַמְתִּין אֶחָד עַל חֲבֵירוֹ
and therefore worshippers had to wait one for another
[תּוֹסָפוֹת שָׁם ב' עַמּוּד א' דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל "מְבָרֵךְ"].
[Tosafot there, Berakhot 2a s.v. mevarekh].
וּבַהַמְתָּנָה סַגִּי כְּמַה שֶׁאָמְרוּ שָׁם מ"ג עַמּוּד ב' דִּלִשְׁנַיִם אֵין מַזִּיק, וְכֵן אִיתָא שָׁם ג' עַמּוּד ב' דִּבִּתְרֵי לֵיכָּא,
And waiting is sufficient, as stated there on 43b that harmful spirits do not harm two people, and on 3b that in the company of two they do not appear;
וּלְכָךְ כְּשֶׁיִּשָּׁאֵר אֶחָד דַּי כְּמַה שֶׁאָמְרוּ שָׁם ה' סוֹף עַמּוּד ב': שְׁנַיִם שֶׁנִּכְנְסוּ וְכוּלֵי,
and therefore keeping one companion remaining is sufficient, as stated on 5b regarding two who entered to pray, etc.;
וְעַיֵּין שָׁם ו' עַמּוּד א' תּוֹסָפוֹת דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל "הַמִּתְפַּלֵּל", וְיְעוּיַּן שָׁם שֶׁסִּיְּמוּ: וּלְכָךְ בַּלַּיְלָה וְכוּלֵי,
and see Tosafot 6a [listed under 5b on Sefaria] s.v. hamitpalel, where they conclude: 'and therefore at night, etc.',
מַשְׁמָע דְּבַלַּיְלָה גַּם בְּבֵית הַכְּנֶסֶת דִּילַן שֶׁבָּעִיר יֵשׁ לָחוּשׁ.
implying that at night, even in our urban synagogues located in town, there is reason for concern.
וְכֵן מַשְׁמָע מִמַּה שֶּׁכָּתְבוּ בְּדִבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל "מְבָרֵךְ" הַנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל: אֲבָל וְכוּלֵי אֶלָּא בַּלַּיְלָה.
And this is likewise implied from what they wrote in the aforementioned s.v. mevarekh: 'however... only at night.'
אֲבָל צָרִיךְ עִיּוּן, דְּהָא "יִרְאוּ עֵינֵינוּ" נִתְקַן רַק בַּלַּיְלָה,
But this requires study, for the blessing Yir'u Eineinu was instituted specifically at night,
וּמִלְּשׁוֹן "וְדַוְקָא וְכוּלֵי" מַשְׁמָע דְּבְבֵית הַכְּנֶסֶת דִּילַן אֵין צָרִיךְ לוֹמַר "יִרְאוּ עֵינֵינוּ", וְצָרִיךְ עִיּוּן.
and from their phrasing 'and specifically, etc.' it would imply that in our urban synagogues one need not recite Yir'u Eineinu, which requires examination.
וּבָרִי"ף אַהָא דִּשְׁנַיִם שֶׁנִּכְנְסוּ וְכוּלֵי מַשְׁמָע גַּם בִּזְמַנָּם דַּוְקָא בַּלַּיְלָה,
And in the Rif on the passage of two who entered to pray, it implies that even in their day it was strictly at night,
וְיֵשׁ לְפָרֵשׁ דִּבְרֵי הַתּוֹסָפוֹת דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל "הַמִּתְפַּלֵּל" הַנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל קָאֵי בִּזְמַנָּם.
and one may explain that the words of Tosafot s.v. hamitpalel were addressed to their ancient period.

וּלְפִי זֶה יֵשׁ לְהַגִּיהַּ בְּתוֹסָפוֹת דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל "מְבָרֵךְ" הַנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל דְּצָרִיךְ לִהְיוֹת אַחַר תֵּירוּץ הַמַּזִּיקִים "בַּלַּיְלָה", וְתֵיבַת "אֶלָּא בַּלַּיְלָה" טָעוּת סוֹפֵר, וְדָחוּק.

And according to this, one would have to emend Tosafot s.v. mevarekh, placing 'at night' after the answer regarding harmful spirits, treating the phrase 'only at night' as a scribal error, which is forced.
וְעַיֵּין בְּאֹרַח חַיִּים סִימָן צ' סָעִיף ט"ו יֵשׁ לְעַיֵּין,
And see Orach Chayim 90:15 where this warrants careful analysis;
וְנִרְאֶה דְּסָבְרֵי דִּ"יִתְבַּלְבֵּל" שַׁיָּיךְ גַּם בָּעִיר כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּתַלְמִידֵי רַבֵּנוּ יוֹנָה, וְגַם זֶה דַּוְקָא בַּלַּיְלָה.
and it appears they hold that distraction (yitbalbel) applies in the city as well as written in Talmidei Rabbeinu Yonah, and this too specifically at night.

אַךְ עַל הַ"יֵּשׁ אוֹמְרִים" שֶׁבָּרַמָ"א נִרְשָׁם תַּלְמִידֵי רַבֵּנוּ יוֹנָה, מְבוֹאָר דִּלְתַלְמִידֵי רַבֵּנוּ יוֹנָה הוּא הַדִּין בַּיּוֹם, וְכֵן כָּתַב בְּבֵית יוֹסֵף לְהַתַּלְמִידֵי רַבֵּנוּ יוֹנָה, אַךְ לֹא יָדַעְתִּי מִנַּיִן לוֹ.

However, on the 'some say' cited in the Rema, Talmidei Rabbeinu Yonah is referenced, indicating that according to them the same applies by day; and so the Beit Yosef wrote regarding Talmidei Rabbeinu Yonah, yet I do not know his source for this.
וְיֵשׁ לוֹמַר תַּלְמִידֵי רַבֵּנוּ יוֹנָה קָאֵי עַל דִּבְרֵי הָרִי"ף דְּמַיְירֵי בַּלַּיְלָה.
And one can argue that Talmidei Rabbeinu Yonah commented on the Rif who spoke specifically of nighttime.
וְעַיֵּין בַּטּוּר מַה שֶּׁכָּתַב: "וְיֵשׁ אוֹמְרִים דְּאַף בְּשֶׁלָּנוּ וְכוּלֵי", לִכְאוֹרָה הַךְ "יֵשׁ אוֹמְרִים" דִּבְרֵי תַּלְמִידֵי רַבֵּנוּ יוֹנָה וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי.
And see the Tur where he wrote: 'And some say that even in ours, etc.,' which seemingly represents the opinion of Talmidei Rabbeinu Yonah as I suggested.

אַךְ מִמַּה שֶּׁכָּתַב בַּדֵּעָה רִאשׁוֹנָה "בַּשָּׂדוֹת אַף בַּיּוֹם" נִרְאֶה דְּזֶהוּ דַּעַת תַּלְמִידֵי רַבֵּנוּ יוֹנָה, וְהַ"יֵּשׁ אוֹמְרִים" הוּא דַּעַת הָרִי"ף, וְסָבַר דְּקָאֵי אַשֶּׁלָּנוּ, וְכֵן מַשְׁמָע בְּבֵית יוֹסֵף עַיֵּין שָׁם.

Yet from what he wrote in the first opinion—'in the fields even by day'—it appears that this is the view of Talmidei Rabbeinu Yonah, while the 'some say' is the view of the Rif, holding that it applies to our synagogues, and this is implied in the Beit Yosef, see there.
אֲבָל צָרִיךְ עִיּוּן, דְּהָא הָרִי"ף אֵין מְחַלֵּק, וְגַם בַּשָּׂדֶה דַּוְקָא בַּלַּיְלָה.
But this requires study, for the Rif makes no such division, holding that even in the field it applies strictly at night.
וְלָכֵן נִרְאֶה טְפֵי דְּהַ"יֵּשׁ אוֹמְרִים" דַּעַת תּוֹסָפוֹת כַּנִּרְאֶה מִדִּבְרֵיהֶם שֶׁלְּפָנֵינוּ.
Therefore it seems more probable that the 'some say' is the opinion of Tosafot as evident from their text before us.
וּלְפִי זֶה בְּבֵית הַכְּנֶסֶת שֶׁלָּנוּ בַּלַּיְלָה, אִם יֵשׁ חֲשַׁשׁ מַזִּיקִין תַּלְיָא בִּפְלוּגְתָּא.
And according to this, whether there is concern for harmful spirits in our synagogues at night depends on this dispute.
וּבְשֶׁלָּהֶם מַשְׁמָע אַף בַּיּוֹם יֵשׁ חֲשָׁשׁ, וְצָרִיךְ עִיּוּן דְּהָא "יִרְאוּ עֵינֵינוּ" תִּקְּנוּ רַק בַּלַּיְלָה.
And regarding their ancient synagogues it would imply that a concern existed even by day, which requires reflection since Yir'u Eineinu was instituted solely at night.
וְעַיֵּין בְּטוּר וְשֻׁלְחָן עָרוּךְ סִימָן רל"ו טַעַם אַחֵר, דְּהוּא בִּמְקוֹם תְּפִלַּת עַרְבִית דְּגַם כְּשֶׁכֻּלָּם בְּיַחַד יְרֵאִים
And see Tur and Shulchan Arukh Siman 236 for an alternative rationale: that it was instituted to substitute for the evening prayer when, even together, people were fearful

[אוֹ דִּמְקוֹמָן שָׁאנֵי כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל ג' עַמּוּד ב', אוֹ מִשּׁוּם חַיּוֹת וְלִסְטִים, עַיֵּין בַּיְרוּשַׁלְמִי רֵישׁ פִּרְקִין, וְעַיֵּין פְּסָחִים ב' עַמּוּד א' וּבְתוֹסָפוֹת, וְיוֹמָא כ"א עַמּוּד א'].
[or perhaps their physical location was uniquely perilous as noted on 3b, or because of wild beasts and bandits, see Yerushalmi at the start of our chapter, Pesachim 2a and Tosafot, and Yoma 21a].
אַךְ דַּעַת תּוֹסָפוֹת שֶׁכָּתְבוּ טַעַם לְהַמְתִּין צָרִיךְ עִיּוּן, גַּם בְּשֻׁלְחָן עָרוּךְ סִימָן צ' שֶׁכָּתַב מִשּׁוּם בִּלְבּוּל וְלֹא זָכַר מַזִּיקִין צָרִיךְ עִיּוּן קְצָת.

But the opinion of Tosafot explaining the reason to wait requires study, and in Shulchan Arukh Siman 90 which states the reason is distraction without mentioning harmful spirits also requires some reflection.
אָמְנָם בֶּאֱמֶת לֹא מָצִינוּ אִיסּוּר לִיכָּנֵס יְחִידִי בְּבַיִת שֶׁבַּשָּׂדֶה בַּיּוֹם אוֹ שֶׁבָּעִיר בַּלַּיְלָה
Indeed, in truth we do not find a blanket prohibition against entering alone into a house in the field by day or in the city at night
[רַק לִישַׁן יְחִידִי],
[only against sleeping alone in a house],
וְכֵן מִמַּה שֶּׁכָּתוּב ג' עַמּוּד ב' "בְּחָרְבָּא בִּדְבָרָא" מַשְׁמָע דַּוְקָא חָרְבָּה, וּבֵית הַכְּנֶסֶת אֵינוֹ חָרְבָּה כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל דְּגַם בֵּי תִּבְנָא וְצִיבֵי סַגִּי

and likewise from the phrasing on 3b 'a ruin in the field' it implies specifically a ruin, whereas a synagogue is not a ruin as I wrote above, since even housing straw and wood removes the status of a ruin

paragraphs.text: Beit Yosef, Orach Chayim 90:20-21: ““Two people who entered a synagogue, and one finished his prayer before his fellow,” and so forth: this is discussed there, on Berakhot 5b. Rabbeinu Yonah wrote that the same applies when many people entered a synagogue, even if they did not enter together: of those remaining last, one must wait for the other. However, if someone entered alone at a time when he could not finish his prayer with them, his fellow need not wait for him. Since he saw that he could not finish with them and nevertheless entered, he showed that he entered on that understanding and is not afraid to remain alone. He further wrote: When we say that his fellow must wait for him, this applies specifically when he is not prolonging anything beyond his prayer. But if he prolongs petitions and other matters, his fellow is not required to wait for him in any circumstance. This concludes his words. What our author explained in the name of Rabbeinu Chananel was also written by Rabbeinu Yonah in his name, and Tosafot likewise wrote it in the name of Rabbeinu Tam. Rif wrote: “The rabbis explained this and established that it concerns the evening prayer; if he leaves him alone and departs, there is concern that he may come into danger.” Concerning the statement that Ri would wait even in our synagogues during the day: Tosafot’s words indicate that he did so as an additional stringency. Mordechai likewise wrote: “Ri was stringent even in our synagogues. He would prolong his prayer until everyone left; and if someone entered the synagogue in the meantime, he would study a book until that person finished his prayer. It is proper for us too to be stringent.” This concludes his words. Rabbeinu Yonah, however, wrote that this rule appears to apply even in synagogues within the city, because a person’s prayer commonly becomes unsettled when he stands alone in prayer.”

paragraphs.text: Tur, Orach Chayim 236:1: “The custom to interrupt with verses, “May our eyes see,” and Kaddish arose because in earlier days their synagogues were in the fields, and they feared remaining there until the time of the evening prayer. They instituted these verses, which contain eighteen mentions of God’s name corresponding to the eighteen blessings of the evening prayer, and concluded with Kaddish. Now that they have resumed praying the evening prayer in synagogues, the original custom has not been abolished. Nevertheless, one must not interrupt with other matters. Some of the great authorities followed the practice of not reciting these verses.”

p: [לז] "אִשָּׁה בִּדְבָרָא לָא שְׁכִיחָא".
"A woman is not commonly found in the open field" (Berakhot 3b).
שָׂדֶה הוּא הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת לְאֹרֶךְ וָרֹחַב, כְּמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי עַל פָּסוּק (מִשְׁלֵי כד, כז): "וְעַתְּדָהּ בַּשָּׂדֶה לָךְ",
An open field represents expansive extension across length and breadth, as I heard expounded on the verse: "and make it fit for yourself in the field" (Proverbs 24:27);
וְשָׁם לֹא שְׁכִיחַ תַּאֲווֹת גּוּפָנִיּוֹת לָחוּשׁ וְלַחְשׁוֹד עַצְמוֹ בְּכָךְ:
and there, base bodily desires are not commonly aroused so as to be concerned and suspect oneself of such impropriety.

paragraphs.text: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Writings, Proverbs 24:1: ““Prepare your work outside, make it ready for yourself in the field, and afterward build your house.” “Prepare your work outside” means that initially a person must observe all the mitzvot in their plain meaning: to be very careful about every prohibition and turn away from evil. “Make it ready for yourself in the field”: a field signifies expansion, so that all the prohibitions extend for him into safeguards and all the stringencies of the Sages. It is known how far the words of God branch out: even a trace of anger is termed “You shall not murder,” and excessive conversation with a woman is an adjunct of “You shall not commit adultery.” Thus the Gemara in Eruvin 53b records Beruriah saying to Rabbi Yose HaGelili, “You should have said, ‘Which way to Lod?’” “Make it ready” conveys establishment and strengthening, for the boundaries and safeguards sustain the mitzvah itself. “Afterward build your house” means that after you have developed yourself in strength and firmness, you will be bounded on every side and permitted to expand into all your wishes without needing an additional safeguard. Rabbi Yose HaGelili therefore did not in fact transgress “Do not speak excessively,” because he had already attained completeness and did not need those safeguards.”

paragraphs.text: Explanation: Mei HaShiloach explicitly interprets ‘field’ as an expansion of desire, then distinguishes Esav's field from Yaakov's field blessed by Hashem. This helps identify the kind of expansion intended by the siman: its claim that bodily desires are uncommon concerns the spiritual state under discussion. The word ‘field’ by itself does not always signify freedom from bodily desire. This is a conceptual comparison, rather than an identification of the unnamed teaching Rav Tzadok reports hearing.

sections.en: Accustom Your Tongue to Say "I Do Not Know"

p: [לח] "לַמֵּד לְשׁוֹנְךָ לוֹמַר אֵינִי יוֹדֵעַ, שֶׁמָּא תִּתְבַּדֶּה וְתֵאָחֵז" (בְּרָכוֹת ד' עַמּוּד א').
"Accustom your tongue to say 'I do not know,' lest you be trapped into deceit" (Berakhot 4a).
וּרְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר: אַף בִּדְבָרִים הַבְּרוּרִים בַּמַּחֲשָׁבָה, כְּשֶׁבָּאִים לְגִלּוּי שֶׁהוּא הַלָּשׁוֹן הַמּוֹצִיא לַפּוֹעַל מַה שֶּׁבַּכֹּחַ בַּלֵּב – יִהְיוּ תְּלוּיִים בְּסָפֵק,

This means: even regarding matters that appear clear in inner thought, when they are brought into outward expression—which is the tongue actualizing that which is latent in the heart—let them be held in cautious doubt;
כִּי הָאָדָם עָלוּל הַטָּעִיּוֹת.
for man is inherently prone to errors.
וּלְכָךְ צָרִיךְ שֶׁכָּל גִּלּוּי מַעֲשָׂיו יִהְיוּ דְּבָרִים מְבוֹרָרִים לַכֹּל, וְלֹא מַה שֶּׁמְּבוֹרָר רַק לוֹ בְּמַחֲשַׁבְתּוֹ;
And therefore all overt disclosures of his deeds must be matters verified and clear to all, and not merely what appears verified to him alone in his private thought;
אֲבָל בְּמַחֲשַׁבְתּוֹ יָכוֹל לַחְשׁוֹב אַף דְּבָרִים הַמְּבוֹרָרִים רַק לוֹ,
though within his thought he may contemplate even matters clear only to himself,
וּבִכְגוֹן זֶה: לִבָּא לְפוּמָא לָא גַּלְיָא:
and in such an instance: the heart does not disclose its secrets to the mouth.

paragraphs.text: The heart's understanding and its expression

paragraphs.text: A reason's inward force is not transferred intact merely by stating it.

rich.text: A reason's inward force is not transferred intact merely by stating it.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Rav Tzadok · Resisei Layla 16:1: “‘Faces’ means disclosures: the sage shows the grounds for saying what he says. The forty-nine are known to be seven times seven, corresponding to the seven attributes of the structure of revelation. The fiftieth gate corresponds to understanding in the heart: one cannot disclose to another the heart's feeling, the inward taste one feels concerning a matter, for that taste cannot be explained and disclosed. This is as they said in Sanhedrin 35a, ‘The human heart forgets’: it cannot be disclosed in writing, nor can it be disclosed in speech. Rather, the impression in the heart clothes itself in speech. The force of the speech follows the feeling of the reason's taste in the heart, and the heart's feeling can be recognized in the speech; but the actual taste that one feels cannot be disclosed.”

The forty-nine are known to be seven times seven, corresponding to the seven attributes of the structure of revelation. This is as they said in Sanhedrin 35a, ‘The human heart forgets’: it cannot be disclosed in writing, nor can it be disclosed in speech. Rather, the impression in the heart clothes itself in speech. The force of the speech follows the feeling of the reason's taste in the heart, and the heart's feeling can be recognized in the speech; but the actual taste that one feels cannot be disclosed.”

paragraphs.text: Explanation: Resisei Layla distinguishes the reasons a sage can disclose from the inward taste of those reasons in the heart. Speech bears an impression of that understanding but does not reproduce it completely. This explains why the present siman demands a further clarification when a private conviction becomes public speech or action. The comparison preserves both sides: inward understanding has substance, while the speaker's certainty alone does not establish the matter for others.

paragraphs.text: Kohelet Rabbah 12:10: “Rabbi Shaul of Naveh taught in the name of Rabbi Shimon: If someone asks you, “When is the appointed time of redemption?” tell him: It is written, “For a day of vengeance is in My heart.” Rabbi Yehudah son of Rabbi Simon said in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: I gave you three identifying signs and specified them concerning Moshe’s burial place—“in the valley,” “in the land of Moav,” and “opposite Beit Peor.” Nevertheless, “no one knew his burial place.” The heart has not disclosed it to the mouth; to whom, then, could the mouth disclose it?”

paragraphs.text: Context: The Midrash uses this expression for what Hashem has kept undisclosed, in its discussion of the time of redemption and Moshe’s burial place. Rav Tzadok applies the expression here to the distinction between an inward conviction and what one can responsibly express to others.

sections.en: Sometimes It Appears to a Person That He Enjoys Heavenly Assistance (siyata Dishmaya) For…

p: [לט] פְּעָמִים נִדְמֶה לָאָדָם שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ סִיַּעְתָּא דִּשְׁמַיָּא לַדָּבָר שֶׁהוּא עוֹשֶׂה, אַל יִסְמוֹךְ עַל זֶה לוֹמַר שֶׁדָּבָר טוֹב הוּא,
Sometimes it appears to a person that he enjoys Heavenly assistance (siyata dishmaya) for the action he is undertaking; yet let him not rely upon this to conclude that it is necessarily a good thing,
דְּלוּלֵי כֵן לֹא הָיָה הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא עוֹזְרוֹ, שֶׁרַק לַבָּא לִטָּהֵר מְסַיְּעִין אוֹתוֹ, אֲבָל בְּבָא לִטָּמֵא אָמְרוּ: רַק פּוֹתְחִין לוֹ וְלֹא מְסַיְּעִין.

arguing that were it not good, the Holy One would not have helped him—reasoning that only to one who comes to purify himself do they grant assistance, whereas to one who comes to defile himself they merely open the door without assisting.
דְּמִכָּל מָקוֹם פְּעָמִים יֵשׁ דִּלְנִסָּיוֹן סִיְּעוּהוּ וְכַיּוֹצֵא,
For nonetheless, there are times when Heaven assists a person as a severe spiritual trial or the like,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּמִיכָה שֶׁאָמַר (שׁוֹפְטִים יז, יג): "עַתָּה יָדַעְתִּי כִּי יֵיטִיב ה' לִי, כִּי הָיָה לִי הַלֵּוִי לְכֹהֵן",
as written concerning Micah who declared: "Now I know that Hashem will prosper me, seeing I have a Levite as my priest" (Judges 17:13)
[וְשֵׁם זֶה בַּהֲוָיָ"ה שֶׁהוּא קֹדֶשׁ כִּדְאִיתָא בִּשְׁבוּעוֹת (לה:)],
[and this divine Name was the Tetragrammaton which is holy, as brought in Shevuot 35b],
הֲרֵי חָשַׁב שֶׁהָיָה לוֹ סִיַּעְתָּא דִּשְׁמַיָּא וְעֵזֶר אֱלֹהִי לְהַזְמִין לוֹ הַלֵּוִי לְכֹהֵן וּלְהֵיטִיב לוֹ.
so that Micah actually believed he had Heavenly assistance and divine aid in having the Levite arranged as his priest to bring him good fortune.
אָמְנָם רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה אָמְרוּ בְּתַנָּא דְבֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ (סֵדֶר אֵלִיָּהוּ רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה כו) כִּי מִיכָה כָּפַר בְּ"אָנֹכִי",
True, our Sages of blessed memory stated in Tanna DeBei Eliyahu that Micah denied the principle of 'I am Hashem,'
וּבְמָקוֹם אַחֵר בֵּיאַרְתִּי שֶׁהוּא כְּפִירָה בַּשּׁוֹרֶשׁ הַיִּשְׂרְאֵלִי, עַיֵּין שָׁם בְּבֵיאוּרוֹ.
and elsewhere I explained that this constitutes a denial of the intrinsic Jewish spiritual root, see there.
וְרַק בְּכָאֵלֶּה נִמְצָא זֶה, מִי שֶׁהוּא חַס וְשָׁלוֹם שׁוֹרֶשׁ פּוֹרֶה וְכוּלֵי.
And this occurs only in such extreme cases, in one who is, Heaven forbid, a root producing gall and wormwood (Deuteronomy 29:17).
אֲבָל אַטּוּ אֲנַן מִי יָדְעִינַן מֵהֵיכָא קָאָתֵינַן וְכוּלֵי (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ קִדּוּשִׁין עא:),
But do we know whence our soul originates? (Kiddushin 71b);
וְהָעֵצָה לָזֶה תְּפִלָּה וְתַחֲנוּנִים לְרַחֲמֵי שָׁמַיִם הַמּוֹעִילִים לַהֲפוֹךְ גַּם הַשּׁוֹרֶשׁ,
and the remedy for this is prayer and supplication for Heavenly mercy which can transform even the primordial root itself,
[כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר עַל פָּסוּק: "לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא לִי אֱלֹהִים וְגוֹמֵר", דִּבְרִיאָה בְּכָל מָקוֹם הַיְינוּ יֵשׁ מֵאַיִן כַּנּוֹדָע].
[as I explained elsewhere on the verse 'Create in me a clean heart, O God' (Psalms 51:12), for 'creation' everywhere denotes something from nothing, as is known].
וְעַיֵּין לְקַמָּן אוֹת ס"ד:
And see below, Siman 64.

These are: Micah, Jeroboam, the son of the Israelite woman, the wood-gatherer, Absalom, Joab, Samson, Achan, the witnesses against Naboth, and Ahab. Against “I am the Lord your God,” Micah rebelled.”

paragraphs.text: Yisrael Kedoshim 5:17: “But Micah rebelled against “I am,” which precedes “You shall have no other gods,” the prohibition of idolatry that is among the commandments. “I am,” however, was not expressed as a command at all. As is known, faith is not something to which a command can apply: if a person does not believe in his heart, what would a command accomplish? Israel are “believers, children of believers”; this is the root of Jewish identity present from birth in all the seed of Jacob. A simple declaration therefore suffices: “I am the Lord your God,” and the believing seed of Israel will believe it. Nevertheless, in this world, which is the world of choice, room for choice was granted even in this, so that a person can depart from the root of Jewish identity and deny the fundamental principle.”

Where there is a deficiency at the root, one can repair the root until a new purity is created in one’s heart, brought into being from nothing.”

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Rav Tzadok · Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, The Egyptian Exile 5:8: “Thus, since he [Rabbi Akiva] was descended from converts, through his effort he became holy flesh and an Israelite soul. Previously he had been unlearned and said, ‘If only I had a Torah scholar,’ and so forth (Pesachim 49b): his natural starting point was not good. Only through effort did he merit the Oral Torah, which clarifies that the essential thing is to be of Israel's holy stock; through his effort he brought it about that he belonged to that holy stock. [Effort is effective even in this, and Hashem has many means, as stated in Taanit 25a: ‘Am I asking from someone who does not have it?’ The principal means is Torah, as the Midrash teaches in several places concerning Yitro and his descendants. A person can attain heavenly mercy so that ‘his flesh returns like the flesh of a young child’ (II Kings 5:14), like a convert who converts, who is considered a newborn child (Yevamot 22a), and return to holy flesh. This is as I wrote elsewhere on ‘Create in me a pure heart, God’ (Psalms 51:12): as is known, ‘creation’ everywhere denotes something from nothing. These matters contain great and substantial discussions, whose place is not here.]”

paragraphs.text: Explanation: Ohr Zarua LaTzadik also reads ‘Create in me a pure heart’ as creation from nothing. Its context is Rabbi Akiva's transformation through Torah and effort, followed by the images of a convert as newly born and flesh restored like a child's. This gives the siman's final remedy a concrete meaning: prayer for mercy can seek a renewed spiritual beginning, rather than treating one's present condition as an unchangeable verdict. The matching cross-reference is suggestive; it does not by itself prove which passage the author intended by ‘elsewhere.’

sections.en: The Ultimate Essence of Repentance Is Reached When Hashem Illuminates a Person's Eyes So…

p: [מ] עִיקַּר הַתְּשׁוּבָה הוּא עַד שֶׁיָּאִיר ה' עֵינָיו שֶׁיִּהְיוּ זְדוֹנוֹת כִּזְכִיּוֹת,
The ultimate essence of repentance is reached when Hashem illuminates a person's eyes so that willful transgressions are transformed into merits,
רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר שֶׁיַּכִּיר וְיָבִין שֶׁכָּל מַה שֶּׁחָטָא הָיָה גַּם כֵּן בִּרְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
which means that he recognizes and understands that everything he sinned was likewise encompassed within the ultimate will of the Blessed Name,
כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת לא סוֹף עַמּוּד ב): ג' פְּסוּקִים וְכוּלֵי, "וְאַתָּה הֲסִבֹּתָ אֶת לִבָּם אֲחֹרַנִּית", "וַאֲשֶׁר הֲרֵעֹתִי" וְכוּלֵי.
as our Sages of blessed memory expounded (Berakhot 31b): three verses imply this, including "You have turned their heart back" (I Kings 18:37) and "whom I have afflicted" (Micah 4:6).
וּכְטַעַם יְדִיעָה וּבְחִירָה שֶׁבֵּיאַר הָאֲרִ"י זַ"ל בְּסוֹף סֵפֶר אַרְבַּע מֵאוֹת שֶׁקֶל כֶּסֶף,
This mirrors the dynamic of divine Foreknowledge and human Free Will explained by the holy Ari at the end of Sefer Arba Meot Shekel Kesef:
שֶׁשְּׁנֵיהֶם אֱמֶת, כָּל אֶחָד בְּמָקוֹם בִּפְנֵי עַצְמוֹ:
that both are absolute truth, each within its own distinct domain;
בִּמְקוֹם הַבְּחִירָה שָׁם אֵין מָקוֹם לִידִיעָה,
in the realm of Free Choice there is no place for Foreknowledge,
וּבִמְקוֹם הַיְדִיעָה שָׁם בֶּאֱמֶת אֵין מָקוֹם לַבְּחִירָה.
while in the realm of Foreknowledge there is in ultimate truth no room for Free Choice.
וּכְשֶׁמַּשִּׂיג לְאוֹר זֶה הָעָצוּם,
And when a person attains this sublime, overwhelming illumination,
אָז שָׁבוּ כָּל זְדוֹנוֹתָיו בִּלְתִּי יוֹצְאִים מֵעוֹמֶק יְדִיעַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
then all of his willful sins are seen as never having deviated from the unfathomable depth of the knowledge of the Blessed Name,
וְהוּא וְדַעְתּוֹ וּרְצוֹנוֹ הַכֹּל אֶחָד.
and He, His knowledge, and His will are entirely One.
וּמֵאַחַר שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ רָצָה כֵּן, הֲרֵי הַכֹּל זְכִיּוֹת,
And since the Blessed Name willed it so, behold all those deeds are converted into merits,
וְזוֹכֶה לְכַפָּרָה גְּמוּרָה שֶׁבְּיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים,
and he merits the absolute atonement of Yom Kippur,
שֶׁזֶּה סוֹד הַשָּׂעִיר לַעֲזָאזֵל,
which is the inner mystical secret of the scapegoat sent to Azazel:
שֶׁאִלּוּ עֲשָׂאוּהוּ הָאָדָם עַצְמוֹ הָיָה עוֹבֵד עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה גָּמוּר,
for had a person performed this act on his own initiative, he would be a complete idolater,
וְהוּא "לֹא יִהְיֶה לְךָ" שֶׁהוּא יְסוֹד כָּל הַמִּצְווֹת לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה וְכָל הָעֲבֵירוֹת וְהַהֲסָרוֹת מֵרְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
violating "You shall have no other gods," which is the foundation of all negative prohibitions, all sins, and all departures from the will of Hashem.
רַק שֶׁהַשָּׂעִיר הוּא עַל יְדֵי רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁהוּא מִצְוָה לְשַׁלְּחוֹ לוֹ, נַעֲשָׂה עוֹד מִצְוָה וְלֹא עֲבֵירָה.
Yet because the scapegoat is dispatched through the explicit command and will of the Blessed Name, it becomes a supreme mitzvah rather than a sin.
וְכָךְ פֵּירְשׁוּהוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (פִּרְקֵי דְּרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר פֶּרֶק מו),
And so our Sages of blessed memory explained (Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer 46),
וְעַיֵּין בָּרַמְבַּ"ן פָּרָשַׁת אַחֲרֵי,
and see Ramban in Parashat Acharei Mot:
שֶׁאָנוּ נוֹתְנִים חֵלֶק לַעֲזָאזֵל שֶׁהוּא הָרַע מִצַּד מַה שֶּׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ צִוָּה לָתֵת לוֹ,
that we offer a portion to Azazel—the side of evil—specifically because the Blessed Name commanded us to give it to him,
וְנִמְצָא הָעֲבֵירָה מִצְוָה:
and consequently the apparent sin is revealed to be a holy mitzvah.

paragraphs.text: Introduction to Siman 40: Divine knowledge and human choice (yedi’ah u-vechirah) in Rav Tzadok and the school of Izbica–Radzin

rich.text: Introduction to Siman 40: Divine knowledge and human choice (yedi’ah u-vechirah) in Rav Tzadok and the school of Izbica–Radzin

paragraphs.text: Rambam asked how a person’s choice can be free if Hashem knows beforehand whether he will be righteous or wicked, and answered that His knowledge is not like ours (Hilchot Teshuvah 5:5; see note 282 below). Rav Tzadok holds that this admission is itself the true answer, and he explains it, after Tikkunei Zohar Chadash and the Ari’s Arba Me’ot Shekel Kesef, as two truths that stand in two different “places”: “In the place of knowledge there is no choice, and in the place of choice there is no grasp of His knowledge; choice exists only from the side of this world” (Takanat HaShavin 6). The place of knowledge is hidden in this world and will be revealed in the future, when the evil inclination is removed and choice falls away (Machshavot Charutz 8; Resisei Layla 50). Elsewhere he spells out that this is Rambam’s answer itself: for us two opposites cannot rest in one subject, but for Hashem they can (citing Maharal’s introduction to Gevurot Hashem); “for us there is choice, and for Hashem knowledge,” and when we merit such a revelation of Godliness that “the righteous will be called by the name of the Holy One” (Bava Batra 75b), we will see that there was no room for choice at all (Likkutei Maamarim, On Shimshon 17).

paragraphs.text: The root is his teacher, the Izbica Rebbe. On “And Sarah denied” he writes that “All is in the hands of Heaven except the fear of Heaven” (Berakhot 33b) holds “only according to the limit of human understanding; in truth all is in the hands of Heaven, even the fear of Heaven, and only in this world has Hashem concealed His way” (Mei HaShiloach, vol. I, Vayera). Even mitzvot and their opposite are from Hashem, and only at times does He ascribe them to man, as He testified of Judah, “She is righteous; from Me” (Sotah 10b; Mei HaShiloach, vol. I, Vayeshev). Yet he limits this to hindsight: Aaron would raise Israel’s deeds “until they became as merits, and this is only after the deed; before the deed a person may not rely on this, but must take care as far as his hand reaches” (Mei HaShiloach, vol. I, Beha’alotcha); and “all the good you do, ascribe to Hashem, and all the failings, ascribe to yourselves” (Mei HaShiloach, vol. I, Ha’Azinu).

paragraphs.text: Radzin teaches the same. On “You shall see My back” (Exodus 33:23), R’ Gershon Chanoch of Radzin writes that only after the deed is it shown how it was bound to Hashem’s will, “but at the time of the deed you cannot see it, for if this were openly revealed there would be no room for divine service” (Sod Yesharim, Purim 4); and one who already in this world takes the stance that all is in Heaven’s hands, even the fear of Heaven, is called “lost” (Sod Yesharim, Rosh Hashanah 1; compare Tiferet Yosef, Shabbat Chol HaMoed Pesach). Rav Tzadok records it as a teaching he heard: “‘You shall see My back’—after the deed one can grasp what Hashem intended by it; but ‘My face,’ before the deed, was not revealed even to Moses” (Resisei Layla 52:2).

paragraphs.text: This siman applies the principle to repentance. Repentance from love raises a person to the place of knowledge, and from there his past sins are seen within Hashem’s will and become merits (Yoma 86b); in the future Hashem will make this clear to all, “when all Israel repent from love, so that willful sins become merits” (Peri Tzadik, Vayeshev 11). It holds only after the deed: one who relies on it beforehand is “one who says, I will sin and repent,” who is not given the chance to repent (Yoma 85b; Peri Tzadik, Masei 11). In practice the two meet in Israel as “we will do and we will hear”: while striving, a person must know that his striving is from Hashem; while recognizing that all is in Heaven’s hands, he must still strive (Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:68).

paragraphs.text: R’ Yisrael Salanter, in one of his late letters, takes up the same question from another side: Hashem knows the outcome, yet He conducts His world as though it were not known. His knowledge of human choice, he writes, is of two kinds. One is “absolute knowledge,” and “one cannot conceive how it does not contradict choice” (as Rambam explained in Hilchot Teshuvah 5). The other is “rational knowledge,” according to a person’s conduct, nature and the chain of cause and effect, “and by this knowledge the Holy One governs His world for good.” For “in the aspect of absolute knowledge the Holy One does not govern His world, which hangs on human choice; it has nothing to do with absolute knowledge,” since “at every moment a person stands in his choice without hindrance.” This is how he reads the Yerushalmi. To the question “Does the Holy One not see what will be?” it answers, “The Holy One judges a person only as he stands at that moment,” as it is said of Ishmael, “where he is” (Genesis 21:17; Yerushalmi Rosh Hashanah 1:3). He sees what will be, yet He judges a person only by what he is now; and for good He even gives in advance, “on credit,” before the deed (Ohr Yisrael, Letter 30).

paragraphs.text: Takanat HaShavin 5:7: “Likewise, with all the transgressions that brought a person to return and to attain the level of a penitent—of which the Sages said that even the completely righteous cannot stand in that place—the distancing has become the cause of closeness.”

paragraphs.text: Takanat HaShavin 5:8: “This level comes through repentance out of love, with greater closeness after the distancing. As the Sages explained the impurity of a menstruant: it is so that she should become beloved to her husband. The deliberate sins thus become like merits, for they are what bring about the closeness.”

paragraphs.text: Context: These passages explain why the section begins with teshuvah and ends with transformed sins. The transformation is realized through repentance out of love: the earlier distance has led to deeper attachment. It is not a claim that a person may choose a transgression in advance and call it a mitzvah. The act of the scapegoat later in this section is a mitzvah because Hashem explicitly commands it.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Rav Tzadok · Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 15:3: “Then Elijah said the verse, “You have turned their heart backward.” Of this they said, “Elijah hurled words toward Heaven,” and they said that the Holy One, blessed be He, afterward acknowledged his argument, as it is written, “Whom I afflicted.” There it says, “Were it not for these three verses, their feet would have faltered.” At that moment there appeared to them something of the concealed light from the Ancient One. This is the meaning of “If your sins are like these years, ordered and coming since the six days of Creation, they shall become white as snow.” In the utterance of Creation it says “formless and void,” which alludes to the deeds of the wicked, as Bereishit Rabbah says. When, through repentance from love, one merits the revelation of this light, “they shall become white as snow”: his deliberate sins become like merits.”

paragraphs.text: Explanation: In Chanukah, Rav Tzadok returns to the very verses quoted in this siman and identifies the means of the revelation: repentance from love. This makes the siman’s language about divine will more precise. The light is disclosed through a repaired relationship with Hashem; it is not an inference a person can use beforehand to authorize a transgression. The siman’s own example of the goat sent to Azazel preserves that distinction: an explicit command makes that particular act a mitzvah.

The light is disclosed through a repaired relationship with Hashem; it is not an inference a person can use beforehand to authorize a transgression. The siman’s own example of the goat sent to Azazel preserves that distinction: an explicit command makes that particular act a mitzvah.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Rav Tzadok · Peri Tzadik, Lech Lecha 7:3: “This is the meaning of “Yours is the dew of your youth”: it is the dew of Atika, the Ancient One. It corresponds to what they said (Shabbat 89b): “If your sins are like years”—like these years that have been ordered and have come from the six days of Creation until now—“they shall become white as snow.” Through repentance from love it becomes clear that in the utterance “Bereishit,” in which “And He said” does not appear and which signifies an understanding concealed from every conception, “formlessness and emptiness” had already been mentioned. These allude to the deeds of the wicked, as is taught in Bereishit Rabbah. This was the intention: first darkness, then light, so that light should gain its advantage from within darkness. It corresponds to the Zohar’s statement (II, 184a), “There is no light except that which emerges from darkness.” Then “they shall become white as snow”: they become merits. This is the meaning of “Yours is the dew of your youth”: it was the blessed God’s intention that the forty-eight years should come first and that afterward Abraham our father should recognize his Creator. This is what they said: “Just as dew flies away, so your sins fly away.” It had been ordered from the utterance “Bereishit,” from Atika, and “they shall become white as snow,” becoming merits. “Just as dew is a sign of blessing for the world, so you are a sign of blessing for the world.””

paragraphs.text: Explanation: Peri Tzadik supplies Abraham’s youth as a concrete setting for the difficult retrospective claim in Tzidkat HaTzadik. The first darkness becomes part of a greater light through repentance from love, and the image of dew places this recognition within Shabbat’s revelation. It illustrates the transformation after return while leaving intact the distinction between human choice and the illumination of Divine knowledge.

paragraphs.text: Arba Meot Shekel Kesef, fol. 79b: “One difficult question must be asked. We have seen in the books of Kabbalah that when God is engaged with Beriah [the realm of Creation], He does not know, whereas in Atzilut [the realm of Emanation] He knows. Thus it would seem that in Atzilut there is knowledge and compulsion. But this presents a difficulty concerning our Sages’ teaching on “Hashem said to Moses: Speak to the priests”: the first king who would arise over Israel would be pierced by a sword. He said to Him, “And to me You say, ‘Speak to the priests’?”—for Saul had killed Nob, the city of priests. It would follow that His knowledge compelled Saul, whether in Beriah or in Atzilut; in either case it compelled him.

paragraphs.text: The answer that my master, of blessed memory, gave is this: it is true that there is knowledge in Atzilut, but a person has the power to choose otherwise. Scripture says, “See, I have set before you today life and good, death and evil”; and, “Choose life, so that you and your offspring may live.” Saul’s case appears to imply compulsion, whereas Scripture demonstrates choice by saying, “Choose.” Our Sages also said that no evil descends from above. Above, in Atzilut, everything is simple, and that knowledge does not descend below to compel a person. Above there is no reward and punishment, and no choice and will. This is the secret of “Is not Esau Jacob’s brother? declares Hashem; yet I loved Jacob.” Does Hashem say that Esau is like Jacob? The Torah has already testified that Jacob dwelt in tents, whereas Esau served idolatry, and Hashem chooses the righteous. How, then, does Hashem subsequently say “I loved Jacob,” when one is righteous and the other wicked? The meaning is that above, in Atzilut, Esau is like Jacob, for there is no reward and punishment there. This is the secret of “Is not Esau Jacob’s brother? declares Hashem,” referring to Atika Kadisha [the Holy Ancient One], as the Idra explains concerning “By Myself I have sworn”: “declares Havayah” [the declaration of Ze’ir Anpin], “declares Hashem,” is Atika Kadisha. [The Holy One, blessed be He, says through Malachi there:] You must therefore listen to My voice and accept My sovereignty, because I chose Jacob although he is like Esau.

paragraphs.text: Also, [there is a proof that there is no knowledge in the realm of Beriah:] if we posit compelling knowledge, there is no need to teach or command, since a person is already fixed in his actions. The tanna, Rabbi Chananya ben Akashya, likewise says, “The Holy One, blessed be He, wished to confer merit upon Israel; therefore He gave them abundant Torah and commandments.” If there were compelling knowledge, abundant commandments would serve no purpose. The meaning, then, is that above, in Atzilut, there is knowledge; the knowledge of a person’s evil does not descend from above, for it remains there. The person, who possesses choice, has the power to choose otherwise. That is why the Torah commanded its commandments. If a person cleaves to Torah, he draws good upon himself. Evil does not descend of itself from above; the person draws the evil upon himself or brings it down.

paragraphs.text: This also explains the teaching in the Zohar, Vayikra, III 13b, on “If a soul sins and hears the voice of an oath, and he is a witness, whether he has seen or known.” It says that before the soul descends below, the Holy One, blessed be He, makes it swear: “Be righteous and do not be wicked.” If we posit knowledge, He would be making it swear falsely, since He knows that it will sin, yet makes it swear. The same applies to our Sages’ statement, “They make him swear: Be righteous and do not be wicked.” If we posit knowledge, He would be making us swear falsely, and Hashem does not desire false oaths in His name. These statements, and many verses, demonstrate that at the time of Creation [in the realm of Beriah], He has no knowledge.

paragraphs.text: What we have explained also shows that even the knowledge of Atzilut is simple knowledge and depends upon human will. He [the person] has already been told that he is like his Maker, who [Hashem] possesses choice and will. Scripture says, “For Yah has chosen Jacob for Himself; Israel, as His treasured possession,” indicating choice and will. Likewise, it says, “I will accept you [declares the Lord Hashem],” and so forth. Thus the verses show that he [the person] possesses [choice]. He also likens Israel to Himself, saying, “You shall be holy, for I am holy”: just as I am holy, so you shall be holy. [Hashem calls them] “My brothers and companions,” “My children,” “in His image,” and “according to His likeness.” For if one says that He has knowledge but that it does not compel, as the master [Rambam], of blessed memory, said, then Saul, whom His knowledge compelled, has grounds for complaint. But if we explain it as we have done, everything accords with truth and faith. This is the meaning of Job’s statement: “Far be it from God to do wickedness, and from the Almighty to do injustice; for He repays a person according to his deed, and brings upon each according to his way.” Examine carefully the meaning of “He repays a person according to his deed, and brings upon each according to his way”; investigate the matter well and you will find its true answer. May you be at peace, and all that is yours be at peace.”

paragraphs.text: Context: This is the passage attributed to the Ari that Rav Tzadok names here. The terms Atzilut and Beriah distinguish levels in the kabbalistic discussion; the passage explicitly insists that the higher knowledge does not descend to compel a person and that Torah, choice, and accountability remain meaningful. Rav Tzadok states his own formulation in the following phrases: each truth has its own domain.

paragraphs.text: Mishneh Torah, Repentance 5:5: “You may ask: Does the Holy One, blessed be He, not know all that will happen? Before it happens, does He know that this person will be righteous or wicked, or does He not know? If He knows that the person will be righteous, it is impossible for him not to be righteous; and if you say that He knows he will be righteous but he may be wicked, then He does not know the matter clearly. Know that the answer to this question is longer than the earth and broader than the sea; many great principles and lofty mountains depend upon it. But you must know and understand what I say here. We have already explained in the second chapter of the Laws of the Foundations of the Torah that the Holy One, blessed be He, does not know through a knowledge external to Himself, as human beings and their knowledge are two things. Rather, He, exalted be His name, and His knowledge are one, and human understanding cannot grasp this matter fully. Just as a person cannot grasp and discover the truth of the Creator, as it is said, ‘A person cannot see Me and live,’ so a person cannot grasp and discover the Creator’s knowledge. This is what the prophet said: ‘My thoughts are not your thoughts, and your ways are not My ways.’ Since this is so, we lack the power to know how the Holy One, blessed be He, knows all creatures and deeds. Nevertheless, we know without doubt that a person’s action lies in his own hands, and the Holy One, blessed be He, neither draws him nor decrees that he act in a particular way. We know this not only from received religion but also through clear rational proofs. Therefore prophecy says that a person is judged for his actions according to what he has done, whether good or evil. This is the principle upon which all the words of prophecy depend.”

paragraphs.text: Takanat HaShavin 6:4: “As is known concerning the secret of divine knowledge and free choice, over which Rambam found difficulty: he revealed there the culmination of his knowledge by saying that he did not know a solution, because our knowledge is not like His knowledge. This is the true answer to the question, unlike Raavad, who wrote that he had left it as a difficulty. Its secret is known in Tikkunei Zohar Chadash and the Ari’s Arba Meot Shekel Kesef. The essence is that in the place of knowledge there is no choice, and in the place of choice there is no apprehension of His knowledge. Choice belongs to the standpoint of this world, for as long as a person remains attached to materiality and is not entirely attached to Him. He has not yet reached the ultimate perfection of choice, which is to cleave entirely to the living God. When he reaches that level, he apprehends the truth that there is no choice, and that it is not through his own righteousness and uprightness of heart. Pride arises from the lowliness and materiality within him; then Hashem is also exalted beyond him. If he recognized that Hashem is with him and that everything is from Him, there would be no place for pride. There, in the place of His greatness, is His humility. Thus humility is the greatness of a person whose soul cleaves to its source.”

paragraphs.text: Context: Rav Tzadok here explicitly connects Rambam’s discussion to the Ari’s two-domain account. paragraphs.text: Machshavot Charutz 8:1: “The question of divine knowledge and free choice is well known. Zohar Chadash and the Ari’s Arba Meot Shekel Kesef resolve it according to the esoteric teaching. The root of the matter is that they occupy two different places. In the place of knowledge there truly is no room for choice; but this place is concealed in this world and will be revealed in the future, when the evil inclination is removed and choice is in fact annulled. As Shabbat 151b says, “Days in which there is no desire” are the days of the Messiah. Then it will also become clear concerning all Israel’s sins that they were ordered from the six days of Creation, as stated in the chapter Rabbi Akiva. This means that the knowledge will be revealed: everything was within His knowledge at the beginning of Creation. But this world is the place of choice.”

paragraphs.text: Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah 2:10: “The Holy One, blessed be He, apprehends His own truth and knows it as it is. He does not know through a knowledge external to Himself, as we know. We and our knowledge are not one, but the Creator, blessed be He, His knowledge, and His life are one from every side, every aspect, and every form of unity. If He lived through a life or knew through a knowledge outside Himself, there would be many divinities—Him, His life, and His knowledge. This is not so; He is one from every side, every aspect, and every form of unity. Thus you say: He is the knower, He is the known, and He is knowledge itself—all are one. This is something that the mouth cannot express, the ear cannot hear, and the human heart cannot fully apprehend.”

The passage then turns the accuser into a witness to Israel’s purity. Ramban cites this Midrash in explaining that the goat is sent solely at Hashem’s command. That is the connection to Rav Tzadok’s contrast between an independently initiated act of worship and the commanded mitzvah. The continuation in 46:9 supplies the outcome of the gift described in 46:8. The printed Midrash’s description of Hashem’s lot as a “burnt offering” is retained as its wording; it is not a statement that the Torah classifies that goat as an olah.

paragraphs.text: Ramban on Leviticus 16:8: “The intention concerning the scapegoat is not, Heaven forbid, that it should be an offering from us to him. Rather, our intention is to fulfill the will of our Creator, who commanded us to do so. The analogy is someone who prepares a feast for a master, and the master tells the person preparing it, ‘Give one portion to such-and-such servant of mine.’ The person preparing the feast gives nothing of his own to that servant and does not act in his honor. Everything was given to the master; the master gives a portion to his servant, while this person keeps his command and does all that he commanded in the master’s honor. The master, in compassion for the host, wished all his servants to enjoy the feast, so that they would speak his praise and not his disparagement. This is the reason for the lots. Had the priest verbally consecrated the goats to Hashem and to Azazel, he would have been like someone worshipping him and making a vow in his name. Instead, he placed them before Hashem at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting, for both are a gift to Hashem. He gives His servant the portion that comes to him from Hashem: He cast their lot and His hand apportioned it to them, as it is said, ‘The lot is cast into the lap, but all its judgment is from Hashem.’ Even after the lot, he would place the goat before Hashem, to declare that it belongs to Him and that in sending it we intend only to fulfill Hashem’s will, as it says, ‘It shall stand alive before Hashem, to atone over it and send it,’ and so forth. For this reason, we do not slaughter it at all.”

sections.en: "I Am the Lord Your God" Precedes "You Shall Have No Other Gods"

p: [מא] "אָנֹכִי" קוֹדֵם לְ"לֹא יִהְיֶה לְךָ",
"I am the Lord your God" precedes "You shall have no other gods,"
כִּי עַל יְדֵי הַהִתְבּוֹנְנוּת הַגְּמוּרָה בְּ"אָנֹכִי" מִצַּד אֱמוּנָה הַבְּרוּרָה בַּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁהוּא מָצוּי
— for through complete and profound contemplation of "I am" arising from lucid faith in the Blessed Name that He is existent,
הוּא נִיצּוֹל מִ"לֹא יִהְיֶה" וְנִשְׁמָר מִכָּל מִינֵי הֲסָרוֹת וּנְזָקִין,
a person is saved from "You shall have no," and is preserved against all forms of spiritual departure and harm;
כִּי אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מִדְרָשׁ תַּנְחוּמָא וַיֵּצֵא): עָשָׂה מִצְוָה אַחַת מוֹסְרִין לוֹ מַלְאָךְ אֶחָד לְשָׁמְרוֹ.
for our Sages of blessed memory stated (Midrash Tanchuma, Vayeitzei): "If one performs a single mitzvah, a single angel is assigned to him to guard him."
וְהִנֵּה מִדָּה כְּנֶגֶד מִדָּה: כָּל הַמִּצְווֹת קִבְּלוּ עַל יְדֵי שָׁלִיחַ, נִמְסָר מַלְאָךְ;
And behold, it is measure for measure: for all the commandments they received through an emissary [Moshe], an angel is assigned;
וְ"אָנֹכִי" וְ"לֹא יִהְיֶה" שָׁמְעוּ מִפִּי הַגְּבוּרָה,
whereas "I am" and "You shall have no" they heard directly from the mouth of the Almighty,
לְכָךְ בִּשְׂכַר "אָנֹכִי" הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא בְּעַצְמוֹ שׁוֹמְרוֹ.
and therefore, in reward for "I am," the Holy One, blessed be He, guards him Himself.
וּבְמָקוֹם אַחֵר אָמְרוּ כִּי מִמִּצְוָה נִבְרָא מַלְאָךְ,
And elsewhere they stated that from a mitzvah an angel is created,
וּבְמִצְוַת "אָנֹכִי" נִבְרָא כִּבְיָכוֹל הִתְגַּלּוּת הַשְׁגָּחַת הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא בְּעַצְמוֹ בְּמוֹחוֹ וְדַעְתּוֹ שֶׁל זֶה,

yet through the commandment of "I am," there is created, as it were, the revelation of the personal providence of the Holy One, blessed be He, Himself within the mind and consciousness of this person,
בְּרִיאָה מַמָּשׁ יֵשׁ מֵאַיִן בְּמוֹחַ וְלֵב אָטוּם
an absolute creation of something from nothing (yesh me'ayin) within an obtuse brain and sealed heart,
לִהְיוֹת מָצוּי אֶצְלוֹ תָּמִיד
so that He is constantly present with him,
עַל יְדֵי אִתְעָרוּתָא כְּחֻדָּהּ שֶׁל מַחַט מִתַּתָּא
whereby through an awakening from below as small as the point of a needle,
נִפְתַּח אַחַר כָּךְ כְּפִתְחוֹ שֶׁל אוּלָם:
it is subsequently opened wide like the portal of the Temple Hall.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Ishbitz–Radzin · Tiferet Yosef, Talmud Anthology, Berakhot 7: “He explained that this was among Hashem's kindnesses. If the statement ‘You shall have no other gods,’ which signifies turning from evil, had preceded ‘I am,’ which signifies doing good, then someone not yet clean in turning from evil would have no place to perform any mitzvah, because he was not yet purified in turning from evil. Hashem's saying ‘I am’ first teaches that even if someone has, Heaven forbid, stumbled in something bad, repentance is not withheld from him, and he can perform mitzvot even while he is not yet clean in turning from evil.”

paragraphs.text: Explanation: Tiferet Yosef draws another consequence from the same order of commandments. If removal of evil were an absolute precondition for every positive act, someone not yet purified would have no beginning. Anokhi comes first as divine kindness that leaves repentance and mitzvot open even while repair remains incomplete. This complements the siman's account of faith leading to protection; it does not turn unfinished repair into permission to continue the wrongdoing.
