sections.en: In Every Action of Man

p: [קמה] בְּכָל פְּעֻלַּת הָאָדָם, הַמַּעֲשֶׂה הוּא כְּמוֹ גּוּף וְהַמַּחֲשָׁבָה נְשָׁמָה, וְגוּף בְּלֹא נְשָׁמָה אֵינוֹ כְּלוּם;
In every action of man, the physical deed is like a body and the thought is the soul, and a body without a soul is nothing;
לְכָךְ מִתְעַסֵּק פָּטוּר, וְאֵינוֹ כְּשׁוֹגֵג, דְּעַל כָּל פָּנִים מִתְכַּוֵּין לַמַּעֲשֶׂה, מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן מִתְעַסֵּק שֶׁאֵין שׁוּם כַּוָּנַת הַמַּחֲשָׁבָה.

therefore one who acts without intent (mit'asek) is exempt, unlike an inadvertent transgressor (shogeg) who at least intended the physical act, whereas the mit'asek had no mental intention whatsoever.

רַק בַּחֲלָבִים וַעֲרָיוֹת שֶׁכֵּן נֶהֱנֶה, וּבַהֲנָאַת אָדָם אִי אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁלֹּא יִתְכַּוֵּין בְּהֶעְלֵם כָּל שֶׁהוּא עַל כָּל פָּנִים, שֶׁבְּטֶבַע הָאָדָם מַרְגִּישׁ בַּהֲנָאָתוֹ אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין יוֹדֵעַ בְּעַצְמוֹ, שֶׁאֵינוֹ זוֹכֵר.

Except regarding forbidden fats and illicit relations where he derived physical pleasure, and in human bodily pleasure it is impossible that there was not some minute hidden intent at least, for by nature a person senses his pleasure even if he is unaware of it in his conscious memory.
וְיָדוּעַ: "נְשָׁמָה שֶׁנָּתַתָּ בִּי טְהוֹרָה", וּלְכָךְ מַחֲשָׁבָה רָעָה אֵין הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מְצָרְפָהּ לְמַעֲשֶׂה (קִדּוּשִׁין מ.),
And it is known: "the soul which You gave within me is pure," and therefore an evil thought is not combined by the Holy One with action (Kiddushin 40a),
כִּי בֶּאֱמֶת כָּל מַחֲשָׁבוֹת רָעוֹת הוּא מֵרוּחַ שְׁטוּת, שֶׁהוּא דִּמְיוֹן הַמִּתְדַּמֶּה לְחָכְמָה כְּקוֹף בִּפְנֵי אָדָם כַּיָּדוּעַ,
for in truth all evil thoughts stem from a spirit of folly, which is an illusion mimicking wisdom like an ape before a man as is known,
רַק כְּשֶׁיּוֹצֵא לַפּוֹעַל בְּמַעֲשֶׂה, וּבַעֲשִׂיָּה שָׁם הוּא מְקוֹם שְׁלִיטַת הָרָע וְכֹחַ הַדִּמְיוֹן.
save when it breaks forth into deed, for in the physical World of Action lies the dominion of evil and the power of illusion.
וּבִתְשׁוּבָה, שֶׁלּוֹקֵחַ כָּל הַמַּחֲשָׁבוֹת וּמַחֲזִירָן לִמְקוֹרָן, מִמֵּילָא נִשְׁאֲרוּ הַפְּעֻלּוֹת גּוּף מֵת בְּלִי חַיּוּת;
And in repentance, wherein one takes all the thoughts and restores them to their divine Source, the physical deeds automatically remain like a dead corpse devoid of vitality;
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם צָרִיךְ סִגּוּפִים לַגּוּף נֶגֶד הַגּוּף שֶׁיִּכְלֶה מַהֵר, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ עוֹד.
and nonetheless one requires bodily fasts and self-afflictions counter to the physical body that it may be rapidly purified, and this is not the place to elaborate further.
וְכֵן בְּמַעֲשֵׂה הַמִּצְווֹת, דְּשָׁם מַחֲשָׁבָה טוֹבָה מִצְטָרֶפֶת שֶׁהוּא בֶּאֱמֶת.
And so too in the performance of mitzvot: there a good thought is combined by God, for it is rooted in eternal truth.
וּמַעֲשֶׂה בְּלֹא מַחֲשָׁבָה הוּא בְּעוֹלַם עֲשִׂיָּה, וְעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר: "אַשְׁרֵי אִישׁ יָרֵא אֶת ה' בְּמִצְוֹתָיו חָפֵץ מְאֹד" (תְּהִלִּים קיב, א),

And an action without thought remains confined to the World of Action, and concerning this it is stated: "Praiseworthy is the man who fears Hashem, that delights greatly in His commandments" (Psalms 112:1),
וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת ח.): דְּ"טוֹב לָךְ" לֹא כְּתִיב,
and our Sages stated (Berakhot 8a): it does not write "and it shall be good with you,"
כִּידוּעַ "אַשְׁרֶיךָ" – בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, "וְטוֹב לָךְ" – לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא שֶׁהוּא בְּיוֹ"ד עַל שֵׁם הַמַּחֲשָׁבָה, כִּדְפֵירֵשׁ רַשִּׁ"י עַל פָּסוּק "אָז יָשִׁיר".

for as is known: "praiseworthy are you" refers to this world, while "and it shall be good with you" refers to the World to Come, which is designated by the letter Yud alluding to Thought, as Rashi explains on "Then sang Moses" (az yashir).
וִירֵא ה' הָעוֹבֵד בְּמַעֲשֶׂה – רַק "אַשְׁרֶיךָ" בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה;
And one who fears Hashem serving solely through physical deed receives only "praiseworthy are you" in this world;
אֲבָל מִכָּל מָקוֹם גַּם דָּבָר זֶה בְּטוֹבָה חַיִּים לָעַד, כִּי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הִבְטִיחַ גַּם כֵּן תְּחִיַּת הַמֵּתִים לְהַשְׁאָרַת הַגּוּפִים הַטּוֹבִים.
yet nonetheless even this physical deed endures in goodness for eternity, because the Blessed Name also promised the resurrection of the dead for the preservation of worthy physical bodies.
לְכָךְ דָּבָר זֶה הוּא שֶׁבַח וְאִישּׁוּר בְּכָל הָעוֹלָמוֹת מַה שֶּׁזֶּה מְאֻשָּׁר בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה לְצַדִּיק,
Therefore this status is praised and confirmed throughout all worlds, wherein he is affirmed in this world as righteous,
וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁשָּׁם אֵינוֹ כֵּן, מִכָּל מָקוֹם כָּךְ מְאֻשָּׁר שָׁם בְּמַעֲלָה זוֹ שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה הוּא צַדִּיק.
and even though in the higher realm it is not so elevated, it is nonetheless affirmed there that in this world he is a righteous man.
אֲבָל הַנֶּהֱנֶה מִיגִיעַ כַּפָּיו הוּא שֶׁאֵינוֹ מִתְעַסֵּק כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל שֶׁכֵּן נֶהֱנֶה, שֶׁהַהֲנָאָה הוּא הַרְגָּשַׁת הַמַּחֲשָׁבָה.
But one who derives pleasure from the labor of his hands is one who does not act merely as a mit'asek, for he derives pleasure, and spiritual pleasure is the conscious feeling of Thought.
וְדָבָר זֶה כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (קִדּוּשִׁין מא.): לְאָדָם טוֹב מַטְעִימִין לוֹ מִפְּרִי מַעֲשָׂיו וְכוּלֵי,
And this matches what they taught (Kiddushin 41a): to a good person they grant a foretaste of the fruit of his deeds,
וְהוּא בָּא אַחֲרֵי הַיְגִיעַ כַּפַּיִם בְּמַעֲשֶׂה, אַחַר כָּךְ מְהַנִּים אוֹתוֹ מִלְּמַעְלָה מֵעֵין עוֹלָם הַבָּא,
which follows after physical toil in practical deed, whereupon they bestow pleasure upon him from Above as a foretaste of the World to Come,
וְאָז זוֹכֶה לְ"טוֹב לָךְ" גַּם בָּעוֹלָם הַבָּא:
and then he merits "and it shall be good with you" in the World to Come as well.

paragraphs.text: Divrei Soferim 35:1: “Our Sages said that the Holy One, blessed be He, joins a good thought to a deed. It seems to me that this means joining it to some deed that was performed without thought, when at another time he has the thought without the deed. Above, beyond time, the Holy One, blessed be He, joins the good thought with the good deed as though everything occurred together. For this reason, the intention need not necessarily be present at the very time of performing the mitzvah, the prayer, or a similar act. Although it is certainly best for his intention to be proper at the time of the act, there is nevertheless a remedy even for someone who did not then intend it: if afterward he merits a proper intention in a holy thought, the Holy One, blessed be He, joins and connects it to the deed and speech, so that they are regarded as having occurred together.”

We have learned that the yod is stated on account of the thought. This resolves the plain meaning.”

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Rav Tzadok · Peri Tzadik, Sukkot 35:1: “It is known that the reward of a mitzvah is the mitzvah itself: one merits that very matter. Thus Torah scholars have no rest in the world to come, as it says, ‘They go from strength to strength’ (Berakhot 64a). Through their engagement in Torah in this world, they merit delighting in Torah in the world to come. Likewise, through the mitzvah meal they observe in this world, they merit the feast of the righteous in the future, which is the culmination of holy delight, as explained in the holy books. As the Sages said: through fulfilling the mitzvah of sukkah one merits sitting in the sukkah of Leviathan's skin.”

Through their engagement in Torah in this world, they merit delighting in Torah in the world to come. paragraphs.text: Explanation: Peri Tzadik explains the continuity between a person's embodied service and the good tasted afterward. Torah and the mitzvah meal become the very forms of future delight, rather than a reward detached from the service. This develops the siman's final distinction between the deed alone and enjoyment that makes its inward life perceptible.

p: [קמו] (מִכְּתַב יַד קָדְשׁוֹ)

(From his holy handwriting.) [This section was left out of the first printed edition (Lublin, 1902). R' Michael Mokotowski, a chasid of Rav Tzadok, copied it from the author's own manuscript into his copy of the book, and it was first printed in Tzidkas HaTzaddik HaMalei (Jerusalem, 1968), edited by his son R' Avraham Eliyahu Kitov.]
הַיִּרְאָה הִיא הַמַּגְדֶּרֶת הַגּוּף,
Fear and awe (yirah) are that which fence in and constrain the body,
וּלְכָךְ שְׂכָרוֹ רַק "אַשְׁרֵי",
and therefore its designated reward is stated merely as 'happy' (ashrei),
דְּהַיְינוּ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה וְלֹא "טוֹב לָךְ" לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא.
meaning in this world, and not 'it is good for you' in the World to Come.
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בָּבָא מְצִיעָא פד.):
Just as our Sages of blessed memory said (Bava Metzia 84a):
"שׁוּפְרָךְ לִנְשֵׁי".
'Your beauty is appropriate for women.'
וְיָדוּעַ יֹפִי בְּכָל מָקוֹם הוּא כְּשֶׁהַגּוּף מוּגְדָּר בַּתַּאֲווֹת,
And it is known that beauty in every place refers to when the body is fenced in and guarded regarding desires,
שֶׁעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר: "שְׁחוֹרָה אֲנִי וְנָאוָה",
concerning which it is stated: 'I am black but comely' (Song of Songs 1:5),
וְהַיֹּפִי רַק לַגּוּף.
for beauty pertains exclusively to the body.

"אַדְּרַבָּא, אִי הֲווֹ סְנוּ – טְפֵי הֲווֹ גְּמִירֵי".

וְזֶה אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן חֲנַנְיָה
And this was articulated by Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya,
בַּר פְּלוּגְתֵּיהּ דְּרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר שֶׁהָיוּ בָּנָיו יְפֵיפִין בְּיוֹתֵר כְּמוֹ שֶׁאִיתָא בִּנְדָרִים (כ:),
the disputant of Rabbi Eliezer whose children were extraordinarily handsome, as brought in Nedarim (20b),
וּמִפְּנֵי הַגְדָּרָתוֹ הָעֲצוּמָה בַּתַּאֲוָה, עַיֵּין שָׁם,
and this was due to his immense self-restraint and discipline in physical desire, see there,
וְהָאָב זוֹכֶה לַבֵּן.
for a father confers merit and traits unto his son.

paragraphs.text: A pleasing outward form and an inward spiritual quality are distinct matters.

rich.text: A pleasing outward form and an inward spiritual quality are distinct matters.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Ishbitz–Radzin · Sod Yesharim, Rosh Hashanah 18:2: “Ashur and Egypt are alluded to in ‘I have seen servants on horses, and princes walking like servants on the earth’ (Ecclesiastes 10:7). My holy father explained: servants on horses indicate very beautiful and clean garments, while there is a deficiency at the root. As the Tikkunei Zohar says (Tikkun 60), evil within and a beautiful garment outside—of this it says, ‘I have seen servants on horses.’ Princes walking like servants on the earth indicate coarse and darkened garments, while at their root there is no deficiency.”

rich.text: : “Ashur and Egypt are alluded to in ‘I have seen servants on horses, and princes walking like servants on the earth’ (Ecclesiastes 10:7). My holy father explained: servants on horses indicate very beautiful and clean garments, while there is a deficiency at the root. As the Tikkunei Zohar says (Tikkun 60), evil within and a beautiful garment outside—of this it says, ‘I have seen servants on horses.’ Princes walking like servants on the earth indicate coarse and darkened garments, while at their root there is no deficiency.”

paragraphs.text: Explanation: Sod Yesharim develops the same verse about servants on horses and princes walking on the ground. Its contrast concerns the relation between outward garment and root: an attractive appearance can conceal a deficiency, while a coarse appearance can conceal a root without that deficiency. This explains the siman's distinction without making bodily appearance alone a reliable measure of a person's inward quality.

p: וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (יוֹמָא סו:):
And our Sages of blessed memory said (Yoma 66b):
"אֵין חָכְמָה לְאִשָּׁה וְכוּלֵי",
'A woman's wisdom is only at the spindle, etc.,'
רַק דַּרְגָּא דְּיִרְאָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב "אִשָּׁה יִרְאַת ה' וְגוֹמֵר".
holding only the spiritual level of fear/awe, as it is written: 'a woman who fears Hashem, she shall be praised' (Proverbs 31:30).
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (נִדָּה מה:):
And as they said (Niddah 45b):
"וַיִּבֶן ה' אֶת הַצֵּלָע" – שֶׁנָּתַן הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא בִּינָה יְתֵירָה בְּאִשָּׁה יוֹתֵר מִבְּאִישׁ.
'And the Lord God built the side'—teaching that the Holy One, blessed be He, endowed greater understanding (binah) in woman than in man.
כִּי כֹּחוֹת הַגּוּף נִמְשָׁכִים מִן הַלֵּב,
For the powers of the physical body are drawn from the heart,
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן הַחָכְמָה מִן הַמּוֹחַ שֶׁלְּמַעְלָה מִמֶּנּוּ,
whereas wisdom is drawn from the brain which is positioned above it,
וּמוֹחַ וְלֵב הֵם עוֹלָם הַבָּא וְעוֹלָם הַזֶּה,
and brain and heart correspond to the World to Come and this world,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְנוּ לְעֵיל קל״ב.
as we have written above in Ot 132.

paragraphs.text: Poked Akarim 6:2: “The apprehension of the Oral Torah is principally in the wisdom of the mind. Nevertheless, its foundation too depends upon the heart; otherwise it is called, “Why is there a price in a fool’s hand to acquire wisdom, when there is no heart?” The exposition in Yoma applies this to one who has Torah but lacks fear of Heaven: his Torah and wisdom are only like the price with which to buy, without his actually acquiring, for he is in truth a fool. This is “Fear of Hashem is his treasure”: the storehouse that holds wisdom, and this is in the heart.”

sections.en: Through Awe and Fear of Heaven a Person Merits Children

p: [קמז] עַל יְדֵי הַיִּרְאָה אָדָם זוֹכֶה לְבָנִים, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "כִּי כֵן יְבֹרַךְ גָּבֶר יְרֵא ה'" (תְּהִלִּים קכח, ד).
Through awe and fear of Heaven a person merits children, as it is written: "Behold, for surely thus shall the man (gever) be blessed that fears Hashem" (Psalms 128:4).
וְ"גֶבֶר" נִקְרָא הָאִישׁ מִצַּד כֹּחוֹ – כֹּחַ גַּבְרָא
And a man is designated as gever specifically from the perspective of his physical virility—the generative power of manhood
[וְלָכֵן נִקְרָא כֵּן הַתַּרְנְגוֹל כִּדְאָמְרוּ שָׁם (בְּרָכוֹת כב.): שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיוּ וְכוּלֵי כְּתַרְנְגוֹלִים],
[which is why the rooster is termed gever, as our Sages stated in Berakhot 22a: so that Torah scholars should not frequent their wives like roosters],
וְגַם שֵׁם הַגְּבוּרָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ: "אֵיזֶהוּ גִבּוֹר וְכוּלֵי" (אָבוֹת פֶּרֶק ד, א).
and it also partakes of the name of gevurah (might), as in: "Who is mighty? He who subdues his inclination" (Avot 4:1).
וּכְשֶׁהוּא בְּאוֹתוֹ כֹּחַ יָרֵא, פֵּירוּשׁ מוּגְדָּר שֶׁלֹּא יַעֲשֶׂה רַק לִרְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ
And when a person exercises holy awe within that very physical power—meaning he bounds and restricts himself not to act except purely for the will of the Blessed Name
[וְגַם יִרְאָה זוֹ בּוּשָׁה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּנְדָרִים (כ.) שֶׁמִּתְבַּיֵּישׁ בְּחַדְרֵי חֲדָרִים מִפְּנֵי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ],
[and this awe also embodies modesty and shame, as stated in Nedarim 20a, feeling shame even in the innermost chambers before the Blessed Name],
אָז זוֹכֶה לִשְׂכַר פְּרִי הַבֶּטֶן.
then he merits the reward of the fruit of the womb.
שֶׁ"הַגֶּפֶן פֹּרִיָּה" עוֹשָׂה פֵּירוֹת זֵיתִים,
For "the fruitful vine" (Psalms 128:3) yields olive-like children,
כִּי שֶׁמֶן הוּא חָכְמָה וְגֶפֶן יִרְאָה כַּנּוֹדָע, וְ"רֵאשִׁית חָכְמָה יִרְאַת ה'" (שָׁם קיא, י), וְ"אִי יִרְאַת ה' אוֹצָרוֹ – אִין וְכוּלֵי" (שַׁבָּת לא.).

for olive oil represents Chokhmah (Wisdom) and the vine represents fear of Heaven as is known, and "the beginning of wisdom is the fear of Hashem" (Psalms 111:10), and "if the fear of Hashem is his storehouse, yes, etc." (Shabbat 31a).
וְ"יַיִן יְשַׂמַּח לֵבָב" (תְּהִלִּים קד, טו), כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּתַנָּא דְבֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ (סֵדֶר אֵלִיָּהוּ רַבָּה רֵישׁ פֶּרֶק ג): יָרֵאתִי מִתּוֹךְ שִׂמְחָתִי וְשָׂמַחְתִּי מִתּוֹךְ יִרְאָתִי;
And "wine gladdens the heart of man" (Psalms 104:15), as stated in Tanna DeBei Eliyahu Rabbah (chapter 3): "I feared out of my joy, and I rejoiced out of my fear";
כִּי כְּשֶׁיּוֹדֵעַ שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ פּוֹעֵל הַכֹּל וְהוּא הַנּוֹתֵן לוֹ כֹּחַ וּגְבוּרָה, מִזֶּה נִמְשָׁךְ יִרְאָה וְגַם שִׂמְחָה.
for when a person knows that the Blessed Name operates all things and it is He Who grants him strength and might, from this awareness flows awe and likewise joy.

וְיָדוּעַ שֶׁזֶּהוּ כַּוָּנַת רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת ד:) עַל "אֵיזֶהוּ בֶּן הָעוֹלָם הַבָּא? זֶה הַסּוֹמֵךְ גְּאוּלָּה לִתְפִלָּה", וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה: כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל יֵשׁ לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא.

And it is known that this is the intent of our Sages (Berakhot 4b) on: "Who is destined for the World to Come? He who juxtaposes redemption to prayer," and our Sages stated that all Israel have a share in the World to Come.

כִּי בֶּאֱמֶת כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל הֵם בְּמַדְרֵגָה זוֹ, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וּמִסְפָּר אֶת רֹבַע יִשְׂרָאֵל" (בַּמִּדְבָּר כג, י), שֶׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מַכְנִיס עַצְמוֹ בָּזֶה, מִמֵּילָא אֵין לָחוּשׁ.

For in truth all Israel stand on this level, as written: "or the number of the fourth part (rova, also alluding to marital intimacy) of Israel" (Numbers 23:10), for the Holy One enters Himself into this union, and consequently there is no cause for apprehension.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ עַל זֶה (נִדָּה ט.): "מִי יִתֵּן טָהוֹר מִטָּמֵא? לֹא אֶחָד" (אִיּוֹב יד, ד) – יְחִידוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם;
And as our Sages expounded on this (Niddah 9a): "'Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? Not one' (Job 14:4)—the Unique One of the world";
דְּלוּלֵא הַיִּחוּד הַגָּמוּר אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְהָבִין זֶה, כִּי בְּתַאֲוָה זוֹ הוּא מְקוֹר הַחֶסְרוֹנוֹת שֶׁמִּן הַנָּחָשׁ,
for without His absolute divine Unity it would be impossible to comprehend this, seeing that in this bodily appetite lies the primal source of human deficiencies introduced by the Serpent,
כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מִדְרָשׁ רַבָּה רֵישׁ פָּרָשַׁת תַּזְרִיעַ יד, ה): בֶּעָווֹן מָלֵא וְכוּלֵי, וְהוּא יִשַׁי שֶׁמֵּת בְּעֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ;
as our Sages stated (Midrash Rabbah, Tazria 14:5): in total iniquity, etc., exemplified by Jesse who died solely through the counsel of the Serpent (Shabbat 55b);
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה סוֹף פָּרָשָׁה יח): "הַנָּחָשׁ הִשִּׁיאַנִי" – רָאָה אוֹתָן עֲסוּקִים וְכוּלֵי,
and as stated (Bereishit Rabbah 18:6): "'The serpent beguiled me'—he saw them engaged in intimacy, etc.,"
וְאַחַר כָּךְ נוֹלַד לָהֶם הַבּוּשָׁה בָּזוֹ וְיָדְעוּ כִּי עֵירֻמִּם, דִּלְמִצְוָה אֵין בּוּשָׁה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּיַעֲקֹב (תַּעֲנִית ה:) [דְּלֹא מֵת, שֶׁהוּא תִּיקֵּן זֶה].

and afterward there was born within them shame over this, and they knew that they were naked (Genesis 3:7), for in a pure mitzvah there is no shame, as they said of Jacob (Taanit 5b) [that he did not die, having rectified this primal flaw].
וּלְכָךְ: שִׁדְרוֹ שֶׁל אָדָם לְאַחַר שֶׁבַע שָׁנִים נַעֲשֶׂה נָחָשׁ וְכוּלֵי (בָּבָא קַמָּא טז.)
And therefore: the spine of a person after seven years becomes a serpent, etc. (Bava Kamma 16a)
[דְּשִׁדְרָה הוּא מַהֲלַךְ הַזֶּרַע מִן הַמּוֹחַ כַּנּוֹדָע, וְשֶׁבַע שָׁנִים הוּא סֵדֶר שָׁלֵם, וְלָכֵן אָמְרוּ זְמַן זֶה לְעִיבּוּרוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ בִּבְכוֹרוֹת (ח.), וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ.

[for the spinal cord is the conduit of the seminal fluid descending from the brain as is known, and seven years represents a complete cycle, which is why they identified this duration for the gestation of a snake in Bekhorot 8a, and this is not the place to elaborate.
וְ"לֹא כָרַע בְּמוֹדִים" הַיְינוּ שֶׁאֵין לוֹ שׁוּם יִרְאָה, כִּי הַכְּרִיעָה הוּא מִפְּנֵי הַיִּרְאָה וּבוּשָׁה.
And 'he did not bow at Modim' means that he lacks all awe, for bowing is the bodily expression of awe and modesty.
וְזֶה אִי אֶפְשָׁר בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (יְבָמוֹת עט.): שְׁלֹשָׁה סִימָנִים וְכוּלֵי, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּנְדָרִים (כ.): בְּיָדוּעַ שֶׁלֹּא וְכוּלֵי].

And this defect is impossible in Israel, as stated in Yevamot 79a: there are three distinguishing signs in Israel—they are bashful, merciful, and do kindness; and in Nedarim 20a: it is known that his ancestors did not stand at Mount Sinai, etc.].

וּלְכָךְ בִּלְעָם שֶׁהָיָה מִשּׁוֹרֶשׁ רַע לֹא הֶאֱמִין בָּזֶה, וְאָמַר: מִי שֶׁהוּא טָהוֹר וְקָדוֹשׁ וְכוּלֵי (נִדָּה לא.), כִּי לֹא יָדַע כְּלָל שֶׁאֶפְשָׁר לִהְיוֹת בָּזֶה גַּם כֵּן קְדוּשָׁה וְטָהוֹר מִטָּמֵא.

And therefore Balaam, who derived from a corrupt root, did not believe in this possibility, cynically challenging: "Would He Who is pure and holy look upon such base matters?!" (Niddah 31a), because he could not fathom that within this bodily act holiness can reside and purity emerge from uncleanness.
וּמִי שֶׁעִיקָּרוֹ חָסֵר, הַיְינוּ שֶׁהָעִיקָּר טָמֵא בֶּאֱמֶת, שֶׁמִּזֶּה הוּא שׁוֹרֶשׁ הָאָדָם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "הֵן בְּעָווֹן חוֹלָלְתִּי וְגוֹמֵר" (תְּהִלִּים נא, ז).

And one whose essential foundation is lacking represents one whose root is intrinsically defiled, for from this is the origin of man, as written: "Behold, I was brought forth in iniquity, etc." (Psalms 51:7).
רַק שֶׁבֶּאֱמֶת יֵשׁ בָּזֶה גַּם כֵּן קְדוּשָׁה וְטָהֳרָה.
Yet in ultimate truth, within this realm there also abides holiness and purity.
אֲבָל בִּלְעָם עִיקָּרוֹ חָסֵר, שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה בְּעִיקָּרוֹ שׁוּם טוֹב וְטָהֳרָה, לְכָךְ לֹא יָדַע לְהָבִין זֶה;
But Balaam was fundamentally deficient, possessing in his primordial root no goodness or purity whatsoever; therefore he could not comprehend this;
רַק בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁדְּבֵקִים בִּיחִידוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "שְׁמַע יִשְׂרָאֵל ה' אֱלֹהֵינוּ ה' אֶחָד" (דְּבָרִים ו, ד):
it is grasped only by the children of Israel who cleave unto the Unique One of the world, as written: "Hear, O Israel: Hashem our God, Hashem is One" (Deuteronomy 6:4).

paragraphs.text: Pirkei Avot 4:1: ‘Ben Zoma says: Who is wise? Someone who learns from every person, as it says: ‘From all my teachers I have gained understanding, for Your testimonies are my meditation’ (Psalms 119). Who is mighty? Someone who masters his inclination, as it says: ‘One who is slow to anger is better than a mighty warrior, and one who rules his own spirit is better than one who captures a city’ (Proverbs 16). Who is wealthy? Someone who rejoices in his portion, as it says: ‘When you eat the labor of your hands, you are fortunate, and it is good for you’ (Psalms 128). ‘You are fortunate’ refers to this world; ‘it is good for you’ refers to the World to Come. Who is honored? Someone who honors other people, as it says: ‘Those who honor Me I will honor, and those who despise Me will be held in contempt’ (I Samuel 2).’

paragraphs.text: Peri Tzadik, Kuntres Amalah shel Torah 4:1: “Every fear of something arises when one fears that some harm will befall him, and he wishes and desires not to have that fear, because being afraid causes him pain. The fear of the Lord is different. It is taught in Tanna Devei Eliyahu Rabbah, chapter 3: “I feared through my joy, and I rejoiced through my fear.” Joy in the Lord brings one to fear Him because of His exaltedness, blessed be He, which one recognizes through that joy, as it is written, “Rejoice with trembling.” Likewise, from the fear that comes through sensing the light of His revealed indwelling presence within one’s heart, as stated above, one comes to joy.”

paragraphs.text: Purity within the same garment
The higher unity can reveal purity where the outward form had seemed to show its opposite.

rich.text: The higher unity can reveal purity where the outward form had seemed to show its opposite.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Ishbitz–Radzin · Sod Yesharim, Parashat Parah 4:1: “It is written (Job 14:4), ‘Who can bring pure from impure—is it not One?’ This means being able to see purity in the very form of the garment that previously appeared to show its opposite, without the garment itself changing. This is possible only when illumination shines from the highest place, called One, indicating One beyond reckoning: illumination from the higher will that is removed from all garments and free of all forms.”

rich.text: : “It is written (Job 14:4), ‘Who can bring pure from impure—is it not One?’ This means being able to see purity in the very form of the garment that previously appeared to show its opposite, without the garment itself changing. This is possible only when illumination shines from the highest place, called One, indicating One beyond reckoning: illumination from the higher will that is removed from all garments and free of all forms.”

paragraphs.text: Explanation: Sod Yesharim explains the same question, ‘Who can bring pure from impure—is it not One?’ Its point is the disclosure of purity within the very garment that previously seemed impure, rather than merely replacing that garment. This develops why Rav Tzadok links the paradox to divine unity and why Bilaam's view of the outward act alone misses the source of its holiness.

paragraphs.text: Lech Lecha uses Yishai to explain why an inherited element of self-enjoyment can remain even in a deeply righteous life.

rich.text: Lech Lecha uses Yishai to explain why an inherited element of self-enjoyment can remain even in a deeply righteous life.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Rav Tzadok · Peri Tzadik, Lech Lecha 9:8: “This corresponds to “from your father’s house,” for it says, “Indeed, in iniquity I was formed.” The Midrash teaches: even the most pious of the pious cannot be without one aspect of iniquity—that is, he is not entirely free of his own enjoyment. This comes from the serpent’s counsel. Shabbat 55b says that Scripture explicitly identifies Jesse, David’s father, as having died through the serpent’s counsel. Concerning him, the Midrash expounds “in iniquity” as a full spelling. The Messiah son of David will repair even the serpent’s counsel and draw true life into the world, as it says, “He asked You for life; You gave it to him.” He will be the final culmination that repairs everything in the world, and “He will swallow up death forever.””

This comes from the serpent’s counsel. Shabbat 55b says that Scripture explicitly identifies Jesse, David’s father, as having died through the serpent’s counsel. Concerning him, the Midrash expounds “in iniquity” as a full spelling. The Messiah son of David will repair even the serpent’s counsel and draw true life into the world, as it says, “He asked You for life; You gave it to him.” He will be the final culmination that repairs everything in the world, and “He will swallow up death forever.””

paragraphs.text: Explanation: The Lech Lecha passage develops the same example of Yishai and identifies the serpent’s remaining trace with an inability to be entirely free of self-enjoyment. This clarifies the present siman’s claim that holiness can be found within bodily life despite its inherited mixture. The final removal of that root belongs to Mashiach ben David. The siman’s present avodah is therefore awe, restraint, and directing the bodily power toward Hashem’s will, rather than assuming that any remaining mixture makes holiness impossible.

paragraphs.text: Tosafot on Bava Kamma 16a:22:1: ““Provided that he did not bow at Modim”: because it is a mitzvah to bow, and when one straightens up one straightens like a serpent, as we find concerning Rav Sheshet in Berakhot. Measure for measure, he becomes a serpent; this is his punishment, for becoming a serpent is a disgrace to him. A marginal comment: Some explain this by the Midrash’s statement that there is a bone in a person’s spine from which he will be formed in the future. That bone is so strong and hard that fire cannot burn it; now, when that bone becomes a serpent, he will not live in the future. But it is unreasonable to say that so great a punishment would come for this sin, for all Israel have a share in the World to Come.”

sections.en: There Is a Torah Scholar Who Merits That His Teachings Are Widely Disseminated Throughout…

p: [קמח] יֵשׁ תַּלְמִיד חָכָם שֶׁזּוֹכֶה דִּשְׁמַעְתָּתֵיהּ מִבַּדְּרִין בְּעָלְמָא, וְיֵשׁ שֶׁאֵין זוֹכֶה לְכָךְ,
There is a Torah scholar who merits that his teachings are widely disseminated throughout the world, and there is one who does not merit this,
וְאֵין זֶה רְאָיָה שֶׁזֶּה גָּדוֹל מִזֶּה,
and this disparity is no proof that the former is greater than the latter,
שֶׁלִּפְעָמִים יֵשׁ דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה יְקָרִים בְּפִי מִי שֶׁהוּא.
for sometimes precious words of Torah are placed in the mouth of anyone.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָנוּ רוֹאִים בְּבִלְעָם שֶׁאָמַר פָּרָשָׁה שְׁלֵימָה בְּתוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב
Just as we see concerning Balaam, who uttered an entire section in the Written Torah

[וּלְיוֹדְעֵי חֵ"ן, כִּי גַּם כָּל הַדִּבּוּרִים מִפַּרְעֹה וַאֲבִימֶלֶךְ וְעֵשָׂו שֶׁנִּזְכַּר בַּתּוֹרָה, הֲרֵי הֵם דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה מַמָּשׁ, וְהָיָה זֶה אֶצְלָם, וְעַל יְדֵי דִּבּוּרָם נִתְגַּלָּה לָנוּ].

[and to the initiates of esoteric wisdom, all the utterances of Pharaoh, Abimelech, and Esau recorded in the Torah are actual words of Torah, which were latent within them and through their speech were revealed to us].

וְכֵן אִיתָא בְּפֶרֶק חֵלֶק (סַנְהֶדְרִין קו:) עַל דּוֹאֵג, דְּמִתְּחִלָּה בִּקֵּשׁ דָּוִד עָלָיו שֶׁלֹּא יָבוֹא לְעָלְמָא דְּאָתֵי, וְאַחַר כָּךְ דְּלָא לֵימְרוּ שְׁמַעְתָּא בֵּי מִדְרְשָׁא מִשְּׁמֵיהּ;

And so it is stated in chapter Chelek (Sanhedrin 106b) regarding Doeg, that initially David prayed concerning him that he not enter the World to Come, and subsequently that they not cite teachings in the house of study in his name;
הֲרֵי דְּאֶפְשָׁר שֶׁיֹּאמְרוּ שְׁמַעְתָּא מִשְּׁמֵיהּ, אַף עַל פִּי דְּאֵין לוֹ חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא.
which proves that it is possible for a halakhic teaching to be cited in a person's name even though he has no portion in the World to Come.
וְכֵן בְּאַחֵר, מִתְּחִלָּה בְּחַיֵּי רַבִּי מֵאִיר אָמְרוּ שֶׁהָיָה מִשְׁפָּטוֹ דְּלָא לֵיתֵי לְעָלְמָא דְּאָתֵי, וַאֲפִילּוּ הָכֵי אָמַר רַבִּי מֵאִיר שְׁמוּעוֹת מִמֶּנּוּ,

And likewise with Acher (Elisha ben Avuyah): initially during the lifetime of Rabbi Meir they declared that his judgment was not to enter the World to Come, yet even so Rabbi Meir transmitted teachings from him,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתְבוּ הַקַּדְמוֹנִים דִּבְכָל מָקוֹם "אֲחֵרִים" הַיְינוּ מַה שֶּׁלָּמַד מֵאַחֵר.
and as the early authorities wrote, wherever the Talmud cites "Acheirim say," it refers to what Rabbi Meir learned from Acher.

וְכֵן אַחַר כָּךְ עֲדַיִן הָיָה בְּגֵיהִנָּם עַד זְמַן רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן כִּדְאִיתָא בַּחֲגִיגָה (טו:), וַאֲפִילּוּ הָכֵי רַבִּי שֶׁסִּידֵּר הַמִּשְׁנָיוֹת קָבַע שְׁמוּעָה בִּשְׁמוֹ בְּאָבוֹת (פֶּרֶק ד, כ), לְפִי שֶׁשְּׁמוּעוֹתָיו הֵם תּוֹרַת אֱמֶת וְדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה מַמָּשׁ.

And likewise afterward Acher still remained in Gehenna until the days of Rabbi Yochanan as brought in Chagigah 15b, and even so, Rebbe who redacted the Mishnayot canonized a teaching in his name in Avot (4:20), because his teachings are Torah of truth and authentic words of Torah.
אֲבָל צָרִיךְ רַחֲמִים גְּדוֹלִים שֶׁיִּהְיוּ דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה נִבְלָעִים בְּלִבּוֹ, וְשֶׁיִּהְיֶה הוּא כָּךְ כְּמוֹ הַדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה שֶׁמַּשִּׂיג וּמוֹצִיא מִפִּיו.
But a person requires vast divine mercy so that words of Torah be absorbed into his heart, and that he himself embody that reality just like the words of Torah he grasps and expresses with his mouth.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּפֶרֶק חֵלֶק (שָׁם) בְּתוֹרָתוֹ שֶׁל דּוֹאֵג "מִן הַשָּׂפָה וְלַחוּץ", פֵּירוּשׁ וְאֵין נִבְלָע בַּלֵּב לִהְיוֹת כָּךְ;
And as stated in chapter Chelek (ibid.) concerning the Torah of Doeg which was "from the lip outward," meaning it was not absorbed into the heart to become integrated as his character;
וְכִדְאִיתָא הָתָם: רְבוּתָא לְמִיבְעֵי בָּעֲיָא וְכוּלֵי, אֶלָּא הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לִבָּא בָּעֵי.
and as stated there: Is it such a great feat to raise conceptual queries, etc.? Rather, the Holy One desires the heart.
פֵּירוּשׁ, הַבְּעָיוֹת הֵם סְפֵקוֹת בַּעֲבוֹדַת ה' וּמִצְווֹתָיו, וְאִם הֵם כָּךְ בַּלֵּב – אָז הוּא רְבוּתָא, וְלֹא בַּפֶּה:

The explanation is: queries represent analytical doubts in the service of Hashem and His commandments, and if they resonate with genuine longing in the heart—then it is a great virtue, and not when merely formulated with the mouth.

paragraphs.text: Chagigah 15b:6-10: “How did Rabbi Meir learn Torah from Acher’s mouth? Did not Rabbah bar bar Chana say in Rabbi Yochanan’s name: What is meant by “For a priest’s lips should guard knowledge, and Torah should be sought from his mouth, for he is an angel of Hashem of hosts”? If the teacher resembles an angel of Hashem of hosts, seek Torah from his mouth; otherwise, do not seek Torah from his mouth. Reish Lakish said: Rabbi Meir found a verse and expounded it: “Incline your ear and hear the words of the wise, and set your heart to My knowledge.” It does not say “to their knowledge,” but “to My knowledge.” Rav Chanina derived it from here: “Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people and your father’s house.” Do the verses contradict one another? There is no difficulty: one concerns a mature student, the other an immature student. When Rav Dimi came, he said: They say in the West, “Rabbi Meir ate the date and cast the pit away.” Rava expounded: What is meant by “I went down to the nut garden to see the greenery of the valley”? Why are Torah scholars compared to a nut? To tell you: just as, although a nut is soiled with mud and filth, what is inside it is not made repulsive, so too, although a Torah scholar has gone astray, his Torah is not made repulsive.”

sections.en: A Person's True Spiritual Perfection Is Reached When He Actually Embodies the Perfection That…

p: [קמט] שְׁלֵימוּת הָאָדָם הוּא כְּשֶׁיִּהְיֶה כָּךְ כְּמוֹ שֶׁהוּא מַשִּׂיג הַשְּׁלֵימוּת שֶׁצָּרִיךְ לִהְיוֹת.
A person's true spiritual perfection is reached when he actually embodies the perfection that he intellectually grasps ought to be.

וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁכָּל הַדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה שֶׁהוּא מַשִּׂיג וְהַהַנְהָגָה הַתּוֹרִיִּית אֵיךְ שֶׁאֶפְשָׁר לָאָדָם הַשָּׁלֵם לְהַשִּׂיג, זֶה הוּא שְׁלֵימוּתוֹ: מַה שֶּׁאֶפְשָׁר לוֹ לְהַשִּׂיג וְצָרִיךְ לְהַשִּׂיגוֹ.

That is, all the words of Torah that he perceives and the Torah conduct which a perfected person can comprehend—this defines his personal perfection: what is possible for him to grasp and what he is destined to attain.
כִּי הַשָּׂגַת הָאָדָם וְחָכְמָתוֹ הוּא עֶצֶם שׁוֹרֶשׁ נִשְׁמָתוֹ וְחַיּוּתוֹ,
For a person's comprehension and wisdom constitute the essential root of his soul and vitality,
וְכָל אֶחָד יֵשׁ לוֹ שׁוֹרֶשׁ בִּפְנֵי עַצְמוֹ כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת נח.) שֶׁאֵין בְּנֵי אָדָם דּוֹמִין זֶה לָזֶה בְּפַרְצוּפֵיהֶן;
and each individual possesses an independent soul-root, as our Sages stated (Berakhot 58a) that no two people are identical in their facial appearance;

וְהַפַּרְצוּף הוּא מֵעִיד עַל פְּנִימִיּוּת הַלֵּב כַּנּוֹדָע, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר (יִתְרוֹ ע עַמּוּד א) מֵחָכְמַת הַפַּרְצוּף, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "חָכְמַת אָדָם תָּאִיר פָּנָיו" (קֹהֶלֶת ח, א),

and the facial visage bears witness to the interior of the heart as is known, and as written in the Zohar (Yitro 70a) concerning the physiognomy of the face, and as stated: "A man's wisdom makes his face to shine" (Ecclesiastes 8:1),
וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁפְּנִימִיּוּת הַלֵּב וְכֵן עֹמֶק חָכְמַת כָּל אֶחָד מִשְׁתַּנֶּה זֶה מִזֶּה.
meaning that the interior of the heart and the depth of wisdom of each person differ one from another.
וְלָכֵן אָמְרוּ (שְׁמוֹת רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה נב) עַל פָּסוּק "הֹלֵךְ הָאָדָם אֶל בֵּית עוֹלָמוֹ" (קֹהֶלֶת יב, ה), שֶׁכָּל אֶחָד יֵשׁ לוֹ עוֹלָם בִּפְנֵי עַצְמוֹ;

And therefore they expounded (Shemot Rabbah 52) on the verse "man goes to his long home (beit olamo, the home of his world)" (Ecclesiastes 12:5), that every person possesses an entire world of his own;
וְהוּא הַנִּקְרָא אֶצְלָם בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר (שַׁבָּת קנב.): כָּל אֶחָד יֵשׁ לוֹ מָדוֹר לְפִי כְּבוֹדוֹ,
and this is what they termed elsewhere (Shabbat 152a): each person has a dwelling according to his honor,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּתִּיקּוּנִים (רֵישׁ תִּיקּוּן סט) דְּעוֹלָם בִּפְנֵי עַצְמוֹ רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר עוֹלָם קָטָן שֶׁלּוֹ.
and as written in the Tikkunim (beginning of Tikkun 69) that "his own world" denotes his individual microcosm.
וּרְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר שֶׁכָּל אֶחָד כּוֹלֵל כָּל כֹּחוֹת הָעוֹלָם כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "בְּצַלְמֵנוּ כִּדְמוּתֵנוּ" (בְּרֵאשִׁית א, כו),
That is, each person encompasses all the cosmic forces of the universe, as written: "in Our image, after Our likeness" (Genesis 1:26),
וּכְשֶׁמַּגִּיעַ לִשְׁלֵימוּתוֹ, זֶה נִקְרָא בִּלְשׁוֹן רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה "קוֹנֶה עוֹלָמוֹ", כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (יז.): יֵשׁ קוֹנֶה עוֹלָמוֹ וְכוּלֵי,

and when he reaches his ultimate fulfillment, this is termed in the language of our Sages "acquiring his world," as stated in Avodah Zarah 17a: "There is one who acquires his world in a single hour, etc.,"
וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁעוֹלָם שֶׁלּוֹ הוּא אֶצְלוֹ בְּקִנְיָן.
meaning that his personal world is possessed by him as an enduring acquisition.
כִּי יֵשׁ שֶׁמַּשִּׂיג וְאֵינוֹ כָּךְ כְּמוֹ שֶׁמַּשִּׂיג, וְאָז הַשָּׂגָתוֹ רַק בִּרְאִיָּה לְבַד.
For there is one who perceives lofty ideals yet does not embody what he perceives, and then his perception remains merely in external sight.
וְזֶהוּ הַתְחָלַת כְּנִיסַת הָאָדָם לְדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בָּרוֹקֵחַ: אֵין חֹזֶק כַּחֲסִידוּת בִּתְחִלָּתוֹ, אֲבָל הוּא רַק בִּרְאִיָּה;
And this marks the initial entry of a person into words of Torah, as written in the Rokeach: there is no fervor like pious devotion at its outset, yet it exists only in vision;
וְצָרִיךְ הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת עַד שֶׁמַּגִּיעַ לִהְיוֹת כָּךְ בְּקִנְיָן וְנִבְלָע בַּלֵּב כָּל מַה שֶּׁמַּשִּׂיג, וְאָז נִקְרָא "קוֹנֶה עוֹלָמוֹ".

and one requires long exertion until he reaches the state where it becomes an internalized acquisition and all that he perceives is absorbed into his heart, and then he is termed "one who acquires his world."
וְאָז הוּא עֵת הַפְּטִירָה כִּלְשׁוֹן הַגְּמָרָא דַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה שָׁם,
And that corresponds to the hour of passing, matching the idiom of the Gemara in Avodah Zarah there,
וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁאֵין לוֹ עוֹד מַה לְּהִשְׁתַּדֵּל בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה שֶׁהוּא הַפְּרוֹזְדּוֹר וְעוֹלַם הַמַּעֲשֶׂה וְהַהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת, וְהוּא לֹא יוּכַל לְהַגִּיעַ יוֹתֵר מֵעוֹלָמוֹ שֶׁלּוֹ.
meaning that he has nothing left to labor for in this world—which is the antechamber and the realm of action and exertion—since he cannot surpass his own personal universe.
וּלְכָךְ בְּעֵת מַתַּן תּוֹרָה, שֶׁאָז הָיָה הַבְלָעַת דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה בְּקִנְיָן [אַחַר שֶׁקָּדְמָה הָרְאִיָּה בִּקְרִיעַת יַם סוּף: "רָאֲתָה שִׁפְחָה וְכוּלֵי"] כַּנּוֹדָע,

And therefore at the Giving of the Torah, when the absorption of words of Torah occurred as an absolute acquisition [following the preliminary vision at the Red Sea where 'a maidservant saw, etc.'] as is known,
אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שַׁבָּת פח:): שֶׁיָּצְתָה נִשְׁמָתָם וְהוֹרִיד הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא טַל שֶׁל תְּחִיָּה,
our Sages stated (Shabbat 88b): their souls departed and the Holy One, blessed be He, brought down the dew of resurrection,
וּכְאָמְרָם זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (פִּרְקֵי דְּרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר פֶּרֶק לד) עַל פָּסוּק "לֹא יִרְאַנִי הָאָדָם וָחָי" (שְׁמוֹת לג, כ) – שֶׁבִּשְׁעַת מִיתָתוֹ רוֹאֶה.
and as they taught (Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer 34) on the verse "man shall not see Me and live" (Exodus 33:20)—at the hour of his death he sees.
וְהַיְינוּ דִּכְשֶׁמַּגִּיעַ לְתַכְלִית הַקִּנְיָן זוֹכֶה לִרְאִיָּה שֵׁנִית כִּי חוֹזֵר לַהַתְחָלָה, וּמִיָּד מִסְתַּלֵּק לְעוֹלָם מְחוּדָּשׁ, וְהוּא עוֹלָם הַבָּא:

That is, when one reaches the ultimate culmination of acquisition, he merits a second vision because he returns to the beginning, and immediately departs to a renewed world, which is the World to Come.

footnotes.enAnchorPrefix: For a person's comprehension and wisdom constitute the essential root of his soul and vitality,

paragraphs.text: Peri Tzadik, Parshat Shekalim 1:2: “Each of the other members of Israel has some secret of His wisdom hidden in the root of his soul, of which he himself is unaware; it is the root of his life, as it is written, “Wisdom gives life to its possessor.” Through this, each has a distinction over all Israel, because of the portion of divinity from above at his soul’s root, in which there is a secret hidden from all Israel. This is why the chapter HaRoeh says that their minds are not alike and their faces do not resemble one another. The difference in a person’s outward form follows the difference in each one’s understanding, for the human face is in the image of God, and this comes from the soul, the portion of divinity. “A person’s wisdom illuminates his face”: according to the point of wisdom and understanding within each person, which is unlike that of his fellow, the light of his face is likewise different.”

paragraphs.text: Explanation: Resisei Layla explains the transition from receiving a soul to calling its completed world one's own. The initial gift comes from Hashem; through Torah and mitzvot it becomes attributed to the person who has worked for it. This clarifies the siman's contrast between an insight that is only seen and a perfection that has become a settled acquisition.

sections.en: When the Holy One, Blessed Be He, Exalts a Particular Good Quality in The…

p: [קנ] כְּשֶׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מְרוֹמֵם אֵיזֶה דָּבָר טוֹב בָּעוֹלָם, אָז מִמֵּילָא אוֹתוֹ דַּרְגָּא בְּסִטְרָא אָחֳרָא מִשְׁתַּפֵּל;
When the Holy One, blessed be He, exalts a particular good quality in the world, that corresponding rung in the Other Side (Sitra Achra) automatically sinks low;
וְכֵן לְהֵיפֶךְ: כְּשֶׁרוֹאֶה אֵיזֶה דָּבָר רַע בְּתַכְלִית הַשִּׁפְלוּת, יֵדַע כִּי אוֹתוֹ דָּבָר בִּקְדוּשָׁה הוּא בְּתַכְלִית הָרוֹמְמוּת.
and likewise conversely: when one sees a particular evil matter at the absolute depth of degradation, let him know that that very attribute in holiness stands at the pinnacle of exaltation.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "כִּי לִי כָל בְּכוֹר בְּיוֹם הַכֹּתִי כָל בְּכוֹר בְּאֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם" (בַּמִּדְבָּר ג, יג).
As it is written: "for all the firstborn are Mine; on the day that I smote all the firstborn in the land of Egypt I hallowed unto Me all the firstborn in Israel" (Numbers 3:13).
וְנֶאֱמַר: "וְכָל קַרְנֵי רְשָׁעִים אֲגַדֵּעַ, תְּרוֹמַמְנָה קַרְנוֹת צַדִּיק" (תְּהִלִּים עה, יא) – בְּאוֹתוֹ דָּבָר שֶׁזֶּה נִגְדָּע, זֶה נִתְרוֹמֵם;

And it is stated: "All the horns of the wicked also will I cut off; but the horns of the righteous shall be lifted up" (Psalms 75:11)—in the exact matter wherein the former is severed, the latter is exalted;

וְנֶאֱמַר: "אִמָּלְאָה הָחֳרָבָה" (יְחֶזְקֵאל כו, ב), וְדָרְשׁוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מְגִילָּה ו.): קֵיסָרִי וִירוּשָׁלַיִם וְכוּלֵי, פֵּירוּשׁ שֶׁשְּׁנֵיהֶם בְּמַדְרֵגָה אַחַת בְּמַלְכוּת.

and it is stated: "I shall be replenished, now that she is laid waste" (Ezekiel 26:2), which our Sages expounded (Megillah 6a): Caesarea and Jerusalem, if one is full the other is desolate, meaning that both occupy one identical level in the realm of sovereignty.
וְכָל אוּמָּה יֵשׁ לָהּ כֹּחַ מַה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (יְרוּשַׁלְמִי שְׁקָלִים א, א): אָפְיָהּ שֶׁל אוּמָּה זוֹ וְכוּלֵי;
And each nation possesses a distinct spiritual faculty, as they said: 'the character (lit. face) of this nation, etc.';

וּלְכָךְ יִרְמְיָה קוֹנֵן עַל אָבְדַן אֻמּוֹת עוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "לִבִּי לְמוֹאָב כַּחֲלִלִים יֶהֱמֶה" (יִרְמְיָה מח, לו), וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּבַמִּדְבָּר רַבָּה (רֵישׁ פָּרָשַׁת בָּלָק כ, א),
and therefore Jeremiah lamented over the destruction of gentile nations, as written: "My heart moans for Moab like flutes" (Jeremiah 48:36), and in Bemidbar Rabbah (beginning of Parashat Balak 20:1),
וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁבְּאָבְדַן אוֹתָהּ אוּמָּה נִתְבַּטֵּל אוֹתוֹ כֹּחַ (כְּמוֹ שֶׁנִּתְבָּאֵר לְעֵיל אוֹת מ"ז, עַיֵּין שָׁם).
meaning that with the destruction of that nation that spiritual power was abolished (as explained above in Section 47, see there).
וּבְכָל דָּבָר יֵשׁ גַּם כֵּן טוֹב כַּיָּדוּעַ, וְאָז נִתְרוֹמֵם אוֹתוֹ כֹּחַ הַטּוֹב.
And within every trait there also resides good as is known, and then that corresponding power of good is exalted.
וּכְמוֹ בְּאָבְדַן סְדוֹם שֶׁהָיוּ אַבִּירֵי לֵב הָרְחוֹקִים מִצְּדָקָה, נִתְבַּשֵּׂר לֵידַת יִצְחָק שֶׁהָיָה גַּם כֵּן גִּבּוֹר הַלֵּב כַּנּוֹדָע.
And as with the destruction of Sodom who were stout-hearted and far from charity, the birth of Isaac was announced, who was likewise a mighty warrior of the heart in holiness as is known.
וְכֵן בְּאָבְדַן מִצְרַיִם הָיָה הֲכָנָה לְמַתַּן תּוֹרָה, כִּידוּעַ מֵחָכְמַת מִצְרַיִם שֶׁהָיְתָה מֻפְלֶגֶת;
And so the downfall of Egypt was the preparation for the Giving of the Torah, as is known from the wisdom of Egypt which was extraordinarily vast;

וּלְכָךְ יְחֶזְקֵאל שֶׁנְּבוּאָתוֹ חָכְמָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (נז:): יְצַפֶּה לְחָכְמָה, אָמַר כַּמָּה פָּרָשִׁיּוֹת עַל חוּרְבַּן מִצְרַיִם, שֶׁעַל יְדֵי זֶה תְּרוֹמַמְנָה קַרְנוֹת חָכְמַת הָאֱמֶת.

and therefore Ezekiel whose prophecy was wisdom—as stated in Berakhot 57b: one who sees Ezekiel should anticipate wisdom—uttered several prophecies concerning the destruction of Egypt, through which the horns of authentic wisdom were lifted up.
וְכֵן אָמַר כַּמָּה פָּרָשִׁיּוֹת עַל צוֹר שֶׁגַּם כֵּן הָיְתָה מְפוֹאָרָה בְּחָכְמָה כַּנּוֹדָע, רַק צוֹר הָיְתָה מֻפְלֶגֶת בְּחָכְמוֹת שִׂכְלִיּוֹת מִפְּעֻלּוֹת בְּנֵי אָדָם
And likewise he uttered several passages concerning Tyre which was also celebrated for wisdom as is known, only that Tyre was distinguished in intellectual philosophies emerging from human actions

[צוֹר לְשׁוֹן צַיָּיר וְצָר צוּרָה; וּמָלֵא וָא"ו שֶׁהוּא אוֹת אֱמֶת כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר (רֵישׁ וַיִּקְרָא ב.), לְפִי שֶׁנִּתְעַסְּקוּ בְּבִנְיַן בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ וְהָיָה לִפְעֻלָּתָם אֲחִיזָה בְּחַיֵּי עוֹלָם.

[Tyre (Tzor) shares the root of tzayyar (artisan) and shaping a form; and it is spelled fully with a Vav which is the letter of truth as written in Zohar III:2a, because they participated in the building of the Temple and their actions had a hold in eternal life.
אֲבָל "צָר" חָסֵר [לְשׁוֹן צַר וְצוֹרֵר] בְּמַלְכוּת רְבִיעִית הַכָּתוּב מְדַבֵּר (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה סוֹף פָּרָשָׁה סא),
However, 'Tzar' spelled deficiently without a Vav [alludes to an adversary], referring to the Fourth Kingdom (Rome) as in Bereishit Rabbah 61 end,

paragraphs.text: The prophet’s lament and the good still to be gathered

rich.text: The prophet’s lament and the good still to be gathered

paragraphs.text: The fall of a counterpart can narrow a field of service while some good remains for later collection.

rich.text: The fall of a counterpart can narrow a field of service while some good remains for later collection.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Ishbitz–Radzin · Sod Yesharim, The Seventh Day of Pesach 10:1: “The matter is like what we find when a prophet foretold a nation's calamity: he lamented, as it says (Isaiah 15:5), ‘My heart cries out for Moav,’ and in chapter 16, ‘My innards sound like a harp for Moav, and my inward parts for Kir Cheres.’ He grieved over the nation's loss, because through this its inclination was annulled, and the power of service corresponding to that particular matter was thereby diminished. Yet in Egypt, although it says (Deuteronomy 17:16), ‘You shall not return by this way again’—even residence in Egypt was forbidden, alluding even to the inanimate—and the Sages said that it was made like a deep place without fish (Berakhot 9b), some points nevertheless remained there that would still enter holiness, to be gathered by Israel from a distance. Of them it says (Psalms 68:32), ‘Nobles will come from Egypt.’ As Pesachim 118b teaches: Egypt will bring a gift to Mashiach. He thinks he should not accept it, but the Holy One tells him to accept it, for they provided lodging for His children in Egypt. Immediately, ‘Nobles will come from Egypt.’”

paragraphs.text: Explanation: Sod Yesharim expressly explains the prophet's lament over another nation's fall: the corresponding field of human service becomes smaller when its opposing inclination disappears. Its Egypt example adds that some good remains to be gathered from a distance afterward. This develops the siman's reciprocal powers while preserving the reason for lament and the possibility of later collection.

sections.en: Periods of Spiritual Descent Which a Person Experiences

p: [קנא] עִתּוֹת הַיְּרִידָה שֶׁיֵּשׁ לָאָדָם שֶׁאֵין לוֹ שׁוּם חֵשֶׁק לְתוֹרָה וַעֲבוֹדָה – זֶהוּ הֲכָנָה לַעֲלִיָּה גְּדוֹלָה,
Periods of spiritual descent which a person experiences, wherein he feels no desire for Torah and divine service, are the preparation for a great ascent.
וְהַיְינוּ עַל יְדֵי הַצְּעָקָה שֶׁצּוֹעֵק כְּשֶׁמִּתְבּוֹנֵן עַל דְּרָכָיו וְרוֹאֶה שִׁפְלוּתוֹ וִירִידָתוֹ.
And that is achieved through the heartfelt outcry he raises when he contemplates his ways and beholds his lowliness and descent.

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וַיִּסְעוּ מֵרְפִידִים וַיָּבֹאוּ מִדְבַּר סִינַי" (שְׁמוֹת יט, ב), וְיָדוּעַ דְּרָשַׁת רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סַנְהֶדְרִין קו.) עַל "רְפִידִים" – שֶׁרָפוּ יְדֵיהֶם מִדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה;

As it is written: "And they departed from Rephidim, and came to the wilderness of Sinai" (Exodus 19:2), and known is the exposition of our Sages (Sanhedrin 106a) on Rephidim—that they slackened their hands from words of Torah;
וְזֶה הָיָה הֲכָנָה לְמַתַּן תּוֹרָה, שֶׁהוּא תַּכְלִית הַחִיזּוּק יָדַיִם בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה.
and this very slackening was the preparation for the Giving of the Torah, which is the ultimate strengthening of hands in words of Torah.

וְנֶאֱמַר: "וְהַנְּשִׂאִם הֵבִיאוּ אֵת אַבְנֵי הַשֹּׁהַם" (שָׁם לה, כז), וְדָרְשׁוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בַּמִּדְבָּר רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה יב, טז): "נְשִׂאִם" חָסֵר, לְפִי שֶׁנִּתְעַצְּלוּ וְכוּלֵי;

And it is stated: "And the rulers (nesi'im) brought onyx stones" (Exodus 35:27), where our Sages expounded (Bemidbar Rabbah 12:16): nesi'im is spelled deficiently without a Yud because they were sluggish in bringing their gifts;
וּבַגְּמָרָא (יוֹמָא עה.): נְשִׂיאִים מַמָּשׁ וְכוּלֵי.
and in the Gemara (Yoma 75a): literal clouds (nesi'im) brought them.
פֵּירוּשׁ שֶׁעַל יְדֵי הָעַצְלוּת, וְצָעֲקוּ לַה', זָכוּ לְכָךְ שֶׁהַנְּשִׂיאִים מַמָּשׁ – הֵם הָעֲנָנִים – הֵבִיאוּ לָהֶם אַבְנֵי הַשֹּׁהַם;
The meaning is that through their realization of sluggishness, and their crying out to Hashem, they merited that the literal nesi'im—the clouds—brought them the onyx stones;
מִסְּתָמָא לְכָל נָשִׂיא הִמְצִיא אֶבְנוֹ, וְזֶה דָּבָר יָקָר יוֹתֵר מִכָּל הַנְּדָבוֹת, וְאִלּוּ הֵבִיאוּ נִדְבָתָם מִקּוֹדֶם לֹא הָיָה לָהֶם זֶה עֲדַיִן.

presumably providing each prince with his own designated tribal stone, which was far more precious than all other donations, whereas had they brought their gifts at the outset they would not yet have possessed this miraculous elevation.
וְהַמָּשָׁל בִּנְשִׂיאִים – שֶׁהוּא חֹשֶׁךְ עַל פְּנֵי הָעוֹלָם, וּמִמֶּנָּה הָאוֹרָה יֵצֵא לְכָל בָּאֵי עוֹלָם.
And the parable of the clouds (nesi'im) is that they bring darkness over the face of the world, yet from that darkness rain and light issue forth unto all mankind.
וְכֵן שָׁמַעְתִּי עַל פָּסוּק: "הַמְכַסֶּה שָׁמַיִם בְּעָבִים", וְאַחַר כָּךְ עַל יְדֵי זֶה "הַמֵּכִין לָאָרֶץ מָטָר" (תְּהִלִּים קמז, ח).
And so I heard expounded on the verse: "Who covers the heaven with clouds," and immediately through this, "Who prepares rain for the earth" (Psalms 147:8).
וְכֵן עָשׂוּ הֵם: מִתְּחִלָּה הָעַצְלוּת הוּא הַחֹשֶׁךְ:
And so it occurred with them: initially the sluggishness constituted the dark cloud.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Rav Tzadok · Peri Tzadik, Yitro 10:1: “It also teaches us how to attain such desire. Of this it says, “They journeyed from Rephidim”: this self-abandonment is not so difficult. As soon as they departed Rephidim, which signifies weakening their hands in Torah, and set their hearts to rouse themselves and seek Hashem’s will, the one who comes to purify himself is helped. When he opens an opening as small as a needle’s point, the Holy One opens entrances through which wagons and carriages can pass. They can therefore immediately reach the wilderness of Sinai, the self-abandonment needed to receive Torah.”

paragraphs.text: Explanation: Peri Tzadik returns to the same journey from Rephidim to Sinai and identifies its active turning point: they set their hearts to seek Hashem’s will. This explains the condition within the present siman. Weakness does not improve a person by itself; the recognition of it and the renewed movement for divine help can open a greater readiness for Torah.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Ishbitz–Radzin · Tiferet Yosef, Shavuot 4: ““They journeyed from Rephidim and came to the wilderness of Sinai.” The Gemara explains Rephidim as their weakening themselves from Torah. Through this failure before the giving of the Torah, Hashem showed them that the different failures sometimes found in Israel can all be repaired through Torah. We see that there are teachings a person cannot attain without first stumbling, as the Gemara says of “this stumbling block is under your hand”: a person does not grasp words of Torah unless he has stumbled in them. Hashem thus showed them that through Torah they could repair everything.”

paragraphs.text: Explanation: Tiferet Yosef explains the same journey as disclosure that Torah can repair earlier failures. Its full discussion also identifies the error of imagining that divine favor makes human service unnecessary. Read beside the siman's explicit crying out, the parallel describes how a failure becomes the occasion for return and greater reception, rather than recommending weakness or delay as a spiritual technique.

paragraphs.text: Tzidkat HaTzadik 14:1: “Even during the day there are sometimes clouds that obstruct the light without making it dark. They are beneficial, because one who looks at the sun damages his eyesight, and they also prevent the intensity of the heat that sometimes harms a person, as we find concerning Nadav and Avihu. Their principal benefit is also as I heard explained concerning the verse, “Who covers the heavens with clouds, who prepares rain for the earth”: through this He brings a fresh drop into the body that causes growth. Yet rain itself is beneficial only at its proper time. Sometimes the cloud is harmful, when the full heat is needed—at the completion of the harvest, which is the completion of action, called harvesting, as stated at the end of the first chapter of Bava Kamma, as I explained elsewhere.”

sections.en: In Proportion to a Person's Distancing of Himself from Evil—meaning from All Worldly Delights…

p: [קנב] כְּפִי הִתְרַחֲקוּת הָאָדָם מִן הָרַע, וְהַיְינוּ מִכָּל חֲמוּדוֹת הָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה וּתְשׁוּקוֹת דִּלְגַרְמֵיהּ, כָּךְ הוּא מִתְקָרֵב לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וּמַשִּׂיג אוֹרוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ,
In proportion to a person's distancing of himself from evil—meaning from all worldly delights and self-centered desires—so does he draw near unto the Blessed Name and attain His divine illumination,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "הֲשִׁיבֵנוּ... וְהָאֵר פָּנֶיךָ" (תְּהִלִּים פ, ד).
as it is written: "Restore us... and cause Your face to shine" (Psalms 80:4).
וְכֵן לְהֵיפֶךְ: כְּפִי הַשָּׂגָתוֹ מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, כָּךְ מִתְרַחֵק מֵעִנְיְנֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "אָנֹכִי" וְ"לֹא יִהְיֶה לְךָ".
And likewise conversely: in proportion to his spiritual perception of the Blessed Name, so does he withdraw from worldly pursuits, as in "I am Hashem your God" and "You shall have no other gods."
וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ: אִם אֵין יִרְאָה אֵין חָכְמָה, אִם אֵין חָכְמָה אֵין יִרְאָה (אָבוֹת פֶּרֶק ג, יז).
And concerning this they taught: "If there is no fear, there is no wisdom; if there is no wisdom, there is no fear" (Avot 3:17).
חָכְמָה הוּא הַשָּׂגַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וְיִרְאָה הוּא מִן הַחֵטְא, וְהָא בְּלָא הָא לָא סַגִּי.
Wisdom is the perception of the Blessed Name, while fear is dread of sin, and neither can function without the other.
וְיִרְאָה נִקְרָא "אוֹצָר" וּכְלִי קִבּוּל, שֶׁהַלֵּב מִתְפַּנֶּה מִכָּל מִינֵי תְּשׁוּקוֹת וַחֲמוּדוֹת, וּמִמֵּילָא הוּא כְּלִי פָּנוּי לְקַבֵּל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה,
And fear is termed a "treasury" and a receptive vessel, wherein the heart empties itself of all base longings and lusts, automatically becoming a cleared vessel to receive words of Torah,
וּכְמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה: יָצָא דָּבָר שֶׁל לֵיצָנוּת – נִכְנַס דָּבָר שֶׁל תּוֹרָה, יָצָא דָּבָר שֶׁל תּוֹרָה – נִכְנַס שֶׁל לֵיצָנוּת.
as our Sages of blessed memory expounded: when levity departs, words of Torah enter; when words of Torah depart, levity enters.
כִּי כְּשֶׁהַלֵּב פָּנוּי מִדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, מִמֵּילָא הוּא מוּכָן לְקַבֵּל כָּל מִינֵי תַּאֲווֹת, כִּי אִי אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁיִּהְיֶה פָּנוּי לְגַמְרֵי.
For when the heart is vacant of words of Torah, it is automatically primed to absorb every worldly lust, since it is impossible for the human heart to remain completely empty.
וּלְכָךְ הֵם שְׁנֵיהֶם בְּיַחַד וְאֵין הָאֶחָד קוֹדֵם לַחֲבֵירוֹ רַק בְּרֶגַע כְּמֵימְרֵיהּ, אֲבָל תֵּיכֶף תָּכוּף לוֹ מַדְרֵגָה הָאַחֶרֶת.
Therefore both go hand-in-hand, neither preceding the other except for a split second, the alternate level following immediately in its wake.
וְהַמְפַנֶּה לִבּוֹ לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, תֵּיכֶף הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מַשְׁרֶה אוֹרוֹ שָׁם;
And whoever clears his heart for the Blessed Name, the Blessed Name instantly causes His light to dwell there;
כִּי הַיִּרְאָה הִיא מַה שֶּׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שׁוֹאֵל מִבְּנֵי אָדָם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וְעַתָּה... מָה ה' אֱלֹהֶיךָ שֹׁאֵל מֵעִמָּךְ כִּי אִם לְיִרְאָה" (דְּבָרִים י, יב),
for fear is what the Blessed Name asks of mortal man, as it is written: "And now... what does Hashem your God ask of you but to fear" (Deuteronomy 10:12),
וְהַחָכְמָה מַה שֶּׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מַשְׁפִּיעַ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "יָהֵב חָכְמְתָא לְחַכִּימִין" (דָּנִיֵּאל ב, כא), וְנֶאֱמַר: "כִּי ה' יִתֵּן חָכְמָה וְגוֹמֵר" (מִשְׁלֵי ב, ו).
whereas wisdom is what the Blessed Name generously bestows, as it is written: "He gives wisdom unto the wise" (Daniel 2:21), and: "For Hashem gives wisdom, etc." (Proverbs 2:6).
וְאִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְתַתָּא צָרִיךְ לִהְיוֹת מִקּוֹדֶם,
And an awakening from below must precede;
וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ (שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים רַבָּה ה, ב): "פִּתְחוּ לִי כְּחֻדָּהּ שֶׁל מַחַט", כִּי דַּי בְּכָל שֶׁהוּא יִרְאָה, וְאָז יֻשְׁפַּע בְּלִבּוֹ נֶגְדּוֹ כָּךְ חָכְמָה.

and regarding this our Sages expounded (Shir HaShirim Rabbah 5:2): "Open for Me an opening like the eye of a needle"—for a minute fraction of fear is sufficient, and then a corresponding measure of wisdom will be poured into his heart.
וּמִמֵּילָא עַל יְדֵי הַחָכְמָה תָּבִיא לוֹ עוֹד יִרְאָה, וְאָז תָּבוֹא עוֹד חָכְמָה, וְחוֹזֵר חָלִילָה עַד שֶׁיִּהְיוּ פְּתָחִים שֶׁיִּהְיוּ וְכוּלֵי.
And automatically that wisdom will bring him further fear, which in turn brings greater wisdom, cycling continuously until portals open wide.
וְאָמְרוּ קַדְמוֹנִים: וּבִלְבַד שֶׁיִּהְיֶה נֶקֶב מְפוּלָּשׁ מֵעֵבֶר לְעֵבֶר,
And the early masters stated: provided that this aperture penetrates entirely from side to side;
וּרְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר שֶׁיִּהְיֶה מִמַּעֲמַקֵּי לִבּוֹ הִתְעוֹרְרוּת גָּמוּר דַּעֲזִיבַת הַחֵטְא, וְלַעֲזוֹב כָּל עִנְיְנֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה, אֲפִילּוּ רֶגַע אֶחָד דַּי:
meaning that from the innermost depths of his heart there must arise a sincere, total awakening to renounce sin and abandon all worldly attachments—and even for a single moment, it is sufficient.

paragraphs.text: Guarding the heart prepares a vessel for the light of truth

paragraphs.text: The relation of Yosef’s holiness to Yaakov’s truth gives a concrete expression to the reciprocal growth of awe and wisdom.

rich.text: The relation of Yosef’s holiness to Yaakov’s truth gives a concrete expression to the reciprocal growth of awe and wisdom.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Rav Tzadok · Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 17:5: “And nonetheless there is required for this also the holiness of Joseph: to be guarded in his spirit holding fast to his stronghold in the fear of Hashem, guarding the Covenant, whereby is achieved the connection and unification of the Holy One and His Shechinah, which is the union of Truth and Faith through the agency of Joseph; for it is impossible for the light of Truth to enter the heart and experience "Hashem is my light" when the heart is brimming with physical lusts. And through the holiness of Joseph one can merit the holiness of Jacob, the dimension of Truth.”

rich.text: : “And nonetheless there is required for this also the holiness of Joseph: to be guarded in his spirit holding fast to his stronghold in the fear of Hashem, guarding the Covenant, whereby is achieved the connection and unification of the Holy One and His Shechinah, which is the union of Truth and Faith through the agency of Joseph; for it is impossible for the light of Truth to enter the heart and experience "Hashem is my light" when the heart is brimming with physical lusts. And through the holiness of Joseph one can merit the holiness of Jacob, the dimension of Truth.”

paragraphs.text: Explanation: Chanukah describes guarding the covenant and holding fast to fear of Hashem as the preparation through which the light of truth can enter the heart. This develops the vessel described in the present siman: a heart occupied by self-directed desires is unavailable for that illumination. The parallel gives the process a particular form, while this siman explains its continuing movement—an act of awe opens reception of wisdom, and the wisdom received deepens awe in turn.

paragraphs.text: Pirkei Avot 3:17: ‘Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya says: If there is no Torah, there is no proper conduct; if there is no proper conduct, there is no Torah. If there is no wisdom, there is no fear; if there is no fear, there is no wisdom. If there is no understanding, there is no knowledge; if there is no knowledge, there is no understanding. If there is no flour, there is no Torah; if there is no Torah, there is no flour. He used to say: To what can someone whose wisdom exceeds his deeds be compared? To a tree with many branches and few roots: the wind comes, uproots it, and topples it facedown, as it is said: ‘He shall be like a shrub in the desert and shall not see when good comes; he shall dwell in parched places in the wilderness, in a salt land that is uninhabited’ (Jeremiah 17). But to what can someone whose deeds exceed his wisdom be compared? To a tree with few branches and many roots: even if all the winds in the world come and blow against it, they cannot move it from its place, as it is said: ‘He shall be like a tree planted beside water, sending its roots toward a stream. It does not notice when heat comes; its leaves remain fresh. In a year of drought it is not anxious, and it does not cease producing fruit’ (ibid.).’

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Rav Tzadok · Yisrael Kedoshim 6:4: “Through the completion of fear, wisdom and Torah too become complete, for the two depend on one another: “Without fear there is no wisdom; without wisdom there is no fear.” Shabbat therefore compares fear to outer keys and Torah to inner keys, apparently reversing its other image of gate and dwelling. Both are true. At the beginning Torah must be fixed in the heart as the inheritance of the congregation of Yaakov, acquired within each Jew. By entering this gate of Torah through an opening like a needle's point, one can then enter service with fear in the heart, the purpose of “Hashem asks of you.””

Both are true. At the beginning Torah must be fixed in the heart as the inheritance of the congregation of Yaakov, acquired within each Jew. By entering this gate of Torah through an opening like a needle's point, one can then enter service with fear in the heart, the purpose of “Hashem asks of you.””

paragraphs.text: Explanation: Yisrael Kedoshim explicitly asks why fear is called the outer key to Torah while elsewhere Torah is called the gate into fear. Its answer distinguishes the inherited Torah that permits entry from the fuller wisdom received through developed fear. This gives the siman's repeated movement a concrete structure: an initial opening does not exhaust either fear or wisdom, and each prepares a deeper reception of the other.

sections.en: The Anguish of Soul That a Person Endures Over His Iniquities Substitutes for Physical…

p: [קנג] הָעָגְמַת נֶפֶשׁ שֶׁיֵּשׁ לָאָדָם עַל עֲווֹנוֹתָיו הוּא תְּמוּרַת יִסּוּרִין, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר (וַיַּקְהֵל ריב עַמּוּד א) מִמָּשִׁיחַ, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
The anguish of soul that a person endures over his iniquities substitutes for physical suffering, as written in the Zohar (Vayakhel 212a) regarding the Messiah, see there.
וְיָדוּעַ דְּנֶפֶשׁ מַנְהִיג הַדּוֹר הוּא הַכּוֹלֶלֶת כָּל נַפְשׁוֹת הַפְּרָטִיּוֹת שֶׁבַּדּוֹר.
And it is known that the soul of the leader of the generation encompasses all the individual souls within that generation.
וְנֶפֶשׁ מָשִׁיחַ הוּא כְּלַל נַפְשׁוֹת כָּל הַדּוֹרוֹת אַחַר הַשְּׁלֵימוּת שֶׁל הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתָם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
And the soul of the Messiah comprises the collective souls of all generations following the completion of their spiritual toil in this world
[כְּמוֹ שֶׁהָאָבוֹת כּוֹלְלִים נַפְשׁוֹת כָּל הַדּוֹרוֹת בְּהַתְחָלָתָם וְשָׁרְשָׁם וּמְקוֹר מוֹצָאָם],
[just as the Patriarchs encompass the souls of all generations at their inception, root, and origin];
וְנִמְצָא בְּכָל נֶפֶשׁ פְּרָטִי נְקֻדַּת הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתוֹ אֶל הַתַּכְלִית הָאֲמִיתִּי הוּא נְקֻדַּת מָשִׁיחַ,
and it turns out that within each individual soul, the focal point of its striving toward the ultimate Truth is the spark of the Messiah,
וּבְאוֹתוֹ נְקֻדָּה הוּא סוֹבֵל צַעַר עַל עֲווֹנוֹת, כְּטַעַם "מְדֻכָּא מֵעֲוֹנֹתֵינוּ" (יְשַׁעְיָה נג, ה), וּמֵקֵל בָּזֶה הָעֳנָשִׁים דְּיִסּוּרִין.
and within that point he bears grief over sins, in the sense of "crushed because of our iniquities" (Isaiah 53:5), thereby lightening the retributions of bodily afflictions.

וְעַיֵּין שָׁם דִּמְקַבְּלָם בְּגַן עֵדֶן, רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר שֶׁמִּתְעוֹרֵר עַל זֶה מִכֹּחַ דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, עַיֵּין שָׁם (רי עַמּוּד א) דִּרְקִיעַ שֶׁעַל הַגַּן עֵדֶן נַעֲשֶׂה מִדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, עַיֵּין שָׁם,

And see there in the Zohar that he receives them in Gan Eden—meaning that he is awakened to this remorse through the power of Torah study, as stated there (210a) that the firmament above Gan Eden is formed from words of Torah—
וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁרוֹאֶה חוֹמֶר הָעֲווֹנוֹת וְכַיּוֹצֵא.
for through Torah he perceives the profound gravity of sin.
וְעַל יְדֵי הַצַּעַר וְהָעָגְמַת נֶפֶשׁ שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ בִּנְקֻדַּת הַלֵּב מֵעֲווֹנוֹתָיו, עַל יְדֵי זֶה מִתְעוֹרֵר תֹּקֶף נְקֻדַּת מָשִׁיחַ הַגְּנוּזָה בּוֹ וּמֵאִיר לוֹ.
And through the grief and anguish of soul he endures in the core of his heart over his sins, the power of the spark of the Messiah hidden within him is awakened and shines upon him.

And see there (211b) that fire from Gehenna reaches Gan Eden,

paragraphs.text: Sha'arei Teshuvah 4:12: “He should continually sigh in the bitterness of his heart, as we explained in the first gate on repentance, and put the abundance of that bitterness in place of suffering. As it says, “A person’s spirit sustains his illness, but a broken spirit—who can bear it?” The meaning is that when the body falls ill, the soul bears its illness; this is the sense of “Who can endure the day of His coming?” It helps and supports the body by speaking to its heart and consoling it so that it can accept and endure. But when the soul is ill and broken by sorrow and anxiety, who will console the soul, and who will bear and support it? Thus anxiety and bitterness of heart are heavier than bodily illness: the soul supports the body in illness, but when the soul is ill and broken by grief, the body does not support it.”

paragraphs.text: Remorse and the gradual repair of the hidden root

rich.text: Remorse and the gradual repair of the hidden root

paragraphs.text: The grief is directed toward the inward source of the fault and its eventual repair.

rich.text: The grief is directed toward the inward source of the fault and its eventual repair.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Rav Tzadok · Machshavot Charutz 7:13: “But the serpent's counsel, from which the root of “the first of the nations” extends, is a root of that root and is present even in the hidden part of the heart. It is effaced through visitation, which belongs to hidden thought; its effacement comes through suffering and grief in the heart over the sin. This is “I shall visit their sin upon them”: He brings it into their hearts to feel deep bitterness over the root of the heart's inclination toward it. This is through burning the heifer to ashes, which purifies contact with the dead, meaning contact with the fundamental source of impurity, the serpent's counsel. Now, when we have neither the heifer's ashes nor the practical performance of the mitzvah, “we shall render the bulls with our lips”: reading the passage gradually brings this into the heart. It comes before Pesach to merit through it the resurrection of the dead that will take place at Pesach, which is why we read the prophecy of the dry bones on Shabbat Chol HaMoed Pesach.”

paragraphs.text: Explanation: Machshavot Charutz distinguishes repair of an openly expressed fault from the gradual repair of its hidden root. The latter involves sorrow in the heart and Torah that gradually makes a person aware of that root, in preparation for renewed life. This explains why the present siman places the significance of remorse in the point directed toward ultimate completion. The comparison concerns the spiritually productive movement of teshuvah described by these texts; the paragraph does not equate every experience of distress with completed repair.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Ishbitz–Radzin · Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayera 1: “‘Hashem appeared to him in the terebinths of Mamre, while he sat at the entrance of the tent in the heat of the day.’ It is written (Malachi 3:20), ‘For you who fear My name, a sun of righteousness will shine, with healing in its wings.’ ‘Those who fear My name’ are those who have a grasp of Torah and Hashem, which brings them true awe. Hashem promises that the sun of righteousness will shine for them—that is, clarified words of Torah. ‘Healing in its wings’ means confidence and strength in Hashem and Torah, like wings, which are a strong support for winged creatures.”

sections.en: Just as a Person Is Required to Believe in the Blessed Name

p: [קנד] כְּשֵׁם שֶׁצָּרִיךְ אָדָם לְהַאֲמִין בַּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, כָּךְ צָרִיךְ אַחַר כָּךְ לְהַאֲמִין בְּעַצְמוֹ.
Just as a person is required to believe in the Blessed Name, so too must he subsequently believe in himself.
רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר, שֶׁיֵּשׁ לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עֵסֶק עִמּוֹ, וְשֶׁאֵינֶנּוּ פּוֹעֵל בָּטֵל "שֶׁבִּן לַיְלָה" וְכוּלֵי (יוֹנָה ד, י), וּכְחַיְתוֹ שָׂדֶה שֶׁלְּאַחַר מִיתָתָם נֶאֶבְדוּ וְאֵינָם.

That is to say, he must believe that the Blessed Name has purposeful dealings with him, and that he is not a pointless creature who sprang up overnight and perishes (Jonah 4:10), or like wild beasts that after death vanish into nothingness.
רַק צָרִיךְ לְהַאֲמִין כִּי נַפְשׁוֹ מִמְּקוֹר הַחַיִּים יִתְבָּרַךְ שְׁמוֹ, וְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מִתְעַנֵּג וּמִשְׁתַּעֲשֵׁעַ בָּהּ כְּשֶׁעוֹשָׂה רְצוֹנוֹ.
Rather, he must believe that his soul stems from the Source of Life, blessed be His Name, and that the Blessed Name delights and revels in it when it fulfills His will.
וְזֶה פֵּירוּשׁ: "וַיַּאֲמִינוּ בַּה' וּבְמֹשֶׁה עַבְדּוֹ" (שְׁמוֹת יד, לא)
— And this is the inner meaning of: "and they believed in Hashem, and in Moses His servant" (Exodus 14:31)—
פֵּירוּשׁ, "מֹשֶׁה" רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר כְּלַל שִׁשִּׁים רִבּוֹא נַפְשׁוֹת יִשְׂרָאֵל בַּדּוֹר הַהוּא, הֶאֱמִינוּ שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ חָפֵץ בָּהֶם
"Moses" denotes the collective sum of the 600,000 souls of Israel in that generation; they believed that the Blessed Name desired them

[וּמִמֵּילָא גַּם כֵּן בְּמֹשֶׁה, אֲשֶׁר הוּא מַמָּשׁ הֵם, וּכְמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא קכא:) שֶׁכָּל זְמַן שֶׁהָיוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל נְזוּפִים לֹא נִתְיַיחֵד הַדִּבּוּר לְמֹשֶׁה.

[and automatically they believed in Moses, who was essentially identical with them; as our Sages stated in Bava Batra 121b that all the years Israel were under censure in the wilderness, divine communication was not granted uniquely to Moses.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר, כִּי בְּכָל חֲטָאֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל חָטָא גַּם כֵּן מֹשֶׁה שֶׁהוּא כְּלָלוּתָם:
And as I wrote elsewhere, in all sins committed by Israel Moses likewise stumbled in an aspect thereof, since he was their aggregate:

כְּמוֹ בָּעֵגֶל הָיָה חֵטְא מֹשֶׁה בִּשְׁבִירַת הַלּוּחוֹת, וּבֶאֱמֶת הוּא דָּבָר תָּמוּהַּ וְזָר מְאֹד אֲפִילּוּ לִקְרוֹעַ סֵפֶר תּוֹרָה בַּחֲמָתוֹ וּלְהַשְׁלִיכָהּ לָאָרֶץ מִכְּתַב יַד סוֹפֵר דְּעָלְמָא, כָּל שֶׁכֵּן הַלּוּחוֹת מִכְּתַב ה'.

as with the Golden Calf, Moses's counterpart was breaking the Tablets; and in truth it is an astonishing and bizarre thing even to tear a Torah scroll written by a simple scribe in one's anger and cast it to the ground, all the more so the Tablets inscribed by the hand of God!
וְהוּא מַמָּשׁ חֵטְא דְּעֵגֶל כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר,
And that was the precise parallel to the sin of the Calf, as I wrote elsewhere;
וּכְשֶׁנֶּאֱמַר לוֹ: "יִישַׁר כֹּחֲךָ שֶׁשִּׁבַּרְתָּ", יָדַע כִּי גַּם בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל כֵּן, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (ה.): "בּוֹאוּ וְנַחֲזִיק טוֹבָה לַאֲבוֹתֵינוּ וְכוּלֵי".

and when God told him: "Congratulations that you broke them" (Shabbat 87a), he knew that this applied to the children of Israel as well, as in Avodah Zarah 5a: "Come and let us acknowledge the good of our forefathers, etc."
וּבְקִבְרוֹת הַתַּאֲוָה אָמַר: "הֲצֹאן וּבָקָר יִשָּׁחֵט לָהֶם וּמָצָא לָהֶם" (בַּמִּדְבָּר יא, כב), וְכֵן בְּמֵי מְרִיבָה;
And at Kivrot HaTa'avah he sinned when saying: "If flocks and herds be slain for them, will they suffice?" (Numbers 11:22), and so too at the Waters of Meribah;
וּבַמְרַגְּלִים הָיָה חֶטְאוֹ הַשְּׁלִיחוּת, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ: "שְׁלַח לְךָ" – לְדַעְתְּךָ, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ לְהַאֲרִיךְ בְּכֻלָּם] –
and with the Spies his flaw lay in dispatching them, as stated: "Send for yourself"—according to your own reasoning; and this is not the place to elaborate upon all of them]—
וְרוֹצֶה וּמְקַבֵּל נַחַת רוּחַ מִן חֵלֶק הַטּוֹב שֶׁבָּהֶם:
and they believed that Hashem desires them and receives deep gratification from the portion of good within them.

paragraphs.text: Explanation: Dover Tzedek develops the same approval of Moshe’s breaking the tablets by emphasizing that broken and whole tablets share the Ark’s holiness. This supports the siman’s demand to believe that one’s life matters to Hashem. A visible break does not prove the disappearance of the underlying kedushah; the account calls for renewed fidelity rather than declaring that every present action is right.

: “You should have understood: the hearts of human beings are in My hand, to turn according to My will. If I sent you, you should have trusted that I would place it in their hearts to be compelled to hear you.”

paragraphs.text: Explanation: Mei HaShiloach places Moshe's uncertainty about Israel's belief within his divine commission: the One who sends him can also turn hearts. Its surrounding argument questions Moshe's wish to possess an independent power of compulsion. This illuminates the siman's qualification of believing in oneself: the confidence is that one has a real place in Hashem's concern and service, while its power remains received from Him.

paragraphs.text: Context: These sources clarify two images in this sentence. A po’el batel is paid for remaining idle; Rav Tzadok says that a person’s service of Hashem has real purpose. The overnight image recalls Jonah’s short-lived plant. Even a long human lifetime can appear like a passing night before Hashem, as Psalm 90 says. Rav Tzadok nevertheless insists that a person’s work and the moments of his life have lasting significance.

paragraphs.text: Rashi on Yoma 82b:1:3: ““What makes you see that your blood is redder?” That is: What is your reasoning for permitting the act because “he shall live by them,” rather than die by them? But now, when an Israelite is being killed and the commandment is also set aside, why should it be preferable before the Omnipresent to transgress His commandment? Why should your blood be dearer to Him than the blood of your fellow Israelite?”

paragraphs.text: Context: Psalm 37:18 and Rashi’s explanation illuminate why a person must believe that his soul and every moment of his life matter to Hashem. Rashi’s setting is the preservation of life: a commandment is ordinarily set aside to save life, while killing another person cannot be justified by claiming that one’s own life is more valuable. This illustrates the preciousness of life; Rav Tzadok’s further point is that Hashem takes delight in the soul’s fulfillment of His will.

paragraphs.text: Peri Tzadik, Pesach 45:1: “This is what Moses meant when he said that they would therefore not believe him: they felt that they themselves possessed no merit through which they could deserve redemption. Hashem answered him that they were believers, children of believers—children of Abraham, who believed in Me, that I can send illumination into a person’s heart even when he possesses none of his own. This was their faith in Egypt, as it says, “The people believed.” So it was: Hashem sent them illumination and abundant love and brought them out from there. But Hashem’s true desire was that they should also experience an awakening from themselves, without an awakening from above.”

paragraphs.text: Peri Tzadik, Pesach 45:1: “Afterward it says, “They believed in Hashem and in Moses His servant.” Moses comprised all the souls of the six hundred thousand of Israel. As the Mekhilta teaches concerning “The children of Israel were fruitful and multiplied,” six hundred thousand were born in one womb—and who was this? Moses. For Moses our teacher comprised all the souls of Israel. This explains the Gemara’s question, “Is fear such a small matter?” and its answer, “Yes, for Moses it is a small matter”: for Moses, the source of Israel’s souls, it was easy for them to reach the quality of fear. This is “They believed in Hashem and in Moses His servant”: since they believed that Moses was Hashem’s servant and that they were branches of him, through this they attained complete faith. This is what they attained at the splitting of the sea.”

paragraphs.text: Context: Peri Tzadik, Pesach 45, develops this extended parallel. The first two excerpts explain why a person’s lack of merit does not sever his relation to Hashem: divine assistance can illuminate his heart while still allowing his own response to count as his achievement. The final excerpt explains the same verse used here: believing in Moses includes recognizing the worth and spiritual capacity of the souls comprised within him. The three excerpts are selected passages from the same discourse; intervening material develops the stages of faith before the sea split.

paragraphs.text: Context: The discussion explains one reason for the joy of the fifteenth of Av. The sentence begins at the end of 121a and continues on 121b: until the wilderness generation’s deaths ended, Moses lacked the former mode of divine speech. Rashbam qualifies this as the loss of ordinary direct communication, not the claim that no necessary divine message reached Moses during those years. This is the connection between Israel’s condition and Moses’ prophecy used here.
