sections.en: All Elevation and Sovereignty in the World Occur Through the Torah

p: [קעח] כָּל הִתְנַשְּׂאוּת הוּא עַל יְדֵי הַתּוֹרָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "בִּי מְלָכִים יִמְלֹכוּ" (מִשְׁלֵי ח, טו);
All elevation and sovereignty in the world occur through the Torah, as it is written: "By me kings reign" (Proverbs 8:15);
אֲפִילּוּ מַלְכֵי אֻמּוֹת עוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים יֵשׁ בָּהֶם חִדּוּשִׁין דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא בְּסוֹד הַגָּלוּת.
even the kings of the gentile nations hold Torah novellae (chiddushin de-Oraita), through the mystery of the exile.
כִּי בֶּאֱמֶת, הָאוֹמֵר: יֵשׁ תּוֹרָה בְּאֻמּוֹת עוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים – אַל תַּאֲמֵן (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ מִדְרָשׁ רַבָּה אֵיכָה ב, ט), כִּי "לֹא עָשָׂה כֵן לְכָל גּוֹי" (תְּהִלִּים קמז, כ).
For in truth, if one says: there is Torah among the gentiles—do not believe it (Eichah Rabbah 2:9), for "He has not dealt so with any nation" (Psalms 147:20).
אֲבָל מִכָּל מָקוֹם, הֲרֵי אֲפִילּוּ בְּתוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב נִכְתַּב הַרְבֵּה דִּבְרֵי רִשְׁעֵי אֻמּוֹת עוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים וְהֵם מִכְּלַל הַתּוֹרָה, וְכֵן בִּנְבִיאִים וּכְתוּבִים.
Yet nonetheless, even within the Written Torah many utterances of wicked gentiles are recorded, and they form an integral part of the Torah, and likewise throughout the Prophets and Writings.
וְהֵם עַצְמָם לֹא יָדְעוּ מַה הֵם מְדַבְּרִים, רַק הַנָּבִיא וְיִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁבְּתוֹכָם יָדְעוּ שֶׁזֶּהוּ דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, וְכָל כֹּחָם מִזֶּה;
And they themselves did not comprehend what they were uttering, but the prophet and Israel amidst them recognized that it was words of Torah, and all their royal power derived from this;
וּמִיָּד שֶׁהוֹצִיאוּ בִּלְעָם מִפִּיהֶם, נִתְבַּטְּלָה מַלְכוּתָם.
and the moment they gave up what they had swallowed, their kingdom was abolished.
וּמִתּוֹךְ הַגְּזֵירוֹת מְבִינִים בַּמֶּה כֹּחָם בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה,
And from the oppressive decrees they issue, we can understand wherein lies their spiritual hold in words of Torah,

וְשׁוֹרֶשׁ כָּל גְּזֵירוֹתָם הוּא "תָּא נֶהֱוֵי לְעַמָּא חַד", שֶׁזֶּהוּ עִיקַּר בִּנְיַן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מִימוֹת חוּרְבַּן רִאשׁוֹן וְאֵילָךְ: לַהֲפוֹךְ גַּם עַל כָּל עַמִּים שָׂפָה בְרוּרָה לִקְרוֹא בְּשֵׁם ה'.

and the inner root of all their decrees is "come, let us become one people," which is the overarching design of the Blessed Name from the destruction of the First Temple onward: to turn unto all nations a pure language, that they may all call upon the Name of Hashem (Zephaniah 3:9).
וְהֵם נֶחְלָקִים בִּפְרָטִים: אִם הוּא עַל מִצְוָה פְּרָטִית – רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לְהִתְחַזֵּק יוֹתֵר בָּהּ,
And they divide into specific details: if a decree targets a particular mitzvah, it signifies that the will of the Blessed Name is that Israel strengthen themselves all the more in that mitzvah,

כְּעִנְיַן הַפְטָרָה שֶׁנִּתְקַן עַל יְדֵי גְּזֵירָה שֶׁלֹּא לִקְרוֹת בַּתּוֹרָה, וְהֵבִינוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה דִּרְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ אַדְּרַבָּה דְּקוֹרִין רַק מְעַט, וּדְצָרִיךְ לְהוֹסִיף עוֹד קְרִיאַת מַפְטִיר בַּנְּבִיאִים.

like the institution of the Haftarah, which was established due to a decree forbidding the reading of the Torah, and our Sages understood that the will of the Blessed Name was, on the contrary, that they had been reading too little, and that they needed to add the reading of the Haftarah from the Prophets.
וְכַיּוֹצֵא בוֹ בַּאֲמִירַת "שְׁמַע יִשְׂרָאֵל" בִּקְדֻשַּׁת מוּסָף שֶׁנִּתְקַן בִּגְזֵירָה עַל יְדֵי רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּסֵפֶר הָאֶשְׁכּוֹל
And similar to this is reciting "Shema Yisrael" in the Kedushah of Musaf, which was instituted during a decree by our Sages, as written in Sefer HaEshkol
[וְכַיּוֹצֵא בָּזֶה אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מִדְרָשׁ רַבָּה אֶסְתֵּר פָּרָשָׁה ז) בְּהָמָן שֶׁלִּגְלֵג שֶׁהַיּוֹם פֶּסַח וְכוּלֵי: חַיֶּיךָ עוֹד מוֹסִיפִים מוֹעֵד עַל מַפַּלְתְּךָ].
[and similarly our Sages stated (Esther Rabbah 7) concerning Haman who mocked that today is Passover, etc.: by your life, they will add yet another festival celebrating your downfall].
גַּם תְּקִיעוֹת בְּמוּסָף נִתְקַן עַל יְדֵי גְּזֵירָה (רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה לב:)
Also blowing the shofar during Musaf was instituted on account of a decree (Rosh Hashanah 32b)

[וְשָׁמַעְתִּי לְפִי שֶׁהוּא שֶׁלֹּא עַל פִּי דִּין, דְּמִדִּין רָאוּי לִהְיוֹת זְרִיזִים מַקְדִּימִים, וְדָבָר כָּזֶה אִי אֶפְשָׁר לִהְיוֹת עַל יְדֵי חַכְמֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל, רַק נַעֲשָׂה עַל יְדֵי גְּזֵירָתָם],

[and I heard that this was because it seemed counter to standard law, where by right the zealous act early in Shacharit, and such a postponement could not have been introduced by the sages of Israel except through the pressure of their persecution],
וְנִמְצָא הֵם הֵבִיאוּ חִדּוּשׁ תּוֹרָה זֶה לָעוֹלָם;
and thus it turns out that the persecutors brought this novel Torah practice into the world;
וְאַחַר שֶׁנִּתְחַדְּשָׁה הֲלָכָה זוֹ, פָּקַע כֹּחָם וְנִתְבַּטְּלָה גְּזֵירָתָם, כִּי זֶהוּ כָּל עִיקַּר כֹּחָם: לְהוֹצִיא דְּבַר הֲלָכָה זוֹ:
and once this halakhah was innovated, their power expired and their decree was annulled, for this was the entire purpose of their power: to bring forth this particular halakhah.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Ishbitz–Radzin · Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Lech Lecha 6: “It is written (Proverbs 8:15), ‘By Me kings reign.’ In ordinary syntax it could have said, ‘By Me reign kings.’ This hints that the Holy One appoints as king only someone who can first rule over himself; him He appoints over others, as it says (Avot 4:1), ‘Who is mighty? One who conquers his inclination.’ ‘By Me kings reign’ means: someone who rules himself, whose understanding governs his desire, will then reign—he will be king over all. He need not heed the person opposing him, since his entire intention is for Heaven.”

paragraphs.text: The distinction explains how words spoken without understanding can become Torah for the prophet and Israel who understand them.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Rav Tzadok · Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 5:6: “This occurred because the heart was diminished through the husk of Greek wisdom, which was without heart. As we explained concerning the Midrash, ‘If they say there is Torah among the nations, do not believe it,’ for ‘there is no Torah among the nations’: their wisdom is from the lips outward and does not instruct the heart. Torah’s wisdom is different; its essential acquisition is in the heart, as it says, ‘In the heart of every wise-hearted person I have placed wisdom.’ This is the meaning of the Sages’ statement that the Greeks defiled all the oils: the wisdom in the heart, for they darkened Israel’s eyes.”

rich.text: : “This occurred because the heart was diminished through the husk of Greek wisdom, which was without heart. As we explained concerning the Midrash, ‘If they say there is Torah among the nations, do not believe it,’ for ‘there is no Torah among the nations’: their wisdom is from the lips outward and does not instruct the heart. Torah’s wisdom is different; its essential acquisition is in the heart, as it says, ‘In the heart of every wise-hearted person I have placed wisdom.’ This is the meaning of the Sages’ statement that the Greeks defiled all the oils: the wisdom in the heart, for they darkened Israel’s eyes.”

paragraphs.text: Explanation: Chanukah contrasts wisdom remaining at the lips with Torah whose essential acquisition is in the heart. This clarifies the present siman’s otherwise surprising observation that wicked speakers can supply words later recorded in Torah. The speaker’s outward utterance and the prophet’s recognition of its Torah-content are different attainments. The siman’s claim about those words sustaining a temporary kingdom should therefore not be confused with its denial that the speaker has acquired Torah inwardly.

paragraphs.text: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 11:5: “This explains why the words of Avimelech, Pharaoh, Bilam, and the like were written in the Torah: those utterances that expressed their entire vitality, reaching the holy spark within them, were taken into the words of Torah. Even Pharaoh’s words, “Who is Hashem, that I should listen to His voice?”—since they were written in the Torah—are words at the root of his vitality, where Hashem established this claim of “Who is Hashem?” For concealment too comes from Hashem, from His true will at the root of creation: that darkness should come first, and light afterward. “He forms light and creates darkness”: creation is a higher level, as is known, for darkness issues from a deeper will, since there is also a need for darkness. Thus Hashem established that the Egyptian exile would prepare for the giving of the Torah; the existence of Egypt and Pharaoh was therefore necessary, for Hashem willed the existence of these creatures who say, “Who is Hashem?””

paragraphs.text: Mishnah Berurah 284:2: ““From the Prophets, etc.” The reason is that on one occasion a decree was imposed on Israel forbidding them to occupy themselves with Torah. Seven people read from the Prophets and recited blessings over them, corresponding to the seven who should have been called to read from the Torah. They did not read fewer than three verses with each person, making twenty-one verses altogether. Therefore, even though the decree was annulled, the practice was not annulled. For this reason they instituted that the maftir read no fewer than twenty-one verses from the Prophets, and that he first read from the Torah out of respect for the Torah, as explained in section 282, Mishnah Berurah 28. The maftir recites seven blessings—the two he recites over the Torah, before and after, one before the prophetic reading, and four afterward—corresponding to the seven who read from the Torah.”

paragraphs.text: Kol Bo 37:13: “The author of HaEshkol wrote: In Musaf on Shabbat, festivals, and Yom Kippur, and at Ne’ilah, one says “Shema Yisrael” and “I am Hashem your God,” which are the beginning and end of the recitation of Shema. This is because a persecutory decree forbade the recitation of Shema altogether. They therefore instituted this Kedushah in every prayer service. sections.en: "In All Your Ways Acknowledge Him" (Proverbs 3:6)

p: [קעט] "בְּכָל דְּרָכֶיךָ דָעֵהוּ" (מִשְׁלֵי ג, ו) מְפוֹרָשׁ בְּשׁוֹחֵר טוֹב (מִזְמוֹר קמד) דְּהַיְינוּ שֶׁיֵּדַע בְּכָל דָּבָר שֶׁלֹּא הוּא הַפּוֹעֵל כְּלָל, רַק הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
"In all your ways acknowledge Him" (Proverbs 3:6) is explained in Shocher Tov (Psalm 144) as meaning that one should know in every matter that it is not he who acts at all, but only the Blessed Name.
וּבַזֹּהַר אִיתָא: דַּע ה"וּ – גַּם כֵּן לְכָךְ נִתְכַּוֵּין,
And in the Zohar it is brought: "Know Vav-Hei" (forming the word Da'ehu)—which intends the same concept,

כִּידוּעַ דְּוָא"ו הֵ"א הוּא קוּדְשָׁא בְּרִיךְ הוּא וּשְׁכִינְתֵיהּ, וְיִחוּדָם הַיְינוּ שֶׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא שׁוֹכֵן בְּתוֹךְ בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וְהוּא חַד עִם כְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל, וְאֵין הֵם דָּבָר נִבְדָּל מִמֶּנּוּ כְּלָל.

for as is known, Vav-Hei represents the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shechinah, and their unification means that the Holy One dwells within the children of Israel and is one with the Congregation of Israel, they not being separate from Him at all.
וְרַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה אָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (סג.): אֲפִילּוּ לִדְבַר עֲבֵירָה,
And our Sages stated in Berakhot 63a: "even regarding a matter of transgression,"

הַיְינוּ שֶׁבְּלֶכְתּוֹ לַעֲבֵירָה, אִם יָשִׂים אֶל לִבּוֹ דְּכֹחוֹ זֶה לָלֶכֶת לַהַמְרוֹת רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ גַּם הוּא מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, כִּי בִּלְתּוֹ מֵאַיִן לוֹ שׁוּם כֹּחַ כְּלָל – עַל יְדֵי זֶה יֵחָלֵשׁ כֹּחַ הַיֵּצֶר.

meaning that on his way to a sin, if he takes to heart that this very strength to go and rebel against the will of the Blessed Name likewise derives from the Blessed Name—for without Him, whence would he have any power at all?—through this the power of the inclination will weaken.
וְזֶהוּ (שָׁם ה.): לְעוֹלָם יַרְגִּיז וְכוּלֵי, יִקְרָא קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע – הַיְינוּ "דָּעֵהוּ".
And this is (ibid. 5a): "A person should always stir up the good inclination against the evil inclination... let him recite the Shema"—which is "acknowledge Him."
וְגַם בֶּעָבָר, עַל יְדֵי זֶה: "וְהוּא יְיַשֵּׁר אֹרְחֹתֶיךָ" (מִשְׁלֵי ג, ו);
And regarding the past as well, through this: "and He shall make your paths straight" (Proverbs 3:6);
"דֶּרֶךְ" נִקְרָא דֶּרֶךְ הַמֶּלֶךְ, וְ"אֹרַח" הוּא מִן הַצַּד,
a "way" (derekh) denotes the king's highway, while a "path" (orach) is from the side,
וּכְשֶׁמְּקַיֵּים "דָּעֵהוּ" אָז נִקְרָא הַכֹּל "דֶּרֶךְ" שֶׁהוּא דֶּרֶךְ הַמֶּלֶךְ.
and when one fulfills "acknowledge Him," then everything is called a "way," which is the king's highway.

אֲבָל גַּם "אֹרְחֹתֶיךָ" שֶׁכְּבָר עָבַרְתָּ וְהִטִּיתָ מִן הַצַּד וְחוּץ מִדֶּרֶךְ הָרָאוּי, אִם עַכְשָׁו מְקַיֵּים "דָּעֵהוּ", יֵדַע שֶׁגַּם זֶה הָיָה מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וְאִם כֵּן הוּא מְיוּשָּׁר:

But even "your paths" where you have already transgressed and strayed off to the side, outside the proper way—if you now fulfill "acknowledge Him," you will realize that this too was encompassed by the Blessed Name, and if so, it is made straight.

paragraphs.text: Midrash Tehillim 144: ‘‘Of David. Blessed is Hashem, my Rock,’ and so on. Solomon said: ‘In all your ways know Him’ (Proverbs 3:6). What does ‘In all your ways know Him’ mean? Keep Him in your heart, before you, on every path you take, as David used to do. He was a king, yet said: ‘I am not king; He is King, and He made me king.’ Thus it says: ‘David knew that Hashem had established him as king over Israel’ (II Samuel 5:12). He was mighty, yet said: ‘I am not mighty.’ He was wealthy, yet said: ‘I am not wealthy.’ Thus he proclaimed: ‘Yours, Hashem, are greatness and might,’ and so on (I Chronicles 29:11). Thus it also says: ‘David administered justice and righteousness for all his people’ (II Samuel 8:15). He went down to battle and won, yet said: ‘I did not win through my own might. Rather, He helped me, He enabled me to win, and I won; He formed me to wage war.’ Thus it says: ‘The God who girds me with strength’ (Psalms 18:33). Therefore he said: ‘Blessed is Hashem, my Rock,’ and so on.’

paragraphs.text: Recognizing that even one’s capacity to act comes from Hashem can weaken the impulse to act against His will.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Ishbitz–Radzin · Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayigash 4: “"If he conquers it, well and good; and if not, let him recite the Shema": for within the study of Torah there is an element of spiritual self-elevation and vigor, so that through Torah study a person might feel emboldened in his soul and still fail to arrive at complete, humble clarity regarding his desire; therefore the third test is to recite the Shema ("Hashem is One"), for the essence of the Shema corresponds to what is explained in the Gemara (Ta'anit 31a), that in the future the Holy One, blessed be He, will make a circle-dance (machol) for the righteous— meaning that all will see that everything is equally in the hand of Hashem, blessed be He, and no individual has any superiority or self-exaltation over his fellow, just like a circle which has no head or end; and the unification of the Shema alludes to this complete nullification of self.”

paragraphs.text: Explanation: Mei HaShiloach explains the same counsel to recite Shema as the recognition that everything is in Hashem’s hand and no person possesses independent superiority. This clarifies the practical direction of “know Him” here. Recognizing the source of one’s power is meant to break the autonomous posture of the yetzer, rather than certify the act it is urging.

paragraphs.text: Kometz HaMinchah 2:79:9: “Since Hashem wished to be called Lord and King, and there is no king without a people, He restricted the spread of His light so that the creatures could apprehend that light, which is their vitality and continued existence, as it is written, “You give life to them all.” This is the name Adnut, indicating that He is Lord of all and that they serve Him. This is called Shechinah: that which dwells within the children of Israel. Within a person, in the depth of the heart, dwell the light and apprehension of Hashem. By contrast, apprehending Hashem as infinite and without limit is called “the Holy One, blessed be He.” Holiness always means separation: this is removed from human apprehension, consecrated beyond it with ten sanctifications, and called holy, concealed by its abundant holiness. This is the meaning of the hidden name Havayah. Its revelation—that is, its spoken pronunciation—is through the name Adnut, which is what is revealed to human hearts.”

paragraphs.text: Tomer Devorah 1:2: “The first quality: “Who is a God like You?” This teaches that the Holy One, blessed be He, is a King who bears insult, enduring an offense beyond what thought can encompass. Certainly nothing is hidden from His supervision. Moreover, there is no moment in which a person is not nourished and sustained by the supernal power flowing upon him. You will therefore find that no person has ever sinned against Him without His supplying, at that very moment, the flow of the person’s existence and the movement of his limbs. Although the person sins with that very power, He does not withhold it at all. Rather, the Holy One, blessed be He, bears such insult by continuing to supply the power that moves his limbs, while the person uses that power at that very moment for sin and iniquity, provoking Him—and the Holy One bears it. Do not say that He cannot withhold that good, Heaven forbid: He has the power in an instant to wither the person’s hands and feet, as He did to Yerovam. Yet, although He has the power to withdraw the power He supplies, and could say, “Since you sin against Me, sin with what is yours, not with what is Mine,” He does not on that account withhold His goodness from the person. He bears the insult, supplies the power, and bestows His goodness on the person. This is insult and forbearance beyond description. For this reason the ministering angels call the Holy One, blessed be He, the King who bears insult. This is the meaning of “Who is a God like You?” You are God, possessing kindness and bestowing good; God, possessing the power to exact retribution and reclaim what is Yours; yet You endure and bear insult until the person returns in repentance.”

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Ishbitz–Radzin · Tiferet Yosef, Talmud Anthology, Berakhot 7: “The Zohar in Shemini likewise teaches: when the Holy One wished to create the world, the Torah said before Him, “This person You are about to create is destined to sin before You.” He replied, “Is it for nothing that I am called patient?” The Midrash on Vaetchanan compares prayer to a mikveh and teshuvah to the sea. Just as a mikveh is sometimes open and sometimes closed, prayer is sometimes open and sometimes closed; but just as the sea is always open, so the Holy One's hand is always open to receive those who return. All this shows that even if a person has failed in a bad act, Heaven forbid, teshuvah is not withheld from him. This is the saying, “Know Him in all your ways,” upon which all the essentials of Torah depend, as Rava concludes, “Even concerning a transgression.” It means that a person must not despair after the failure of sin, for teshuvah is always available to him. This is a principle among the essentials of Torah.”

paragraphs.text: Explanation: Tiferet Yosef discusses the same Berakhot statement and explains its application after a failure: a person must not despair of return. The surrounding teaching explains why “Anochi” precedes “You shall have no other gods”: a person who is not yet free of wrongdoing must still have a place to do mitzvos. This complements the existing Shema note, which addresses temptation as it arises, with a source focused on the already-diverted path at the end of the siman.

paragraphs.text: Explanation: Siman 128 explicitly uses “In all your ways know Him” while retaining the need for atonement even for an act understood through a holy purpose. This is an important companion to the retrospective conclusion here. The knowledge that one's power came from Hashem is meant to weaken the urge to disobey and open return; it is not a self-issued exemption from the work of repair.

sections.en: Even Though Our Sages Stated in Bava Batra 9a: "If One Does Not Merit…"

p: [קפ] אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּבָבָא בַּתְרָא (ט.): "לֹא זָכָה – מְרוּדִים", הַיְינוּ מִשּׁוּם דִּכְשֶׁזּוֹכֶה אֵין צָרִיךְ לְכָךְ;
Even though our Sages stated in Bava Batra 9a: "if one does not merit, his resources go to the oppressive rulers (merudim)," that is because when one merits, he has no need for this;
אֲבָל אִם לֹא זָכָה, כַּפָּרָה גְּדוֹלָה הוּא בִּמְרוּדִים,
however, if he did not merit, there is great atonement through the oppressive rulers,
כִּידוּעַ מֵהַזֹּהַר דְּשָׂעִיר הַמִּשְׁתַּלֵּחַ הוּא סוֹד הַמִּנְחָה שֶׁשָּׁלַח יַעֲקֹב לְעֵשָׂו.
as is known from the Zohar that the scapegoat sent away is the mystical secret of the gift that Jacob sent to Esau.
וְיָדוּעַ דְּכָל מַה שֶּׁנּוֹתְנִים לְאֻמּוֹת עוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים, הַכֹּל הוּא מִמַּעֲשֵׂה אָבוֹת בְּאוֹתוֹ דּוֹרוֹן – סִימָן לַבָּנִים.
And it is known that all which Israel gives to the gentile nations derives from the deeds of the Patriarchs in that gift—a sign for the children.
וַהֲרֵי אֵין לְךָ בְּכָל הַקָּרְבָּנוֹת כַּפָּרָה גְּדוֹלָה כְּמוֹ שָׂעִיר הַמִּשְׁתַּלֵּחַ, שֶׁהוּא מְכַפֵּר עַל כָּל עֲבֵירוֹת שֶׁבַּתּוֹרָה.
And behold, you have no atonement among all the sacrifices greater than the scapegoat, which atones for all transgressions in the Torah.
וּלְכָךְ כְּשֶׁלֹּא זָכָה וְצָרִיךְ כַּפָּרָה, מַזְמִינִים לוֹ מְרוּדִים שֶׁזֶּה מְכַפֵּר
And therefore, when one did not merit and requires atonement, oppressive rulers are summoned upon him, which brings atonement
[לְפִי שֶׁנַּפְשׁוֹ דּוֹאֵב לוֹ עַל נְתִינַת הַמָּעוֹת לְמָקוֹם שֶׁאֵין שׁוּם מִצְוָה, מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן לַעֲנִיִּים שָׂמֵחַ שֶׁעוֹשֶׂה מִצְוָה עַל יָדָם];
[because his soul aches over surrendering money to a place where there is no mitzvah, whereas when giving to the poor he rejoices that he fulfills a mitzvah through them];
אֲבָל אַשְׁרֵי לְמִי שֶׁזָּכָה וְאֵין צָרִיךְ לְכַפָּרָה כְּלָל.
but praiseworthy is he who has merited and needs no such painful atonement at all.

וְכֵן יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם נֶעֱנַשׁ עַל זֶה תֵּיכֶף בִּצְלִיעָתוֹ בְּרַגְלָיו, עַל יְדֵי נְתִינַת מָעוֹת לְנָכְרִי, שֶׁזֶּה נִקְרָא "הַיְקוּם" שֶׁמַּעֲמִידוֹ עַל רַגְלָיו כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (פְּסָחִים קיט.).

And so our father Jacob, peace be upon him, was punished for this immediately by limping upon his thigh, through giving money to a stranger—wealth being called "the substance" (yekum) that establishes a man upon his feet, as our Sages stated (Pesachim 119a).

וְכֵן כְּשֶׁהֶאֱכִיל לוֹ עֲדָשִׁים, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהָיָה בִּשְׁבִיל קְנִיַּת הַבְּכוֹרָה, מִכָּל מָקוֹם נֶאֱמַר תֵּיכֶף אַחַר כָּךְ: "וַיְהִי רָעָב בָּאָרֶץ" (בְּרֵאשִׁית כו, א) – עַל יְדֵי שֶׁהֶאֱכִיל לְנָכְרִי בָּא רְעָבוֹן לַצַּדִּיקִים, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהוּא לְצוֹרֶךְ.

And likewise when he fed Esau lentils, even though it was for the purchase of the birthright, it is stated immediately thereafter: "And there was a famine in the land" (Genesis 26:1)—through feeding a stranger, famine came upon the righteous, even though it was for a necessary purpose.
וְאַחַר כָּךְ "וַיָּבֹא יַעֲקֹב שָׁלֵם" (שָׁם לג, יח), וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שַׁבָּת לג:): שָׁלֵם בְּגוּפוֹ וְכוּלֵי,
And afterward: "And Jacob came whole" (Genesis 33:18), concerning which our Sages stated (Shabbat 33b): whole in his body, whole in his wealth;

paragraphs.text: His distress concerned the right relation of the property to its root of life.

rich.text: His distress concerned the right relation of the property to its root of life.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Rav Tzadok · Peri Tzadik, Vayishlach 10:1: “Yaakov was distressed over the gift he sent Esav: “the gift passed before him,” and he was in distress. He had already clarified his flocks: the Midrash says he had six hundred thousand flocks, corresponding to the number of the roots of Israel's souls, each root becoming a complete flock. Now that he had to send some to Esav, he feared that his property was not yet clarified. Later it became clear to him that he was complete in his property and nothing was lacking from that gift: the portion belonged to the relation with Esav, and through the gift he extracted the holy sparks from him.”

rich.text: : “Yaakov was distressed over the gift he sent Esav: “the gift passed before him,” and he was in distress. He had already clarified his flocks: the Midrash says he had six hundred thousand flocks, corresponding to the number of the roots of Israel's souls, each root becoming a complete flock. Now that he had to send some to Esav, he feared that his property was not yet clarified. Later it became clear to him that he was complete in his property and nothing was lacking from that gift: the portion belonged to the relation with Esav, and through the gift he extracted the holy sparks from him.”

paragraphs.text: Explanation: Vayishlach explains that Yaakov's distress was not merely the loss of a quantity: he feared that his already clarified property was still not rightly sorted. The later completeness disclosed that the portion sent to Esav had a relation to the work of extracting the holy sparks. This develops the siman's final link between restored money and restored bodily wholeness through the spiritual relation of the property, rather than reducing the passage to a financial calculation.

sections.en: Every Person Possesses a Specific, Dominant Desire

p: [קפא] כָּל אָדָם יֵשׁ לוֹ חֶמְדָּה מְיוּחֶדֶת,
Every person possesses a specific, dominant desire,
וּבְאוֹתוֹ דָבָר שֶׁחֶמְדָּתוֹ וְתַאֲוָתוֹ גּוֹבֶרֶת בְּיוֹתֵר, בְּדָבָר זֶה עַצְמוֹ הוּא כְּלִי מוּכָן לְקַבֵּל בִּרְכַּת ה' אִם יָשׁוּב אֶל ה' בְּכָל לִבּוֹ,
and in that very matter wherein his passion and lust surge most intensely, in that exact thing itself he is a vessel primed to receive Hashem's blessing if he returns to Hashem with all his heart,
הַיְינוּ לְהַכִּיר שֶׁחֶמְדָּה זוֹ הַנְּטוּעָה בּוֹ מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הוּא.
that is, to recognize that this very longing planted within him originates from the Blessed Name.
וְזֶה שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא קי.) עַל פָּסוּק "וּשְׁבוּאֵל בֶּן גֵּרְשׁוֹם בֶּן מֹשֶׁה נָגִיד עַל הָאֹצָרוֹת" (דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים א כו, כד):
And this is what our Sages of blessed memory expounded (Bava Batra 110a) on the verse "and Shevuel son of Gershom, son of Moses, was overseer of the treasuries" (I Chronicles 26:24):
כֵּיוָן שֶׁרָאָה דָוִד שֶׁמָּמוֹן חֲבִיבָה עָלָיו בְּיוֹתֵר, מִנָּהוּ עַל הָאוֹצָרוֹת וְכוּלֵי.
once David saw that money was exceedingly beloved to him, he appointed him over the treasuries, etc.
וַהֲרֵי הָאוֹצָרוֹת אֵין שֶׁלּוֹ, וְלֹא נָתַן לוֹ הָאוֹצָרוֹת כְּלָל, וּבַמֶּה הִשְׂבִּיעַ חֶמְדָּתוֹ?
Now behold, the treasuries were not his personal property, and David did not give him the treasuries at all, so how did this satisfy his craving?
אִם בִּשְׁבִיל פְּרָס שֶׁקִּבֵּל, הוּא הַדִּין אִם הָיָה מְמוּנֶּה עַל דָּבָר אַחֵר.
If it was merely for the salary he received, that would be equally true had he been appointed over anything else!
אַךְ בֶּאֱמֶת דָּרְשׁוּ שָׁם: "וּשְׁבוּאֵל" – שֶׁשָּׁב בְּכָל לִבּוֹ,
But in truth they expounded there: "Shevuel"—that he returned (shav) to God with all his heart,
וְהַתְּשׁוּבָה הַיְינוּ שֶׁמֵּשִׁיב חֶמְדָּה זוֹ לִמְקוֹרָהּ, וּמַכִּיר שֶׁלּוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ הַכֶּסֶף וְהַזָּהָב.
and repentance means that he traced this very longing back to its divine Source, recognizing that the silver and the gold belong to Him, blessed be He.
וּלְכָךְ הוּא רָאוּי לִהְיוֹת עַל הָאוֹצָרוֹת דְּדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, שֶׁמַּלְכוּתוֹ מִדַּת מַלְכוּת שָׁמַיִם,
And therefore he was uniquely suited to oversee the treasuries of King David, peace be upon him, whose earthly monarchy embodied the Kingdom of Heaven,
וְכָל מִינּוּיוֹ הַיְינוּ שֶׁהַמְמוּנֶּה עַל אוֹתוֹ הַדָּבָר הָיָה מַכִּיר וְיוֹדֵעַ לְהַקְנוֹת הַכֹּל לְעֶלְיוֹן קוֹנֵה שָׁמַיִם וָאָרֶץ.
where every administrative appointment meant that the official over that area recognized and knew how to consecrate everything entirely to the Most High, Possessor of heaven and earth.
וְגַם בְּרָכָה בָּאוֹצָרוֹת בָּא עַל יָדוֹ, כֵּיוָן שֶׁיְּצָרוֹ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בַּבְּרִיאָה חוֹמֵד מָמוֹן, עַל כָּרְחֲךָ יֵשׁ בּוֹ כֹּחַ עָצוּם בָּזֶה,

Furthermore, blessing flowed into the treasuries through him, for since the Blessed Name fashioned him at birth with a passion for wealth, perforce an immense spiritual capacity was invested in him in that area,
וְכֵיוָן שֶׁשָּׁב בְּכָל לִבּוֹ, הֲרֵי בִּרְכַּת ה' בְּמָמוֹן עַל יָדוֹ.
and once he repented with all his heart, Hashem's blessing in wealth rested upon his hands.
וְגַם נֶאֱמַר: "טוֹב עַיִן הוּא יְבֹרָךְ" (מִשְׁלֵי כב, ט), וְהוּא הָיָה צַר עַיִן בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּיְרוּשַׁלְמִי (פֶּרֶק הָרוֹאֶה הֲלָכָה ב),
And it is also stated: "He that has a generous eye shall be blessed" (Proverbs 22:9), whereas he had originally been grudging when serving idolatry, as brought in the Yerushalmi (Berakhot 9:2),
וְהַיְינוּ מִשּׁוּם חֶמְדַּת מָמוֹן עֵינוֹ צָרָה בְּשֶׁל אֲחֵרִים,
meaning that out of greed for money his eye had been begrudging toward others' possessions,
וּבִמְקוֹם צָרוּת עַיִן הוּא טוֹבַת עַיִן כְּשֶׁשָּׁב כַּנּוֹדָע, לְכָךְ הַבְּרָכָה עַל יָדוֹ
and in the very place of a begrudging eye resides a generous eye when one repents, as is known, which is why blessing flowed through him
[וְעַיֵּין שָׁם בַּיְרוּשַׁלְמִי דְּהוּא נָבִיא זָקֵן דְּבֵית אֵל,
[and see there in the Yerushalmi that he was the old prophet of Bethel (I Kings 13),
וּבְסַנְהֶדְרִין (קד.) אָמְרוּ עָלָיו: גְּדוֹלָה לְגִימָה שֶׁמַּשְׁרָה וְכוּלֵי,
and in Sanhedrin 104a they said of him: great is hospitality (legimah), for it causes the Shechinah to rest, etc.,
דְּפֶלֶא, אַטּוּ אֶחָד מַאֲכִיל לַחֲבֵירוֹ?
which is wondrous—can merely feeding someone cause prophecy to rest?
רַק לְפִי שֶׁבְּטוֹב עַיִן נֶאֱמַר "כִּי נָתַן מִלַּחְמוֹ לַדָּל", וְהוּא אָז חָזַר לְקִלְקוּלוֹ וְהָיָה צַר עַיִן,
Rather, because regarding a generous eye it is written: 'for he gives of his bread to the poor' (Proverbs 22:9), and he later regressed to his spiritual flaw and was begrudging,
לְכָךְ אֶצְלוֹ הוּא רְבוּתָא גְּדוֹלָה, כִּי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ דָּן כָּל אֶחָד כְּפִי מַה שֶּׁהוּא בְּמִדּוֹתָיו]:
so for him to feed another was a tremendous spiritual feat, as the Blessed Name judges each person according to his unique traits].

paragraphs.text: Shevuel’s attachment to money is treated as a particular power that can be returned to its source.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Rav Tzadok · Yisrael Kedoshim 5:15: “this occurred later, after the Philistines injected into her [Delilah] the lust for money, mirroring the primeval Serpent; and when they could not seduce her through food or promiscuity, they schemed to corrupt her through monetary greed, the root of all desires; wherefore silver (keseph) shares the root of kisufin, yearning and craving; being the all-inclusive desire through which all worldly acquisitions are obtained. Wherefore even one immersed in another desire is never free from this one; and those who are clean from all other bodily appetites are often not clean from monetary greed; for there are mortals who cherish their money more than their bodies [Berakhot 61b]; showing an obsession with money even when it satisfies no physical appetite and harms the body, loving wealth for its own sake; after the manner of "the mouse lying upon gold dinars" (Sanhedrin 29b); this being the root of the Serpent who bites without deriving any pleasure (Koheles Rabbah 10:11 on Koheles 10:11). And therefore through monetary greed comes the ultimate forgetting of Hashem more than through any other appetite;”

Wherefore even one immersed in another desire is never free from this one; and those who are clean from all other bodily appetites are often not clean from monetary greed; for there are mortals who cherish their money more than their bodies [Berakhot 61b]; showing an obsession with money even when it satisfies no physical appetite and harms the body, loving wealth for its own sake; after the manner of "the mouse lying upon gold dinars" (Sanhedrin 29b); this being the root of the Serpent who bites without deriving any pleasure (Koheles Rabbah 10:11 on Koheles 10:11). And therefore through monetary greed comes the ultimate forgetting of Hashem more than through any other appetite;”

paragraphs.text: Explanation: Yisrael Kedoshim explains why money can be desired for itself even when it no longer serves bodily enjoyment: it gathers many forms of longing into one apparently enduring possession. This makes David’s appointment intelligible. The repair is not simply giving Shevuel enough money to satisfy him, but turning a powerful attachment into responsible service of an entrusted store. The quoted discussion concerns Delilah. Citation correction: the teaching that some people value their money more than their bodies is in Berakhot 61b; the supplied Hebrew’s reference to Pesachim 105a has been corrected in square brackets.

paragraphs.text: Resisei Layla 17:1: “Song arises from longing, which is why there are “songs of desire.” When a person’s soul longs entirely for the blessed Lord and is sick with love for Him, his mouth opens to sing before Him. No songs awaken Israel’s love for their Father in Heaven and their union with Him like the Song of Songs. This love is the opposite of love for this world; therefore it is the holy of holies, belonging entirely to the blessed Lord and wholly separated from all the desires of this world, with no connection to them at all. This is the pattern: that same heart which tastes darkness to its furthest limit and seeks the Lord from there tastes light to its furthest limit, until it attains that there is no darkness—“even darkness does not darken,” and “night shines like day.” So it is with all the traits: in the place of a begrudging eye there is a generous eye, and in the place of an evil heart, a good heart.”

paragraphs.text: A person's natural traits affect the labor required and the significance of overcoming them.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Ishbitz–Radzin · Tiferet Yosef, Talmud Anthology, Taanit 19: “The explanation is this: in actual conduct they were equally righteous. But one needed to labor and endure so that he could turn himself away from a bad trait, while the other did not need that labor. It is like two people: one is naturally, from birth, not prone to anger; the other is prone to anger, suffers from it and labors not to be angry. Hashem therefore gives him greater reward. Although his companion also has no anger, this person suffered and labored against it more than his companion; therefore Hashem gives him greater reward.”

paragraphs.text: Explanation: Tiferet Yosef explains why the Talmud's account of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva need not mean that their outward righteousness differed. One may need to labor against a trait that costs the other no struggle. This directly develops the siman's closing statement that Hashem judges each person according to his particular qualities.

sections.en: The Torah Is Called an Outcry (shav'ah)

p: [קפב] הַתּוֹרָה נִקְרָא "שַׁוְעָה", כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (ג:) עַל פָּסוּק "קִדַּמְתִּי בַנֶּשֶׁף וָאֲשַׁוֵּעָה" (תְּהִלִּים קיט, קמז): עַד חֲצוֹת הָיָה וְכוּלֵי;
The Torah is called an outcry (shav'ah), as stated in Berakhot 3b on the verse "I rose early in the dawn and cried (va-ashave'ah)": until midnight he engaged in Torah, etc.;
כִּי עַל יְדֵי דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה קוֹרִין לְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שָׁם כא.) עַל פָּסוּק "כִּי שֵׁם ה' אֶקְרָא" (דְּבָרִים לב, ג) – בִּרְכַּת הַתּוֹרָה, עַיֵּין שָׁם.

for through words of Torah we call upon the Holy One, blessed be He, as stated (ibid. 21a) on the verse "When I call upon the Name of Hashem" (Deuteronomy 32:3), from which the blessing over Torah study is derived, see there.
כִּי הַתּוֹרָה כֻּלָּהּ שְׁמוֹתָיו וְכוּלֵי, כִּי הַשֵּׁם הוּא הַמִּדּוֹת, וְאֵין סוֹף עַצְמוֹ אֵין לוֹ שֵׁם כְּלָל כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר;
For the entire Torah consists of His holy Names, and a divine Name denotes His attributes, while the Infinite (Ein Sof) Himself has no name at all, as written in the Zohar;
רַק מִדּוֹתָיו, רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר רְצוֹנוֹ הַמִּתְפַּשֵּׁט בַּבְּרוּאִים, וְהַתּוֹרָה כֻּלָּהּ הִיא כְּלָלוּת רְצוֹנוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ.
rather His attributes denote His will expanding within creation, and the entire Torah is the comprehensive embodiment of His blessed will.
וְלָכֵן אָמְרוּ בְּרֵישׁ בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה שֶׁהוּא דְּפוּס מַעֲשֵׂה בְרֵאשִׁית, וּלְכָךְ הִיא שְׁמוֹתָיו, וְלִמּוּדָיו, דְּהַיְינוּ יְדִיעַת זֶה
Therefore they said at the beginning of Bereishit Rabbah that the Torah is the architectural blueprint of Creation; thus it is His Names, and its study—namely the comprehension of this
[וְכֵן נִתְקַן בְּבִרְכַּת הַתּוֹרָה: "יוֹדְעֵי שְׁמֶךָ וְלוֹמְדֵי וְכוּלֵי"],
[and so was it instituted in the blessing of the Torah: 'those who know Your Name and study, etc.'],
נִקְרָא "קְרִיאָה".
is called a calling (keri'ah).
וּכְמוֹ קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע, וּכְמוֹ הַקּוֹרֵא לַחֲבֵירוֹ בִּשְׁמוֹ, כְּשֶׁצּוֹוֵחַ שְׁמוֹ נִקְרָא שֶׁקּוֹרֵא, שֶׁרוֹצֶה שֶׁיָּבוֹא אֶצְלוֹ וְיִפְנֶה לוֹ.
It is like the reading (keri'at) of Shema, and like one calling his fellow by name: when he calls his name it is termed calling, for he desires that he come to him and turn toward him.

וְכֵן תּוֹרָה עַל מְנָת לַעֲשׂוֹת, הַיְינוּ: "הִדָּבֵק בְּמִדּוֹתָיו וְכוּלֵי", הַיְינוּ לִהְיוֹת כִּרְצוֹנוֹ, שֶׁזֶּהוּ שֶׁיָּבוֹא אֶצְלוֹ, כְּעִנְיַן "וְשָׁכַנְתִּי בְּתוֹכָם" (שְׁמוֹת כה, ח), שֶׁזֶּהוּ עַל יְדֵי דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה.

So too, Torah studied in order to practice means: "cleave unto His attributes, etc.," meaning to conform to His will, which draws Him near, in the spirit of "and I will dwell among them" (Exodus 25:8), which is achieved through words of Torah.
וּלְכָךְ נִקְרָא "שַׁוְעָה", דְּהוּא מֵעֲשָׂרָה לְשׁוֹנוֹת שֶׁל תְּפִלָּה (מִדְרָשׁ רַבָּה רֵישׁ פָּרָשַׁת וָאֶתְחַנַּן),
And therefore it is called an outcry (shav'ah), which is one of the ten expressions of prayer (Devarim Rabbah, Va'etchanan),
וּבַזֹּהַר (שְׁמוֹת יט סוֹף עַמּוּד ב): אֵין לְךָ שַׁוְעָה אֶלָּא בִּתְפִלָּה וְכוּלֵי, וּבַכָּתוּב דְּמַיְיתֵי נִזְכַּר תְּפִלָּה וְשַׁוְעָה.
and in the Zohar (Shemot 19b end): there is no shav'ah except in prayer, etc., and in the verse cited there prayer and shav'ah are linked.
רַק "שַׁוְעָה" לְשׁוֹן שְׁעִיָּה, רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר שֶׁיִּפְנֶה אֵלָיו, עַל דֶּרֶךְ קְרִיאָה
Only that shav'ah is related to she'iyah (turning toward), meaning that He turn toward him, by way of calling

[שֶׁהוּא גַּם כֵּן מִלְּשׁוֹנוֹת שֶׁל תְּפִלָּה; וּבְדִבְרֵי רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה מוּרְגָּל "הַקּוֹרֵא בַּתּוֹרָה" וְלֹא בִּתְפִלָּה, כִּדְאָמְרוּ (עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה נח:): לְשׁוֹן תּוֹרָה לְחוּד וּלְשׁוֹן חֲכָמִים לְחוּד;

[which is likewise one of the expressions of prayer; and in rabbinic idiom it is common to say 'one who reads in the Torah' and not in prayer, reflecting Avodah Zarah 58b: the language of the Torah is distinct from the language of the Sages;

כִּי בִּלְשׁוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הַקְּרִיאָה קָרוּי תְּפִלָּה, וְתוֹרָה נִקְרָא הַקְּבִיעוּת בַּלֵּב וּבְמַעֲשֶׂה, דְּהַיְינוּ הָעֲנִיָּה, וְזֶהוּ בֶּאֱמֶת תּוֹרַת ה', אֲבָל לְשׁוֹן חֲכָמִים הַקְּרִיאָה הוּא הַתּוֹרָה, וְהָבֵן זֶה],

for in God's language, calling is termed prayer, while Torah is the engraving in heart and action, namely the divine response, which is truly Hashem's Torah; but in the Sages' tongue, reading is termed Torah, and understand this],
דְּהַיְינוּ הַשְׁרָאַת הַשְּׁכִינָה בַּלֵּב, כְּמוֹ בְּקַבָּלַת הַקָּרְבָּן שֶׁהוּא הַשְׁרָאַת הַשְּׁכִינָה נֶאֱמַר בְּקַיִן שֶׁלֹּא קִבֵּל לְשׁוֹן "לֹא שָׁעָה" (בְּרֵאשִׁית ד, ה).

which means causing the Shechinah to dwell in the heart, just as regarding the acceptance of an offering—which represents the resting of the Shechinah—it was said of Cain, whose offering was rejected, "He had no respect (lo sha'ah)" (Genesis 4:5).
וּמַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב אֵין וְכוּלֵי אֶלָּא בִּתְפִלָּה, הַיְינוּ כַּנּוֹדָע דְּאֵין תּוֹרָה אֶלָּא בִּמְקוֹם תְּפִלָּה, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּמְגִילָּה (כט.).
And what was stated, that there is no shav'ah except in prayer, aligns with the known principle that Torah belongs in the place of prayer, as stated in Megillah 29a.
כִּי תְּפִלָּה נִקְרָא יִרְאָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (ט:) עַל פָּסוּק "יִירָאוּךָ עִם שָׁמֶשׁ" (תְּהִלִּים עב, ה);
For prayer is termed fear/awe, as stated in Berakhot 9b on the verse "They shall fear You while the sun endures" (Psalms 72:5);
וְדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה שִׂמְחָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "פִּקּוּדֵי ה' יְשָׁרִים מְשַׂמְּחֵי לֵב" (שָׁם יט, ט);
and words of Torah are joy, as written: "The statutes of Hashem are right, rejoicing the heart" (Psalms 19:9);
וְזֶהוּ יַחַד, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּתַנָּא דְבֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ רַבָּה (רֵישׁ פֶּרֶק ג): אֲנִי יָרֵאתִי מִתּוֹךְ שִׂמְחָתִי וְכוּלֵי,
and these two unite, as stated in Tanna DeBei Eliyahu Rabbah (chapter 3): "I feared out of my joy, etc.,"
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּאָבוֹת (פֶּרֶק ג, יז): אִם אֵין יִרְאָה וְכוּלֵי,
and as stated in Avot (3:17): "If there is no fear, there is no wisdom, etc.,"
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּתִּיקּוּנִים (תִּיקּוּן י) דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא בְּלָא דְחִילוּ וּרְחִימוּ לָא פָּרְחַת לְעֵילָא,
and as stated in the Tikkunim (Tikkun 10) that Torah without awe and love does not fly upward,
וְאִם כֵּן אֵין כָּאן קְרִיאָה כְּלָל.
and if so, there is no true calling upon God at all.
אֲבָל תּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּמְקוֹם תְּפִלָּה נִקְרָא "שַׁוְעָה".
But Torah studied in the place of prayer is termed an outcry (shav'ah).
וְזֶהוּ "וַתַּעַל שַׁוְעָתָם אֶל הָאֱלֹהִים מִן הָעֲבֹדָה" (שְׁמוֹת ב, כג),

paragraphs.text: Torah's many divine names concern the powers disclosed to created understanding, while their source remains one.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Rav Tzadok · Sichat Malakhei HaSharet, From Tanchuma 1: “In truth, at their root all is one, singular and united, just as before the world was created. Only in the created being's perception is there a perception of different powers, and according to each power He is named. Therefore the entire Torah, which includes the order of all the powers found in creation, consists of the names of Hashem, the source of life and existence for all these powers. Within every power we recognize that Hashem is the master of that power; He is therefore named for us as the master of that power, and so with every particular. These are deep matters, clear to one who understands.”

paragraphs.text: Explanation: Sichat Malakhei HaSharet explains the premise behind calling through Torah: a name makes a particular revealed power recognizable, and Torah orders the powers present in creation. The multiplicity belongs to the recipient's apprehension, while the source remains one. This gives content to the siman's distinction between the infinite source beyond names and the divine will expressed in the Torah and its commandments.

paragraphs.text: Calling in truth through Torah
The closeness of Torah explains a calling that reaches beyond the ordinary favorable time for prayer.

rich.text: The closeness of Torah explains a calling that reaches beyond the ordinary favorable time for prayer.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Rav Tzadok · Machshavot Charutz 15:7: “It uses the expression ‘he entreated,’ which the Sages explained in Sukkah 14a as turning judgment to mercy like a pitchfork. Every prayer needs a favorable time, as it says (Psalms 69:14), ‘My prayer to You, Hashem, is at a favorable time,’ and as the Sages said (Berakhot 8a), there are appointed times for prayer. At a time of judgment, which is not favorable, he is not answered. Torah, however, is above the sun and time. Of this it says (Psalms 145:18), ‘Hashem is near to all who call Him, to all who call Him in truth,’ and truth means Torah (Berakhot 5b). Through calling Him by means of Torah, He is close always, to every soul and at every time, for this is attachment to the living God, with nothing intervening.”

paragraphs.text: Explanation: Machshavot Charutz uses the same verse and the same identification of truth with Torah. It distinguishes prayer's favorable time from the connection through Torah described as having no barrier. This explains why the siman calls Torah joined with prayer a cry that rises beyond prayer alone, while preserving the surrounding requirement of awe and actual inward connection.

sections.en: "Conversing" (Sichah) Denotes Mundane Conversation

p: [קפג] "שִׂיחָה" נִקְרָא מִילֵּי דְּעָלְמָא, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּסֻכָּה (כא:): מִשִּׂיחָתוֹ שֶׁל רַבָּן גַּמְלִיאֵל וְכוּלֵי, וּבְעֵירוּבִין (נד:) עַל פָּסוּק "עַל דֶּרֶךְ שִׂיחוּ" – אֵלּוּ וְכוּלֵי;

"Conversing" (sichah) denotes mundane conversation, as stated in Sukkah 21b: from the casual conversation of Rabban Gamliel, etc., and in Eruvin 54b on the verse "tell of it, you that walk by the way" (Judges 5:10)—these are the masters of Talmud;
אֲבָל "דִּבּוּר" הוּא דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּתַעֲנִית (י:) עַל פָּסוּק "הָלוֹךְ וְדַבֵּר", עַיֵּין שָׁם.
but "speech" (dibbur) denotes words of Torah, as stated in Ta'anit 10b on the verse "as they went on and talked" (II Kings 2:11), see there.
רַק רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר שֶׁלֹּא בְּכַוָּנָה גְּמוּרָה, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (יג:) עַל פָּסוּק "לְדַבֵּר בָּם" – כִּי הֵיכִי דְּלִיגְרְסוּ.
Only that it implies articulation without deep meditative intention, as stated in Berakhot 13b on "to speak of them"—so that they may recite (ligresu).
וְגִירְסָא הַיְינוּ הֲגַם דְּלָא יָדַע מַאי קָאָמַר, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (יט.) עַל פָּסוּק "גָּרְסָה נַפְשִׁי" (תְּהִלִּים קיט, כ).
And girsa (vocal recitation) applies even when one does not fully understand what he is saying, as stated in Avodah Zarah 19a on "my soul breaks (garsah) for the longing."
אֲבָל הַיְּדִיעָה הַגְּמוּרָה נִקְרָא לִמּוּד וְעֵסֶק בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה, שֶׁעַל זֶה מְבָרְכִין "לַעֲסוֹק בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה".
But thorough comprehension is termed study (limud) and engagement in words of Torah, over which we recite the blessing "to engage in the words of Torah."
וּמִמַּה שֶׁאָמְרוּ שָׁם: אַגְמִירוּ וְכוּלֵי כִּי הֵיכִי דְּלִיגְרְסוּ, נִרְאֶה דִּבְהַתְחָלָה צָרִיךְ לְיַגֵּעַ שֶׁיִּהְיוּ דְּבָרִים הַיּוֹצְאִים מִן הַלֵּב;
And from what is stated there—teach them so that they recite—it appears that initially one must labor so that words emerge from the heart;
אֲבָל אַחַר כָּךְ זוֹכֶה לְדִבּוּר וְגִירְסָא הֲגַם דְּלָא יָדַע מַאי קָאָמַר, שֶׁזֶּה נִקְרָא פִּטְטַיָּא דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא, גַּם כֵּן הוּא דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה גָּמוּר.
but subsequently one merits verbal articulation and recitation even when he does not fully grasp what he is saying, which is termed casual chatter of the Torah, and is likewise authentic Torah.
וְהוּא מַה שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (שָׁם): בַּתְּחִלָּה תּוֹרַת ה', וְאַחַר כָּךְ תּוֹרָתוֹ;
And this is what is stated in Avodah Zarah (ibid.): initially it is called Hashem's Torah, and afterward his own Torah;

וּכְשֶׁזּוֹכֶה דְּהוּא תּוֹרָתוֹ, דּוּגְמַת אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם נַעֲשׂוּ שְׁתֵּי כִּלְיוֹתָיו וְכוּלֵי (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה סא), גַּם דִּבּוּר שֶׁהוּא מֵהַשָּׂפָה וְלַחוּץ הוּא דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה.
and when one merits that it becomes his own Torah, like our father Abraham whose two kidneys became like two teachers (Bereishit Rabbah 61:1), even speech that is from the lips outward is Torah.
וּמַה שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּדוֹאֵג בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין (קו:) שֶׁכָּל תּוֹרָתוֹ וְכוּלֵי מִשָּׂפָה וְלַחוּץ, הַיְינוּ שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה לוֹ הַהַתְחָלָה;
And what was stated of Doeg in Sanhedrin 106b that all his Torah was from the lip outward was because he never experienced the holy beginning;
וְגַם כִּי עַל יְדֵי לָשׁוֹן הָרָע נִתְקַלְקֵל הַדִּבּוּר שֶׁמֵּהַשָּׂפָה וְלַחוּץ.
and also because through slander his external speech became ruined.

וְזֶה שֶׁפָּתַח בִּדְבָרִים רַבָּה בְּפָסוּק "מַרְפֵּא לָשׁוֹן וְגוֹמֵר" (מִשְׁלֵי טו, ד) עַיֵּין שָׁם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (זֹהַר חֵלֶק ג, רסא עַמּוּד א): מִשְׁנֵה תּוֹרָה מֹשֶׁה מִפִּי עַצְמוֹ אֲמָרָן.

And this explains why Devarim Rabbah opened with the verse "A soothing tongue is a tree of life" (Proverbs 15:4), see there, for the Zohar (Part III, 261a) states: the Book of Deuteronomy Moses uttered from his own mouth.

כִּי מִפִּי הַגְּבוּרָה הַיְינוּ שְׁכִינָה מְדַבֶּרֶת מִתּוֹךְ גְּרוֹנוֹ, שֶׁזֶּה נִקְרָא דְּבָרִים הַיּוֹצְאִים מִן הַלֵּב, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּשִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים רַבָּה עַל פָּסוּק "וְלִבִּי עֵר" – שֶׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לִבָּן שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל.

For from the mouth of the Almighty means the Shechinah speaks through his throat, which is termed words emerging from the heart, as stated in Shir HaShirim Rabbah on "my heart was awake"—the Holy One is the heart of Israel.
אֲבָל לְשׁוֹן "אֵלֶּה הַדְּבָרִים אֲשֶׁר דִּבֶּר וְגוֹמֵר" (דְּבָרִים א, א) מַשְׁמָע מִשָּׂפָה וְלַחוּץ, דְּלֹא יָדַע וְכוּלֵי,
But the phrasing "These are the words which Moses spoke" implies from the lip outward, where he did not consciously generate it,
פֵּירוּשׁ: מַדְרֵגַת הַדַּעַת שֶׁהוּא מַדְרֵגַת מֹשֶׁה – שְׁכִינָה מְדַבֶּרֶת וְכוּלֵי – לֹא הָיָה אָז, רַק מִפִּי עַצְמוֹ.
meaning the level of Da'at which is the stature of Moses—where the Shechinah speaks—was not operating then, but he spoke from his own mouth.
וּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם אָמַר "לֹא אִישׁ דְּבָרִים", כִּי הוּא מַדְרֵגַת בַּעְלָהּ דְּמַטְרוֹנִיתָא שֶׁכָּל דְּבָרָיו נִקְרָא תּוֹרַת ה', וּמִלָּתוֹ לְבַד עַל לְשׁוֹנוֹ.

And Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, had said "I am not a man of words" (Exodus 4:10), because his level was the Husband of the Matronita, where all his words were Hashem's Torah, His word alone upon his tongue.
וְזֶה נִקְרָא "עֵץ חַיִּים" כַּאֲשֶׁר יוֹצֵא מִן הַלֵּב שֶׁמִּמֶּנּוּ תּוֹצְאוֹת חַיִּים.
And this is termed a "tree of life" when it emerges from the heart from which flow the issues of life (Proverbs 4:23).
וְזֶהוּ "מַרְפֵּא לָשׁוֹן" – שֶׁיָּכוֹל לְדַבֵּר אַחַר כָּךְ דְּבָרִים בַּלָּשׁוֹן לְבַד.
And this is "a soothing tongue"—that one can subsequently speak words through the tongue alone.
וְהֵם שָׁלֹשׁ מַדְרֵגוֹת: בַּעֲלֵי מִקְרָא – זֶהוּ תּוֹרַת ה', וּבַעֲלֵי מִשְׁנָה – זֶהוּ תּוֹרָתוֹ,
And these form three rungs: masters of Scripture represent Hashem's Torah; masters of Mishnah represent his own Torah;
וּבַעֲלֵי תַלְמוּד הוּא שֶׁאַחַר כָּךְ זוֹכֶה לְמַדְרֵגַת הַשִּׂיחָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ: "שִׂיחוּ" – אֵלּוּ בַּעֲלֵי תַלְמוּד, שֶׁכָּל שִׂיחָתָן וְכוּלֵי:
and masters of Talmud represent one who subsequently merits the level of casual conversation, as stated: "tell of it"—these are the masters of Talmud, all of whose conversation is Torah.

paragraphs.text: Sefer HaZikhronot 14:2: “It appears, however, that their language and their reading are included in the commandment of Torah study, like one studying Ezekiel’s passage of the Chariot: he is certainly called one who studies Torah, although he understands only the plain narrative. We read the Chariot as the haftarah on Shavuot; although none of us knows the extent of its mysteries, the reader is considered to be studying the words of the Prophets. In the first chapter of Avodah Zarah, concerning the revealed parts of Torah as well, they said: “Let a person recite, even though he does not know what he is saying.” The same applies to its hidden parts: since they are actual words of Torah, even though he does not understand, he has studied Torah. The Ari, our honored teacher Rabbi Yitzḥak of blessed memory, said that the language of the holy Zohar is beneficial to the soul. It seems that the intention is that familiarity with its language helps one arrive at true understanding.”

paragraphs.text: Context: Rav Tzadok distinguishes the value of reading Torah from having already attained its inner meaning. The continuation does not make reading esoteric books obligatory and rejects adopting mystical prayer intentions without understanding them. The positive point relevant here is that faithful recitation can prepare the way for genuine understanding.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Rav Tzadok · Peri Tzadik, Rosh Chodesh Shvat 6:2: “It further says: because Moses said, “I am heavy of mouth,” and “I am not a man of words,” he merited the Holy One’s saying to him, “Mouth to mouth I speak with him,” and merited saying, “These are the words.” This is as stated in Tanchuma, Devarim 2, and in the Midrash Rabbah there: “Yesterday you said, ‘I am not a man of words,’ and now you speak so much,” and so forth; “Study the Torah and be healed,” and so forth. As it says, “A healing tongue is a tree of life.” The book of Deuteronomy is the root of the whole Oral Torah, as stated in Zohar III, 261a: “The Written Torah and the Oral Torah,” and “it is called Torah and Mishneh Torah.” Moses our teacher said this on Rosh Chodesh Shevat, as it says, “In the eleventh month, on the first of the month, Moses spoke,” and so forth—the month formed with the letter tzadi.”

rich.text: : “It further says: because Moses said, “I am heavy of mouth,” and “I am not a man of words,” he merited the Holy One’s saying to him, “Mouth to mouth I speak with him,” and merited saying, “These are the words.” This is as stated in Tanchuma, Devarim 2, and in the Midrash Rabbah there: “Yesterday you said, ‘I am not a man of words,’ and now you speak so much,” and so forth; “Study the Torah and be healed,” and so forth. As it says, “A healing tongue is a tree of life.” The book of Deuteronomy is the root of the whole Oral Torah, as stated in Zohar III, 261a: “The Written Torah and the Oral Torah,” and “it is called Torah and Mishneh Torah.” Moses our teacher said this on Rosh Chodesh Shevat, as it says, “In the eleventh month, on the first of the month, Moses spoke,” and so forth—the month formed with the letter tzadi.”

paragraphs.text: Explanation: The Shvat passage presents Moshe’s later speech as the result of an earlier encounter with Torah that transformed his capacity to speak. This helps explain the order emphasized in the present siman: inward Torah comes first; only afterward can speech emerging readily from the person be called his own Torah. ‘From his own mouth’ thus describes an attained expression of Torah, not an independence from its divine source or a claim that every unprepared utterance has the same standing.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Ishbitz–Radzin · Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Noach 6: “‘The whole earth had one speech and common words.’ It does not say one tongue. The principal tongue is the holy tongue, which is implanted deep in the heart and flows from the root of life. Other tongues are called a stammering tongue, as it says (Isaiah 33:19), ‘A stammering tongue without understanding’: it has no root of life in the heart, for understanding is in the heart. Although the generation of the dispersion spoke the holy tongue, it had no root of life in them; they spoke it only from the lips outward, like the chatter and chirping of birds and other creatures. So too concerning the serpent: the commentators ask why its curse does not mention taking away its tongue. In truth it had no tongue at the root, since it spoke slander against its Creator. Understand this.”

paragraphs.text: Explanation: Mei HaShiloach contrasts holy language rooted in the heart with outward use of the same words by the generation of the dispersion. Its final harmful-speech example also matches the siman's qualification concerning Doeg. This helps distinguish superficial recitation without an inward beginning from the speech that remains Torah after such a beginning has been acquired.

Rabban Gamliel possessed this power in particular, as they said (Eruvin 64b): “From here we learned that Rabban Gamliel discerned correctly through the holy spirit.” The holy spirit means that the speech flows from the supernal holiness mentioned above. sections.en: The Beginning of Words of Torah Is Passionate Desire

p: [קפד] הַהַתְחָלָה לְדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה הוּא הַחֵשֶׁק, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "כִּי אִם בְּתוֹרַת ה' חֶפְצוֹ" (תְּהִלִּים א, ב), וְאָז נִקְרָא תּוֹרַת ה' כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (יט.),
The beginning of words of Torah is passionate desire, as written: "his delight is in the law of Hashem" (Psalms 1:2), and then it is termed Hashem's Torah, as stated in Avodah Zarah 19a;
וְאַחַר כָּךְ הַהַשָּׂגָה שֶׁנִּקְרָא "וּבְתוֹרָתוֹ יֶהְגֶּה וְגוֹמֵר" (שָׁם).
and afterward comes comprehension, termed "and in his law does he meditate, etc." (ibid.).

וְהַחֵשֶׁק גָּדוֹל יוֹתֵר, כְּמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי עַל פָּסוּק "טוֹב שֵׁם מִשֶּׁמֶן טוֹב" (קֹהֶלֶת ז, א) וְעַל מַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה: גְּדוֹלָה שִׁמּוּשָׁהּ וְכוּלֵי (בְּרָכוֹת ז:).

And desire is greater, as I heard expounded on "A good name is better than precious oil" (Ecclesiastes 7:1) and on the rabbinic dictum: "Greater is the serving of Torah than its study, etc." (Berakhot 7b).

וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם זֶהוּ בַּהַתְחָלָה וּבְיַלְדוּת שֶׁאָז הַחֵשֶׁק גּוֹבֵר, וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ שִׁילְהֵי שַׁבָּת (קנב.): יַנְקוּתָא כְּלִילָא דְּוַרְדָּא וְכוּלֵי, עַיֵּין שָׁם שְׁבַח הַיַּלְדוּת וּגְנוּת הַזִּקְנָה שֶׁאָז הַחֵשֶׁק כָּבָה.

Nonetheless, this belongs to the beginning and to youth when desire surges, concerning which they stated at the end of Shabbat (152a): youth is a crown of roses, etc., see there the praise of youth and the dispraise of old age when desire cools.

וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה: זִקְנֵי תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים וְכוּלֵי, וְכֵן בְּכַמָּה מְקוֹמוֹת נִשְׁתַּבְּחוּ זְקֵנִים, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּשְׁמוֹת רַבָּה (פָּרָשָׁה ה) וּבְוַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה (סוֹף פָּרָשָׁה יא),
Yet our Sages stated: as elderly scholars age their minds settle, and the elderly are praised in several places, as in Shemot Rabbah (chapter 5) and Vayikra Rabbah (end of chapter 11);
דְּבֶאֱמֶת אָמְרוּ (תַּעֲנִית ז.): הַרְבֵּה לָמַדְתִּי מֵרַבּוֹתַי וְכוּלֵי וּמִתַּלְמִידַי יוֹתֵר וְכוּלֵי, וּמֵרַבּוֹתַי הַיְינוּ הַהַתְחָלָה וְהַחֵשֶׁק.
for in truth they taught (Ta'anit 7a): "I have learned much from my teachers, and from my disciples more than from all of them," where learning from teachers represents the beginning and the desire.
וְאַחַר פְּטִירַת הָרַב, וְנִקְרָא "תּוֹרָתוֹ" שֶׁיָּגַע מֵעַצְמוֹ לְלַמֵּד לַאֲחֵרִים, אָז לָמַד יוֹתֵר וּמוֹסִיפִים חָכְמָה,
And after the teacher's passing, when it is called "his own Torah" as he toils on his own to teach others, then he learns more and increases in wisdom;

רַק שֶׁהַהַשָּׂגָה הוּא מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, כִּי "ה' יִתֵּן חָכְמָה", וְהַכֹּל בִּידֵי שָׁמַיִם חוּץ מִיִּרְאַת שָׁמַיִם שֶׁהוּא מִדַּת הַנּוּקְבָא וְהָאִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְתַתָּא בְּחֵשֶׁק וְרָצוֹן כַּנּוֹדָע, זֶהוּ בִּידֵי אָדָם, לְכָךְ זֶהוּ טוֹב וְגָדוֹל.

only that comprehension is from the Blessed Name, for "Hashem gives wisdom" (Proverbs 2:6), and all is in the hands of Heaven except the fear of Heaven, which is the feminine attribute and the awakening from below in desire and will, which is in human hands, making it good and great.
מִכָּל מָקוֹם הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עוֹשֶׂה מִתּוֹרַת ה' תּוֹרָתוֹ, וְאוֹמֵר שֶׁגַּם זֶה שֶׁלּוֹ וְהוּא הַמְחַדֵּשׁ הַחִדּוּשִׁין דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא,
Nevertheless, the Blessed Name transforms Hashem's Torah into the person's own Torah, affirming that this too is his and that he is innovating novel Torah insights,
וְהוּא מַדְרֵגָה גְּדוֹלָה כְּעִנְיַן: עֲתִידִים צַדִּיקִים שֶׁיִּקָּרְאוּ בִּשְׁמוֹ שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא עה:);
which is an exalted level, akin to: the righteous are destined to be called by the Name of the Holy One, blessed be He (Bava Batra 75b);
כִּי הַתּוֹרָה כֻּלָּהּ שְׁמוֹתָיו שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא – וְזֶהוּ מִצַּד תּוֹרַת ה',
for the entire Torah is the Names of the Holy One—which is from the side of Hashem's Torah;
וְגַם שְׁמוֹתָן שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל כַּנּוֹדָע דְּיֵשׁ שִׁשִּׁים רִבּוֹא אוֹתִיּוֹת לַתּוֹרָה – וְזֶהוּ מִצַּד תּוֹרָתוֹ.
and it is also the names of Israel, as known that there are 600,000 letters in the Torah—which is from the side of his own Torah.
וּלְכָךְ פְּתִיחַת סֵפֶר שְׁמוֹת שֶׁהוּא סֵפֶר מַתַּן תּוֹרָה בְּ"וְאֵלֶּה שְׁמוֹת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל" (שְׁמוֹת א, א).
And therefore the opening of the Book of Shemot, which is the book of the Giving of the Torah, begins with: "Now these are the names of the children of Israel" (Exodus 1:1).
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי, כִּי פְּתִיחַת כָּל סֵפֶר וּפָרָשָׁה הוּא צוּרְתָא דִּשְׁמַעְתָּא שֶׁל אוֹתוֹ סֵפֶר וּפָרָשָׁה,
And as I heard, the opening of every book and section is the thematic essence (tzurata dishemata) of that book and section,
וְכָךְ קְרִיאַת שֵׁם הַסֵּפֶר "שְׁמוֹת" עַל שֵׁם שְׁמוֹת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל, שֶׁזֶּהוּ כְּלָלוּת הַתּוֹרָה, כִּי הַשֵּׁם הוּא יְסוֹד הַדָּבָר.
and so naming the book Shemot (Names) reflects the names of the children of Israel, which is the totality of the Torah, for the name is the essence of a thing.
וּלְכָךְ אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן קָרָא שֵׁמוֹת וְהַמַּלְאָכִים לֹא יָדְעוּ, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה יז),
And therefore Adam the First assigned names while the angels could not, as our Sages stated (Bereishit Rabbah 17),
דְּמַלְאָכִים אֵין לָהֶם שֵׁם, דִּלְפִי שְׁלִיחוּתוֹ נִקְרָא (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ שָׁם פָּרָשָׁה עח).
for angels possess no fixed names, being named according to their temporary mission (ibid. 78).

וְהוּא עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁכָּתְבוּ הַקַּדְמוֹנִים, כִּי מִנְהַג מִצְרַיִם גַּם כֵּן וְאֶרֶץ הַקֶּדֶם שֶׁהָאֲדוֹנִים יִקְרְאוּ לְעַבְדֵיהֶם שֵׁמוֹת כִּרְצוֹנָם, לְהוֹרוֹת כִּי אֵינוֹ רְשׁוּת וּבַעַל בְּחִירָה בִּפְנֵי עַצְמוֹ כְּלָל.

And this is in line with what early authors wrote, that in ancient Egypt and the East masters assigned names to their servants at will, to signify that the servant has no independent agency or free choice at all.

וּכְפִי הַשָּׂגַת הַמַּלְאָכִים שֶׁאֵין לָהֶם בְּחִירָה, כָּךְ תְּפִיסָתָם בְּכָל הַנִּבְרָאִים, וּמִי שֶׁאָמַר לַשֶּׁמֶן וְיִדְלַק יֹאמַר לַחֹמֶץ וְיִדְלַק, אִם כֵּן אֵין לְשׁוּם דָּבָר שֵׁם מְיוּחָד.

And according to the perception of angels who lack free will, such is their grasp of all creations: He Who commanded the oil to burn can command vinegar to burn, so nothing has an intrinsic, unalterable name.

רַק הָאָדָם שֶׁנִּבְרָא בִּבְחִירָה, הוּא מַשִּׂיג הַנִּבְרָאִים מִצַּד כֹּחַ בְּחִירָתוֹ – כֹּחַ טִבְעָם הַמּוּטְבָּע, כְּאִלּוּ הוּא דָּבָר נִפְרָד וְנִבְדָּל וְעוֹמֵד בִּפְנֵי עַצְמוֹ בְּטִבְעוֹ, לְכָךְ יֵשׁ לוֹ שֵׁם.
Only man who was created with free will perceives creations through the power of choice—their embedded natural character—as though an entity stands distinct in its nature; hence it has a name.
וְהַהַתְחָלָה לְדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה הוּא מִצַּד הַבְּחִירָה, זֶה נִקְרָא שְׁמוֹת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל, וְהַסִּיּוּם – שְׁמוֹת הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא.
And the beginning of Torah study is from the side of choice, termed the names of the children of Israel, while its conclusion is the Names of the Holy One, blessed be He.
אֲבָל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא אוֹמֵר לְהֵיפֶךְ: בַּתְּחִלָּה תּוֹרַת ה' וְכוּלֵי.
But the Holy One says the reverse: initially it is Hashem's Torah, etc.
וְכַיּוֹצֵא בוֹ בִּבְרָכוֹת (לה.): "לַה' הָאָרֶץ וּמְלוֹאָהּ" (תְּהִלִּים כד, א) קוֹדֶם בְּרָכָה,
And similarly in Berakhot 35a: "The earth is Hashem's and the fullness thereof" applies prior to a blessing,
שֶׁכְּשֶׁסָּבוּר שֶׁזֶּה נִבְדָּל מִצַּד מִדַּת הַבְּחִירָה אָז "לַה' הָאָרֶץ",
for when one thinks it stands independent through the dimension of choice, then "the earth is Hashem's";
וְאַחַר הַבְּרָכָה שֶׁמַּכִּיר שֶׁהַכֹּל שֶׁלּוֹ, אָז "הָאָרֶץ נָתַן לִבְנֵי אָדָם" (שָׁם קטו, טז).
and after the blessing when he recognizes that all is His, then "the earth has He given to the children of men" (Psalms 115:16).
וְכֵן כָּאן: אָז נִקְרָא תּוֹרָתוֹ.
And so here: then it is called his own Torah.
וְצַדִּיקִים נִקְרְאוּ בִּשְׁמוֹתָיו שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא, כִּי שְׁמוֹת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל הֵם עַצְמָם שְׁמוֹת הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל, וּלְכָךְ הַזִּקְנָה מְשֻׁבַּחַת.
And the righteous are called by the Names of the Holy One, because the names of the children of Israel are themselves the Names of the Holy One as noted above; therefore old age is praiseworthy.
רַק מִצַּד הַכְּלִילָא וְהַכֶּתֶר שֶׁהוּא מִצַּד בְּחִירַת הָאָדָם, הַיַּנְקוּת טוֹב וְגָדוֹל כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל:
Only that from the perspective of the crown rooted in human choice, youth is precious and great as noted above.

paragraphs.text: Chanukah’s language of education explains how an initial enthusiasm can remain fruitful when its first intensity has cooled.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Rav Tzadok · Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 7:1: “Chanukah means a beginning, when a person begins to educate himself. Through this something remains fixed for all time, as he accustoms himself through the desire and will of his youthful days, as it says: ‘Educate the youth according to his way; even when he grows old, he will not depart from it.’”

rich.text: : “Chanukah means a beginning, when a person begins to educate himself. Through this something remains fixed for all time, as he accustoms himself through the desire and will of his youthful days, as it says: ‘Educate the youth according to his way; even when he grows old, he will not depart from it.’”

paragraphs.text: Explanation: Chanukah connects the beginning of self-education with habit formed through youthful desire. This helps resolve the present siman’s praise of both youth and old age. Desire has a distinctive greatness as the person’s awakening, while its lasting fruit appears in a learned way that continues into mature understanding and teaching. The cooling of the first excitement need not mean the loss of what that desire established.

paragraphs.text: Mei HaShiloach, Volume II, Five Scrolls, Ecclesiastes 5: ““A good name is better than good oil.” A name alludes to desire, as explained in many places in the first volume. Thus “David made a name” means diligence and exertion in serving God, as stated in the holy Zohar, Vayera 116b. Good oil signifies clarity and wisdom in Torah. “A good name” thus means that desire and diligence are better than knowledge and wisdom. Just as someone satisfied with one loaf should not envy someone who needs many loaves, a person who studies one chapter all day should not envy a person of broad understanding who studies several chapters. The essential thing is diligence and desire: this is precious before God. How long a person takes to grasp a matter makes no difference to this value. This is “a good name is better than good oil.””

paragraphs.text: Resisei Layla 52:2: “Our Sages, of blessed memory, said (Berakhot 7b, end): “Serving Torah is greater than studying it.” I heard that study has a limit: how much a person comprehends. Service, however, is the longing and love of the one who serves, which move him to serve and to strive to raise the banner of Torah; this has no limit. He does not comprehend the substance of the Torah revealed to the sages, but only desires and yearns for Torah—that is, for the root of the whole Torah. Thus, service also encompasses the power of the hidden fiftieth gate.”

paragraphs.text: Longing expands an initial reception of Torah into continuing growth.

rich.text: Longing expands an initial reception of Torah into continuing growth.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Ishbitz–Radzin · Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Bereshit 15: “‘This is the book of Adam's generations; in God's likeness He made him.’ The secret of image and likeness is this: image is the substance of life without expansion, like a newborn infant at its first instant. Afterward it begins to expand through its desires, such as the desire to eat. Through that desire it eats, and its life grows continually until it matures in breadth and height. That expansion is called likeness. So too in the soul: the first drop of Torah entering a person is called image; the yearning for Torah is called likeness. Through that yearning more Torah is continually added. This is ‘On the day God created Adam, in God's likeness…’: the principal purpose of man's creation was to desire continually the increase of Torah. This is the meaning of the saying (Berakhot 7b), ‘Serving Torah is greater than its study’: serving Torah is called the yearning. ‘This is the book of Adam's generations’ means that if a person merits image and likeness as explained, he will continually see new Torah, count his years and generations, and lengthen his days.”

This adds a mechanism for the siman's valuation of early desire while its later discussion preserves the value of mature attainment.

paragraphs.text: Shabbat 152a: ‘It was taught: Rabbi Yosei bar Kisma says: Two [legs] are better than three [with a staff]. Woe for the one thing that goes and does not return. What is it? Rav Chisda said: Youth. When Rav Dimi came, he said: Youth is a wreath of roses; old age is a wreath of nettles. It was taught in Rabbi Meir’s name: Chew with your teeth, and you will find the benefit in your steps, as it is said: ‘We had our fill of bread and were well, and we saw no harm.’ Shmuel said to Rav Yehuda: ‘Sharp one, open your sack [your mouth] and let in your bread. p: [קפה] שָׁלֹשׁ מַדְרֵגוֹת לְתַלְמִיד חָכָם: רַב, וְחָבֵר, וְתַלְמִיד, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּתַעֲנִית (ז.): הַרְבֵּה לָמַדְתִּי מֵרַבּוֹתַי, וּמֵחֲבֵירַי וְכוּלֵי, וּמִתַּלְמִידַי וְכוּלֵי

There are three stages for a Torah scholar: master, colleague, and disciple, as stated in Ta'anit 7a: "I have learned much from my teachers, from my colleagues more, and from my disciples most of all"
[וְהֵם עַצְמָן ג' מַדְרֵגוֹת הַנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל אוֹת קפ"ג, כָּל אֶחָד בִּשְׁעָתוֹ, כַּמּוּבָן לַמַּשְׂכִּיל];
[and these are the very three rungs mentioned above in Section 183, each in its time, as understood to the discerning];
וּשְׁתֵּי רִאשׁוֹנוֹת הֵם בְּיָדוֹ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּפֶרֶק א דְּאָבוֹת: "עֲשֵׂה וְכוּלֵי וּקְנֵה וְכוּלֵי", מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן תַּלְמִיד, עַיֵּין שָׁם בְּתוֹסְפוֹת יוֹם טוֹב.
and the first two are in his direct control, as stated in Avot (1:6): "Make for yourself a master, and acquire for yourself a colleague," unlike acquiring a student, see Tosafot Yom Tov there.
רַק הַסִּיּוּם "וֶהֱוֵי דָן וְכוּלֵי", נִרְאֶה דְּזֶהוּ כְּלַפֵּי הַתַּלְמִידִים, לֹא כְּרַבָּן גַּמְלִיאֵל שֶׁאָמַר בִּבְרָכוֹת (כח.): כָּל תַּלְמִיד שֶׁאֵין תּוֹכוֹ כְּבָרוֹ וְכוּלֵי;

Rather, the conclusion "and judge every person favorably" relates to students, not like Rabban Gamliel who said in Berakhot 28a: "Any disciple whose inside does not match his outside may not enter the study hall";
דְּעַל תַּלְמִיד שֶׁאֵינוֹ בְּיָדוֹ לֹא שַׁיָּיךְ אַזְהָרָה, רַק שֶׁהוּא מִמֵּילָא, מִי שֶׁעָשָׂה שְׁנֵי דְבָרִים הַקּוֹדְמִים זוֹכֶה אַחַר כָּךְ גַּם כֵּן לְתַלְמִידִים.

for regarding students, which is not in his control, an explicit injunction is inapplicable, rather it follows naturally: whoever fulfilled the two preceding directives subsequently merits students as well.

וּכְלַפֵּי מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ אַנְשֵׁי כְּנֶסֶת הַגְּדוֹלָה: "הַעֲמִידוּ תַלְמִידִים הַרְבֵּה" (אָבוֹת פֶּרֶק א, א), אָמַר הוּא בְּלָשׁוֹן אַחֵר: "הֱוֵי וְכוּלֵי", דְּגַם כֵּן עַל יְדֵי זֶה יִהְיוּ הַרְבֵּה.

And facing what the Men of the Great Assembly said, "Raise up many disciples" (Avot 1:1), Yehoshua ben Perachyah formulated it differently: "Judge favorably," for through this too disciples will multiply.

וּלְפִי שֶׁרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן פְּרַחְיָה הָיָה יוֹצֵאת בִּרְחוֹבוֹתָיו מֵאוֹתוֹ תַּלְמִיד (בְּרָכוֹת יז רֵישׁ עַמּוּד ב), וְהָיָה סָלְקָא דַעְתָּךְ שֶׁלֹּא לְהַרְבּוֹת תַּלְמִידִים, לְפִיכָךְ אָמַר בְּלָשׁוֹן זֶה: לוֹמַר שֶׁאֵין לָחוּשׁ לְכָךְ, וְאַתְּ הֱוֵי דָן וְכוּלֵי, כָּל שֶׁמַּעֲשָׂיו סְתוּמִים, וּבַהֲדֵי כַּבְשֵׁי דְּרַחֲמָנָא לְמָא לָךְ.

And because Yehoshua ben Perachyah suffered public calamity from that disciple Jesus (Berakhot 17b), and one might think not to multiply students, he therefore taught in this language to show one must not hold back: judge favorably whenever a person's deeds are ambiguous, for why meddle in the hidden ways of the Merciful One?

וְהַלִּמּוּד מֵרַב הוּא הַהַתְחָלָה, וְזֶה נִקְרָא בִּבְרָכוֹת (ו.): אֶחָד שֶׁיּוֹשֵׁב וְעוֹסֵק בַּתּוֹרָה שֶׁשְּׁכִינָה עִמּוֹ מִקְּרָא דְּ"אַזְכִּיר אֶת שְׁמִי" (שְׁמוֹת כ, כא), דְּהַתּוֹרָה נִקְרָא שֵׁם ה' כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שָׁם כא.), וְ"אַזְכִּיר" הַיְינוּ דְּהוּא תּוֹרַת ה' כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל אוֹת קפ"ד, וְנִקְרָא עַל שֵׁם הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁמַּזְכִּיר וּמְלַמֵּד.

And learning from a master is the beginning, termed in Berakhot 6a "one who sits and engages in Torah, the Shechinah is with him," derived from "wherever I cause My Name to be mentioned" (Exodus 20:21), for Torah is called Hashem's Name (Berakhot 21a), and "cause to be mentioned" means Hashem's Torah as noted in Section 184, named after the Blessed Name Who mentions and teaches it.

וְזֶהוּ בְּיָחִיד שֶׁיּוֹשֵׁב וְעוֹסֵק; וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּנְדָרִים (פא.): מִפְּנֵי מָה אֵין תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים מְצוּיִים לִהְיוֹת בְּנֵיהֶם וְכוּלֵי? שֶׁלֹּא בֵּרְכוּ וְכוּלֵי, כִּי בִּרְכַּת הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁמְּבָרֵךְ "הַמְלַמֵּד תּוֹרָה לְעַמּוֹ יִשְׂרָאֵל", וּמַכִּיר שֶׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מְלַמֵּד וְהִיא תּוֹרַת ה', אָז נַעֲשֵׂית תּוֹרָתוֹ לְאַחַר בְּרָכָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל בְּאוֹת קפ"ד.

And this applies to an individual sitting and learning; as stated in Nedarim 81a: why is it uncommon for scholars' sons to be scholars? Because they did not recite the blessing over Torah first, for through blessing "Who teaches Torah to His people Israel," recognizing that God teaches and it is Hashem's Torah, it becomes his own Torah after the blessing, as I wrote in Section 184.
וְאָז זוֹכִים לְבָנִים תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים, דְּהַיְינוּ לִהְיוֹת שְׁנַיִם שֶׁיּוֹשְׁבִים וְעוֹסְקִים בַּתּוֹרָה
And then they merit scholar sons, which means becoming two who sit and learn together
[וְזֶהוּ מַדְרֵגַת "אָז נִדְבְּרוּ יִרְאֵי ה' וְגוֹמֵר" (מַלְאָכִי ג, טז), מַדְרֵיגַת הַדִּבּוּר שֶׁנִּתְבָּאֵר לְעֵיל אוֹת קפ"ג שֶׁהוּא מַקְבִּיל לָזֶה כְּמוֹ שֶׁנִּתְבָּאֵר].
[which is the rung of "Then they that feared Hashem spoke often, etc." (Malachi 3:16), the level of speech explained in Section 183].

וְנִקְרָא "יִרְאֵי ה' אִישׁ אֶל רֵעֵהוּ" – מַדְרֵגַת חָבֵר, כִּי יִרְאַת שָׁמַיִם הוּא הַבְּחִירָה שֶׁבִּידֵי אָדָם, וְהַבְּחִירָה בְּעַצְמָהּ בֶּאֱמֶת גַּם כֵּן מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁיָּצַר הָאָדָם בַּעַל בְּחִירָה.

And they are called "they that feared Hashem, one to his fellow"—the stage of a colleague, for fear of Heaven is human choice, and choice itself is likewise from Hashem Who created man with free will.
רַק יִרְאַת שָׁמַיִם, דְּהַיְינוּ הַהַכָּרָה שֶׁהַבְּחִירָה גַּם כֵּן מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, זֶה נִקְרָא יִרְאַת שָׁמַיִם שֶׁיָּרֵא לִבְחוֹר בָּרָע – זֶהוּ בִּידֵי אָדָם.
But fear of Heaven—recognizing that choice also derives from Hashem, so that one fears choosing evil—this is in human hands.
וְהַתְחָלַת הַחֵשֶׁק לִלְמוֹד מֵרַב הוּא הַבְּחִירָה עַצְמָהּ, וְהוּא בְּסוֹד נָעוּץ סוֹפָן בִּתְחִלָּתָן שֶׁזֶּה גַּם כֵּן מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בֶּאֱמֶת, וְלָכֵן נִקְרָא תּוֹרַת ה'.
And the initial desire to learn from a master is choice itself, in the mystery of "their end is wedged in their beginning," which is truly from Hashem; thus it is called Hashem's Torah.

paragraphs.text: Tosafot Yom Tov on Pirkei Avot 1:6:1: “Midrash Shmuel writes in the name of Rabbi Yehudah Lerma that he asked why it did not instruct one to take students, since they said, “From my students more than from all.” He explained that students wish only to learn, and therefore learn where their heart desires or from someone from whom they think they will learn more. Since a person may not find someone willing to be his student, the tanna did not instruct him about them.”

paragraphs.text: Self-scrutiny is not the measure for judging another

rich.text: Self-scrutiny is not the measure for judging another

paragraphs.text: The responsibility to own one's own deficiency does not authorize assigning the same inward fault to another person.

rich.text: The responsibility to own one's own deficiency does not authorize assigning the same inward fault to another person.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Ishbitz–Radzin · Tiferet Yosef, Talmud Anthology, Taanit 16: “This applies only to a person judging himself. If he sees a deficiency in another, he is not entitled to attribute the deficiency to that person; he must judge him favorably, holding that the person is surely inwardly clear of the bad traits that appear in him and that the failing is like an error proceeding from the ruler. This was the matter here: Rabbi Elazar saw bad traits in a person and judged that the person himself was not refined and possessed those traits. The person answered him: Although I myself must attribute the deficiency to myself, even when it seems to me that I am clear of those bad traits, it is otherwise with you. You are not entitled to attribute the deficiency to me; you must judge me favorably. Go to the Craftsman who made me and say to Him, ‘How ugly is this vessel You made.’”

This was the matter here: Rabbi Elazar saw bad traits in a person and judged that the person himself was not refined and possessed those traits. The person answered him: Although I myself must attribute the deficiency to myself, even when it seems to me that I am clear of those bad traits, it is otherwise with you. You are not entitled to attribute the deficiency to me; you must judge me favorably. Go to the Craftsman who made me and say to Him, ‘How ugly is this vessel You made.’”

paragraphs.text: Explanation: Tiferet Yosef reads the encounter with the apparently ugly person as a warning about interpreting another's character. The person must examine himself; the observer must allow for what he cannot see. This clarifies why the present siman places favorable judgment beside the work of finding friends and raising students. The discipline that makes a person demanding of himself need not become suspicion that closes the door to another's Torah growth.
