sections.en: During the Time of Prayer Delusions Surge Most Intensely within a Person

p: [רט] בְּעֵת הַתְּפִלָּה בְּיוֹתֵר הַדִּמְיוֹנוֹת גּוֹבְרִים בָּאָדָם, וְזֶהוּ עִיּוּן תְּפִלָּה שֶׁאֵין אָדָם נִיצּוֹל בְּכָל יוֹם (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא קסד:).
During the time of prayer delusions surge most intensely within a person, which is the "iyun tefillah," the lapse of focus in prayer, from which no one escapes a single day (Bava Batra 164b).
וְהַתּוֹסָפוֹת וְהָרַ"ן בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה (טז:) הֵבִיאוּ עַל זֶה הַיְרוּשַׁלְמִי דְּפֶרֶק הָיָה קוֹרֵא: "אֲנָא מִן יוֹמָא לָא כַּוְּונִית וְכוּלֵי" כִּפְשָׁטֵיהּ.
And Tosafot and the Ran in Rosh Hashanah 16b cite on this the Yerushalmi in chapter Hayah Korei: "In all my days I never concentrated, etc.," according to its literal reading.
וּבֶאֱמֶת עַל אֲנָשִׁים גְּדוֹלִים כָּאֵלֶּה רָחוֹק מִלִּשְׁמוֹעַ זֶה, בִּפְרָט רַבִּי חִיָּיא דְּאָמְרוּ עָלָיו בְּבָבָא מְצִיעָא (פה:) שֶׁאָמַר: מַשִּׁיב הָרוּחַ – נָשֵׁיב זִיקָא וְכוּלֵי.

But in truth, regarding such towering spiritual giants it is far-fetched to understand this literally, especially Rabbi Chiya of whom Bava Metzia 85b relates: when he recited "He causes the wind to blow," the wind blew, etc.
וְיֵשׁ לְפָרֵשׁ: "לָא כַּוְּונִית" – לֹא הוּצְרַךְ;
And it may be explained: "I never concentrated"—meaning he never needed to exert effort to concentrate;
דְּכַוָּנַת הַלֵּב שַׁיָּיךְ בְּבַעַל דִּמְיוֹן וּמַחֲשָׁבוֹת, שֶׁהַלָּשׁוֹן מְשׁוּלָּח לְדַבֵּר אַף שֶׁלִּבּוֹ בַּל עִמּוֹ, וְצָרִיךְ לְכַוֵּין לִבּוֹ.
for directing the heart is necessary only for one prone to imagination and stray thoughts, whose tongue runs ahead while his heart is not present, requiring deliberate focus.

וְהוּא לֹא הוּצְרַךְ מֵעוֹלָם לָזֶה, שֶׁמֵּעוֹלָם לֹא הָיָה בְּמַחֲשַׁבְתּוֹ דָּבָר אַחֵר, רַק הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ נוֹכַח עֵינָיו, וְלֹא הָיָה מְדַבֵּר אֶלָּא כִּמְדַבֵּר לִפְנֵי מֶלֶךְ מַלְכֵי הַמְּלָכִים לְעוֹלָם.
But he never needed this, for never did any extraneous thought enter his mind, having the Blessed Name constantly before his eyes, praying always as one speaking directly before the King of kings.

וְ"יוֹמָא חַד בָּעֵי כַּוְּונִית וְכוּלֵי" – פֵּירוּשׁ הוּצְרַךְ לְכָךְ, שֶׁהָיָה לוֹ מַחֲשָׁבוֹת מַטְרִידִים, וְאוּלַי הַיְינוּ עוּבָדָא דְּבָבָא מְצִיעָא (שָׁם) דְּאֵלִיָּהוּ טַרְדִינְהוּ, עַיֵּין שָׁם.

And "one day I sought to concentrate, etc."—meaning on that one day he was compelled to make an effort because distracting thoughts besieged him, perhaps identical with Bava Metzia 85b where Elijah troubled them, see there.
וְאָז הוּצְרַךְ לְכַוֵּין הַלֵּב לְהַעֲמִיד מַחְשְׁבוֹתָיו כָּרָאוּי, וְלֹא הוֹעִיל מֵאַחַר שֶׁמִּן הַשָּׁמַיִם הִטְרִידוּהוּ.
And then he needed to direct his heart to stabilize his thoughts properly, yet it did not avail since from Heaven they disturbed him.
וְכֵן אִינָךְ אָמוֹרָאֵי שָׁם (שֶׁהִרְהֲרוּ בְּדָבָר אַחֵר) – הַיְינוּ בְּעֵת שֶׁאֵירַע לָהֶם טִרְדָּא מִן הַשָּׁמַיִם עַד שֶׁהֻוצְרְכוּ כַּוָּנָה.
And so with the other Amoraim mentioned there (who thought of other matters)—it was at an hour when distraction was brought upon them from Heaven so that deliberate effort was required.
אֲבָל תָּמִיד לָא צְרִיכֵי כַּוָּנָה כְּלָל, דְּמִמֵּילָא צָעַק לִבָּם אֶל ה' בְּעֵת הַתְּפִלָּה בְּמִי שֶׁאֵינוֹ בַּעַל דִּמְיוֹן.
But ordinarily they required no deliberate effort at all, their heart crying out spontaneously to Hashem during prayer, as is true of anyone free from delusion.
אֲבָל בְּכָל אָדָם כִּמְעַט אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְהִנָּצֵל כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל.
But for ordinary man it is virtually impossible to be spared from this, as noted above.
וְעַל זֶה תִּקְּנוּ בַּתְּחִלָּה: "אֲדֹנָי שְׂפָתַי תִּפְתָּח וְגוֹמֵר" (תְּהִלִּים נא, יז), שֶׁהַשֵּׁם אֲדֹנָ"י מוֹרֶה עַל שְׁכִינָתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁבְּקֶרֶב לִבּוֹת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל;
And for this reason they instituted at the opening: "O Lord, open my lips, etc." (Psalms 51:17), for the Name Adonai alludes to His Shechinah dwelling within the hearts of the children of Israel;
וּמְבַקְּשִׁים שֶׁהִיא תִּפְתַּח הַפֶּה, וְלֹא שֶׁהַפֶּה יְדַבֵּר מֵעַצְמוֹ, רַק מַה שֶּׁהַלֵּב יִפְתָּחֶנּוּ,
and we plead that the Shechinah open the mouth, so that the mouth does not speak mechanically on its own, but solely what the heart opens,
וְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לִבָּן שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "צוּר לְבָבִי" כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּשִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים רַבָּה (פָּרָשָׁה ה), וְהַיְינוּ מִדַּת הַשֵּׁם הַנִּזְכָּר כַּנּוֹדָע.
and the Holy One is the heart of Israel—"God is the rock of my heart" (Shir HaShirim Rabbah 5)—which is the attribute of this Name as is known.
וּבַסּוֹף: "יִהְיוּ לְרָצוֹן וְגוֹמֵר" (תְּהִלִּים יט, טו), שֶׁעַל הֶעָבָר מְבַקֵּשׁ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה הֶגְיוֹן הַלֵּב לְרָצוֹן אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהָיָה מְעוֹרָב בְּדִמְיוֹנוֹת וּמַחֲשָׁבוֹת זָרוֹת,

And at the conclusion: "Let the words of my mouth... be acceptable, etc." (Psalms 19:15), where regarding the past he pleads that the meditation of the heart be acceptable even though it was mingled with delusions and alien thoughts,
כִּי "אַתָּה צוּרִי" – הוּא מִדַּת "צוּר לְבָבִי" הַנִּזְכָּר, וּמִמְּךָ הַכֹּל, כָּל מַחְשְׁבוֹת הַלֵּב;
for "You are my Rock"—which is the attribute of "the rock of my heart," and from You is all, even all inward thoughts;
וְ"גֹאֲלִי" הוּא הַגְּאוּלָּה הַנִּזְכֶּרֶת לְעֵיל אוֹת ר"ח: לִגְאוֹל דְּבַר אֱמֶת מִדִּמְיוֹן שֶׁהוּא מְלוּבָּשׁ בּוֹ וּכְאִלּוּ שָׁבוּי אֶצְלוֹ.
and "my Redeemer" is the redemption mentioned in Section 208: to redeem the spark of truth from the illusion wherein it was enclothed and held captive.
וְטַעַם: מַצְלֵי הֵיכָא דְּגָרְסֵי (בְּרָכוֹת ח.) גַּם כֵּן, כִּי הַתּוֹרָה מוֹצִיאָה דִּמְיוֹן שֶׁהוּא הֶפְכּוֹ כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל.
And the reason one should pray where he studies Torah (Berakhot 8a) is likewise because the Torah expels illusion, which is its opposite.
וְלִהְיוֹת מַחֲשָׁבוֹת זָרוֹת מִן הָאֲוִירִים כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל אוֹת ר"ה, אֲוִיר שֶׁל אַרְבַּע אַמּוֹת שֶׁל הֲלָכָה מַכְנִיס בַּלֵּב מַחֲשֶׁבֶת דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה וּמוֹצִיא דִּמְיוֹן;
And since alien thoughts enter from environmental atmospheres (Section 205), the atmosphere of the four cubits of Halakhah instills thoughts of Torah and drives out illusion;
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן מְקוֹם תְּפִלָּה, הַתְּפִלָּה אֵינוֹ הֵיפֶךְ הַמַּחֲשָׁבוֹת זָרוֹת, אַדְּרַבָּה אָז מִתְגַּבְּרִים כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל, אֵין אֲוִירוֹ מוֹצִיא מַחֲשָׁבָה זָרָה מִלֵּב.

whereas in a place devoted to prayer alone, prayer is not the direct conceptual antithesis of alien thoughts—on the contrary, then they surge—so its atmosphere does not automatically purge extraneous thoughts.

וְשָׁמַעְתִּי כִּי אַרְבַּע אַמּוֹת שֶׁל הֲלָכָה יֵשׁ לוֹ קְדוּשַּׁת אֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל, וְאִם כֵּן אֲוִירָהּ מַחְכִּים כְּמוֹ אֲוִיר אֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל, וְחָכְמָה הוּא הִיפּוּךְ דִּמְיוֹן, כְּשֶׁזֶּה קָם זֶה נוֹפֵל.
And I heard that the four cubits of Halakhah possess the sanctity of the Land of Israel, whose air makes one wise; and wisdom is the opposite of illusion: when one rises, the other falls.
וּ"מֵסִיר אָזְנוֹ מִשְּׁמֹעַ תּוֹרָה, גַּם תְּפִלָּתוֹ תוֹעֵבָה" (מִשְׁלֵי כח, ט; שַׁבָּת י.) – פֵּירוּשׁ: "תּוֹעֵבָה" נִקְרָא כְּשֶׁמְּלֵאָה מַחֲשָׁבוֹת זָרוֹת וְדִמְיוֹנוֹת;

And "He that turns away his ear from hearing the Torah, even his prayer is an abomination" (Proverbs 28:9; Shabbat 10a)—meaning it is called an abomination when it is filled with alien thoughts and delusions;

וְהַתְּפִלָּה הוּא עֲבוֹדָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב, וּמֵאַחַר שֶׁהַלֵּב מָלֵא מַחְשֶׁבֶת פִּגּוּל, הוּא חַס וְשָׁלוֹם כְּמוֹ עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה וְתוֹעֵבָה, רַק דְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ צוּרוֹ וְגוֹאֲלוֹ כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל.
and prayer is the service of the heart, so when the heart is full of contaminated thoughts, it is like idolatry and an abomination, save that Hashem is his Rock and Redeemer as noted.

אֲבָל אִם מֵסִיר אָזְנוֹ מִשְּׁמוֹעַ תּוֹרָה שֶׁהִיא הַמַּצֶּלֶת מִדִּמְיוֹן, וְהוּא פּוֹשֵׁעַ בְּעַצְמוֹ שֶׁלֹּא לְהִנָּצֵל, אָז חַס וְשָׁלוֹם "תְּפִלָּתוֹ וְכוּלֵי", שֶׁאֵין הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ גּוֹאֲלוֹ.
But if he deliberately turns his ear away from hearing Torah which saves from illusion, being willfully negligent, then "his prayer is an abomination," for Hashem will not redeem him.

אֲבָל אִידַךְ סָבַר זְמַן תּוֹרָה לְחוּד, וְתַלְיָא בִּפְלוּגְתָּא דִּבְרָכוֹת (לא.): אִם עוֹמְדִין לְהִתְפַּלֵּל מִתּוֹךְ הֲלָכָה פְּסוּקָה שֶׁהִיא הַמְזַכֶּכֶת הַמַּחֲשָׁבָה, אוֹ מִתּוֹךְ כֹּבֶד רֹאשׁ

— But the opposing sage holds the time for Torah is distinct from prayer, which depends on the dispute in Berakhot 31a: whether one stands to pray out of an established halakhah which refines thought, or out of reverent solemnity (koved rosh)—
זֶהוּ כְּדִבְרֵי הָאוֹמֵר זְמַן תְּפִלָּה לְחוּד שֶׁאֵין לוֹ חִבּוּר עִם תּוֹרָה, רַק עַל יְדֵי כֹּבֶד רֹאשׁ מִיִּרְאַת שָׁמַיִם שֶׁבְּלִבּוֹ יוֹצִיא הַמַּחֲשָׁבוֹת זָרוֹת וְהַדִּמְיוֹנוֹת מֵהַלֵּב:
the latter reflecting the view that the time of prayer is separate and unconnected to Torah, driving out alien thoughts through solemn fear of Heaven alone.

paragraphs.text: Tosafot on Rosh Hashanah 16b:5:1: “Rabbeinu Tam says that “examination of prayer” here is like that in “Get Pashut,” where it is counted among three things from which a person is not saved each day: namely, that he does not direct his heart in prayer. As the Jerusalem Talmud says: Rabbi Chiyya the Great said, “All my days I have not concentrated. Once I sought to concentrate, and I thought in my heart: Who enters before the king first, the chief officer or the exilarch?””

paragraphs.text: Context: Tosafot records this explanation and the Yerushalmi passage, but then rejects it as the meaning of the particular warning in Rosh Hashanah, interpreting that warning as confident expectation of an answer. The lack-of-concentration explanation applies to the daily failing in Bava Batra. Rav Tzadok is examining the Yerushalmi’s account of the sages’ concentration.

paragraphs.text: Ran on Rosh Hashanah 3b:4: ““Examination of prayer”: He relies on his prayer and is confident that it will be heard. As for what we say in the chapter Get Pashut, that there are three transgressions from which no person is free each day, one of which is examination of prayer—the examination of prayer there is not the same as here. Were it the same, how could it say that no one is free of it each day? There are many people who do not rely on their prayer every day. Rather, examination of prayer there means that he does not attend to his prayer. It therefore says that no one is free of it, for no one directs his attention as he should. As we read in the Jerusalem Talmud, Berakhot: Rabbi Ḥiyya said, “All my days I have not concentrated. Once I came to concentrate, and I thought in my heart: Who enters before the king first, the chief official or the exilarch?” Shmuel said, “I counted chicks.” Rabbi Bun, son of Rabbi Ḥiyya, said, “I counted rows of masonry.” Rabbi Matanya said, “I am grateful to my head, for when it reached Modim it bowed of itself.” This is what is meant in the chapter Kol Kitvei HaKodesh: “May I be rewarded for having fulfilled examination of prayer.” It is also what is meant in the chapter Mefannin: There are six things whose fruits a person enjoys in this world, one of which is examination of prayer—that is, he attends to it and directs his intention in it.”

paragraphs.text: Peri Tzadik, Vayeshev 3:1: “One may explain that this is what Rabbi Ḥiyya the Great meant by “All my days I have not concentrated”: he did not need to straighten his heart and direct it to his Father in Heaven through preparation in Torah or fear, by waiting before prayer. Rather, he would rise and find his heart hoping toward love and fear, as in Rabbi Elazar’s prayer, “May we rise,” and so forth. “Once I wished to concentrate”: on that occasion he needed to prepare for prayer and wait an hour beforehand, and he was unsure which preparation to make—according to the Mishnah or according to the baraita. This is what he meant by “I thought in my heart: Who enters before the king first, the chief official or the exilarch?” The chief official signifies a Torah scholar, as we find in Zevaḥim: “The chief official took my hand, and his scent reached my hand”—because you went before Rav Sheshet, have you become like Rav Sheshet? Rav Sheshet was a Sinai, as it says in Eruvin: “Rav Ḥisda’s lips trembled before the teachings of Rav Sheshet.” This is the meaning of the chief official. The expression concerning the grasp and the scent follows what is said in the Zohar: They caused Issachar to come into the world, because the scent of Torah rose before the Holy One, blessed be He; this is “the mandrakes gave forth their scent.” It also follows the teaching that with each utterance the whole world filled with fragrance. The exilarch, however, is a ruling scepter, as it says in Sanhedrin: “The scepter shall not depart from Judah”—these are the exilarchs in Babylonia, who rule Israel with a rod. We also find in Ḥullin: “For you have striven with divine beings and men”—He alluded to the exilarchs in Babylonia and the patriarch in the Land of Israel. The patriarch’s role is in Torah, as Rashi explains that those ordained are called elohim; the exilarchs are the “men,” the ruling scepter. We find in Berakhot that once a king bows, he does not straighten up, for he is full of fear, submission, and dread. Rabbi Ḥiyya was therefore unsure which preparation to make in order to direct and straighten his heart to his Father in Heaven: through gravity, submission, and fear, signified by the exilarch’s level and corresponding to the Mishnah; or through a conclusive halakhah, corresponding to the baraita and signified by the chief official. This is what he meant: Who enters before the King first—the chief official, signifying Torah, or the exilarch, signifying fear? In truth, both are one, as it says in Avot: “If there is no wisdom, there is no fear; if there is no fear, there is no wisdom.” Rabbi Ḥiyya was unsure only where the awakening should begin: with Torah, or with fear and submission. “Who enters before the King first” means which should come first.”

paragraphs.text: Resisei Layla 31:1: “Isaac came and added that even prayer without deliberate concentration is prayer. This was his level: he would show them the Holy One, blessed be He, before their very eyes (Shabbat 89b)—how the whole earth is filled with His glory, literally present before the eye. With such clear recognition, deliberate concentration of the heart no longer makes a difference, as it says (Jerusalem Talmud, Berakhot 2:4): “All my days I did not concentrate,” and so forth. For when a person has such clear recognition, this itself is a comprehensive intention encompassing all his thoughts, words, and deeds. Even his ordinary conversation is entirely from the blessed God alone, and there is none besides Him. There is no difference between concentrating this way or that, for which he must make an effort; instead he should leave everything to the blessed God and exert himself only in the fundamental intention, “I have set the Lord before me always”—literally before me. Then, of itself, when he fulfills “Commit,” and so forth, “they shall be established,” and so forth. This is called an unintended act, rather than mere unawareness, for a comprehensive intention is nevertheless required, as explained above, and he must know that he is going to pray.”

paragraphs.text: Kometz HaMinchah 2:32:1: see note 1733 (Vol. I).

Explanation: Kometz HaMinchah connects David's ‘I am prayer’ to the request ‘Adonai, open my lips.’ Accepting divine lordship allows speech to become an expression of that relation. This illuminates the siman's distinction between a mouth moving on its own and speech opened from the heart. The full attained condition is a model toward which the ordinary opening request turns, rather than something proved merely by pronouncing its words.

paragraphs.text: Tzidkat HaTzadik 233:1: “To be saved all day from alien thoughts and thoughts outside the will of the blessed God is possible only for one entirely free of personal self-interest. This is when he has already killed the evil inclination, as did King David, peace be upon him; “whoever wins the battle is given” prayer, as stated at the end of Tikkun 13. Whoever is not free of alien thoughts all day will not escape alien thoughts in prayer either. Thus Bava Batra says that no one is free of examination of prayer, apparently speaking of every person. The words of the Yerushalmi cited by Tosafot, “All my days I have not concentrated,” then retain their plain meaning: he could not escape every flash of an alien thought throughout the entire prayer. The thought “Who enters before the king?” concerns honor. Because of an attachment to honor, this thought entered on the day he wished to concentrate, when he prepared himself like the early pious ones who waited in order to direct their hearts—that is, to straighten the heart so that it would contain no self-interest or desire apart from the will of the blessed God. Perhaps at that moment the blessed God would help him win the battle and remove the inclination from within him. The thoughts “I counted chicks” and “rows of masonry,” concerning possessions, arise from an attachment to the desire for money. “I am grateful to my head” means that envy brings an alien thought at Modim, the thanksgiving for God’s kindnesses: the envious person feels deprived and does not thank the blessed God for His benefits, but instead complains that He gives benefit to another. This is the meaning of Bava Kamma’s teaching about a person’s spine, applying it to one who did not bow at Modim, for “envy rots the bones.” The serpent’s root is envy, as the Sages said: he saw and became envious. Eve likewise fed Adam because of envy. It is known that almost no one is entirely free of these three—envy, desire, and honor. As I wrote above, “Who can stand before envy?” Concerning desire, the Sages said, “Even the most pious of the pious,” and so forth. All the more so honor, which includes both, as is known. Therefore no one escapes alien thoughts.”

paragraphs.text: The spoken words and the hidden heart

rich.text: The spoken words and the hidden heart

paragraphs.text: The closing verse includes what can be articulated and what remains hidden, with a demand to relinquish private motives.

rich.text: The closing verse includes what can be articulated and what remains hidden, with a demand to relinquish private motives.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Ishbitz–Radzin · Tiferet Yosef, Talmud Anthology, Pesachim 1: “It is written (Psalms 19:15), ‘May the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable before You…’ The Zohar says (Vayishlach 169a): King David said, ‘The words of my mouth’—these are expressed words; ‘the meditation of my heart’—these are hidden words that a person cannot express with his mouth, the meditation in the heart. One corresponds to the lower level and one to the upper level; expressed speech corresponds to the lower level. My holy grandfather explained that a person has actions in which he does not recognize Heaven's honor, to the point that he himself doubts whether his intention was clearly for Hashem's will. Actual mitzvot give him great assurance, for he knows that he fulfilled Hashem's will through them, as the Midrash says (Tanchuma, Ki Tavo): see what assurance and room to speak those who perform mitzvot have. But in ordinary optional matters he may doubt whether his intention was expressly to fulfill Hashem's will. This gives rise to accusations that perhaps this was not his intention. The counsel is to remove, from his side, every private interest, so that he has no worldly stake in these matters; then all the accusing powers will fall away.”

paragraphs.text: Explanation: Tiferet Yosef explains the same closing prayer verse through the Zohar's distinction between expressed words and inward matters that cannot be articulated. It then requires the person to remove private worldly interests. This gives a complementary account of asking that both mouth and heart be accepted, while preserving the siman's acknowledgment that the actual prayer may still contain distracting thoughts.

paragraphs.text: Tzidkat HaTzadik 223:1: “As I heard, the four cubits of halakhah are holy with the holiness of the Land of Israel. The air of the lands of the nations is expelled from them entirely on every side by the double-edged sword, and the holy air of words of Torah enters. This is the air of the Land of Israel, which therefore imparts wisdom, like Torah’s quality of making the simple wise. But the synagogue and prayer do not help when a person has already encountered and become entangled in alien thoughts, for his entire prayer will likewise be full of alien thoughts. Rather, he must direct his heart to distance himself from alien thoughts; then through prayer he can bring holy thoughts into the depth of the heart and kill the evil from afar, as in “their tongue is a sharpened arrow.” The tongue is like an arrow that kills from a distance, and this is through prayer, as stated in the Tikkunim, at the end of Tikkun 13 and elsewhere: he shoots arrow after arrow at it.”

sections.en: When Seeking to Concentrate

p: [רי] כְּשֶׁרוֹצֶה לְכַוֵּין, כָּתַב תַּלְמִידֵי רַבֵּנוּ יוֹנָה בִּבְרָכוֹת (פֶּרֶק ה, כה עַמּוּד ב) בְּשֵׁם הַקַּדְמוֹנִים: שֶׁיִּפְשׁוֹט גּוּפוֹ מִנִּשְׁמָתוֹ, עַיֵּין שָׁם, פֵּירוּשׁ כֵּן: לִבּוֹ לְמַעְלָה (יְבָמוֹת קה:).

When seeking to concentrate, Talmidei Rabbeinu Yonah in Berakhot (chapter 5) write in the name of the early masters that one should divest his body from his soul, meaning directing his heart on high (Yevamot 105b).
וּבְטוּר וְשֻׁלְחָן עָרוּךְ סִימָן צ"ח נִקְרָא זֶה "הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת הַגַּשְׁמִיּוּת", וְשֶׁהוּא קָרוֹב לִנְבוּאָה.
And in the Tur and Shulchan Arukh (Orach Chayim 98) this is termed the "divestment of physical corporeality" (hitpashtut ha-gashmiyut), which borders on prophecy.

וּבֶאֱמֶת זֶהוּ מַדְרֵגַת הַנְּבִיאִים כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּמוֹרֶה נְבוּכִים, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּשָׁאוּל שֶׁהָלַךְ וּמִתְנַבֵּא עָרוֹם (שְׁמוּאֵל א יט, כד), פֵּירוּשׁ שֶׁהַגּוּף הוּא לְבוּשׁ לַנֶּפֶשׁ כַּנּוֹדָע, וְהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּתוֹ נִקְרָא עָרוֹם;

And in truth this is the level of the prophets as written in the Guide for the Perplexed, and as written of Saul who prophesied naked (I Samuel 19:24), for the body is a garment for the soul, and stripping it away is termed nakedness;
וְתַרְגּוּם יוֹנָתָן שָׁם: "בַּרְשָׁן", פֵּירוּשׁ מְשֻׁגָּע, שֶׁאֵינוֹ פּוֹנֶה כְּלָל לְגוּפוֹ, וּפְעֻלַּת הַגּוּף הֵם כִּמְעַט בְּלֹא יְדִיעָתוֹ כְּלָל וּכְמוֹ מְשֻׁגָּע.
and Targum Yonatan translates there "barshan," meaning seemingly crazed, completely paying no heed to his body, physical bodily actions occurring almost without his conscious awareness.
וְכֵן קָרְאוּ לַנָּבִיא גַּבֵּי יֵהוּא (מְלָכִים ב ט, יא): "הַמְשֻׁגָּע".
And so they termed the prophet regarding Jehu: "that madman" (II Kings 9:11).

וּמַדְרֵגַת הַנְּבוּאָה הָיוּ מַגִּיעִים עַל יְדֵי הַתְּפִלָּה, כִּדְאָמְרוּ בִּמְגִילָּה (כז.): אֱלִישָׁע דַּעֲבַד בְּרַחֲמֵי, וְהַיְינוּ עַל יְדֵי הַדְּבֵיקוּת בַּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וְהַכָּרַת הַנּוֹכַח.
And to prophecy they ascended through prayer, as stated in Megillah 27a: Elisha acted through prayers for mercy, achieved through cleaving to Hashem and direct awareness of His Presence.
וְדָבָר זֶה כְּבָר נִיטְּלָה, וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם אָמְרוּ בְּבָבָא בַּתְרָא (יב.): מִן הַחֲכָמִים לֹא נִיטְּלָה;
And this capacity was formally taken away, yet Bava Batra 12a states: from the sages it was not taken away;

כִּי עַל יְדֵי תּוֹרָה גַּם כֵּן נֶאֱמַר: "בְּאַהֲבָתָהּ תִּשְׁגֶּה [תָמִיד]" (מִשְׁלֵי ה, יט), וּכְמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (עֵירוּבִין נד:) עַל רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן פְּדָת שֶׁשּׁוֹכֵחַ עִנְיְנֵי הַגּוּף, וְהוּא בְּהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת הַגַּשְׁמִיּוּת עַל יְדֵי דְּבֵיקוּתוֹ בַּתּוֹרָה, זֶה אֶפְשָׁר גַּם בַּזְּמַן הַזֶּה.

for through Torah it is likewise said: "be enraptured [always] with her love" (Proverbs 5:19), as our Sages stated (Eruvin 54b) of Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat who forgot bodily needs, divesting physical corporeality through cleaving to Torah, which remains possible even in our times.

וּבֶאֱמֶת זֶהוּ עִיקַּר הַדְּבֵיקוּת בַּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (כְּתוּבּוֹת קיא:): וְכִי אֶפְשָׁר לִדְבַּק בַּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ? אֶלָּא הַמַּשִּׂיא וְכוּלֵי, וְזֶהוּ בְּעַם הָאָרֶץ כְּשֶׁנִּדְבָּק לְתַלְמִיד חָכָם.

And in truth this is the essence of cleaving unto Hashem, as stated in Ketubot 111b: Is it possible to cleave unto the Blessed Name? Rather, marrying one's daughter to a scholar, which applies to a commoner attaching himself to a sage.

וְהַתַּלְמִיד חָכָם כְּשֶׁדָּבוּק בַּתּוֹרָה הוּא דָּבוּק בַּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, כִּי אוֹרַיְיתָא וְקוּדְשָׁא בְּרִיךְ הוּא חַד, כִּי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הוּא וְחָכְמָתוֹ וּרְצוֹנוֹ אֶחָד כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב הָרַמְבַּ"ם בְּהִלְכוֹת יְסוֹדֵי הַתּוֹרָה (פֶּרֶק ב הֲלָכָה י), וְהַתּוֹרָה הִיא חָכְמָתוֹ וּרְצוֹנוֹ, וְהַדָּבוּק בָּהּ דָּבוּק בַּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וּבְאוֹתוֹ עֵת הוּא בְּמַדְרֵגַת נְבוּאָה, רַק חָכָם עָדִיף.

And the scholar cleaving to Torah cleaves to Hashem, for the Torah and the Holy One are One, Hashem and His wisdom and will being unified (Rambam, Yesodei HaTorah 2:10), so that he who cleaves to Torah cleaves to Hashem, standing at that hour on the level of prophecy, with the sage being superior.
וּבַזֹּהַר שְׁמוֹת (ו סוֹף עַמּוּד ב) הַטַּעַם דִּלְנָבִיא הוּא רַק לְזִמְנִין וְכוּלֵי;
And in Zohar Shemot (6b end) the reason is given why for a prophet it is only occasional;

וְהַיְינוּ כִּי הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת הַגַּשְׁמִיּוּת עַל יְדֵי דְּבֵיקוּת בַּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּהַכָּרַת הַנּוֹכַח – זֶה אִי אֶפְשָׁר כְּלָל לִהְיוֹת בִּתְמִידוּת, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (לא.): יָכוֹל יִתְפַּלֵּל כָּל הַיּוֹם כֻּלּוֹ? תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר: וְזִמְנִין וְגוֹמֵר, שֶׁזֶּה אִי אֶפְשָׁר כְּלָל לִהְיוֹת כָּל הַיּוֹם בִּתְפִלָּה לִפְנֵי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וְאֵינוֹ בְּכֹחַ אָדָם שֶׁבַּגּוּף כְּלָל, וַאֲפִילּוּ הֶאָרַת פָּנִים לַמַּלְאָכִים אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא כְּמַרְאֵה הַבָּזָק כְּרֶגַע וּמִיָּד נִתְעַלֵּם.

for divesting corporeality through cleaving to Hashem in direct conscious presence cannot possibly be continuous, as in Berakhot 31a: might one pray all day long? Scripture states: three times a day, for it is impossible to pray before Hashem all day, being beyond human bodily capacity, and even the angels perceive the divine Face only as a flash of lightning for an instant, immediately receding.

וְרַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן דּוֹרְדְּיָא בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (יז.) הִרְבָּה בִּתְפִלָּה עַד שֶׁיָּצְתָה נִשְׁמָתוֹ – הַיְינוּ מִכֹּחַ רִבּוּי הַתְּפִלָּה, כִּי אֵין בְּכֹחַ אָדָם לִסְבּוֹל, כִּי זֶה נִקְרָא עֲבוֹדָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב וּמְיַגַּעַת הָאָדָם.

And Rabbi Elazar ben Dordaya in Avodah Zarah 17a prayed intensely until his soul departed—from the sheer force of continuous prayer, for human strength cannot endure it, being the exhausting service of the heart.
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן הַתּוֹרָה נִקְרָא לֶחֶם וּמָזוֹן וְעֵץ חַיִּים שֶׁהִיא הַנּוֹתֶנֶת קִיּוּם לָאָדָם עַל יְדֵי שִׂמְחָתוֹ בְּחָכְמָתוֹ,
In contrast, Torah is called bread, sustenance, and the Tree of Life, sustaining man through his intellectual joy in its wisdom.
וְלָכֵן נֶאֱמַר בָּהּ: "לֹא יָמוּשׁ וְגוֹמֵר" (יְהוֹשֻׁעַ א, ח), שֶׁיָּכוֹל לִהְיוֹת דָּבוּק בָּהּ שֶׁלֹּא יִתְבַּטֵּל אֲפִילּוּ רֶגַע אֶחָד.
Therefore it is said of it: "it shall not depart out of your mouth" (Joshua 1:8), for one can cleave to it without ceasing even for a single moment.

וְזֶה טַעַם עֶבֶד לִפְנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ וְשַׂר לִפְנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ בִּבְרָכוֹת (לד:) לוּלֵי פֵּירוּשׁ רַשִּׁ"י, רַק הַשַּׂר הוּא תָּמִיד בְּבֵית הַמֶּלֶךְ, אֲבָל הָעֶבֶד רַק בְּעֵת שֶׁצָּרִיךְ לְשִׁימּוּשׁוֹ.

And this explains "a servant before the King" versus "a minister before the King" in Berakhot 34b, were it not for Rashi's explanation: the minister is constantly in the palace, while the servant enters only when needed for service.

וְרַבִּי חֲנִינָא בֶּן דּוֹסָא לֹא תִּמְצָא בְּכָל הַשַּׁ"ס מִמֶּנּוּ שׁוּם הֲלָכָה זוּלַת הַהִיא דְּאָבוֹת: "כָּל שֶׁיִּרְאַת חֶטְאוֹ וְכוּלֵי וְכָל שֶׁמַּעֲשָׂיו וְכוּלֵי" (פֶּרֶק ג, ט), וּבִשְׁאָר מְקוֹמוֹת סִפּוּרָיו מִמּוֹפְתָיו בִּתְפִלּוֹתָיו, כִּי זֶה כָּל עִסְקוֹ;

And of Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa you will not find in the entire Talmud a single legal ruling, save that in Avot 3:9: "He whose fear of sin precedes his wisdom, etc., and whose deeds exceed his wisdom," while all other passages recount the wonders of his prayers, for this was his entire occupation;

וְשׁוֹרֶשׁ נַפְשׁוֹ בַּתּוֹרָה הוּא בְּאוֹתָהּ מֵימְרָא דְּ"כָל שֶׁיִּרְאַת חֶטְאוֹ וְכוּלֵי", שֶׁזֶּה הָיָה הַבְּלִיטָה מִנַּפְשׁוֹ, וּמוֹרֶה עַל אוֹתוֹ דָּבָר שֶׁאֵין הַחָכְמָה הָעִיקָּר, רַק הַיִּרְאַת חֵטְא צָרִיךְ שֶׁיִּקְדַּם וְהַמַּעֲשֶׂה יִהְיֶה מְרוּבֶּה, כִּי זֶה כָּל עִסְקוֹ בִּתְפִלָּה שֶׁנִּקְרָא עֲבוֹדָה וְיִרְאָה כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שָׁם ט:) עַל פָּסוּק "יִירָאוּךָ עִם שָׁמֶשׁ",

and his soul-root in Torah was expressed in that very dictum, teaching that wisdom is not paramount, but fear of sin must precede and action must abound, for his occupation was prayer, termed service and awe (Berakhot 9b on "They shall fear You with the sun").
וְזֶהוּ מַדְרֵגַת עֶבֶד הָעוֹבֵד עֲבוֹדָה.
And this is the level of a servant performing service.

וְרַבָּן יוֹחָנָן בֶּן זַכַּאי דָּבוּק בַּתּוֹרָה שֶׁהִיא דְּבֵיקוּת תְּמִידִי נִקְרָא "שַׂר", וְלוֹ נִפְתָּחִין כָּל סוֹדוֹת הַמֶּלֶךְ, וּבְוַדַּאי כָּל דְּעָבֵיד רַחֲמָנָא לְטָב, וּמְגַלֶּה לוֹ הַטּוֹבָה שֶׁיֵּשׁ כְּשֶׁלֹּא יִפְעַל בִּתְפִלָּתוֹ, וּלְכָךְ אֵין מַשְׁגִּיחִין עָלָיו [לִפְעוֹל בְּנֵס בִּתְפִלָּתוֹ].

And Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, cleaving continuously to Torah, is called a "minister," to whom the King's secrets are open, knowing that whatever the Merciful One does is for the good, realizing the hidden good in a prayer not being answered, which is why they did not heed him [to overturn decrees by miracles through his prayer].

מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן הָעֶבֶד שֶׁאִי אֶפְשָׁר לְגַלּוֹת לוֹ רָזֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ, וְהוּא מְבַקֵּשׁ טוֹבָתוֹ וּרְצוֹנוֹ לְפִי דַעְתּוֹ, הַמֶּלֶךְ מוּכְרָח לְמַלֹּאות לוֹ רְצוֹנוֹ מֵאַחַר שֶׁלְּפִי דַעְתּוֹ בְּעִנְיָן אַחֵר הוּא רַע לְפָנָיו;

In contrast, the servant, to whom the King's hidden counsels cannot be revealed, pleads according to his own perspective, and the King grants his wish since otherwise it appears tragic to the servant;
וְאַחַר כָּךְ הוּא מוּכְרָח בֶּאֱמֶת לִרְאוֹת שֶׁיִּהְיֶה גַּם זֶה לְטוֹב אֲמִיתִּי לוֹ:
and subsequently the King ensures that this fulfillment also yields genuine eternal good for him.

footnotes.enAnchorPrefix: When seeking to concentrate, Talmidei Rabbeinu Yonah in Berakhot (chapter 5) write in the name of the early masters that one should divest his body from his soul, meaning directing his heart on high (Yevamot 105b).

paragraphs.text: Rabbeinu Yonah on Berakhot 22b:3: ““He must direct his eyes downward and his heart upward”: This means that he should think in his heart as though he were standing in heaven, and remove from his heart all the pleasures of this world and all bodily enjoyments, as the ancients said: “When you wish to concentrate, strip your body away from your soul.” After reaching this thought, he should also imagine himself standing in the Temple below, for through this his prayer will be more acceptable before the Omnipresent.”

paragraphs.text: Yevamot 105b:5: “He said to them: Thus my father said: One who prays must direct his eyes downward and his heart upward, so that both these verses may be fulfilled.”

Rav Tzadok explains these expressions as inward concentration beyond bodily sensation, not a physical act.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Rav Tzadok · Sichat Malakhei HaSharet 3:25: “And these two sublime faculties are spiritual states operating beyond the physical limbs; unlike mental thought which remains linked to the brain as a physical bodily organ; for these two higher levels transcend the body, termed in the Shulchan Aruch (Orach Chayim 98:1) "the stripping away of corporeality" (hitpashtut hagashmiyut); wherein reaching these rungs one loses all physical awareness of the body, as recorded of Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat (Eruvin 54b) who embodied "be you ravished always with her love" Proverbs 5:19.”

rich.text: : “And these two sublime faculties are spiritual states operating beyond the physical limbs; unlike mental thought which remains linked to the brain as a physical bodily organ; for these two higher levels transcend the body, termed in the Shulchan Aruch (Orach Chayim 98:1) "the stripping away of corporeality" (hitpashtut hagashmiyut); wherein reaching these rungs one loses all physical awareness of the body, as recorded of Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat (Eruvin 54b) who embodied "be you ravished always with her love" Proverbs 5:19.”

paragraphs.text: Explanation: Sichat Malakhei HaSharet uses the same Shulchan Aruch reference and Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat’s immersion in Torah to explain this language. In its preceding paragraph, the two powers are identified as chayah and yechidah, modes of the soul’s attachment to its source. This clarifies that the discussion concerns the direction and absorption of awareness, rather than a physical separation that one attempts to perform.

paragraphs.text: Radak on I Samuel 19:24:1: ““He too stripped off his clothes”: This teaches that the other prophets stripped off their clothes, for “he too” includes them. The matter is that when prophecy comes upon a person, his senses cease to function and he falls, as it says of Balaam, “fallen, with eyes uncovered,” and as Daniel says, “I was in a deep sleep on my face, with my face to the ground.” Sometimes he strips off his clothes because of the great cessation of his sensory and psychic activities, and he remains with the intellectual faculty alone.”

paragraphs.text: Tanya, Part I; Likkutei Amarim 5:2-6: “When any intellect understands and apprehends an intelligible matter, the intellect grasps and encompasses it in the mind, and the intelligible matter is grasped, encompassed, and clothed within the intellect that has apprehended and understood it. The intellect is also clothed in that intelligible matter while apprehending and grasping it. For example, when a person correctly and thoroughly understands a halakhah in the Mishnah or Gemara, his intellect grasps and encompasses it, while his intellect is also clothed in it at that time. This halakhah is the wisdom and will of the Holy One, blessed be He: it arose in His will that if, for example, Reuven makes one claim and Shimon another, the ruling between them shall be such and such. Even if such a case never has and never will come to judgment with these claims and demands, nevertheless, since it arose in the will and wisdom of the Holy One, blessed be He, that if one makes this claim and the other that claim, the ruling shall be so, when a person knows and intellectually apprehends that ruling as set out in the Mishnah, Gemara, or legal authorities, he thereby apprehends, grasps, and encompasses in his intellect the will and wisdom of the Holy One, blessed be He. No thought can grasp Him, His will, or His wisdom except as they are clothed in the halakhot set before us; his intellect is also clothed in them. This is a wondrous union, with no comparable union or equivalent anywhere in physical existence: they become actually one and united in every respect.”

paragraphs.text: Tanya, Part I; Likkutei Amarim 5:9-13: “Because, through knowing Torah, Torah is clothed in the person’s soul and intellect and encompassed within them, it is called “bread” and “food for the soul.” Just as physical bread nourishes the body when brought inside it and becomes blood and flesh like its own flesh, enabling it to live and endure, so through knowing and apprehending Torah in the soul—learning it thoroughly through intellectual examination until it is grasped by the intellect and united with it—it becomes food for the soul and life within it, from the Life of life, the blessed Infinite, clothed in His wisdom and Torah within it. This is the meaning of “Your Torah is within my inward parts.” As Etz Ḥayyim, Gate 44, chapter 3, explains, the soul’s garments in the Garden of Eden are the commandments, while Torah is the food of the souls that engaged in Torah for its own sake in this world, as also stated in Zohar, Vayakhel 210. “For its own sake” means in order to bind one’s soul to God through understanding Torah, each according to his intellect, as explained in Peri Etz Ḥayyim. [The food is inward light, while the garments are surrounding lights. Therefore our Sages said that Torah study is equivalent to all the commandments, for the commandments are garments alone, while Torah is both food and a garment for the understanding soul, which clothes itself in Torah through its examination and study. All the more so when one expresses it aloud, for the breath of speech becomes surrounding light, as explained in Peri Etz Ḥayyim.]”

sections.en: Torah and Prayer Are Both Required Together by Man

p: [ריא] תּוֹרָה וּתְפִלָּה צְרִיכִים שְׁנֵיהֶם בְּיַחַד לָאָדָם, וְלֹא גָּרְסֵי אֶלָּא הֵיכָא דִּמְצַלֵּי (מְגִילָּה כט.) וְכֵן לְהֵיפֶךְ (בְּרָכוֹת ח.);
Torah and prayer are both required together by man: one should study only where he prays (Megillah 29a) and conversely pray where he studies (Berakhot 8a);

וְאָמְרוּ בִּיבָמוֹת (קט:): כָּל הָאוֹמֵר אֵין לִי אֶלָּא תּוֹרָה וְכוּלֵי, שֶׁעַל יְדֵי זֶה חַס וְשָׁלוֹם יָבוֹא לִשְׁכּוֹחַ שֶׁצָּרִיךְ לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, שֶׁזֶּהוּ עִנְיַן הַתְּפִלָּה – הַהַכָּרָה שֶׁהוּא חָסֵר וּמְבַקֵּשׁ לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁיְּמַלְּאֶנּוּ.

and they stated in Yevamot 109b: whoever says he has nothing but Torah does not even possess Torah, for through this he might forget his utter dependence upon Hashem, which is the essence of prayer—the realization that he is deficient, beseeching Hashem to replenish him.
וְעַל יְדֵי הַתּוֹרָה יַחְשׁוֹב שֶׁהוּא מָלֵא, וְאָז אֲפִילּוּ תּוֹרָה אֵין לוֹ;
And through isolated Torah study he might imagine himself self-sufficient, and then he lacks even Torah;
כִּי לֹא נִיתְּנָה תּוֹרָה אֶלָּא לַחֲסֵרִים וּמַכִּירִים חֶסְרוֹנָם וּמְבַקְּשִׁים לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁיּוֹשִׁיעֵם,
for the Torah was given solely to those who are deficient, who recognize their lack and plead before Hashem to save them,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "הָעֲנִיִּים וְהָאֶבְיוֹנִים מְבַקְשִׁים מַיִם וָאַיִן לְשׁוֹנָם בַּצָּמָא נָשָׁתָּה" (יְשַׁעְיָה מא, יז), וְאֵין מַיִם אֶלָּא תּוֹרָה (בָּבָא קַמָּא יז.).
as written: "The poor and needy seek water, and there is none, and their tongue fails for thirst" (Isaiah 41:17), and there is no water other than Torah (Bava Kamma 17a).
וְעִיקַּר רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בִּבְרִיאַת הָעוֹלָם הָיָה רַק לִכְבוֹדוֹ וּלְקִילּוּסוֹ וְשֶׁיְּצַפּוּ לוֹ;
And the primary will of Hashem in creating the world was for His glory, His praise, and that creatures yearn for Him;
וְאָמְרוּ (יְבָמוֹת סד.): הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מִתְאַוֶּוה לִתְפִלָּתָן שֶׁל צַדִּיקִים.
and they taught (Yevamot 64a): the Holy One yearns for the prayer of the righteous.
וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ בְּמִדְרָשׁ רַבָּה (נִצָּבִים): שֶׁמָּא תֹּאמַר לְרָעַתְכֶם נָתַתִּי הַתּוֹרָה? לֹא נִיתְּנָה אֶלָּא לְטוֹבַתְכֶם וְכוּלֵי.
And regarding this they said in Devarim Rabbah (Nitzavim): Lest you say I gave the Torah for your detriment? It was given only for your benefit, etc.

וּבְוַדַּאי חַס וְשָׁלוֹם אֵיךְ יַעֲלֶה עַל הַדַּעַת שֶׁיִּהְיֶה לְרָעַתְכֶם? רַק דְּסָלְקָא דַעְתָּךְ שֶׁזֶּה טוֹב יוֹתֵר שֶׁיְּקַוֶּוה הָאָדָם בְּכָל רֶגַע אֶל הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁיָּאִיר עֵינָיו מַה לַּעֲשׂוֹת וְאֵיךְ לְהִתְנַהֵג, וְלֹא שֶׁיִּהְיֶה לוֹ חֹק קָבוּעַ כְּשֻׁלְחָן עָרוּךְ: זֶה הַדֶּרֶךְ לְכוּ בוֹ, שֶׁאֵין צָרִיךְ לְצַפּוֹת לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּכָל נְתִיבוֹתָיו.

And how could it ever enter the mind that it was for their detriment? Rather, one might think it better that man depend in every moment upon Hashem to enlighten him how to act, without a fixed code like the Shulchan Arukh directing his path, which might reduce his constant yearning for Hashem.

אֲבָל בֶּאֱמֶת הוּא לְטוֹבָתְךָ, שֶׁזֶּה אוֹר הַמֵּאִיר וּמַבְהִיק שֶׁיּוּכַל לְהִשָּׁעֵן עָלָיו, וּבְלֹא הַתּוֹרָה הָיָה עוֹמֵד בְּיִרְאָה בְּכָל דָּבָר שֶׁמָּא טוֹעֶה וְאֵין רָצוֹן אֲמִיתִּי דְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ כֵּן.

But in truth it is for your benefit, providing a radiant light upon which to lean, whereas without the Torah one would stand in perpetual terror in every deed lest he be mistaken and it not be the true will of Hashem.
אֲבָל הַתּוֹרָה נִקְרָא "מִשְׁעָן", כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּחֲגִיגָה (יד.), וְכֵן אִיתָא בְּוַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה (פָּרָשָׁה כא): "עַמּוּד בַּרְזֶל – מִשְׁנָה";
But the Torah is called a "support," as stated in Chagigah 14a, and in Vayikra Rabbah 21: "an iron pillar—this is the Mishnah";

וַהֲרֵי זֶה כְּמוֹ אֲכִילַת מָן, שֶׁהָיוּ מְצַפִּים בְּכָל עֵת לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁיַּשְׁפִּיעַ לָהֶם חַיּוּתָם, נֶאֱמַר בּוֹ: "וַיְעַנְּךָ וַיַּרְעִבֶךָ" (דְּבָרִים ח, ג), שֶׁזֶּה עִנּוּי נֶפֶשׁ, וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (יוֹמָא עד:): רֶמֶז לַסוּמִין וְכוּלֵי שֶׁגַּם הֵם לֹא רָאוּ.

which mirrors the eating of the manna: where they yearned at every moment for Hashem to provide their life, concerning which it is said: "And He afflicted you, and suffered you to hunger" (Deuteronomy 8:3), which was an affliction of soul, as Yoma 74b expounds: like a blind man who cannot see what he eats.
וְכֵן הַתּוֹרָה הוּא אוֹר הַמֵּאִיר, וּבְלָאו הָכִי הוֹלֵךְ בַּחֹשֶׁךְ, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁמּוֹצֵא גַּם בַּחֹשֶׁךְ, אֵין בּוֹ שְׂבִיעָה.
And so the Torah is a shining light, without which one walks in darkness; and even if he finds something in the dark, it brings no satisfaction.
וְלָכֵן אָמְרוּ (בְּרָכוֹת לב:): הַמַּאֲרִיךְ בִּתְפִלָּתוֹ וּמְעַיֵּין בָּהּ וְכוּלֵי, וּמַאי תַּקַּנְתֵּיהּ? יַעֲסוֹק בַּתּוֹרָה וְכוּלֵי;
And therefore they taught (Berakhot 32b): one who prolongs his prayer and expects its fulfillment, his heart becomes sick; what is his remedy? Let him engage in Torah;
שֶׁהַתְּפִלָּה נִקְרָא "תּוֹחֶלֶת מְמֻשָּׁכָה" (מִשְׁלֵי יג, יב), שֶׁאֵינוֹ בְּטִיחוּת גָּמוּר;
for prayer is termed "hope deferred," lacking absolute certainty;

אֲבָל עַל יְדֵי דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, כְּשֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מֵאִיר שֶׁפָּעַל מַה שֶּׁהִתְפַּלֵּל, זֶהוּ מִשְׁעָן חָזָק, וְ"תַאֲוָה בָאָה" כְּאִלּוּ כְּבָר בָּאָה, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁעֲדַיִן לֹא בָּאָה, אֵינוֹ תּוֹחֶלֶת מְמֻשָּׁכָה, מֵאַחַר שֶׁרוֹאֶה בְּבֵירוּר וְנָכוֹן לִבּוֹ בָּטוּחַ בַּה' שֶׁיּוֹשִׁיעוֹ.

but through words of Torah, when Hashem illuminates that his prayer has been effected, it is a firm support, and "desire fulfilled" is as though it has already arrived, no longer deferred hope, since his heart rests securely confident in Hashem that He will save him.

וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מְכִילְתָּא רֵישׁ פָּרָשַׁת בְּשַׁלַּח): לֹא נִיתְּנָה תּוֹרָה אֶלָּא לְאוֹכְלֵי מָן, שֶׁבֶּאֱמֶת גַּם בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה צְרִיכִים לְהִתְנַהֵג כְּאוֹכְלֵי מָן: לְצַפּוֹת בְּכָל רֶגַע לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁיָּאִיר לוֹ אוֹרוֹת מְחוּדָּשׁוֹת בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה, וְלֹא שֶׁיִּסְמוֹךְ עַל מַה דִּכְתִיבָא וּמַנְחָא וְהַמְּפוֹרָשׁ בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה.

And our Sages stated (Mekhilta, Beshalach): the Torah was given only to eaters of the manna, meaning that even in Torah one must conduct himself like the eaters of manna: yearning at every moment for Hashem to radiate fresh lights in Torah, not relying merely on what is written and recorded explicitly.
דִּבֶּאֱמֶת גַּם אַחַר שֶׁנִּיתְּנָה תּוֹרָה, מִכָּל מָקוֹם הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מֵאִיר בְּכָל רֶגַע לִמְבַקְשָׁיו זֶה הַדֶּרֶךְ בִּפְרָטוּת אֵיךְ לְהִתְנַהֵג.
For in truth, even after the Torah was given, the Blessed Name illuminates at every instant for those who seek Him the individualized path of conduct.

וְעַל זֶה בִּקֵּשׁ דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם: "הֲבִינֵנִי וְגוֹמֵר" (תְּהִלִּים קיט, קכה), וְכֵן בְּכַמָּה פְּעָמִים נִדְרָשִׁים בְּשׁוֹחֵר טוֹב שֶׁאֵין לוֹ נִיחָא בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה רַק מַה שֶּׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מֵאִיר וּמְלַמֵּד לוֹ:

And concerning this King David prayed: "Give me understanding, etc." (Psalms 119:125), as expounded in Shocher Tov, that he found no true rest in Torah except in what Hashem personally illuminates and teaches him.

paragraphs.text: Explanation: Mei HaShiloach uses bread to distinguish receiving worldly sustenance from recognizing the divine utterance that gives it life. This sheds light on the siman’s comparison to the manna: a reliable source of nourishment need not produce spiritual self-sufficiency. Recognition of the Giver belongs within the act of receiving and enjoying it.

footnotes.enAnchorPrefix: and they stated in Yevamot 109b: whoever says he has nothing but Torah does not even possess Torah, for through this he might forget his utter dependence upon Hashem, which is the essence of prayer—the realization that he is deficient, beseeching Hashem to replenish him.

paragraphs.text: Resisei Layla 26:1: “In Torah, the levels are determined by excellence: whoever exceeds his fellow in wisdom is the greater. In prayer, however, the reverse is true: the levels are determined by lack, as stated in the Zohar (I, 23b), “A prayer of the poor,” which envelops all prayers, and as in Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai’s analogy of a servant and a minister (Berakhot 34b). For the more a person lacks and the more he needs, the more he can accomplish through his prayer, because his prayer comes from a deeper place in the heart. The essence of prayer arises from lack, as one asks the blessed God to supply what is missing; before the blessed God there is no distinction between the great and the small.”

footnotes.enAnchorPrefix: But in truth it is for your benefit, providing a radiant light upon which to lean, whereas without the Torah one would stand in perpetual terror in every deed lest he be mistaken and it not be the true will of Hashem.

paragraphs.text: Takanat HaShavin 8:5: “In truth, the Holy One, blessed be He, does not deal oppressively with His creatures, imposing decrees on them in order to punish them if they transgress. Concerning this they said in the Midrash: “Do not say that I gave the Torah to your detriment; it was given only for your benefit.” “To your detriment” cannot mean this literally, for such a thought cannot arise, Heaven forbid. Rather, it means that the Torah is not merely an arbitrary decree. If it were, it would be detrimental to those who transgress, who are the majority, for “there is no righteous person on earth,” and so forth, and Bava Batra says, “Most succumb to robbery, a minority to forbidden relations, and everyone to the dust of evil speech.” It would then have been better not to decree and not to punish. In truth, however, the Torah is the pattern of the work of Creation, as they said in Bereshit Rabbah. According to the laws of Creation, keeping the Torah’s laws is necessary to sustain the world. “Evil pursues sinners”—the transgression itself pursues them. One should complain only about oneself, not about the Life of the worlds. God did us a great good in giving the Torah: He made known the things a person should do and live, and repeatedly urged choosing life, for they are intrinsically our life.”

paragraphs.text: Likkutei Maamarim, On Book of Joshua 19: “The revelation of secrets hidden from those who receive them is what is called the Oral Torah. This is “His secrets are concealed”: they are not revealed to everyone, but only to the person to whom God reveals them. If one could learn it from another or from what is written in books, it too would be called “written and already laid down,” as though one did not need God. sections.en: Torah and Prayer Are Both Designated Solely for One Who Is Deficient

p: [ריב] הַתּוֹרָה וְהַתְּפִלָּה שְׁנֵיהֶם רַק לְמִי שֶׁהוּא חָסֵר וּמְבַקֵּשׁ הַשְׁלָמָה עַל יְדֵי הַתְּפִלָּה אוֹ עַל יְדֵי הַתּוֹרָה, שֶׁהִיא תַּבְלִין לַיֵּצֶר הָרָע וּלְיַישֵּׁר הַחִסָּרוֹן שֶׁבַּלֵּב.

Torah and prayer are both designated solely for one who is deficient, seeking replenishment through prayer or through Torah, which is an antidote to the evil inclination to straighten the deficiency in the heart.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּשַׁבָּת (פט.): כְּלוּם יֵצֶר הָרָע יֵשׁ בֵּינֵיכֶם? וְלָמָּה לָכֶם אוֹרָהּ.
And as stated in Shabbat 89a: "Is there an evil inclination among you angels? Why then do you need its light?"
וְלָכֵן תְּחִלַּת שְׁנֵיהֶם הַיִּרְאָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי: כִּי עִיקַּר יִרְאָה פֵּירוּשׁ הַכָּרַת הַחִסָּרוֹן שֶׁמִּפְּנֵי זֶה הוּא מִתְיָירֵא;
Therefore the inception of both is fear, as I heard: for the essence of fear is the recognition of deficiency, on account of which one trembles;
וְכִידוּעַ דְּיִרְאָה נִקְרָא נוּקְבָא, פֵּירוּשׁ שֶׁהִיא חֲסֵרָה וּמְבַקֶּשֶׁת הַשְׁלָמָה.
and as is known, fear is termed the female aspect (Nukva), meaning that which is deficient and seeks completion.
וְעַל יְדֵי תּוֹרָה מִיָּד הוּא הַשְׁלָמַת הַחִסָּרוֹן, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "פִּקּוּדֵי [ה' יְשָׁרִים] מְשַׂמְּחֵי לֵב" (תְּהִלִּים יט, ט), וְשִׂמְחָה הוּא הִיפּוּךְ הַיִּרְאָה.
And through Torah the replenishment of deficiency is immediate, as written: "The statutes [of Hashem are right], rejoicing the heart" (Psalms 19:9), and joy is the opposite of fear.

אֲבָל עַל יְדֵי תְּפִלָּה, אִם הוּא כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (תַּעֲנִית כה סוֹף עַמּוּד ב): אָמַר מַשִּׁיב הָרוּחַ – נָשֵׁיב זִיקָא וְכוּלֵי, עַל זֶה אָמַר: "וְשִׂמַּחְתִּים בְּבֵית תְּפִלָּתִי" (יְשַׁעְיָה נו, ז), שֶׁמִּיָּד מַגִּיעַ הַמִּלּוּי;

But through prayer, if it is like the saying in Ta'anit 25b: when he recited "He causes the wind to blow," the wind blew, etc., concerning this Scripture states: "and make them joyful in My house of prayer" (Isaiah 56:7), for fulfillment arrives immediately;
וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת ז.): "תְּפִלָּתָם" לֹא נֶאֱמַר וְכוּלֵי, כִּי גַּם הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מִתְפַּלֵּל, פֵּירוּשׁ מִתְאַוֶּוה וְרוֹצֶה לְאוֹתוֹ דָּבָר,
and our Sages stated (Berakhot 7a): it does not say "their prayer," but "My house of prayer," for the Holy One likewise prays—meaning He yearns and wills that very outcome,

רַק שֶׁמְּנָעוֹ בִּשְׁבִיל שֶׁמִּתְאַוֶּוה לִתְפִלָּתָן שֶׁל צַדִּיקִים, וְהוּא מוּכָן לַעֲנוֹת, וּמִתְאַוֶּוה שֶׁיִּתְפַּלְּלוּ וְיֵעָנוּ, וְתַאֲוָתוֹ שֶׁל הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הַיְינוּ תְּפִלָּתוֹ, וְאָז "וְשִׂמַּחְתִּים".
only that He held it back because He yearns for the prayer of the righteous, being poised to answer, and His yearning is His prayer, and then "I will make them joyful."
וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ: אִם שְׁגוּרָה וְכוּלֵי, פֵּירוּשׁ בִּמְרוּצָה, כִּי אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְהִתְפַּלֵּל עַל דָּבָר אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן הוּא חָסֵר לָהּ.
And concerning this they said: "If my prayer is fluent (shgura), etc."—meaning running swiftly—for one cannot pray for something unless he acutely lacks it.
וּבְוַדַּאי רַבִּי חֲנִינָא בֶּן דּוֹסָא שֶׁהִתְפַּלֵּל עַל חוֹלִים, כָּל כָּךְ עוֹרְרוּ רַחֲמָיו עַל אוֹתוֹ חוֹלֶה עַד שֶׁהָיָה חָסֵר מְאֹד וּמְצַפֶּה לִישׁוּעָה.
And certainly Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa when praying for the sick had his compassions so aroused for that patient that he felt an immense lack, longing for salvation.
וְאִם הָיָה פּוֹעֵל, אָז תֵּיכֶף הָיָה מַגִּיעַ הַשִּׂמְחָה וּמִלּוּי הַחִסָּרוֹן בְּלִבּוֹ, וְהָיָה יָכוֹל לָרוּץ בִּתְפִלָּתוֹ מִתֵּיבָה לְתֵיבָה כְּדֵי לְהָחִישׁ הַיְשׁוּעָה.
And if his prayer effected its goal, joy and the fulfillment of that lack immediately flooded his heart, and he was able to run swiftly in his prayer from word to word to hasten the salvation.

וְאִם לָאו, הָיָה עֲדַיִן עוֹמֵד בַּחִסָּרוֹן וּבַצִּיפּוּי, וְלֹא הָיָה אֶפְשָׁר לוֹ לָלֶכֶת כְּלָל מִכָּל תֵּיבָה מִן הַתְּפִלָּה וּלְהַרְחִיק מִמֶּנָּה, מֵאַחַר שֶׁעֲדַיִן אֵין לוֹ מִלּוּי לְחֶסְרוֹנוֹ.
But if not, he remained immersed in deficiency and longing, unable to move past each word of the prayer, since he had not yet received fulfillment for his lack.

וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת לב:): כָּל הַמְעַיֵּין בִּתְפִלָּתוֹ וְכוּלֵי, שֶׁאֵין לָאָדָם לִבְטוֹחַ כָּל כָּךְ בְּבֵירוּר עַל הַתְּפִלָּה, רַק: "קַוֵּה אֶל ה' חֲזַק [וְיַאֲמֵץ לִבֶּךָ] וְקַוֵּה אֶל ה'" (תְּהִלִּים כז, יד).

And our Sages stated (Berakhot 32b): whoever expects the fulfillment of his prayer brings heart pain, for one must not rely with definitive certitude upon his prayer, but rather: "Hope in Hashem; be of good courage, [and He shall strengthen your heart;] hope, I say, in Hashem" (Psalms 27:14).

וְלָכֵן נֶאֱמַר: "עִבְדוּ אֶת ה' בְּיִרְאָה" (שָׁם ב, יא), שֶׁהָעֲבוֹדָה דִּתְפִלָּה הִיא בְּיִרְאָה וְלֹא בְּשִׂמְחָה, כִּי אֵינוֹ בָּטוּחַ כָּל כָּךְ, אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן כְּרַבִּי חֲנִינָא בֶּן דּוֹסָא כְּשֶׁשְּׁגוּרָה תְּפִלָּתוֹ.

Therefore it is said: "Serve Hashem with fear" (ibid. 2:11), for the service of prayer is accompanied by fear and not pure joy, as one is not completely certain, unless like Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa when prayer is fluent.
וְ"גִילוּ בִּרְעָדָה" (שָׁם), שֶׁאֲפִילּוּ כְּשֶׁבָּא לוֹ שִׂמְחָה, אִי אֶפְשָׁר לִבְטוֹחַ כָּל כָּךְ, וְצָרִיךְ לִהְיוֹת גַּם כֵּן בִּרְעָדָה.
And "rejoice with trembling" (ibid.), for even when joy arrives, one cannot become overconfident, but must remain with trembling.
רַק בְּמִזְמוֹר לְתוֹדָה נֶאֱמַר: "עִבְדוּ אֶת ה' בְּשִׂמְחָה" (שָׁם ק, ב), כִּי בְּכָל תְּפִלָּה צָרִיךְ לִהְיוֹת הוֹדָאָה עַל הֶעָבָר וּצְעָקָה לֶעָתִיד לָבוֹא.
Only in the Psalm of Thanksgiving is it said: "Serve Hashem with gladness" (ibid. 100:2), for in every prayer there must be thanksgiving for the past and supplication for the future.

וְזֶה טַעַם סְמִיכַת גְּאוּלָּה לִתְפִלָּה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי עַל קְצִיבַת עֵץ דֶּאֱלִישָׁע, שֶׁצָּרִיךְ לְהַרְאוֹת דָּבָר שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עוֹשֶׂה כַּהַאי גַּוְונָא שֶׁהָעֵץ צָף, וְעַל יְדֵי כֵן יָכוֹל לְבַקֵּשׁ בְּחֹזֶק שֶׁגַּם הַבַּרְזֶל יָצִיף, כִּי מַאי נַפְקָא מִינַּהּ לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בֵּין עֵץ לְבַרְזֶל.

And this is the reason for juxtaposing redemption to prayer, as I heard regarding Elisha casting the wood (II Kings 6:6): one must point to a phenomenon where Hashem acts similarly—the wood floating—and through this plead with vigor that the iron axe-head likewise float, for what difference is there to Hashem between wood and iron?

וְכֵן צָרִיךְ לְהַזְכִּיר הוֹדָאָה עַל הֶעָבָר שֶׁגְּאַלְתָּנוּ וּמַה שֶּׁפָּעַלְתָּ יְשׁוּעוֹת, וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה נְבַקֵּשׁ גַּם עַכְשָׁו: הוֹשִׁיעֵנוּ, מַאי נַפְקָא מִינַּהּ לְךָ בֵּין אָז לְעַכְשָׁו.
And so one must articulate thanksgiving for the past—that You redeemed us and wrought salvations—and through this plead now: save us, for what difference is there to You between then and now?
וּלְכָךְ בְּעֵת הַתּוֹדָה וְהוֹדָאַת הֶעָבָר, שֶׁבָּזֶה כְּבָר הָיָה הַמִּלּוּי, שַׁפִּיר נֶאֱמַר בְּשִׂמְחָה.
Therefore during thanksgiving for the past, where fulfillment has already occurred, it is rightly said with joy.
וּמִכֹּחַ זֶה יוּכַל לְהַמְשִׁיךְ גַּם כֵּן שִׂמְחָה עַל הַתְּפִלָּה, שֶׁבְּוַדַּאי יֵעָנֶה מִכֹּחַ טַעֲנָה הַנִּזְכֶּרֶת לְעֵיל.
And through this power he can extend joy over the prayer as well, confident that he will be answered based on that very claim.
וְזֶהוּ סְמִיכַת גְּאוּלָּה לִתְפִלָּה, שֶׁיִּהְיֶה תְּכוּפָה לָהּ וּמְחוּבָּר וּמְיוּחֶדֶת לָהּ, אָז גַּם בִּתְפִלָּה יֵעָנֶה, וְהוּא בֶּן עוֹלָם הַבָּא;
And this is juxtaposing redemption to prayer, that it be immediately adjacent and unified with it, and then he will be answered in prayer, and he is a son of the World to Come;

כִּי "בְּרַתָּא דְּמַלְכָּא דָּא צְלוֹתָא" הִיא מִדַּת אֶרֶץ הָעֶלְיוֹנָה שֶׁנִּקְרָא עוֹלָם הַבָּא, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּרֵישׁ פֶּרֶק חֵלֶק עַל עוֹלָם הַבָּא מִקְּרָא דִּ"לְעוֹלָם יִירְשׁוּ אָרֶץ" (יְשַׁעְיָה ס, כא).
for "the King's daughter is prayer," which is the Supernal Earth termed the World to Come, as Sanhedrin 90a derives from "they shall inherit the land forever" (Isaiah 60:21).

וְלָכֵן תִּקְּנוּ שָׁלֹשׁ רִאשׁוֹנוֹת בְּשֶׁבַח הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לַטַּעַם הַנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל: מֵאַחַר שֶׁאַתָּה יָכוֹל עַל הַכֹּל, עַל יְדֵי זֶה מְבַקְּשִׁים י"ב אֶמְצָעִיּוֹת, וְאַחַר כָּךְ שָׁלֹשׁ אַחֲרוֹנוֹת כְּעֶבֶד הַנּוֹטֵל פְּרָס שֶׁבָּטוּחַ עַל הַמִּלּוּי.

Therefore they instituted the first three blessings in praise of Hashem for the aforementioned reason: since You are omnipotent, through this we petition the twelve middle requests, and then conclude with the final three like a servant receiving a reward, confident of fulfillment.
וּבֶאֱמֶת יֵשׁ לִבְטוֹחַ בַּה' שֶׁיַּעֲנֵהוּ וִיקַבֵּל תְּפִלָּתוֹ, רַק שֶׁלֹּא יְעַיֵּין בָּהּ, וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "יִבְטַח בְּשֵׁם ה' וְגוֹמֵר" (יְשַׁעְיָה נ, י).
And in truth one must trust in Hashem that He will answer and accept his prayer, provided he does not arrogantly expect it, as in: "let him trust in the Name of Hashem, etc." (Isaiah 50:10).
וּתְחִלָּתוֹ: "מִי בָכֶם יְרֵא ה' וְגוֹמֵר" – פֵּירוּשׁ, הֶחָסֵר וּמְבַקֵּשׁ הַשְׁלָמָה עַל יְדֵי תְּפִלָּה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (ו:) עַל זֶה דְּרָגִיל לָבוֹא לְבֵית הַכְּנֶסֶת.

And that verse opens: "Who is among you that fears Hashem, etc."—meaning one who feels deficient and seeks completion through prayer, as Berakhot 6b expounds regarding one accustomed to attending the synagogue.
וְהַיְינוּ דְּ"שֹׁמֵעַ בְּקוֹל עַבְדּוֹ" – הוּא הַשְּׁלִיחַ צִבּוּר כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל אוֹת ר"י כְּעֶבֶד לִפְנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ.
And "hearkens to the voice of His servant"—this is the prayer leader (shaliach tzibbur), who stands like a servant before the King (Section 210).
"הָלַךְ חֲשֵׁכִים", וּפֵירְשׁוּ שָׁם: לִדְבַר הָרְשׁוּת;
"Walks in darkness"—which they explained there: for permitted mundane pursuits;
וּבֶאֱמֶת חֹשֶׁךְ נִקְרָא דְּבַר עֲבֵירָה, רַק נֹגַהּ הוּא דְּבַר הָרְשׁוּת כַּיָּדוּעַ מִסּוֹד הַד' קְלִיפּוֹת.
and in truth "darkness" denotes sin, while "glow" (nogah) denotes permitted matters, as known from the mystery of the four kelipot.
רַק כַּוָּנַת הַכָּתוּב: שֶׁבֶּאֱמֶת אֵין לוֹ נֹגַהּ, וַאֲפִילּוּ לְדִבְרֵי הָרְשׁוּת הוּא חֲשֵׁכִים, כֵּיוָן שֶׁעַל יְדֵי זֶה מוֹנֵעַ מִמִּצְוָה.
But the verse means that he truly lacks glow, and even permitted affairs become darkness since through them he is prevented from a mitzvah.
וְאָמַר: "יִבְטַח וְגוֹמֵר" – פֵּירוּשׁ, שֵׁם ה' הוּא מַה שֶּׁלְּמַעְלָה מֵהַטֶּבַע כַּנּוֹדָע, בָּזֶה יִבְטַח שֶׁיּוּכַל לְהוֹשִׁיעַ לְמַעְלָה מִשִּׂכְלוֹ.
And it states: "let him trust in the Name of Hashem"—the Name Havayah transcending nature, wherein he trusts that He can save beyond human reason.
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם זֶהוּ רַק בִּטָּחוֹן, אֲבָל "יִשָּׁעֵן" – מִשְׁעָן הוּא יוֹתֵר, וּמַה שֶּׁהוּא בְּיָדוֹ וְנִשְׁעָן עָלָיו, זֶהוּ "בֵּאלֹהָיו",
However, that is merely trust; but "and lean upon"—a staff of support is firmer, what is in his hand to lean upon being "upon his God" (Elohav),

כִּידוּעַ דְּשֵׁם זֶה מוֹרֶה עַל כֹּחוֹת הַמּוּטְבָּעִים בַּבְּרוּאִים, וֶ"אֱלֹהָיו" רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר כֹּחוֹתָיו שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ שֶׁנָּתַן לוֹ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לְכַלְכֵּל עַצְמוֹ עַל יָדוֹ בְּכָל צְרָכָיו בְּעֵצוֹת מִדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה וְחָכְמָה וַעֲבוֹדָה – בָּזֶה הוּא עִיקַּר הַשְּׁעִינָה.

for this Name denotes the natural powers embedded in creation, and Elohav refers to the faculties Hashem granted him to sustain himself in all his needs through Torah, wisdom, and divine service—upon which he primarily leans.
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם יִבְטַח בִּישׁוּעָה שֶׁלְּמַעְלָה מִכֹּחוֹ גַּם כֵּן, כִּי אֵין מַעְצוֹר לַה', וְהֵן לֹא קָצְרָה יָדוֹ מֵהוֹשִׁיעַ:
Nonetheless, let him also trust in salvation transcending his natural strength, for there is no restraint to Hashem, nor is His hand shortened from saving.

paragraphs.text: Shabbat 88b:8-89a:1: “The Holy One, blessed be He, said to Moses: ‘Give them an answer.’ He said before Him: ‘Master of the universe, I fear that they may burn me with the breath of their mouths.’ He said to him: ‘Take hold of My Throne of Glory and give them an answer,’ as it is stated: ‘He takes hold of the face of the throne; He spreads His cloud over him.’ Rabbi Nahum said: ‘This teaches that Shaddai spread some of the radiance of His Shekhinah and His cloud over him.’ Moses said before Him: ‘Master of the universe, what is written in the Torah that You are giving me? ‘I am Hashem your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.’’ He said to them: ‘Did you descend to Egypt? Were you enslaved to Pharaoh? Why should the Torah be yours? Again, what is written in it? ‘You shall have no other gods.’ Do you dwell among nations that worship idols? Again, what is written in it? ‘Remember the Shabbat day to sanctify it.’ Do you perform work, so that you need to rest? Again, what is written in it? ‘You shall not take’—are there commercial dealings among you? Again, what is written in it? ‘Honor your father and your mother’—do you have a father and mother? Again, what is written in it? ‘You shall not murder,’ ‘You shall not commit adultery,’ ‘You shall not steal.’ Is there jealousy among you? Is there an evil inclination among you?’ Immediately they conceded to the Holy One, blessed be He, as it is stated: ‘Hashem, our Master, how mighty is Your Name,’ and so on; whereas ‘Set Your splendor upon the heavens’ is not written.”

footnotes.enAnchorPrefix: Therefore the inception of both is fear, as I heard: for the essence of fear is the recognition of deficiency, on account of which one trembles;

paragraphs.text: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayera 9: ““Now I know that you fear God.” The distinction between fear of Hashem and fear of Elohim is as follows. Fear of Elohim is a person’s restraining himself from doing something, such as eating and the like, because he is not yet complete and still has a deficiency. He limits himself according to his understanding; this is called fear of Elohim. Fear of Hashem, however, means that even when a person understands that he could do this thing because his soul has been purified of that deficiency, it remains forbidden to him by God. For God commanded upright precepts for every soul. Since there is someone who has not yet been purified in this respect, God did not permit the thing, because it is not equally suitable for everyone. A person is obligated to bear a prohibition on account of his fellow. This is called fear of Hashem.”

For there is a reverence belonging to Torah that is called the feminine, the Oral Torah, concerning which it is said there, “Then the trees of the forest shall sing.””

paragraphs.text: Tiferet Yisrael, Introduction to Tiferet Yisrael 20: “The meaning is that, through Torah, a person is considered a complete being, and therefore it gladdens his heart. When a person is in a state of completion, he is joyful. The opposite occurs when he is in a state of deficiency: he is in mourning. Therefore, when death occurs among his close relatives, he is in mourning.”

paragraphs.text: Explanation: Tiferet Yosef asks how the Sages can describe righteous prayer as changing the divine measure when Hashem does not change. Its answer locates the change in the recipient's attainment of the gift. This illuminates the present siman's language that Hashem Himself desires the requested fulfillment and waits for prayer. The petition opens a relation of reception; it is not portrayed as persuading an unwilling giver to acquire a new disposition.

paragraphs.text: Be'er HaGolah, Well 4 2:3: “This is what they meant by “From where do we know that the Holy One, blessed be He, prays?” Because He is the true good and abundant in kindness, He is called “desiring kindness” and seeks the good. His praying means seeking the good. Prayer means a request; this is the essential meaning of the word everywhere. In a human being, however, the request is directed to God—otherwise, what would his request accomplish? Nevertheless, prayer means a request. The teaching says that God desires and seeks this: that it be His will for His mercy to overcome His anger, for Him to conduct Himself toward His children with the attribute of mercy, and to go beyond the strict measure of judgment.”

paragraphs.text: Peri Tzadik, Pesach 32:1: “As we find with Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa, who said, “He who told oil to burn will tell vinegar to burn.” Why did he mention “He who told oil to burn”? One must recall that God implanted in the nature of oil that it should burn, and through this one can draw forth His saying that vinegar should burn. This accords with what I heard from the holy master, of blessed memory, concerning Elisha: “He cut a piece of wood, threw it there, and the iron floated.” Why did he need to cut and throw wood? He wished to recall that God implanted in wood the nature of floating on water, and through this he threw it so that God would give the iron this nature as well. Elisha did this through an action, whereas Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa recalled it verbally: “He who told oil to burn,” and so forth. For him, this was not an act of miracles, since otherwise he would certainly not have wished to benefit from a miracle. Rather, it was completely clear before his eyes that there is no independent nature or habit, only what God gives the thing as its nature. The burning of oil was like the burning of vinegar to him. By recalling aloud, “He who told oil to burn,” that it comes only from God’s utterance, he drew forth the influence that would make the vinegar burn. Thus “He made a memorial for His wonders” is explained by “Hashem is gracious and compassionate”: through remembrance they can draw forth the influence from Atika, which is wonder.”

paragraphs.text: Devarim Rabbah 2:10: ““For what great nation,” and so forth. A legal question: May a person of Israel who has recited Shema wait after Shema and then pray? The Sages taught: There are three immediate successions—slaughter immediately after laying hands on the offering; a blessing immediately after washing the hands; and prayer immediately after redemption. What is the reward of one who does this? Rabbah bar Abbahu said: If he lays hands and slaughters, he may be assured that his offering has been accepted. If he washes his hands and immediately blesses, he may be assured that no accuser will prosecute during his meal. If he recites Shema and immediately prays, he may be assured that his prayer is heard.”

paragraphs.text: Using one’s given powers and praying beyond them belong to the same reliance

rich.text: Using one’s given powers and praying beyond them belong to the same reliance

paragraphs.text: The work from below uses all available strength and also asks for the help that strength cannot supply by itself.

rich.text: The work from below uses all available strength and also asks for the help that strength cannot supply by itself.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Rav Tzadok · Peri Tzadik, Rosh Chodesh Kislev 7:4: “At least an awakening from below in prayer is also needed: to ask His help against the inclination that seeks to kill him, which he cannot overcome. God then helps through an awakening from above. Samekh indicates “The Lord supports all who fall,” and the fallen sukkah of David: it surrounds like a sukkah, protecting those who seek His help. From the person’s side, the work of this month is to stir the good inclination against the bad with all his strength, until he cannot overcome it from his own side.”

paragraphs.text: Explanation: Kislev joins full effort against the inclination with the prayer that calls forth assistance from above. This explains the present siman’s distinction between leaning on the powers Hashem has already given and trusting in salvation beyond them. Neither side cancels the other: existing wisdom and ability are themselves gifts to be used, while their limitation gives prayer its honest sense of need. Support is received by the person who turns toward Hashem from within that work.

paragraphs.text: Tanya, Part II; Shaar HaYichud VehaEmunah 6:1-2: “The name Elohim is the name of the attribute of strength and contraction. Therefore it also has the numerical value of hateva, “nature,” because it conceals the supernal light that brings the world into being and gives it life, so that the world appears to stand and operate by nature. This name Elohim is a shield and covering for the name Havayah, concealing the light and vitality that flow from Havayah and bring something into being from nothing, lest they be revealed to the creatures and the creatures lose their independent existence. This strength and contraction are themselves also a form of kindness through which the world is built. This is strength included within kindness.”

sections.en: Whoever Is Deficient and Pleads for Completion

p: [ריג] מִי שֶׁהוּא חָסֵר וּמְבַקֵּשׁ הַשְׁלָמָה, אִי אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לֹא יַעֲנֵהוּ,
Whoever is deficient and pleads for completion, it is impossible that the Holy One, blessed be He, will not answer him,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "קָרוֹב ה' לְנִשְׁבְּרֵי לֵב וְאֶת דַּכְּאֵי [רוּחַ יוֹשִׁיעַ]" (תְּהִלִּים לד, יט),
as it is written: "Hashem is near unto them that are of a broken heart, and the contrite [of spirit He saves]" (Psalms 34:19),
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק ג, קצה עַמּוּד א) דִּתְפִלָּה דְּעָנִי כְּלַל כָּל צְלוֹתִין וּבָקְעֵי רְקִיעִין.
and as written in the Zohar (Part III, 195a) that the prayer of the afflicted man encompasses all prayers and cleaves through the heavens.
וְאֵין עָנִי אֶלָּא בְּדַעַת (נְדָרִים מא.), אֲפִילּוּ אֵין יוֹדֵעַ אֵיךְ לְהִתְפַּלֵּל וּלְרַצּוֹת לְקוֹנוֹ,
And "poor" denotes poor in knowledge (Nedarim 41a), even one who does not know how to pray properly and find favor before his Maker;
וּלְכָךְ נֶאֱמַר בּוֹ: "וְלִפְנֵי ה' יִשְׁפֹּךְ שִׂיחוֹ" (תְּהִלִּים קב, א), וְ"שִׂיחָה" פֵּירוּשׁ מִילֵּי דְּעָלְמָא וְלֹא דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה
and therefore concerning him Scripture states: "and pours out his complaint (sicho) before Hashem" (Psalms 102:1), where sichah signifies mundane everyday words rather than structured words of Torah

[וּבְיִצְחָק נֶאֱמַר גַּם כֵּן "לָשׂוּחַ בַּשָּׂדֶה" (בְּרֵאשִׁית כד, סג), כִּידוּעַ דְּהוּא עַמּוּד הַתּוֹרָה, וְ"שִׂיחוּ" – אֵלּוּ בַּעֲלֵי תוֹרָה שֶׁכָּל שִׂיחָתָן תּוֹרָה (עֵירוּבִין נד:), שַׁיָּיךְ שַׁפִּיר "שִׂיחוֹ"],

[and concerning Isaac it is likewise said "to converse (lasu'ach) in the field" (Genesis 24:63), for as is known he is the pillar of Torah, and "tell of it" denotes the masters of Torah all of whose conversation is Torah (Eruvin 54b), so the term sicho is fitting],

הַיְינוּ שֶׁמְּדַבֵּר בְּלֹא דַעַת, וְ"יִשְׁפֹּךְ" – וְלֹא בְּמָתוֹן וּבְסֵדֶר, רַק שֶׁמִּתּוֹךְ שְׁבִירוּת לִבּוֹ שׁוֹפֵךְ נַפְשׁוֹ לַה' וּדְבָרִים בִּלְתִּי מְסוּדָּרִים וְשֶׁלֹּא בְּדַעַת, וְזוֹ מְקוּבֶּלֶת יוֹתֵר.

meaning that he speaks without sophisticated understanding, and "pours out"—not in measured patience and order, but from the brokenness of his heart he pours out his soul to Hashem with disordered words and lacking eloquence, and this prayer is accepted above all.
וּתְפִלָּה בִּמְקוֹם קָרְבָּנוֹת, וּדְעָנִי נִקְרָא "מִנְחָה", שֶׁחָשׁוּב לִפְנֵי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מַתָּנָה וּמִנְחָה, וְגַם הוּא לְשׁוֹן נִיחָא, כִּי הוּא מְקַבֵּל תֵּיכֶף הַנִּיחָא.

And prayer stands in place of sacrifices, and that of the poor is called a Minchah (meal-offering), which is regarded before the Blessed Name as a gift and tribute (minchah), and is also an expression of rest (nicha), for he immediately receives tranquility.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי: דְּכָל אֶחָד מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁחָסֵר לְאֵיזֶה דָּבָר וּמְבַקֵּשׁ גַּם בַּהַפְלָגָה
And as I heard: every Jew who lacks anything and asks even with expansive audacity
[כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּרָכוֹת נ.) דִּבִּשְׁאֵלָה: "הַרְחֶב פִּיךָ וַאֲמַלְאֵהוּ" (תְּהִלִּים פא, יא)],
[in line with Berakhot 50a that in petition: "open wide your mouth and I will fill it" (Psalms 81:11)],
הָיָה פּוֹעֵל בְּוַדַּאי, רַק שֶׁהוּא מְרוּצֶּה אַחַר כָּךְ בְּכָל שֶׁהוּא.
would certainly effect his salvation, only that he subsequently settles for the slightest partial result.
וְצָרִיךְ לָזֶה דַּעַת שֶׁלֹּא לְהִתְרַצּוֹת, וְלַחְשׁוֹב עַצְמוֹ שֶׁאֵינוֹ חָסֵר רַק בִּישׁוּעָה שְׁלֵימָה.
And for this one requires the resolve not to be placated, viewing himself as entirely lacking until complete salvation arrives.
וְזֶה עֲצַת יַעְבֵּץ שֶׁאָמַר: "אִם בָּרֵךְ [תְּבָרֲכֵנִי] וְגוֹמֵר" (דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים א ד, י),
And this was the counsel of Ya'betz who pleaded: "Oh that You would [bless me] indeed, etc." (I Chronicles 4:10),
וְאָמְרוּ בִּתְמוּרָה (טז.) שֶׁאָמַר: אִם וְכוּלֵי וְאִם לָאו הֲרֵינִי הוֹלֵךְ וְכוּלֵי,
and they expounded in Temurah 16a that he said: if You bless me, yes, and if not, behold I go down to Sheol,
פֵּירוּשׁ שֶׁאָמַר שֶׁאֵינוֹ מְקַבֵּל שׁוּם נִיחָא כְּלָל כָּל זְמַן שֶׁלֹּא יַעֲנֵהוּ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ כְּכָל אֲשֶׁר שָׁאַל, וּבְאִם לָאו הֲרֵי הוֹלֵךְ חַס וְשָׁלוֹם לִשְׁאוֹל וְחָסֵר לְגַמְרֵי.

meaning that he resolved that he would accept no pacification whatsoever so long as the Blessed Name did not answer him in all that he asked, and if not, he was heading unto the grave, completely deficient.
וְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מוּכָן לַעֲזוֹר לְנִשְׁבְּרֵי לֵב, וּמִיָּד: "וַיָּבֵא [אֱלֹהִים אֵת] אֲשֶׁר שָׁאָל" (שָׁם), וּמִלְּשׁוֹן הַגְּמָרָא "מִיָּד" מְבוֹאָר דְּפוֹעֵל תֵּיכֶף.

And the Blessed Name is poised to help the broken-hearted, and immediately: "and [God] granted him that which he requested" (ibid.), where from the Talmudic phrase "immediately" it is evident that it effected results instantly.
וְאָנוּ מְבַקְּשִׁים: "רַחֲמָנָא דְּעָנֵי לִתְבִירֵי לִבָּא וּלְמַכִּיכֵי רוּחָא – עֲנֵינָא".
And we pray in the Selichot: "Merciful One Who answers the broken of heart and the humble of spirit, answer us."
דְּבֶאֱמֶת לָזֶה גּוּפֵיהּ צָרִיךְ סַיַּעְתָּא דִּשְׁמַיָּא: לִהְיוֹת לֵב נִשְׁבָּר וְשֶׁלֹּא לְהִתְרַצּוֹת בְּשׁוּם דָּבָר רַק בִּישׁוּעָה גְּמוּרָה.
For in truth, for this itself one requires Heavenly assistance: to possess a broken heart and refuse to be placated by anything short of absolute salvation.
וְעַל זֶה מְבַקְּשִׁים "רַחֲמָנָא וְכוּלֵי" כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל אוֹת רי"ב מִקְּצִיבַת הָעֵץ:
And regarding this we plead "Merciful One, etc.," in the spirit of Section 212 regarding Elisha casting the wood:
שֶׁהֲרֵי עָנִיתָ לִפְלוֹנִי בְּדָבָר זֶה, וְהוֹשִׁיעַ גַּם לָנוּ אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין אָנוּ כְּמוֹתוֹ, מַאי נַפְקָא מִינַּהּ לְךָ?
seeing that You answered that person in this matter, save us too even though we are not like him, for what difference does it make to You?
כְּעִנְיַן "אִם צָדַקְתָּ מַה תִּתֶּן לוֹ וְגוֹמֵר" (אִיּוֹב לה, ז), כִּי לַאֲמִיתַּת רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מַאי נַפְקָא מִינַּהּ בֵּין צַדִּיק לְרָשָׁע, וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן בָּזֶה.

in the manner of "If you are righteous, what do you give Him, etc.?" (Job 35:7), for in the ultimate depth of the divine will, what difference is there to Him between righteous and wicked, and all the more so in this context.
רַק זֶהוּ מִצַּד הַנְהָגַת הַתּוֹרָה, מִצִּידָּהּ רָאוּי לַעֲנוֹת לְצַדִּיק יוֹתֵר, וְכֵן לְנִשְׁבַּר לֵב יוֹתֵר.
It is only from the perspective of the Torah's legal governance that it is fitting to answer the righteous more, and likewise the broken-hearted more.
אֲבָל בַּקָּשַׁת רַחֲמִים הוּא גַּם שֶׁאֵינוֹ מִשּׁוּרַת מִשְׁפַּט הַתּוֹרָה,
But beseeching mercy applies even where it is not warranted by the strict judgment of the Torah;
וְזֶהוּ "רַחֲמָנָא" – מִצַּד מִדַּת רַחֲמָנוּתְךָ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָנוּ רוֹאִים שֶׁאַתָּה עוֹנֶה לָזֶה, כָּךְ עֲנֵה גַּם לָנוּ:
and this is "Merciful One"—from the aspect of Your quality of mercy, just as we see that You answer this broken-hearted one, so answer us as well.

paragraphs.text: Zohar, Balak 14:188-189: “Why? Because the poor person is brokenhearted, and it is written, “Hashem is close to the brokenhearted.” The poor person constantly disputes with the Holy One, blessed be He, and He attends and hears his words. When he prays, He opens all the windows of the heavens, and that brokenhearted poor person pushes aside all the other prayers ascending above. It is written, “A prayer of the poor when he wraps”: it should have said “when he wraps himself.” Rather, he wraps up all the prayers of the world, and they do not enter until his prayer enters. The Holy One, blessed be He, says: Let all the prayers be wrapped up, and let this prayer come to Me. I do not want a court here to judge between us. Let his complaints be before Me, and let him and Me be alone. The Holy One, blessed be He, communes alone with those complaints, with that prayer, as it says, “Before Hashem he pours out his speech”—before Hashem indeed.”

paragraphs.text: The description of unarranged prayer concerns a heart whose lack cannot remain unspoken.

rich.text: The description of unarranged prayer concerns a heart whose lack cannot remain unspoken.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Rav Tzadok · Et HaOchel 14:1: “This is the meaning of eating the bread of poverty, like ‘A prayer of the poor person when he is overwhelmed,’ which envelops all prayers and breaks through the heavens. Because of his great lack, the poor person pours out his speech as the pouring out of his soul, like Channah pouring out her soul. He cannot contain it within his heart, until he speaks with his mouth and raises his voice. That eating has the power to bring forth speech that issues from the heart; the principal vitality is in proportion to the depth of the poverty and the felt need.”

paragraphs.text: Explanation: Et HaOchel develops the same Psalm and the comparison to Channah. Its larger context defines the soul's poverty as acknowledging that it has nothing independently and lives through heavenly mercy. The quoted passage explains why such a prayer can emerge as poured-out speech rather than a polished arrangement. This supports the siman's emphasis on the heart's reality, without making disorder of words a substitute for that reality.

paragraphs.text: Peri Tzadik, Vaetchanan 2:1: “Certainly, in ordinary prayer to the blessed God one should not raise one’s voice; doing so is a sign of little faith. But sometimes a person is in very great distress and can no longer contain within himself the anguish over some matter for which he needs deliverance. Then he cries out from the depth of his heart. He does not intend to raise his voice before the blessed God; rather, the cry comes from the walls of his heart because he has no recourse. As the Sages said concerning “They cried out in a loud voice”: they said, “Woe, woe”—in another language, “Gevalt, gevalt”—because they were greatly distressed by the evil inclination that surrounded them, and there was no way to escape. Prayer with such a cry is accepted before Him, blessed be He, and does not return empty.”

paragraphs.text: Tanya, Part I; Likkutei Amarim 48:3-4: “This is not the place to explain the particulars of the contractions, how and what they are. In general, however, they are the concealment and hiding of the flow of light and vitality, so that it does not shine and flow openly to the lower beings, clothing itself in them, influencing them, and bringing them to life as something from nothing—except for a very minute amount of light and vitality, so that they remain limited and finite. This is an exceedingly small illumination, accounted as nothing in relation to illumination without limit or end; there is no proportion or relation between them at all. The meaning of “proportion” in numbers is known: the number one has a proportion to a million, being one part in a million. But in relation to something entirely without limit or number, no numerical proportion exists. Even a thousand million and myriads of myriads do not have even the proportion of one to a thousand million and myriads of myriads; rather, they are accounted as absolutely nothing. Precisely so is this small illumination, which clothes itself in the higher and lower worlds to influence and give them life, in relation to the hidden and concealed light that is infinite. That light does not clothe itself in and influence the worlds openly to give them life, but encompasses them from above, and is called “that which encompasses all worlds.””
